Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 1:

﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it.﴾

Since the main purpose of this surah is to restrain the polytheists from associating partners with Allah and from its related matters, and to warn them of the evil outcome of that, and since their threats had been repeated earlier in many verses concerning a Day that would be the distinguisher between truth and falsehood, on which their power would vanish and their severity would end, and since they had found that Day slow in coming, to the point that they became confident it would not occur, they began to mock the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, and so they sought to hasten the arrival of that Day.

The surah opens with a threat expressed in the form of a report, that this threatened matter has already arrived. The past tense is used here to mean the future that is certain to happen, and this is indicated by the consequential clause (﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾), because the prohibition against hastening the arrival of that Day implies that it has not yet arrived.

The word "amr" (command) is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, like "wa'd" (promise) in the sense of "mawʿud" (that which is promised), meaning what Allah has commanded, and what is intended by Allah's command is His decree and the will for its occurrence at the appointed term that wisdom requires.

In expressing it as "the command of Allah" there is an ambiguity that conveys its awesomeness and magnitude, since it is attributed to One to whom nothing is great. He has referred to it at times as "the promise of Allah," and at other times as "the term of Allah," and the like.

The address is initially to the polytheists, because seeking the punishment hastily is one of their traits. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 47].

It is also permissible that it includes the believers, because the punishment of Allah, although the disbelievers seek to hasten it mockingly, thinking that it will not come, the believers likewise harbor within their souls a sense of its delay and love to see it hastened upon the disbelievers.

Thus the clause ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ is a consequence of ﴿the command of Allah has come﴾, and it is among the intended objects of the warning.

"Istiʿjal" (seeking hastening) is requesting that something be made to occur sooner, so its object is that which is being hastened, and the verb may take more than one object with the preposition "bi," as they say: "istaʿjil bi-kadhā" (seek to hasten with such-and-such). Allah the Exalted's words ﴿What I have is not what you seek to hasten﴾ [al-An'am: 57] have already passed in surah al-An'am.

So the pronoun in "tastaʿjilūhu" either refers to Allah the Exalted, meaning "do not seek to hasten Allah," and the object of "tastaʿjilūhu" is omitted because the words ﴿the command of Allah has come﴾ indicate it, the implied meaning being: "do not seek to hasten Allah with His command," in the manner of His saying: ﴿Soon I will show you My signs, so do not seek to hasten Me﴾ [al-Anbiya: 37].

It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the command of Allah, and in that case the verb "istiʿjal" is transitive to it by the omission of the preposition.

The meaning of the prohibition here is subtle, and they have not mentioned it among the usages of prohibitive forms. It is fitting that it be for equalization (taswiyah), just as the imperative form may come for equalization, meaning that there is no benefit in seeking to hasten it, because it will not be hastened before its appointed time.

* * *

﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate with Him.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (istinaf ibtidaʾi), because it is the very aim of the threat, since the warning and restraint were only for the sake of nullifying association, so the clause ﴿the command of Allah has come﴾ served as an introduction, and the clause ﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate﴾ serves as the goal.

The "ma" in His words ﴿above what they associate﴾ is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning: above their associating others with Him.

The majority of readers recite "yushrikūna" with the third-person form, following the rhetorical device of iltifat (shift), turning away from direct address so that the disavowal is specifically about their condition, which is that they would descend from the honor of direct address to the third person.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recite it with the second-person form (ta'), in accordance with His words ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 2:

﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command, upon whomever of His servants He wills, [saying]: Warn that there is no god except Me, so fear Me.﴾

Their asking for the punishment to be hastened was mockery of the Messenger ﷺ and denial of him, and it arose from the creed of polytheism, one of whose foundations is the impossibility of God sending messengers from among humans.

The affirmation of the coming of the punishment was followed by the declaration of God's transcendence above having partners, and this was followed by the clearing of the Messenger ﷺ from lying in what he conveys from his Lord. He described for them the sending (of messengers) in a concise description, and this is an interjection in the midst of the argument for monotheism.

By "the angels" is meant one of them, and he is Jibril, peace be upon him.

Al-Ruh (the Spirit) is the revelation. The name "the Spirit" was applied to it by way of metaphor, because revelation, by it, is guidance for minds to the truth. Thus revelation is likened to the spirit, just as true knowledge is likened to life, and ignorance is likened to death. God the Exalted said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We brought him to life?﴾ [al-An'am: 122].

The aspect of likening revelation to the spirit is that when minds comprehend revelation, spiritual life (which is knowledge) comes to be in them, just as when the spirit enters the body, sensory life comes to be in it. God the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52].

The meaning of ﴿from His command﴾ is the genus, i.e., from His affairs, which are His matters and decrees that He has singled out for Himself. This is its attribution to God, as here and as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52], and His saying the Exalted: ﴿They guard him by the command of God﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11], and His saying the Exalted: ﴿Say: The spirit is of my Lord's command﴾ [al-Isra': 85], because of what the attribution conveys of specification.

The majority read (yunazzilu) with a shadda on the zay. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a kasra on the nun.

The majority read (yunazzilu) with a dammed yaa' beneath (i.e., a yā' with a ḍamma as the initial letter, marking the third person), a fatha on the nun, and a shadda on the zay with a kasra. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ruways from Ya'qub read it with a sukun on the nun, a lightened zay with a kasra, and (al-malā'ikata) in the accusative.

Rawh from Ya'qub read it with a fawqiyya (taa') opened, a fatha on the nun, and a shadda on the zay with a fatha, and (al-malā'ikatu) in the nominative, on the basis that its original form is tatanazzalu.

His saying the Exalted ﴿upon whomever of His servants He wills﴾ is a reply to various kinds of their denial, for they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], and they said: ﴿Why, then, were bracelets of gold not cast upon him?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 53], meaning he should have been a king, and they said: ﴿What is with this Messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. The will of God proceeds in accordance with His wisdom. God the Exalted said: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124].

And ﴿an warn﴾ (anzirū) is an explanation of the verb (yunazzilu), because it is in the sense of "He sends down the angels with the revelation."

His saying ﴿with the Spirit by His command upon whomever of His servants He wills﴾ is an interjection and a digression between the verb (yunazzilu) and its explanatory clause.

﴿That there is no god except Me﴾ is connected to (anzirū), with the omission of the preposition before (an), which is regular, and the estimate is: "Warn that there is no god except Me." The pronoun governed by (anna) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). Since this statement is directed at those who took other gods alongside God, and that was misguidance for which they deserve punishment, their being informed of the opposite of their belief, with which they are occupied, was a warning.

Then (fattaqūn) is made to follow from it, and it is a command to taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) that encompasses the whole Shari'a.

The clause ﴿an warn﴾ up to His saying the Exalted (fattaqūn) encompasses the entire Shari'a, because the clause ﴿that there is no god except Me﴾ is an indication of what returns from the Shari'a to the reform of belief, which is the command to the perfection of the intellectual faculty.

The clause (fattaqūn) is an indication of abstention and compliance, which are the two that are the culmination of the perfection of the practical faculty.

[p. 101]

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (*istina' bayani*) arising from His words, exalted is He, ﴿above what they associate﴾ (16:1). When they heard that, they would expect proof that God is exalted above having partners. So the passage begins by indicating that He alone is the Creator and Determiner, and this indicates that what is created cannot be described as divine. This is shown by the consequence that follows these proofs in His later words, ﴿Is one who creates like one who creates not? Will you not remember?﴾ (16:17).

He followed His words, ﴿Glorified is He﴾, with ﴿exalted is He above what they associate﴾ (16:1), to establish the result of the proof. This is like how, in the discipline of logic (*sina'at al-mantiq*), the conclusion is stated before the syllogism (*qiyas*), and then that same conclusion is stated after the syllogism in the form of a result, to confirm monotheism. This is because error in associating partners is the root of the collapse of the beliefs of the people of polytheism. Also, their association of partners is what led them to deny the prophethood of the one who came to forbid them from polytheism. Therefore, the concern with establishing monotheism and refuting polytheism was necessarily given precedence over establishing the truthfulness of the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, which is introduced at the beginning of the surah with His words, ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command﴾ (16:2).

Many proofs from creation were enumerated, all containing abundant blessings upon people, as an embedding (*idmaj*) of acknowledgment of God's blessings upon them. It also contains an allusion (*ta'rid*) that those blessed by Him who worshipped other than Him have denied His blessing upon them, since they thanked what had not blessed them and forgot the One who alone bestows blessings. This is the greatest ingratitude. This is indicated by the conjunction of ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you cannot enumerate it﴾ (16:18) with the clause ﴿Is one who creates like one who creates not?﴾ (16:17).

The proof from the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater and more comprehensive than the other proofs, because they contain everything and because they are among the greatest of existing things. That is why the beginning was with them. However, the generality of what they contain required that it be followed by proof from the kinds of creation and created things. So He repeated with the creation of man and his stages, which is the most wondrous of observed existing things, then with the creation of animals and their conditions, because it includes the kinds that come after man in perfection of craftsmanship, along with the blessings found in their kinds. Then with the creation of what sustains the life of man and animals, namely water and plants. Then with the creation of the causes of times, seasons and appointed periods. Then with the creation of earthly minerals. He then moved to proof from the creation of seas, then from the creation of mountains, rivers, roads and signs of guidance on journeys. Its detail will come later.

The *ba'* in His words ﴿with truth﴾ (*bil-haqq*) is for accompaniment (*mula'abah*), and it is connected to ﴿created﴾ (*khalaqa*), since creation is what accompanies the truth.

The word *al-haqq* here means the opposite of futility (*'abath*), so here it means wisdom and seriousness. Do you not see His words, ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ (44:38), ﴿We created them not except with truth﴾ (44:39), and His words, ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ (38:27)? *Al-haqq* and *al-sidq* are both used as descriptions of a thing's perfection within its kind.

The clause ﴿exalted is He above what they associate﴾ is parenthetical (*mu'taridah*).

[p. 102]

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *ta'ala 'amma tushrikun* (تَعالى عَمّا تُشْرِكُونَ) with a *ta'* at the beginning of the verb (the second person, "you associate"), instead of the *ya'* (the third person, "they associate").

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 4:

﴿He created man from a drop of fluid, and behold, he is an open adversary.﴾ This is also a clarifying resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*), and it is another argument for God's exclusive divinity and His oneness in it. After He had argued against them from the creation of the higher and lower worlds, which are visible to them, He moved on to argue against them from the creation of their own selves, which is known to them. Also, when He argued for His oneness from the creation of the greatest things known to them, He further argued against them from the creation of the thing most wondrous to the one who reflects, namely man, across the two extremes of his stages: from being a base drop to being a rational, eloquent person who makes his purposes and knowledge clear.

The definite article in *al-insan* (man) is for the mental reference (*al-'ahd al-dhihni*), which is the definition of the genus (*ta'rif al-jins*). That is, it refers to the creation of the known genus that you call "man."

Three considerations have been mentioned regarding the lesson drawn from the creation of man: his genus, known through its quiddity and properties, namely animality, rationality, and good form; the rest of his states of being; and the origin of his creation, which is the drop, the most lowly of things, from which the most noble species arose, and the final point to which God elevated him, which is reason. All of this is contained in the two clauses and one prepositional phrase: ﴿He created man from a drop of fluid, and behold, he is an open adversary.﴾

*Al-khasim* (the adversary) is one of the intensive forms (*sigha al-mubalagha*), meaning one who argues very much.

*Mubin* (open, clear) is a second predicate of the pronoun in *fa-idha huwa* (and behold, he is). That is, when he is a speaker who expresses clearly what is in his heart and his intent, whether in truth or in falsehood, and who argues with all kinds of proofs, even sophistry.

The intended meaning is disputation in affirming partners (with God) and nullifying oneness, and denying those who call to monotheism, as indicated by the words of God Most High in Surah Ya-Sin:

[p. 103]
﴿Does man not see that We created him from a drop of fluid, and then he is an open adversary?﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:77] ﴿And he presents Us with an example and forgets his own creation, saying, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:78]

The use of the particle *idha* (behold, suddenly), the particle of suddenness (*idha al-fuja'iyya*), is a subsidiary metaphor (*isti'ara taba'iyya*). The particle that indicates the meaning of suddenness is borrowed for the meaning of a thing following upon something other than what one would expect it to follow from. No particle was assigned to this meaning. There is no true suddenness here, because God was not surprised by this, nor did He surprise anyone. Rather, the meaning is that if an observer were to reflect on the creation of man, he would expect from him acknowledgment of the oneness of his Creator and of His power to restore his creation. So when he hears from him association (of partners with God), argument against oneness, and denial of resurrection, it is as though it has surprised him. And since the particle of suddenness indicates the occurrence of surprise to the one who speaks it, it is necessary that the suddenness be a subsidiary metaphor.

Thus the insertion of the particle of suddenness makes the sentence convey two matters: amazement at man's development from the most base state to the most wondrous state, namely the state of disputation and clear expression arising from thought and reason; and an indication of his ingratitude for the blessing, and his use of what God bestowed upon him to disobey the One who bestowed it. The sentence in itself is an admonition (*tanwih*), and with the addition of the particle of suddenness, amazement is combined with the admonition. Had it been said, "So he is an adversary," or "Then he was an adversary," this eloquent meaning would not have been achieved.

[Page 104]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verses 5–7:

﴿And the cattle He created for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home at evening and when you send them out to pasture.﴾ ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾

It is permissible for والأنعام (al-an'am, "the cattle") to be coordinated (ʿaṭf, conjunction) as a single noun on a single noun, coordinated with الإنسان (al-insan, "man"), meaning: He created man from a drop of semen, and the cattle, which are also created from a drop of semen. Thus a lesson is derived from this wondrous creation, because of its resemblance to the creation of man. In this case the clause خَلَقَها (khalaqaha, "He created them") with its complements is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafa, a new independent clause), and thereby the favour (imtinan) is obtained.

It is also permissible that the coordination is of clause upon clause, so that the accusative of والأنعام is governed by a suppressed verb which the following mentioned verb explains, by way of the construction known as ishtighal (the verb being occupied by the pronoun, so that the noun is governed by a suppressed verb). The estimated sense is: "And He created the cattle; He created them." In this case the statement conveys emphasis (tawkid) for the purpose of strengthening the ruling, out of concern for the benefits that are in the cattle. It is thus a favour upon the addressees, and also an allusion (taʿrid) to them, for they have denied the blessing of God by [His] creating them, and they have made some of their offspring for their associates, and made a share for God. And what ingratitude is greater than seeking nearness through creatures to other than the One who created them? In the statement there is no restriction (hasr) under either of the two estimations.

The clause لكم فيها دفء (lakum fiha dif', "for you in them is warmth") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the object pronoun in خَلَقَها (khalaqaha) under both estimations. However, the first mode is a perfect parallel to His saying, ﴿He created man from a drop; then behold, he is an open adversary﴾ [an-Nahl: 4], in that the lesson is obtained initially, then the allusion to ingratitude is obtained secondarily. By contrast, in the second mode its explicit meaning is favour, and the lesson is obtained by way of metonymy (kinaya) from the concern.

The intended purpose of the argument is His saying ﴿And the cattle He created﴾ and what follows it, as an inclusion (idmaj) of the favour.

والأنعام (al-an'am) are the camels, the cattle, the sheep and the goats, and this was mentioned in the surah of al-An'am. The most famous of the cattle among the Arabs were the camels; therefore the word al-an'am among them commonly refers to camels.

The address is suitable to include the polytheists, who are the primary target of the argument, and also to include all people, especially in what the statement contains of favour.

In it there is a shift (iltifat) from the third-person form of His saying ﴿what they associate﴾ [an-Nahl: 1], in consideration of some of the addressees.

الدِّفء (al-difʾ), with a kasra on the dal, is a noun for that by which one warms oneself, like الملء (al-milʾ) and الحمل (al-himl). It is the garments woven from the wool, fur and hair of the cattle, from which tents and clothing are made.

Since those were the material of weaving, the woven product is treated as if it were contained within the cattle. The warmth was singled out for mention from among the general benefits because of the special care given to it.

The coordination of ومنافع (wa-manafiʿ, "and benefits") upon دفء (difʾ) is a coordination of the general upon the specific, because the matter of warmth is rarely brought to mind.

Then eating from them is coordinated, because it is from their very bodies, not from their fruits.

The clause ﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾ is coordinated upon the clause ﴿for you in them is warmth﴾.

The clause ﴿and from them you eat﴾ is coordinated upon the clause ﴿for you in them is warmth﴾. This is a favour by the blessing of their being subjected for eating from them and for nourishment, and for the restoration of strength that results from their nourishment.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿and from them you eat﴾ is for emphasis, because they are very eager to eat meat, and for the sake of the rhyme (fasila, the closing rhyme of the verse). The use of the imperfect verb in تَأْكُلُونَ (ta'kulun, "you eat") is because that is among the repeated actions.

الإراحة (al-iraha) is the act of ruwah (evening return), which is the returning to the watering and resting places. It is said: "He brought his camels home (arah niʿamahu) when he returned them after the morning pasture."

السُّروح (al-surur) is الإسامة (al-isama, sending out to pasture), that is, going out with them in the morning to the pastures. It is said: sarahaha (with the rāʾ lightened), saraḥan and surūḥan; and sarrahaha (with the rāʾ doubled), tasrihan.

The mention of الإراحة (returning) before التسريح (sending out) is because the beauty is stronger and more delightful at the time of returning, since then they come back with full bellies, udders laden with milk, cheerful with the joy of satiety, and with the desire to return to their dwellings, from the watering places and resting places.

The use of the imperfect in تُريحون (turihun, "you bring home") and تَسْرَحون (tasrahun, "you send out") is because these are repeated states, and in their repetition is the repetition of the blessing with its sights.

The clause ﴿and they carry your loads﴾ is coordinated upon ﴿and for you in them is beauty﴾, so it is also in the position of a circumstantial clause. The pronoun refers to the most famous of the cattle among them, namely the camels, as in the words of [Umm Zar'] in the story of Umm Zara': "He rode a swift horse and took a spear, and brought me abundant cattle," for the cattle that are taken with a spear are camels, since they are seized in a raid.

The pronoun in وتحمل (wa-tahmil, "and they carry") refers to some of the cattle by context, and the choice of the imperfect verb is due to the repetition of that action.

الأثقال (al-athqal) is the plural of ثَقَل (thaqal, with two fathas), which is what is heavy for people to carry by themselves.

The intended meaning of بَلَد (baladun, "a land") is a class of places to which they travel, such as al-Sham and Yemen with respect to the people of the Hijaz, including the people of Makka, in the summer and winter journeys and the journey to the Hajj.

The clause ﴿and they carry your loads﴾ conveys the meaning "they carry you and convey you," by way of a metonymy close to explicit statement. Therefore He followed it with His saying ﴿you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves﴾.

The clause ﴿you could not reach it﴾ is a descriptive clause (sifa) for بَلَد (baladun), and it conveys the meaning of distance, because the arrival of a traveller at a land with hardship is characteristic of a distant land; that is, you would not reach it without the cattle carrying your loads.

الشِّق (al-shiqq), with a kasra on the shin, in the reading of the majority, means المشقة (al-mashaqqa, hardship), and the bāʾ is for accompaniment (mulabasa), and المشقة means severe fatigue.

What comes after the particle of exception is an exception from the states of the addressees' pronoun.

Abu Jaʿfar read ﴿with great hardship to the souls﴾ with a fatha on the shin, and this is a dialectal form of the shiqq with a kasra on the shin.

The clause has negated that they would reach it except with hardship. Its outward meaning therefore conveys that they used to reach it without mounts, with hardship, but this is not the intended meaning, since carrying loads on cattle accompanied the journeys to distant lands. Rather the intended meaning is: "You would not reach it without the camels, or without the camels [as mounts]," and the part was omitted because of the indication of the context.

The clause ﴿Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾ is a justification (taʿlil) for the clause ﴿and the cattle He created﴾; that is, He created them for these benefits, because He is Kind and Merciful toward you.

Then eating from them is coordinated, because it is from their very bodies, not from their fruits.

The clause ﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾ is coordinated upon the clause ﴿for you in them is warmth﴾.

The clause ﴿and from them you eat﴾ is coordinated upon the clause ﴿for you in them is warmth﴾. This is a favour by the blessing of their being subjected for eating from them and for nourishment, and for the restoration of strength that results from their nourishment.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿and from them you eat﴾ is for emphasis, because they are very eager to eat meat, and for the sake of the rhyme (fasila, the closing rhyme of the verse). The use of the imperfect verb in تَأْكُلُونَ (ta'kulun, "you eat") is because that is among the repeated actions.

الإراحة (al-iraha) is the act of ruwah (evening return), which is the returning to the watering and resting places. It is said: "He brought his camels home (arah niʿamahu) when he returned them after the morning pasture."

السُّروح (al-surur) is الإسامة (al-isama, sending out to pasture), that is, going out with them in the morning to the pastures. It is said: sarahaha (with the rāʾ lightened), saraḥan and surūḥan; and sarrahaha (with the rāʾ doubled), tasrihan.

The mention of الإراحة (returning) before التسريح (sending out) is because the beauty is stronger and more delightful at the time of returning, since then they come back with full bellies, udders laden with milk, cheerful with the joy of satiety, and with the desire to return to their dwellings, from the watering places and resting places.

The use of the imperfect in تُريحون (turihun, "you bring home") and تَسْرَحون (tasrahun, "you send out") is because these are repeated states, and in their repetition is the repetition of the blessing with its sights.

The clause ﴿and they carry your loads﴾ is coordinated upon ﴿and for you in them is beauty﴾, so it is also in the position of a circumstantial clause. The pronoun refers to the most famous of the cattle among them, namely the camels, as in the words of [Umm Zar'] in the story of Umm Zara': "He rode a swift horse and took a spear, and brought me abundant cattle," for the cattle that are taken with a spear are camels, since they are seized in a raid.

The pronoun in وتحمل (wa-tahmil, "and they carry") refers to some of the cattle by context, and the choice of the imperfect verb is due to the repetition of that action.

الأثقال (al-athqal) is the plural of ثَقَل (thaqal, with two fathas), which is what is heavy for people to carry by themselves.

The intended meaning of بَلَد (baladun, "a land") is a class of places to which they travel, such as al-Sham and Yemen with respect to the people of the Hijaz, including the people of Makka, in the summer and winter journeys and the journey to the Hajj.

The clause ﴿and they carry your loads﴾ conveys the meaning "they carry you and convey you," by way of a metonymy close to explicit statement. Therefore He followed it with His saying ﴿you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves﴾.

The clause ﴿you could not reach it﴾ is a descriptive clause (sifa) for بَلَد (baladun), and it conveys the meaning of distance, because the arrival of a traveller at a land with hardship is characteristic of a distant land; that is, you would not reach it without the cattle carrying your loads.

الشِّق (al-shiqq), with a kasra on the shin, in the reading of the majority, means المشقة (al-mashaqqa, hardship), and the bāʾ is for accompaniment (mulabasa), and المشقة means severe fatigue.

What comes after the particle of exception is an exception from the states of the addressees' pronoun.

Abu Jaʿfar read ﴿with great hardship to the souls﴾ with a fatha on the shin, and this is a dialectal form of the shiqq with a kasra on the shin.

The clause has negated that they would reach it except with hardship. Its outward meaning therefore conveys that they used to reach it without mounts, with hardship, but this is not the intended meaning, since carrying loads on cattle accompanied the journeys to distant lands. Rather the intended meaning is: "You would not reach it without the camels, or without the camels [as mounts]," and the part was omitted because of the indication of the context.

The clause ﴿Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾ is a justification (taʿlil) for the clause ﴿and the cattle He created﴾; that is, He created them for these benefits, because He is Kind and Merciful toward you.

Thus a lesson is derived from this wondrous creation, because of its resemblance to the creation of man. In this case the clause خَلَقَها (khalaqaha, "He created them") with its complements is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafa, a new independent clause), and thereby the favour (imtinan) is obtained.

It is also permissible that the coordination is of clause upon clause, so that the accusative of والأنعام is governed by a suppressed verb which the following mentioned verb explains, by way of the construction known as ishtighal (the verb being occupied by the pronoun, so that the noun is governed by a suppressed verb). The estimated sense is: "And He created the cattle; He created them." In this case the statement conveys emphasis (tawkid) for the purpose of strengthening the ruling, out of concern for the benefits that are in the cattle. It is thus a favour upon the addressees, and also an allusion (taʿrid) to them, for they have denied the blessing of God by [His] creating them, and they have made some of their offspring for their associates, and made a share for God. By contrast, in the second mode its explicit meaning is favour, and the lesson is obtained by way of metonymy (kinaya) from the concern.

The intended purpose of the argument is His saying ﴿And the cattle He created﴾ and what follows it, as an inclusion (idmaj) of the favour.

**Ibn 'Ashur, al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir, on surah 16, verse 8:**

﴿And horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride, and as adornment.﴾

(Al-Khayla), "the horses," is coordinated with ﴿and the cattle He created﴾ [An-Nahl: 5], so the implied meaning is: "and He created the horses."

The discussion of the basis of the argument and what follows it, namely the expression of favour (al-imtinan), and the lesson in each case, is the same as what was said about His words before this, ﴿and the cattle He created for you, in them is warmth﴾ [An-Nahl: 5], and so on.

The omitted verb is connected to ﴿for you to ride, and as adornment﴾, meaning: God created them so that they would be vehicles for mankind. Had it not been so, their existence would have had no benefit for the building up of the world.

The coordination of (wa-zinatan), "and as adornment," in the accusative, is coordinated with the prepositional phrase in ﴿li-tarkabuha﴾ ("for you to ride them"). Its connection with the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil) has been avoided, because the condition for its being put in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) is fulfilled, since its agent and the agent of its governing verb are one and the same. The governing verb is the verb (khalaqa) in ﴿and the cattle He created﴾ [An-Nahl: 5] up to ﴿and the horses and mules﴾, all of which is the direct object of the verb (khalaqaha).

There is no doubt that the agent of (ja'alaha zinatan), "made them an adornment," is God, the Exalted, because the intended meaning is that they are, in themselves, an adornment. That is, He created them as an adornment for the earth, or He adorned the earth with them, as in His words ﴿And We have certainly adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾ [Al-Mulk: 5].

This accusative form is the clearest evidence that the object of purpose is in the accusative by implication of the particle of causation.

This is in the context of expressing favour, so it is restricted to what the first addressees benefited from in their customs.

He restricted the favour to riding for horses, mules and donkeys, and adornment, and did not mention carrying loads on them, as He said concerning the cattle ﴿and they carry your loads﴾ [An-Nahl: 7]. This is because it was not their custom to carry loads on horses, mules and donkeys. Horses were ridden for raiding and hunting, mules were ridden for walking and raiding, and donkeys were ridden for moving between villages and the like.

In the Hadith of al-Bukhari, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, during the Farewell Pilgrimage, he said: "I came riding a female donkey, while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was leading the people in prayer," and so on.

Abu Sayyara used to lead the people out of 'Arafa in the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period) riding a donkey, and he said about it:

"Make way for Abu Sayyara,
and for his clients, the Banu Fazara,
until he leads, riding his donkey,
facing the Ka'ba, calling on his neighbour."

Therefore, favour does not apply to a blessing that is not used by those upon whom it is bestowed. Even if the thing bestowed has benefits that the addressees do not intend, such as ploughing with camels, horses, mules and donkeys, which Muslims do and which no one is known to have objected to, or benefits that the addressees did not perceive, such as the benefits of medicines derived from animals that were not known to people before, all of this falls within the generality of His words ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [Al-Baqara: 29] in Surat al-Baqara. This is a generality regarding essences, which entails the generality of conditions, except for what the evidence has specified from the verse in al-An'am: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it﴾ [Al-An'am: 145], and so on.

From this it is known that there is no evidence in this verse for the prohibition of eating the flesh of horses, mules and donkeys, because eating them rarely comes to mind, due to its rarity. How could it be otherwise, when the Muslims ate donkey flesh at the Battle of Khaybar without asking the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission, while they were in a state of necessity, and the verse of Surat al-Nahl had been recited for many years by then, yet no one objected to them, nor did the Prophet (ﷺ) object.

As came in the Sahih: he (ﷺ) was told, "The donkeys have been eaten," and he remained silent. Then he was told, "The donkeys have been eaten," and he remained silent. Then he was told, "The donkeys have been finished," so the crier of the Prophet (ﷺ) called out that God and His Messenger forbid you to eat the flesh of donkeys. Then the cooking pots were overturned.

Horses, mules and donkeys are alike in that the verse does not include the ruling on eating them. So the determination of whether eating them is permitted or forbidden is based on other evidence.

As for horses and mules, there is strong disagreement among the scholars regarding the permissibility of eating them. The majority permitted eating them, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and al-Zahiri. It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Asma' bint Abi Bakr, 'Ata', al-Zuhri, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Jubayr.

Malik and Abu Hanifa said: eating the flesh of horses is forbidden. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and they argued with His words ﴿for you to ride them, and as adornment﴾. Had their flesh been permissible to eat, He would have mentioned eating them as a favour, as He did with the cattle in His words ﴿and from them you eat﴾ [An-Nahl: 5]. This is an argument that does not stand on its own, so it is answered by what we have established regarding the discourse being conducted in consideration of the customs of its addressees. Many hadiths are established that Muslims ate horse flesh during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he knew of it, but it was rare in their customs.

There is also a narration from Malik, may God be pleased with him, that the flesh of horses is disliked, and al-Qurtubi chose this view.

As for donkeys, it is established that Muslims ate their flesh on the day of Khaybar, and then they were forbidden from it, as in the hadith mentioned above. The interpretation of this has been disputed. The majority understood it as a prohibition of donkeys themselves. Some understood it to mean that they were their means of transport that day, so if they had continued eating them they would have been left stranded in that place, returning on foot, unable to carry their belongings. This is the opinion of a group of the early scholars. Another group of the early scholars adhered to the apparent meaning of the prohibition and said that the flesh of domestic donkeys is forbidden, because they are the subject of the prohibition, while the wild donkeys remain permitted by original permission. This is the view of the majority of the imams, Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, and others, may God be pleased with them all.

In this, there is the establishment of a ruling of worship (hukm ta'abbudi) in the distinction, and it is not appropriate to adopt such a position in independent reasoning (ijtihad) except on the basis of a text that does not admit of interpretation, as we have explained in our book Maqasid al-Shari'a al-Islamiyya. Moreover, it is not known in the Sharia that a domestic species of an animal should be forbidden while its wild counterpart is not.

As for mules, the majority hold that they are forbidden. As for those who say that eating horses is forbidden, their reason is that mules are a hybrid of two forbidden species, so it is necessarily forbidden to eat them. As for those who say that eating horses is permitted, their reasoning is that the prohibition of one of the two species from which it is composed, namely donkeys, takes precedence over the permission of the other species, namely horses. It is also reported from 'Ata' that he considered them lawful.

Al-Khayl (horses) is a collective noun (ism jam') with no singular form from its own root, according to the more correct view. This was discussed previously at His words ﴿and the marked horses﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14] in Surat Al 'Imran.

Al-Bighal (mules) is the plural of baghl, which is a name for the male. The female is of the same kind as its mother, a mare, and its father is a donkey. It is among the rare species produced by crossing two kinds. The reverse of it is the birdhawn (a horse produced from a mare and a stallion from a donkey). One of the special characteristics of mules is that the females are sterile, so they do not give birth.

Al-Hamir (donkeys) is the broken plural of himar. It is also pluralised as ahmira and humur. It is generally used for the male of the species. The female is called atan. In the plural, the prevalence of the masculine has been observed.

﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾ is a parenthetical clause at the end of the statement, or in its middle, as will be explained later.

(Yakhluqu), "He creates," is a present-tense verb intended to denote the present time, not the future. That is, He is now creating what you do not know, O people, of things created for your benefit, and you are unaware of it. Just as He created the cattle and the horses for them, He creates for them and will continue to create for them other creatures that they do not know now. This includes what is unfamiliar or unknown to the addressees but known to other peoples, such as the elephant among the Abyssinians and Indians; and what is unknown to anyone and then becomes known to people later, such as the animals of the polar regions, like the seal and the white bear, and the animals of the American continent, which were unknown to people at the time the Qur'an was revealed. In this case, the present tense is used for the present with the sense of renewal, meaning: He is the Creator, and He creates.

As has been said, this includes what God creates of created beings in Paradise, but that is specific to the believers. So the apparent meaning is that it is not intended by the context of general favour to people, which is used to establish the proof against those who are ungrateful for the blessing.

What appears to me is that this verse is one of the Qur'an's unseen scientific miracles, and that it is an indication that God will inspire mankind to invent vehicles that are more beneficial to them than horses, mules and donkeys. These include the bicycles that a person rides and moves with his feet, called (biskilat); the trains of the railway lines; the motor cars powered by refined petroleum, called automobiles; and then the aircraft that fly in the air using refined petroleum. All of these are creations that emerged in successive ages, and those who lived before the age in which each of them existed did not know them.

God's inspiring people to invent them is part of God's creation. It is God who inspired the human inventors with the intelligence and knowledge with which He endowed them, and with the gradual progress they made up the ladder of civilisation, and some borrowed from others until they invented them. Therefore they are, in this sense, created by God, the Exalted, because all of it is from His blessing.

[p. 112]

**"And upon Allah is the direction of the way, and among them is that which deviates. And had He willed, He would have guided you all."** This is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'tariḍa*), whose insertion is required by the context of the favor of making travel easy through mounts: horses, mules, and donkeys.

When the favor of making the way easy, which leads to physical destinations, was mentioned, the discourse rose to remind them of the way that leads to spiritual destinations, which is the way of guidance (*al-hudā*). God's assumption of responsibility for this way is therefore a greater favor than the facilitation of physical routes, because through the way of guidance eternal happiness is attained. This way consists of the gift of the human intellect, which distinguishes truth from falsehood, and the sending of messengers to call people to the truth, to remind them of what they neglect, and to guide them to what their intellects cannot reach, or can reach only with hardship and at the risk of falling into the pitfalls of the path.

So "the way" (*al-sabīl*) is a metaphor for the actions people undertake insofar as they lead to the abode of reward or the abode of punishment, as in His saying, **"Say: This is my way"** (Yusuf 12:108). The context also clarifies this meaning: after the proofs of monotheism (*tawḥīd*) were explained, it was appropriate to point out that this is a path to guidance and a removal of excuse, and that among the paths people take there is a path of misguidance and injustice.

The preposition **"upon"** (*ʿalā*) has been used figuratively, in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech extensively, to express the meaning of assuming responsibility (*taʿahhud*), as in His saying, **"Indeed, upon Us is guidance"** (al-Layl 92:12). The commitment to clarifying the way of guidance is likened to a right and an obligation incumbent upon the one who has a claim to it.

The word **"direction"** (*qaṣd*) means the straightness of the path. It occurs here as a description of "the way" in the manner of describing by a verbal noun (*waṣf bi-l-maṣdar*), because one says "a direct way" (*ṭarīq qāṣid*), meaning straight. This is stronger in describing straightness, as is the case with descriptions by verbal nouns. The genitive construction "direction of the way" (*qaṣd al-sabīl*) is an attribute-to-noun construction (*iḍāfat al-ṣifa ilā al-mawṣūf*), and the attribute is restrictive (*ṣifa mukhaṣṣiṣa*), because the definite article in "the way" is generic (*li-l-jins*). It is necessary to posit an omitted noun, because what God has undertaken is the clarification of the way, not the way itself.

The pronoun in **"among them"** (*wa-minhā*) refers to "the way" (*al-sabīl*), on the basis that it is permissible to treat it as feminine.

**"That which deviates"** (*jā'ir*) is a description of "the way" considered in its masculine usage, meaning: of the kind of way, among which is also the direction of a deviating way that is not a true direction.

The deviating (*al-jā'ir*) is that which turns away from straightness. It is used as a metonymy for a path that does not lead to the intended goal, that is, to good, and which leads to harm. Thus it is deviating in respect of its traveler. Its description as deviating is in the manner of rational metaphor (*al-majāz al-ʿaqlī*). The deviating way was not attributed to God, because the path of error was invented by the people of error, an invention that the intellect given by God to humankind does not attest to, and God has forbidden people from following it.

The clause **"And had He willed, He would have guided you all"** is a concluding phrase (*tadhyīl*).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 10:**

﴿It is He who sent down water from the sky; from it is drink, and from it are trees, in which you pasture [your livestock].﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a new sentence that resumes the argument) introducing another proof from the manifestations of God Most High's wondrous creation. Within it is embedded a reminder of the blessings that this marvelous water brings to people: the blessing of drink, and the blessing of food for the animals on which people's lives depend, and for the people themselves.

The form of definition of the subject and predicate (*al-musnad ilayhi* and *al-musnad*) conveys restriction (*hasr*), meaning: He alone, and no other. This is a restriction contrary to the apparent sense, because the addressees do not deny this, nor do they claim any partner with Him in it. However, when they worshipped idols that had not bestowed these blessings upon them, their state became like that of one who claims that the idols bestowed these blessings upon them. Thus they were placed in the position of one who claims a partnership with God in creation. So the restriction is a restriction of singling out (*qasr ifrad*), presented as a departure from the apparent sense of the speech.

The meaning of sending down water from the sky has already been explained at His words, ﴿And He sent down water from the sky and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22], in Surat al-Baqarah.

He mentioned two blessings in the water: the drink from it, and the growth of trees and crops by it.

The clause ﴿for you from it is drink﴾ is a qualifier of *ma'an* (water). *Lakum* (for you) is connected to *sharab* (drink) and was placed before it for emphasis, and *minhu* (from it) is likewise a fronted predicate. Its being fronted permitted the subject to be indefinite (*nakira*).

[Page 114]

*Al-sharab* (drink) is a name for what is drunk: the liquid that the lips sip and that reaches the throat, to be swallowed without chewing.

The *min* in *minhu* is partitive (*tab'idiyyah*). His words ﴿*minhu shajar*﴾ (and from it are trees) are parallel to His words ﴿*minhu sharab*﴾ (from it is drink). The particle *min* was repeated after the conjunctive *wa* because the *min* here is either for origin (*ibtida'*) or causal (*sababiyyah*), and so it would not be good to conjoin *shajar* to *sharab*.

*Al-shajar* (trees) is applied to plants with hard stems, and it is also applied to all herbage and pasture by way of predominance (*taghlib*, the use of one term for a broader category because it predominates).

This predominance was observed here, because it is the chief pasture of the livestock of the people of the Hijaz, owing to the scarcity of pasture in their land. They graze on *al-sha'ari* (scrub) and thickets. In the hadith about the stray camel: "The stray camel drinks water and grazes on the trees until its owner comes to it."

Among the subtle rhetorical points is the use of the locative particle *fi* (in). The grazing (*isama*) in it occurs by eating from it, and eating from what is beneath it of the herbage.

*Al-isama* (grazing): releasing camels to graze, and *al-sawm* is grazing. It is said: *sāmat al-mashiyah* (the livestock grazed), so it is *sa'imah* (grazing), and *asamaha rabbuha* (its owner let it graze).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 11:

﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops, the olives, the date palms, the grapes, and of all the fruits. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought.﴾ The clause (yunbitu, "He causes to grow") is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in (anzala, "He sent down"); that is, God causes to grow for you.

It was not joined by conjunction to the clause (﴿lakum minhu sharab﴾ [al-Nahl: 10], "for you from it is drink") because this is not something that results from the descent of water alone; rather, it requires planting and cultivation alongside it.

This mention is among the proofs of the immense power of the Lord, so its purpose is argument mingled with a reminder of blessing, as indicated by His saying (lakum, "for you"), in the same manner as what preceded in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the cattle—He created them for you; in them is warmth﴾ [al-Nahl: 5], the verse, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the horses, mules, and donkeys, that you may ride them﴾ [al-Nahl: 8], the verse.

The causing to grow was attributed to God because He is the one who inspires its causes and the creator of its roots, as a reminder to people to dispel their delusion of relying on their own power. For this reason He said, ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought﴾, because of the many subtleties contained within it.

The mention of the crops and olives and what accompanies them has already occurred more than once in Surat al-An'am.

Reflection (tafakkur) was discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal? Will you not then reflect?﴾ [al-An'am: 50], in Surat al-An'am.

The insertion of the word qawm (people) serves to indicate that reflection is among their natural dispositions, as was discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed there are signs for a people who use reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿And of all the fruits﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with ﴿the crops and the olives﴾; that is, He causes to grow for you thereby of the fruits what is not mentioned here.

The definite article is the definite article of genus (ta'rif al-jins), and what is meant is the kinds of fruits of the earth that water causes to grow. Each people among mankind has the fruits of its land and its climate. The "min" (of) is partitive (tab'idiyyah), intended to vary the blessing bestowed upon each people by the fruits they receive. It did not enter upon the crops and what is coordinated with them because they are among the fruits that grow in every place.

The clause ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil).

The sign (ayah) is the indication that He, exalted is He, is the Originator, the Wise. And that is the growing of diverse kinds from one water, as He said, ﴿Watered with one water﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4], in Surat al-Ra'd.

The indication of this was attached to the attribute of reflection, because it is a subtle indication, arising gradually. This is also an allusion to the polytheists who did not take guidance from what is in that of indication of God's sole divinity, that they are a people who do not reflect.

Al-Jumhur read (yunbitu) with the third-person masculine ya' (ya' al-ghaybah), while Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read it with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 12:

﴿And He subjected for you the night and the day, and the sun and the moon, and the stars are subjected by His command. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾ These are further signs of the precise craftsmanship and knowledge of God Most High, combined with a favour (imtinan).

What explains this verse has already preceded in the opening of Surah Yunus. The subjection of these things was discussed at His saying, ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command. Surely, His is the creation and the command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], at the beginning of Surah al-A'raf, and at the beginning of Surah al-Ra'd and in Surah Ibrahim.

This is a transition to argue, through the perfection of the craftsmanship, for the oneness (wahdaniyya) of the Creator and His knowledge, and an integration (idmaj) between argument and favour. The indications are linked to the attribute of reason ('aql), because the basic faculty of reason is sufficient to infer from them the oneness and power (of God), since they are clear, manifest indications, present to observation every day and night.

The reason for the insertion of the word "qawm" (people) just above has already been explained, and that the sentence is a concluding phrase (tadhyil).

The majority of readers read all these nouns in the accusative, as objects of the verb sakhkhara. Ibn 'Amir read ﴿wal-shamsu wal-qamaru wal-nujumu﴾ in the nominative, as a subject (mubtada'), and read (musakhkharatun) in the nominative as its predicate (khabar) about them. The nuance of the difference in case-endings is to indicate the distinction between the two kinds of subjection. Hafs read (al-nujumu) and (musakhkharatun) in the nominative. The nuance of the difference in style is the distinction between the two kinds of subjection, in that the first is evident, while the other is hidden, due to the scarcity of those who observe the movements of the stars.

By "His command" is meant the command of creation (amr al-takwin) for the well-known solar system.

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) has offered in his book Durrat al-Tanzil an explanation for the difference between the singular (ayatan) in the first and third occurrences, and the plural (ayat) in the second occurrence: that what is mentioned first and third goes back to what sprouts from the earth, so all of it is one sign, following the creation of the earth, and what it contains (i.e., it is all of one state: the state of plants in the earth in the first, and one state: the state of propagation in animals in the third verse). As for what is mentioned in the second occurrence, it refers to the differing conditions of the sun, the moon, and the planets, each of which has its own system and indications that differ from those of the others, so what is mentioned in that is a collection of signs (i.e., because some of them are accidents such as night and day, and some are bodies with differing systems and multiple indications).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 13:

﴿And what He has created for you on the earth, of diverse colours. Surely in that is a sign for a people who remember.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "the night and the day," meaning: and He subjected to you what He has created for you on the earth. It is evidence of the subtle craftsmanship and wisdom, by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿of diverse colours. Surely in that is a sign for a people who remember﴾, and by "for you" (lakum) He indicated the favour (minnah) it contains.

The dharʾ (ذرء) is creation through procreation and generation through pregnancy and hatching. Plant growth is therefore not dharʾ. It includes livestock and horses, and the favour of it has already passed, and of other things too, such as hunting and guarding dogs, hunting animals, birds, edible wild animals, and trees and plants.

The description of the diversity of its colours is added here, and it is an addition for the sake of wonder, and it has no bearing on the favour (imtinan). It is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4] in Surat al-Ra'd, and His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of diverse hues, and jet-black﴾ [Fatir: 27], and ﴿And among people and moving creatures and cattle, there are diverse colours﴾ [Fatir: 28] in Surat Fatir. With this, this became a独立 sign; therefore He concluded it with the clause ﴿Surely in that is a sign for a people who remember﴾. And because the locus of inference is the diversity of colours together with the unity of the origin of creation, the sign was stated in the singular in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Surely in that is a sign﴾.

The word alwan (ألوان) is the plural of lawn (لون), which is a quality of the surfaces of bodies, perceived by sight, arising from the mixing of some elements with the surface, either by original creation or by dyeing it with a substance of known colour. The mixing of two or more elements produces an unlimited number of colours. It was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its colour is"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 69] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The inference from the diversity of colours is attached to the attribute of remembrance (tadhakkur), because it is an inference that is reached merely by recalling the diverse colours, since they are well known.

The insertion of the word "people" (qawm), and the clause being a concluding remark (tadhyil), were discussed a moment ago.

Al-Fakhr [al-Razi], in Durrat al-Tanzil, offered a reason for the variation of the descriptions in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for a people who give thought﴾ [al-Nahl: 11], His saying ﴿for a people who understand﴾ [al-Nahl: 12], and His saying ﴿for a people who remember﴾: that this is in consideration of the variation in the degree of need for strength of contemplation. The evidence of the creatures produced from the earth requires reflection (tafakkur), which is the exercise of consideration that leads to knowledge. The indication of what He created on the earth of animals requires further contemplation in reflection to infer the variation of their states, their reproduction and their benefits, so they needed reminding (tadhkir), which is reflection together with remembering their kinds and the variation of their properties. As for the indication of the subjection of the night and day and the celestial worlds, it is finer and needs deeper penetration, so He described those who infer from it as "those who understand" (ya'qilun), and understanding (ta'aqqul) is the highest state of inference. End.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 14:

﴿And it is He who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it fresh meat and extract from it ornaments which you wear; and you see the ships ploughing through it, that you may seek of His bounty and perhaps you will be thankful﴾. The discussion of this argument, and the incorporation of the favour within it, is like what preceded it. The discussion of the subjection of ships in the sea and the subjection of rivers has already passed, in the course of Surat Ibrahim.

Page 119

Among the subjection of the sea is its creation in a form that makes swimming and sailing with ships possible, and the enabling of swimmers and sailors to hunt the fish created in it and subjected to the stratagems of hunters. The favour is further emphasised by the fact that the meat of its catch is fresh.

And (min) here is for the beginning of origin, meaning: you eat fresh meat issuing from the sea.

Al-tari (فَطَرِيّ, "fresh") is the opposite of dry, its verbal noun is al-tarawa (الطَّراوَة, freshness), and its verb is tarawa (طَرُوَ), on the pattern of kharusha (خَشُنَ).

Al-hilya (الحِلْيَة, "ornament," i.e., what people adorn themselves with, meaning they beautify themselves) has already been discussed at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿seeking ornament﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17] in Surat al-Ra'd. It refers to pearls and coral. Pearls are found in some seas such as the Persian Gulf, while coral is found in all seas, abundant or scarce. The discussion of pearls will come in Surat al-Hajj and Surat al-Rahman, and the discussion of coral will come in Surat al-Rahman.

Al-istikhraj (الِاسْتِخْراج, "extraction") is an increase in bringing out, so the sin and ta' are for emphasis, like istajaba meaning ajaba.

Al-lubs (اللُّبْس, "wearing") is placing on the body a garment, turban or worked jewellery; one says lubs al-taj (wearing a crown), lubs al-khatam (wearing a ring), lubs al-qamis (wearing a shirt). It was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿We have sent down to you clothing﴾ [al-A'raf: 26] in Surat al-A'raf.

The attribution of wearing the ornament to the masculine plural pronoun is by way of prevalence (taghlib), since most ornaments are worn by women, apart from rings and the ornaments of swords.

The clause ﴿and you see the ships ploughing through it﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the coordinated clauses, though coordination was possible; its purpose is to vary the style, to express wonder at the subjection of sailing in the sea, by calling to mind the strange state through the verb of seeing. This verb is frequently used to express wonder in many forms, such as "if you could see," "have you seen," "what do you see." Introducing the verb of seeing in such contexts conveys urging to know that matter. Thus this arrangement of the speech serves this meaning; without it the speech would be: "and you extract from it ornaments which you wear and seek of His bounty in ships ploughing through it."

Page 120

The coordination of "and that you may seek" upon "you extract" is so that it forms part of the favours which arose from the wisdom of subjecting the sea. It was not made the cause of the ships' ploughing, as was done in Surat Fatir, ﴿and you see the ships ploughing through it that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [Fatir: 12], because that verse was not introduced with the favour of subjecting the sea, but came for another purpose.

The particle of causation is repeated in His saying, ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾, because of the distance caused by the parenthetical clause.

Seeking of Allah's bounty means trade, as it is expressed by that in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The coordination of ﴿and perhaps you will be thankful﴾ upon the remaining causes is because it is among the wisdoms for which Allah subjected the sea to people, to lead them to acknowledge worship of Allah and to renounce associating others with Him therein. It is an allusion against those who associated partners.

[Page 120]

This is a transition to inference and to God's favour through the great creatures on the surface of the earth, whose existence is a kindness to humankind. Since these creatures were made as a complement to the earth and placed on its outer surface, Allah expressed their creation and placement by "casting" (al-ilqa'), which is the throwing of something onto the earth. It is likely that the creation of these was later than the creation of the earth, since the mountains may have burst forth through terrestrial upheavals such as a great earthquake, and then the rivers came into being through the falling of rain. As for the roads and landmarks, the lateness of their existence is evident. So the creation of these four resembles casting something into something after the latter has been completed.

It is likely that the original formation of the mountains was from fragments that the stars threw down, which then landed on the surface of the earth, just as the rains fell and formed the rivers. Thus the comparison of the occurrence of these two to "casting" is clear. Using "casting" for the placing of the roads and landmarks is a case of taghlib (the prevalence of one term over another in a shared description).

Another example of using "casting" for giving and the like is His saying, ﴿Has the Reminder been cast upon him from among us?﴾ [al-Qamar: 25].

*Rawasi* is the plural of *rasin*, an adjective derived from *rasw* (with a fatha on the ra' and a sukun on the sin). It is also said with a damma on the ra' and sin, with the sin doubled and the waw doubled. It means firmness and settledness in a place. God says, ﴿and cooking pots fixed firmly﴾ [Saba': 13].

*Rasin* is used as a name for a mountain, being in the position of a predominant adjective. Its plural follows the pattern *fawa'il*, contrary to the usual analogy. It is one of the rare forms, like *'awadhil* and *fawaris*. Some discussion of it was given earlier at the beginning of al-Ra'd.

His saying, ﴿lest it shake with you﴾ [Luqman: 10], gives the reason for casting the firm mountains onto the earth. *Mayd* means agitation, and the pronoun in *tamida* refers to the earth, by the indication of its being joined with His saying "with you." For when *mayd* is followed by the preposition *bi*, it is understood that the object of *bi* is the thing settled in the thing that shakes. Agitation disrupts people's interests and inflicts pain on them.

Since the context is one of favour, it is understood that the thing given as the reason is the absence of shaking, not its occurrence. The speech proceeds with an ellipsis that the context requires. Similar cases are numerous in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

*So we hastened the hospitality, lest you revile us*

He meant "lest you not revile us," so the cause is the absence of reviling, not its occurrence. The Kufan grammarians explain such cases by the ellipsis of the negative particle after *an* (that/lest), the implied meaning being "so that they do not shake with you" and "so that you do not revile us." This is the apparent reading. The Basran grammarians explain the same by the ellipsis of a governing noun between the verb giving the reason and *an*, the implied meaning being "out of aversion that they should shake with you."

This meaning to which the verse points is an obscure one. It may be that God made the protrusions of the mountains on the earth's surface a counterbalance to its sphericity, such that it is not so smooth as to lessen its motion through space, which would render its agitation severe.

The blessing of the rivers is great, for from them they drink and water their crops, and in them their ships sail for their journeys.

After this last favour He joined to it *wa-subulan* ("and roads"), the plural of *sabil*, which is the road travelled upon by land.

The clause ﴿that you may be guided﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh), meaning "in hope of your being guided." It is an expression with multiple application: it suits being guided to destinations in journeys by marking roads, establishing mooring places on rivers, and calculating distances, and all of this is from God's making, since it is accomplished through His inspiration. It also suits being guided to the true religion, which is the religion of monotheism, since in those things there is a sign pointing to the Creator who is singular in creation.

The *'alamat* ("landmarks") are the signs which God inspired people to set up or to recognise by convention, so that they serve as indicators of distances and of safe routes on land and sea, which travellers then follow.

The clause ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿and He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾, because it has the sense of: "and He guided you by the star, so you are guided by it." This is a favour concerning guidance at night, for roads and landmarks guide only in daytime, whereas a traveller may be compelled to journey at night. The positions of the stars are thus signs for people travelling by night, by which the heavens are known. Those who are most in need of them are sailors, for they cannot anchor every night and so are obliged to sail by night. This is a great guidance at a time when the path is confused for the traveller. For this reason the complement in His saying "and by the star" is placed first, a placement that signifies emphasis, and likewise the predicate in His saying "they are guided" is the verbal predicate.

He turned from the second person to the third person (iltifat, a shift of grammatical person), an expression that alludes to a particular group, namely the wayfarers and the sailors, for their guidance is by these stars alone.

The definiteness in *al-najm* ("the star") is the definiteness of genus, and what is meant by it is the stars that people have come to recognise for guidance, such as the Pole Star. This was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿And it is He who made for you the stars that you may be guided by them﴾ [al-An'am: 97], in Surat al-An'am.

[Page 121]

Placing the subject before the verbal predicate in His saying "they are guided" serves merely to reinforce the judgement, since the context does not permit the intention of restriction (qasr), although it was forced into that sense in al-Kashshaf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verses 17–18:

﴿Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then remember?﴾ ﴿And if you tried to count the favours of God, you could not enumerate them. Indeed, God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾

After the proofs had been established for God's sole creation ex nihilo, beginning from His saying, ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾ [al-Nahl: 3], and after the favour (minnah) had been established and gratitude (shukr) had become obligatory, these two sentences follow from that as conclusions drawn from the preceding proofs, as a denunciation of the polytheists. The interrogation about equality is a denial (istifham inkari), meaning: he who creates is not equal to he who does not create. The particle kaf (in kaman) indicates similitude, and it is the object of the denial, since they made the idols gods as partners with God, Exalted. From the content of the two relative clauses it becomes known which of the two relatives is more worthy of divinity, and thus the object of the denial becomes clear.

Since what is meant by "he who does not create" is the idols, the use of man (من), which is ordinarily used for rational beings, is for the sake of harmonizing with His saying, ﴿Is He who creates﴾.

Following upon the denial of equality is an interrogation about the absence of remembrance, given that equality is negated. So the interrogation in His saying, ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾, is used in the sense of a denial of the absence of remembrance. This varies according to the addressees; it is a denial directed at the polytheists' turning away from remembrance in this matter.

The sentence ﴿And if you tried to count the favours of God, you could not enumerate them﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to the sentence ﴿Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then remember?﴾ and is like a complement to it, because it is a result of what those proofs contained of favour (imtinan), as has preceded. It stands in the position of a concluding summary (tadhyil) for the favour, because it contains a generality that encompasses the favours mentioned and others.

This is a comprehensive statement alerting to the abundance of God's favours upon people, such that those who count cannot enumerate them. When this is the case, alerting to their multiplicity has been achieved by knowing their foundations and the worlds that contain them.

Page 124

In this there is an allusion to increasing in thanks for the favours in general, and an indirect reference to the monstrousness of the disbelief of those who disbelieved in this Benefactor, and to the intensification of the threat against them. Its parallel has preceded in Surat Ibrahim.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verses 17–18:

﴿Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then remember?﴾ ﴿And if you tried to count the favours of God, you could not enumerate them. Indeed, God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾

After the proofs had been established for God's sole creation ex nihilo, beginning from His saying, ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾ [al-Nahl: 3], and after the favour (minnah) had been established and gratitude (shukr) had become obligatory, these two sentences follow from that as conclusions drawn from the preceding proofs, as a denunciation of the polytheists. The interrogation about equality is a denial (istifham inkari), meaning: he who creates is not equal to he who does not create. The particle kaf (in kaman) indicates similitude, and it is the object of the denial, since they made the idols gods as partners with God, Exalted. From the content of the two relative clauses it becomes known which of the two relatives is more worthy of divinity, and thus the object of the denial becomes clear.

Since what is meant by "he who does not create" is the idols, the use of man (من), which is ordinarily used for rational beings, is for the sake of harmonizing with His saying, ﴿Is He who creates﴾.

Following upon the denial of equality is an interrogation about the absence of remembrance, given that equality is negated. So the interrogation in His saying, ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾, is used in the sense of a denial of the absence of remembrance. This varies according to the addressees; it is a denial directed at the polytheists' turning away from remembrance in this matter.

The sentence ﴿And if you tried to count the favours of God, you could not enumerate them﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to the sentence ﴿Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then remember?﴾ and is like a complement to it, because it is a result of what those proofs contained of favour (imtinan), as has preceded. It stands in the position of a concluding summary (tadhyil) for the favour, because it contains a generality that encompasses the favours mentioned and others.

This is a comprehensive statement alerting to the abundance of God's favours upon people, such that those who count cannot enumerate them. When this is the case, alerting to their multiplicity has been achieved by knowing their foundations and the worlds that contain them.
