Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 19:

﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you disclose.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17]. After he had established, through numerous proofs, that Allah alone possesses the attribute of creation to the exclusion of others, and then reinforced that by saying ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], he moves here to establishing that He alone possesses comprehensive knowledge ('ilm).

No argument is put forward before this statement, nor is any proof appended after it, because it is something already indicated by the proofs of Allah's exclusive creation. The Creator of the apparent and hidden parts of the human being must necessarily know the subtle movements of those parts, which are both manifest and concealed; therefore He said ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you disclose.﴾

The addressees here are those addressed in His saying, ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ and there is in it an allusion (taʿrid) to threat and warning, that Allah will hold them accountable for their disbelief.

In it is also an announcement that their idols are otherwise, as indicated by the fronting of the subject (musnad ilayh) before the verbal predicate (khabar fiʿli), which conveys restriction (qasr) in order to refute the claim of partnership.

Hafs read (mā yusirrūna wa mā yuʿlinūna) with the yāʾ (third person) in both, which is an iltifat (shift) from address (khitab) to the third person (ghayba). On his reading, the sentence is more emphatic in threat than in the intent of instruction.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 16, verses 20–21:**

﴿And those whom they call upon besides Allah create nothing, while they are themselves created.﴾ ﴿They are dead, not living; and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾

This is a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) on the sentence ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ (An-Nahl: 17) and the sentence ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ (An-Nahl: 19).

The referent of ﴿alladhīna﴾ (those whom) is the idols. It is evident that the address here is exclusively to the polytheists, who are among those addressed by the pronouns in the preceding verses.

The purpose of this sentence is to state explicitly what was implicitly derived from what precedes it, namely the negation of creative power from the idols and the negation of knowledge from them.

The first predicate, the sentence ﴿they create nothing﴾, is derived from the sentence ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ (An-Nahl: 17). The conjunction of ﴿while they are themselves created﴾ is an ascent (*irtiqāʾ*) in the argument for the negation of their divinity.

The second predicate, the sentence ﴿They are dead, not living﴾, is an explicit statement of what was derived from the sentence ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ (An-Nahl: 19), by the method of negating a thing by negating what necessarily accompanies it (*nafy al-shayʾ bi-nafy malzūmihi*).

[Page 126]

This is the method of *kināya* (allusion), which is like mentioning a thing by its indicator. Thus the negation of life from the idols in the phrase ﴿not living﴾ entails the negation of knowledge from them, because life is a condition for the reception of knowledge. Also, the negation that they know what concerns their own state entails the negation that they know the states of others, by the implication of the wider sense of the address (*fahwā al-khiṭāb*). Whoever is like this is not a god.

The verb ﴿yukhlaqūn﴾ (they are created) is attributed to the substitute subject (*al-nāʾib*, the passive form) because the agent is evident from the context. The meaning is: they are created by Allah, the Exalted. For they are of stone, which is among the creations of Allah, and the carving of stone into images and shapes by humans does not remove the original material from being created by Allah, the Exalted. Just as Allah said, relating the words of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him): ﴿And Allah created you and what you make﴾ (As-Ṣāffāt: 96).

The phrase ﴿not living﴾ is an emphasis of the content of the phrase ﴿dead﴾, to indicate the firmness of the attribute of death in them, that there is no trace of life in it, because they are stones.

Stones are described as dead in regard to the fact that death is the absence of life. It is not a condition in describing something by names of privation (*asmāʾ al-iʿdām*) that the described thing be capable of the quality it lacks, as the philosophers (*al-ḥukamāʾ*) have established as a convention, because that is a logical convention prompted by the organisation of the principles of argumentation.

ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqūb read ﴿yadʿūna﴾ (they call upon) with the third-person (*taḥtiyya*) form, and in it there is an additional clarification directing the address to the polytheists, in contrast to the reading of the majority.

The sentence ﴿and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾ is an incorporation (*idmāj*) to establish the resurrection following the discussion of establishing the oneness of Allah, the Exalted. For these two are the basis of refuting the creed of the polytheists, and a preparation for the reason for the mutual entailment between denying the resurrection and denying monotheism, in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts deny, and they are arrogant﴾ (An-Naḥl: 22). For this reason, the apparent meaning is that the pronouns in ﴿yashʿurūn﴾ (they perceive) and ﴿yubʿathūn﴾ (they are resurrected) refer to the disbelievers, by way of *iltifāt* (shift of address) in the reading of the majority, and in the harmony of pronouns in the reading of ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqūb.

The purpose of negating their perception of the resurrection is to threaten them with the fact that the resurrection they denied is certain, and that they do not know when it will overtake them suddenly, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾ (Al-Aʿrāf: 187).

[Page 127]

Resurrection (*al-baʿth*): its literal meaning is sending from one place to another. It is also used for rousing a crouching animal, and from this comes the expression "I resurrected the camel" (*baʿathtu al-baʿīr*) when I roused it from its resting place. Perhaps this is from applying the name of a thing to its cause. The term *al-baʿth* has become dominant in the terminology of the Qur'an for bringing people to reckoning after death. Whoever of them is dead, his resurrection is his emergence from his grave. Whoever of them is living, and the hour of the end of the world overtakes him so that he dies at that moment, his resurrection is his revival after death. With this interpretation, the attribution of the negation of perception of the time of resurrection to the living disbelievers who are threatened is not problematic, and it is not correct that the pronoun in ﴿yashʿurūn﴾ refers to ﴿those whom you call upon﴾, i.e., the idols.

﴿Ayyāna﴾ (when) is an interrogative noun concerning time, composed of ﴿ayy﴾ (which) and ﴿ān﴾ (time), meaning "which time?" It suspends the verb ﴿yashʿurūn﴾ (they perceive) from acting on its object because of the interrogative sense. The meaning is: they do not perceive the time of their resurrection. ﴿Ayyāna﴾ has already occurred in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the Hour, when will it come to pass?﴾ (Al-Aʿrāf: 187), in Surah Al-Aʿrāf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 22–23:

﴿Your God is one God. But as for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are deniers, and they are arrogant.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾

This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that presents the conclusion of the preceding argument. That is, it has already been established by what came before that the divinity of anything other than Allah is invalid, and therefore it is established that you have one God with no partner. Because what has passed is sufficient to refute their denial of God's oneness, the sentence is left without an emphasizing particle (mu'akkid), in treating the state of the polytheists after they have heard the proofs as the state of one about whom it is not supposed that he would hesitate in this matter. This differs from His saying, ﴿Indeed, your God is one⁠﴾ [al-Saffat: 4] in Surah al-Saffat, because that is the beginning of a statement not preceded by any proof, just as His saying, ﴿And your God is one God⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163] in Surah al-Baqarah is addressed to the People of the Book.

The statement ﴿But as for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are deniers⁠﴾ follows from this. It is a branching of information from information, meaning: upon this decisive matter, established by the proofs mentioned earlier, there branches the information that your hearts are deniers, and you are arrogant, and that this arises from your not believing in the Hereafter.

The expression referring to the polytheists by the relative pronoun and its clause, ﴿those who do not believe in the Hereafter⁠﴾, is used because they have become known for the content of the relative clause and renowned for it, in a manner of reproach and disparagement among the believers, like His saying, ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say: Why are the angels not sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?⁠﴾ [al-Furqan: 21]. It also alludes to the fact that this relative clause is connected to their persistence in obstinacy, because the absence of their belief in resurrection and reckoning has emboldened them to cast aside the call of Islam behind their backs, so they did not expect to be held accountable for rejecting it, even supposing it were true, so that they might examine the proofs of its correctness. Yet they believe in Allah, but they do not believe that He has prepared for people a Day of recompense for their deeds.

The meaning of ﴿their hearts are deniers⁠﴾ is: rejecting what is actually the case. The word denial (inkar) is used for rejecting an established matter, since it is the opposite of affirmation (iqrar). The object of (munkirah) is omitted because the context indicates it, meaning: deniers of God's oneness.

He expressed by the nominal sentence ﴿their hearts are deniers⁠﴾ to indicate that denial is established for them and constant, because of their persistence in denial after the proofs became clear. This indicates that denial has become a disposition for them and has taken firm root in their souls, because they were harmed by it from the standpoint that they do not believe in the Hereafter, so they became accustomed to not reflecting on consequences.

Likewise, the sentence ﴿and they are arrogant⁠﴾ is constructed as a nominal sentence to indicate that arrogance has taken firm hold of them. This has been contrasted in the verse of Surah al-Furqan, ﴿They have indeed become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression⁠﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], because that verse was not preceded by proofs of God's oneness like the proofs mentioned in this verse.

The sentence ﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows⁠﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah) placed between the two conjoined sentences.

Al-jaram (with a vowel on the first letter and a short vowel on the second): its original meaning is "necessity," and it became common in usage until it came to mean "truly." It was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿Undoubtedly, they in the Hereafter are the greatest losers⁠﴾ [Hud: 22] in Surah Hud.

His saying ﴿that Allah knows⁠﴾ is in a position of genitive by a deleted preposition, related to (jaram). The predicate of the negating (la) is deleted because it is evident, since the estimate is: "la jaram" exists. The deletion of the predicate in such a construction is common, and the estimate is: "la jaram" concerning the fact that He knows, or "la jaram" from the fact that He knows, meaning: there is necessarily His knowledge, meaning: there is no doubt in that.

The sentence ﴿that Allah knows⁠﴾ is an informative statement used figuratively (kinayah) to express a warning of requital for what they conceal and what they reveal of denial, arrogance, and other things, a requital of punishment and retribution. Therefore, it is followed by the sentence ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant⁠﴾, which stands in the place of causal explanation and concluding appendage to it, because one who does not love an act, while being capable, will repay its doer with evil.

The definite article in "al-mustakbirin" (the arrogant) is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), because the nature of a concluding appendage is generality, and it includes those being spoken of here. Thus the establishing of punishment for them is like establishing a thing by its own proof.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verses 24–25:

﴿When it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear.﴾

﴿وإذا قِيلَ لَهُمْ﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿قُلُوبُهم مُنْكِرَةٌ﴾ [al-Nahl: 22], because what is contained in this is among their states that were mentioned earlier. For He mentioned their arrogance and their denial of Oneness, and followed this with their false excuses for denying the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, and their barring of people from following Islam. The estimated sense is: "Their hearts are deniers and arrogant; so they do not acknowledge prophethood, nor do they leave a gap between you and those who seek guidance; they are misleaders of people, turning them away from Islam."

The mention of the verb "said" (qāla) requires that it proceed from a speaker who asks them about a matter that occurred among them, and not as a hypothetical supposition; and that they answer with what has been mentioned, as deception toward the religion and a display of the appearance of advisers to those seeking guidance and counsel, supported by the context of His words, ﴿ومِن أوْزارِ الَّذِينَ يُضِلُّونَهم بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ﴾.

"Idhā" (إذا) is an adverb of time carrying the sense of a conditional, and this conditional indicates the repetition of these two statements. The exegetes have mentioned that when the affair of the Prophet ﷺ concerned Quraysh, and they saw the effect of the Qur'an upon people's souls, and the followers of Islam began to increase, and those arriving at Mecca during the pilgrimage season and at other times began to ask people about this Qur'an and what it called to, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira devised for them excuses and fabrications that they would invent in order to convince the inquirers. So he dispatched sixteen men from among them during the days of the season, who would sit at the mountain passes of Mecca and its roads through which people came, saying to whoever asked them: "Do not be deceived by this man who claims that he is a prophet, for he is a madman, or a sorcerer, or a poet, or a soothsayer, and the speech he utters is tales from the tales of the ancients which he has copied down." This has been mentioned at the end of Surat al-Hijr. And al-Nadr ibn al-Harith used to say: "I will recite to you what is more beautiful than the discourse of Muhammad: the stories of Rustam and Isfandiyar." This has been mentioned at His words, ﴿ومَن قالَ سَأُنْزِلُ مِثْلَ ما أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ [al-An'am: 93], in Surat al-An'am.

The questioning of the Arabs about the mission of the Prophet ﷺ was frequent and occurred often, and the most explicit of it is what al-Bukhari narrated, "from Abu Dharr, that he said: I was a man from Ghifar, and news reached us that a man had emerged in Mecca who claims he is a prophet. So I said to my brother Unays: Go to this man, speak with him, and bring me his news. So he went, met him, and then returned. I said: What do you have? He said: By God, I saw a man who commands good and forbids evil. I said: You have not satisfied me regarding the news. So I took a leather bag and a staff, then I headed to Mecca and began not knowing him, and I disliked asking about him, and I drank from the water of Zamzam and remained in the mosque..." up to the end of the hadith.

The inquiry of the questioners seeking news about what was sent down from God indicates that their question was that of one seeking guidance about a claim that had reached them, whose report had spread in the lands of the Arabs, and that they asked with good intention, framing the question about the news as it had reached them of his call.

As for the answer, it is an eloquent reply which contained a clarification of the type of this speech and a refutation that it was sent down from God; for the tales of the ancients are well known, whereas what is sent down from God is by nature something not known beforehand.

"Mādhā" (ماذا) is a compound of "mā" (the interrogative) and the demonstrative noun; after it comes a verb which is a relative clause for an omitted relative pronoun, for which the demonstrative noun stands in, and the meaning is: "What is this that has been sent down?"

"Mā" is used interrogatively to ask about the explanation of the kind and the like, and its position is that it is a predicate preceding its subject, while the demonstrative noun's position is the subject; the estimated sense is: "This that your Lord sent down—what is it?" The grammarians have been lax in saying that "dhā" in their saying "mādhā" has become a relative noun, and this was mentioned at His words, ﴿يَسْألُونَكَ ماذا يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 215], in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿أساطِيرُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject indicated by what is in the question; the estimated sense is: "It is tales of the ancients," i.e., what is asked about is the tales of the ancients.

From this it is known that it is not sent down from their Lord, because tales of the ancients are not sent down from God, as we have said just above. For this reason ﴿أساطِيرُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ did not occur in the accusative; for if it were in the accusative, the estimated sense would be: "He sent down the tales of the ancients," and that is a self-contradictory statement, because the tales of the ancients that preceded are not what God has now sent down.

"Asatir" (الأساطِيرُ) is the plural of "asṭār," which is the plural of "saṭr," so "asatir" is a plural of a plural. Al-Mubarrad said: it is the plural of "usṭūrah" with a damma on the hamza, like "urjūḥah," and it is feminine in consideration that it is a written story. What al-Mubarrad mentioned is preferable, because they are "asatir" mostly, meaning by them stories, not every written book. This has been mentioned at His words, ﴿يَقُولُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إنْ هَذا إلّا أساطِيرُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ [al-An'am: 25], in Surat al-An'am.

The lam in ﴿لِيَحْمِلُوا أوْزارَهُمْ﴾ is a statement of purpose for the verb "they said," and it is a final cause (ghāyah), not a efficient cause ('illah); for when they said ﴿أساطِيرُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾, they did not intend that their saying be a cause for them to bear the burdens of those they mislead. So the lam is used figuratively for the outcome, like His words, ﴿فالتَقَطَهُ آلُ فِرْعَوْنَ لِيَكُونَ لَهم عَدُوًّا وحَزَنًا﴾ [al-Qasas: 8].

The estimated sense is: they said that saying in the manner of one who incites toward what draws to himself an increase of harm, since by it they bore the burdens of those they mislead in addition to their own burdens.

"Awzar" (الأوْزارُ), its literal meaning is loads, the plural of "wizr" with a kasra on the waw and sukun on the zay, which is weight. It is used for crime and sin, because it weighs down its doer, preventing him from escape from pain and hardship. Thus its origin is a metaphor, by likening crime and sin to a load, and this metaphor became common. God said, ﴿وهم يَحْمِلُونَ أوْزارَهم عَلى ظُهُورِهِمْ﴾ [al-An'am: 31], in Surat al-An'am, just as sins are expressed by "burdens"; God said, ﴿ولَيَحْمِلُنَّ أثْقالَهم وأثْقالًا مَعَ أثْقالِهِمْ﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13].

The carrying of burdens is an image of the state of their being entangled in the consequences of their crimes, by the state of one carrying a weight who cannot free himself from it. Since sin was likened to weight, so it was named "wizr," the entanglement in its consequences was likened to carrying weight in the manner of imaginative representation (takhyīl). From the two separate metaphors arose one comprehensive figurative image for the whole configuration, and this is among the most excellent imagery: that the figurative image be capable of being divided into several similes or metaphors.

The attribution of the burdens to the pronoun "them" is because they are their source.

The burdens are described as ﴿كامِلَةً﴾ ("in full") to affirm their completeness and the intensity of their weight, so that this extends to the intensity of their distress in their consequences, since this is the intended purpose from attributing the carrying to the burdens.

"Min" (مِن) in His words, ﴿ومِن أوْزارِ الَّذِينَ يُضِلُّونَهُمْ﴾, is causal, related to a omitted verb indicated by the coordinating particle and the prepositional particle after it, since the prepositional particle must have a complement. Its estimated sense is: "and they bear," and the object of the verb is omitted, indicated by the object of its counterpart. The estimated sense is: "and they bear burdens resulting from the burdens of those they mislead," i.e., burdens arising for them from their causing the misguidance of those who were misled (with a fatha on the lam), for their causing of misguidance requires that the misled share the sinner's crime of misguidance, since had he not misled him, he might have been guided by his own observation or by asking sincere advisers. And in the sound hadith: "Whoever calls to misguidance will have upon him a sin like the sins of whoever follows him, without that diminishing their sins in the least."

﴿بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of object in ﴿يُضِلُّونَهم﴾, i.e., they mislead people who lack knowledge, supposing their misguidance to be counsel. The purpose of this circumstantial clause is to magnify the misguidance, not to restrict it, for misguidance does not occur except from lack of knowledge, wholly or partly.

The clause ﴿ألا ساءَ ما يَزِرُونَ﴾ is a concluding summation (tadhyīl), introduced with the particle of alerting, out of concern for what it contains of warning against falling into it or for abandoning it.

[Page 134]

When he mentioned the consequence of their leading others astray and barring those who asked about the Qur'an and Islam from it in the Hereafter, he followed it with a threat that there would befall them what had befallen their likes in this world of disgrace and punishment. This also carries a discouragement that by their scheming they would not reach the goal they intended, and that they are frustrated in their scheming, just as those before them who schemed against their messengers were frustrated.

Since their answer to those who asked about the Qur'an was to say that it is ﴿fables of the ancients﴾ [an-Nahl: 24], presenting it in the guise of sincere counsel and guidance while they actually wanted to preserve their disbelief, that conduct was called scheming against the believers. Scheming means inflicting harm on another while disguising it as sincere advice and benefit. Their conduct was therefore compared with the scheming of those before them, that is, of the earlier nations who schemed against others, such as the people of Hud, the people of Salih, the people of Lut, and the people of Pharaoh. Concerning the people of Salih, God the Exalted said: ﴿And they schemed a scheme, and We schemed a scheme﴾ [an-Naml: 50], and so on. He also said: ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals to scheme therein; but they scheme only against themselves, and they do not perceive﴾ [al-An'am: 123].
Thus the definiteness of the relative clause in His saying ﴿those before them﴾ is equivalent to definiteness by the article of the genus (lam al-jins, the definite article denoting the whole class).

The meaning of ﴿God came upon their structure﴾ is a metaphor (isti'arah), by likening one who intends to take vengeance to one who comes toward the person he is avenging himself upon. From the same usage is His saying: ﴿So God came upon them from where they did not expect﴾ [al-Hashr: 2].

His saying ﴿God came upon their structure from the foundations﴾ is an allegory (tamthil) for the states of the uprooting of nations. "Al-bunyan" (structure) is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, that is, "what is built" (al-mabni), and here it is used metaphorically for strength, might, protection, and elevated standing.

The use of "building" for such a thing is found in eloquent speech. 'Abdah ibn al-Tabib said:

*Qays's destruction was not the destruction of one man,*
*but the structure of a people that collapsed.*

And Su'dah, the mother of al-Kumayt ibn Ma'ruf, said:

*Ma'ruf built for you a structure which you demolished,*
*and for the ancient nobility there is both builder and demolisher.*

The phrase ﴿from the foundations﴾ is connected to "atā" (came). "Min" here is the min of starting point, and its object is the starting point of the coming, which means uprooting. So it has the sense of demolishing it.
"Al-qawa'id" (the foundations): the bases and the pillars that are set up as columns for the building, on which the roof rests. This is an imaginative figure (takhyil) or a supporting figure of speech (tarshih), since nothing in the statement is likened to the foundations.

"Al-khurur" means falling and dropping. The verb "kharra" is therefore a metaphor for the removal of that which gave protection, like His saying: ﴿They destroy their houses with their own hands﴾ [al-Hashr: 2].

[Page 135]

"Al-saqf" (the roof), in its literal sense, is the covering of the space between the walls of a house, placed on the walls, and it may be made of stone or of timber. Here it is used metaphorically for the same thing for which "building" was used metaphorically.
"From above them" is an emphasis (ta'kid) of the clause ﴿the roof fell upon them﴾.

From the combination of these metaphors the allegorical metaphor (al-isti'arah al-tamthiliyyah) is formed. It is the likening of the state of the people who schemed, in their strength, that God then seized them swiftly and removed that might, to the state of a people who erected a great building with supports and took refuge in it, and God uprooted it from its foundations so that the roof of the building collapsed all at once upon its occupants, and they all perished. This is among the excellences of the allegorical metaphor, since it resolves into several metaphors.

The clause ﴿and the punishment came upon them﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿God came upon their structure from the foundations﴾. The article in "al-'adhab" (the punishment) is the definite article of reference (lam al-'ahd), so it conveys the meaning of His saying "from above them," together with the addition of His saying ﴿from where they did not perceive﴾. Because of this addition, it was coordinated, since it differs in meaning; otherwise, a emphasizing clause is not normally coordinated. The meaning is that the punishment mentioned came upon them suddenly while they did not perceive it. Seizure by surprise is more harmful, because it is accompanied by intense terror, unlike what arrives gradually, for the soul receives that with patience.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 27:

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say: "Where are My partners, concerning whom you used to oppose [the believers]?"﴾ This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿that they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Nahl: 25]; because that is a threat against them, and this is a completion (takmilah) of it.

The plural pronoun in His words, exalted is He, ﴿yukhzihim﴾ ("He will disgrace them") refers back to what the pronoun in the preposition with lam refers to in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And when it is said to them: "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ [al-Nahl: 24], and that refers back to those who do not believe in the Hereafter.

صفحة ١٣٦
And ﴿thumma﴾ ("then") is for sequence in rank (al-tartib al-rutbi), for the disgrace of the Hereafter is greater than the removal of the blessings of this world.
Al-khizy is humiliation (al-ihanah), and it has been discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Then what is the recompense of those among you who do that except disgrace in the life of this world?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The fronting of the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is for emphasis on the Day of Resurrection, because it is the day of the everlasting states, so the punishment in it is awe-inspiring to the hearers.

And ﴿ayna﴾ ("where") is an interrogative about place, and it requires knowledge of the existence of what is located in the place. Since the context here is one of mockery (tahakkum), the interrogation about place is used in mockery, so that it appears to them like those greedily searching for their gods, while they themselves know that there is no existence for them and no place for them to dwell.

The attribution of the partners to the Divine Name (ḍamīr al-jalālah) is an increase in rebuke, because the manifestation of God's greatness on that day, visible to the eye, contradicts that He has any partner; so the addressees then know the impossibility of partnership.

The relative pronoun in His words, ﴿alladhina kuntum tushaqqunna fihim﴾ ("concerning whom you used to oppose"), serves to draw attention to their error and mistake in claiming partnership, similar to the one in the verse of ʿAbdah:

"Indeed, those whom you see as your brothers, their hearts' rage is healed only by your being thrown down."

Al-mushaqqah is vehement contention in dispute, as if it were a dispute with which there is no way to agreement, since each disputant has come to be on a side other than the other's side.

Nafiʿ read ﴿tushaqqūnī﴾ with a kasrah on the nūn, by elision of the first-person yā' (the pronoun "me"), meaning "you oppose Me," and this is by their denial of what God commanded through His Messenger ﷺ. The rest read ﴿tushaqqūna﴾ with a fatḥah on the nūn and the object omitted for knowledge, meaning "you oppose the one who calls you to monotheism."

The ﴿fi﴾ ("concerning") is for figurative location (al-zarfiyyah al-majaziyyah) with the elision of a modifier (muḍāf), since opposition does not occur in the essences but in the meanings, and the implied sense is: "concerning their divinity or concerning their matter."

صفحة ١٣٧
﴿Those who were given knowledge will say: "Indeed, disgrace and misery this day are upon the disbelievers."﴾ This is an independent sentence (jumlah ibtidaʾiyyah) relating the saying of the best of creation when they hear God's words, exalted is He, through the tongue of the angels of punishment: ﴿Where are My partners, concerning whom you used to oppose?﴾

The clause ﴿qāla alladhīna ūtū al-ʿilm﴾ is brought without a conjunction, because it stands in the position of the answer to His words "where are My partners," to draw attention to the fact that those given knowledge rushed to the answer when the polytheists were struck dumb, so they were not left without a response. Those given knowledge answered with a comprehensive reply denying that the alleged partners would avail the polytheists anything, and that disgrace and misery have encompassed the disbelievers.

The expression in the past tense is to affirm the certainty of the saying.

Those "given knowledge" (alladhina ūtū al-ʿilm) are those whom God granted knowledge of realities, from among the messengers and prophets, peace be upon them, and the believers, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And those who were given knowledge and faith will say: "You have remained in the Book of God until the Day of Resurrection."﴾ [al-Rum: 56]. That is, they say, at that standing, upon seeing the readied punishment for the disbelievers, words indicating that disgrace and harm on the Day of Resurrection are restricted to the disbelievers. This is an assertive restriction (qasr idda'i), with the definite article of the genus, to the extreme limit within its genus, so much so that anything else is as if it were not of that genus.

The emphasis of the sentence by the particle of emphasis, by the form of restriction, and by the use of the particle of elevation (ʿalā), which indicates the firm grip of disgrace and misery upon them, conveys the sense of wonder at the terror of what has been prepared for them.

[p. 138]

﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ ﴿and they will offer submission, [saying]: "We did not do any evil." Yes, indeed, God is Knowing of what you used to do."﴾ ﴿So enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein. And how wretched is the abode of the arrogant!﴾ The indication is clear that His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾, is not part of what is said by "those who were given knowledge" on the Day of Resurrection, since there is no connection. The Unbelievers would not be identified on the Day of Resurrection as "those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves," because the present tense in His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿taken in death by the angels﴾, comes close to explicitly indicating that this taking in death is described as occurring at the time it happens, while on the Day of Resurrection their deaths have already passed, and there is no further benefit in mentioning them on that day. Therefore the correct reading is that this is a new, independent statement.

It is related from ʿIkrimah: this verse was revealed in Medina concerning a people who had embraced Islam in Mecca but had not emigrated, so the Quraysh brought them out to Badr against their will, and they were killed at Badr.

The correct reading is that ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾ [al-Nahl: 32] is a substitute (badal) for "those" in His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿But those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Nahl: 22], or a qualifier (sifah) of them, as their description at the end of the verse as "the arrogant" indicates, in His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿And how wretched is the abode of the arrogant!﴾. They are the ones described earlier in His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿and they are arrogant﴾ [al-Nahl: 22], and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ). If you refuse this because of the distance between the one followed and the follower, then make ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾ [al-Nahl: 32] the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), the implied sense being: "They are those whom the angels take in death."

The omission of the subject (ḥadhf al-musnad ilayhi) follows customary usage in such cases, for any subject that has been mentioned earlier in the speech, about which something has been reported and whose situation has been described. This is what al-Sakkaki calls omission that is governed by usage (al-ḥadhf al-muttabaʿ fīhi al-istiʿmāl). Opposite to this is His statement, Exalted is He, later on: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good﴾ [al-Nahl: 32], which is a qualifier of "those who were mindful of God," so this is its parallel.

The purpose of this relative clause is to describe the state of those who die in polytheism. After mentioning the situation of those upon whom punishment descended, leading to their annihilation, and what will befall them on the Day of Resurrection,

[p. 139]

the state of their death is mentioned, which lies between the two states of this world and the Hereafter. It is a state that comes upon all of them, whether among those who were overtaken by annihilation or those who perished before that.

Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) who undertook to connect it with what precedes have agreed to make ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾, the whole verse, a substitute for "the unbelievers" in His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, disgrace and misfortune today are upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Nahl: 27], or a qualifier of it. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) remained silent about it, and that silence is "a golden silence." Al-Khafaji said: "It is valid that it be a statement made by the speech (maqul li-l-qawl), and not included under it." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "It is possible that 'those' is in the nominative case as a new subject (mubtada') separate from what precedes it, and its predicate is in His statement, ﴿and they will offer submission﴾." End of quote.

The verb's attachment to the feminine present prefix ta' (tatawaffāhum), in the reading of the majority, is according to its attribution to the plural group. Ḥamzah and Khalaf read yatawaffāhum with the letter yā' as the original form.

The wronging of oneself (ẓulm al-nafs) is polytheism.

The verb "to cast" (al-ilqāʾ) is used metaphorically for manifesting, accompanied by humiliation, likened to casting down weapons on the ground. That is because they gave up their arrogance and denial and hastened to acknowledge and submit when they tasted the torment of having their souls torn away.

As-salam, with a fatḥah on the sin and a fatḥah on the lam, means submission (al-istislām). The casting and the salam were discussed earlier at His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿and cast to you the peace﴾ [al-Nisa': 90] in Surat al-Nisa', and the literal casting was discussed earlier at His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿and He cast upon the earth firm mountains﴾ [al-Nahl: 15] at the beginning of this surah.

Describing them as ﴿wronging themselves﴾ suggests that the angels' taking them in death is accompanied by severity and punishment. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿If only you could see when the angels take those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal: 50].

The clause ﴿We did not do any evil﴾ is a quoted speech (maqul qawl) of an omitted verb of saying, indicated by "they will offer submission," because the first manifestation of offering submission is speech that shows submission. They say this to the angels who are tearing away their souls, so that the angels will stop the torment of the tearing away. Due to the confusion of their minds, they think that the angels are only testing them with punishment, in order to discover the hidden state of their affairs. So they assume that if they lie to them, their lie will be accepted by the angels, and the angels will stop the punishment for them. For this reason they deny that they had done any evil before.

Therefore the clause ﴿Yes, indeed, God is Knowing of what you used to do﴾ is the angels' reply to them. For this reason it begins with the particle that nullifies negation, which is "yes" (balā). They made God's knowledge of what they used to do a metaphorical expression (kināyah) for refuting their statement ﴿We did not do any evil﴾, and also an indication that they only treated them with punishment by a command from God, Exalted is He, who knows them.

They attributed knowledge to God rather than saying, "We know what you used to do," out of courtesy toward God, and to indicate that they only knew this through instruction from God, Exalted is He.

The consequence expressed in ﴿So enter the gates of Hell﴾ following the refutation of their denial of doing evil is clear, because the affirmation that they used to do evil necessitates their deserving punishment. This is at the time when their final destination is revealed to them, as is found in the hadith: "The grave is either a garden of the gardens of Paradise or a pit of the pits of the Fire." A parallel to this is His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿If only you could see when the angels take those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs, and [saying], "Taste the punishment of the burning"﴾ [al-Anfal: 50].

The clause ﴿And how wretched is the abode of the arrogant!﴾ is a concluding remark (tadhyil). It is possible that it is a quotation of the angels' speech, but the more evident view is that it is a speech of God, Exalted is He, reporting, not a part of what is reported. The description of them as "the arrogant" supports this, since it links this attribute to the one described in His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿Their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant﴾ [al-Nahl: 22]. The lam that enters on "wretched" (bi'sa) is the lam of oath.

Al-mathwa means the place of return, from thawa, meaning "to return," or the dwelling place, from thawa meaning "to dwell." It was discussed earlier at His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿He said, "The Fire is your abode"﴾ [al-An'am: 128] in Surat al-An'am.

He did not refer to Hell as "the home" (al-dar) as He did with Paradise later, in His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿And how excellent is the home of the mindful!﴾ [al-Nahl: 30]. This is to belittle them, and to show that they are not in Hell in the position of the people of the home, but rather they are crowded together in the Fire, and they are in an abode of dwelling, that is, a place of staying.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 30–31:

Page 141
﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Good."﴾
When the description of the evil deeds of the disbelievers and their consequences was opened with the fact that when it was said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they said, "Tales of the ancients" [al-Nahl: 24], here is set the contrast between their state and the state of the good deeds of the believers and the goodness of their consequences. Thus this is opened with the counterpart of what the story of the disbelievers was opened with, and the parallel between the two narratives comes in the most wondrous arrangement.

This sentence is conjoined (ma'tufah) to the sentences before it, and it is inserted, by way of digression (istitrad), within the states of the polytheists. This sentence is not introduced with the conditional particle as its counterpart was introduced with it, "And when it is said to them, 'What has your Lord sent down?'" [al-Nahl: 24]. This is because their saying "Tales of the ancients" [al-Nahl: 24], being a lie they fabricated, is liable to be abandoned by its speaker, who may come back to the truth, and that not everyone who says it agrees upon it. Therefore it was joined to the conditional particle, which requires the repetition of that, to indicate their persistence in disbelief. By contrast, here, truthfulness is liable to be a continuing habit of its speaker, so there is no need to point to a repetition from him.

"Those who were mindful of God" (alladhina ittaqaw): they are the believers, because faith is the mindfulness of God and fear of His anger. The intended ones are the believers known in Makkah, so the relative pronoun is for a known referent (li'l-'ahd).

The meaning is that the believers were asked about the Qur'an and the one who brought it, and they guided the askers, and did not hesitate in disclosing the reality of the Qur'an in the most concise and comprehensive explanation, which is the word (khayran) "good," in the accusative. Its wording encompasses every good in this world and every good in the Hereafter. Its accusative case indicates that they took it as the object of (anzala, "sent down") which occurs in the questioners' question. Thus the accusative indicates that they affirm that the Qur'an was sent down from God. This is the point of difference between the nominative in the answer of the polytheists, when it was said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they said, "Tales of the ancients" [al-Nahl: 24], in the nominative, and the accusative in the speech of the believers, when it was said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they said, "Good," in the accusative. This was mentioned a moment ago at His saying, exalted is He, "They said, 'Tales of the ancients'" [al-Nahl: 24].

﴿For those who did good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better. And excellent is the abode of the mindful. Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter, beneath which rivers flow; they will have therein whatever they wish. Thus does God reward the mindful.﴾
This is an initial resumptive sentence (mustanifah ibtida'iyyah), and it is a speech from God, exalted is He, similar to its counterpart in the verse "Say, O My servants who believe, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good, and the earth of God is spacious" [al-Zumar: 10] in Surah al-Zumar, and it is not part of the quoted speech of those who were mindful of God.

"Those who did good" (alladhina ahsanu): they are the mindful, so this is the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, linking the predicate's construction with the relative pronoun, meaning: their reward is good, because they did good.

His saying, exalted is He, "in this world" (fi hadhihi al-dunya) may be connected to the verb (ahsanu), and it may be a stationary adverbial phrase functioning as a circumstantial qualifier of (hasanah, "good"). Consider what comes in the explanation of this verse in Surah al-Zumar regarding the wisdom of the placement in the middle.

The meaning of "and the abode of the Hereafter is better" is that it is better for them than this world. So if they have good in this world, then they will have what is better in the Hereafter. Just as the disbelievers had the punishment of this world and the punishment of Hell, the mindful had the best of this world and the best of the Hereafter. This is the counterpart of His saying, exalted is He, regarding the polytheists, "That they may bear their burdens in full" [al-Nahl: 25], and His saying, "And the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive" [al-Nahl: 26].

The good of this world is the good life, and what God opened to them of the splendor of this world together with the blessing of faith. The good of the Hereafter is lasting bliss. God, exalted is He, said, "Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do" [al-Nahl: 97].

His saying, exalted is He, "And excellent is the abode of the mindful. Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter" is the counterpart of His saying, exalted is He, regarding their opposites, "Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein. And wretched is the abode of the arrogant" [al-Nahl: 29].

It has already been mentioned what is the reason for calling Hell a "dwelling-place" (mathwa) and Paradise an "abode" (dar).

"Ni'ma" (excellent is) is a verb of praise that is not inflected, and its subject is a fa'il indicating the genus of the one praised. After it is mentioned another nominative called the "specified of praise" (al-makhsus bi'l-madh), which is either a mubtada' whose khabar is omitted or a khabar whose mubtada' is omitted. When something indicating the specified of praise has already preceded, it is not mentioned after that, as here, since the prior mention of "and the abode of the Hereafter" indicates that the specified of praise is the abode of the Hereafter. The meaning: "and excellent is the abode of the mindful: the abode of the Hereafter."

"Gardens of perpetual residence" (jannatu 'adn) is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, from among those whose subject is omitted in accordance with usage when the subject has already been discussed earlier, as mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, "Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves" [al-Nahl: 28]. The estimated form is: "It is the gardens of perpetual residence," i.e., the abode of the mindful is the gardens of perpetual residence.

The clause "which they will enter" (yadkhulunaha) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the mindful." Its purpose is to evoke that wondrous state, the state of their entering the abode of good, the best outcome, and the gardens.

The clause "they will have therein whatever they wish" (lahum fiha ma yasha'un) is a circumstantial clause of a pronoun, from the pronoun of subject in (yadkhuluna ha), and its content completes what is in the clause "which they will enter" of evoking that wondrous state.

The clause "Thus does God reward the mindful" is a new resumptive sentence. The use of the demonstrative (dhalika) serves to distinguish the reward and to draw attention to it, and to make the reward so distinguished and complete that the reward of the mindful is likened to it: the estimated meaning is "God rewards the mindful with a reward like that reward which you have known." It is a concluding sentence (tadhyil), because the definiteness in "the mindful" is for generality.

﴿For those who did good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better. And excellent is the abode of the mindful. Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter, beneath which rivers flow; they will have therein whatever they wish. Thus does God reward the mindful.﴾
This is an initial resumptive sentence (mustanifah ibtida'iyyah), and it is a speech from God, exalted is He, similar to its counterpart in the verse "Say, O My servants who believe, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good, and the earth of God is spacious" [al-Zumar: 10] in Surah al-Zumar, and it is not part of the quoted speech of those who were mindful of God.

"Those who did good" (alladhina ahsanu): they are the mindful, so this is the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, linking the predicate's construction with the relative pronoun, meaning: their reward is good, because they did good.

His saying, exalted is He, "in this world" (fi hadhihi al-dunya) may be connected to the verb (ahsanu), and it may be a stationary adverbial phrase functioning as a circumstantial qualifier of (hasanah, "good"). Consider what comes in the explanation of this verse in Surah al-Zumar regarding the wisdom of the placement in the middle.

The meaning of "and the abode of the Hereafter is better" is that it is better for them than this world. So if they have good in this world, then they will have what is better in the Hereafter. Just as the disbelievers had the punishment of this world and the punishment of Hell, the mindful had the best of this world and the best of the Hereafter. This is the counterpart of His saying, exalted is He, regarding the polytheists, "That they may bear their burdens in full" [al-Nahl: 25], and His saying, "And the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive" [al-Nahl: 26].

The good of this world is the good life, and what God opened to them of the splendor of this world together with the blessing of faith. The good of the Hereafter is lasting bliss. God, exalted is He, said, "Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do" [al-Nahl: 97].

His saying, exalted is He, "And excellent is the abode of the mindful. Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter" is the counterpart of His saying, exalted is He, regarding their opposites, "Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein. And wretched is the abode of the arrogant" [al-Nahl: 29].

It has already been mentioned what is the reason for calling Hell a "dwelling-place" (mathwa) and Paradise an "abode" (dar).

"Ni'ma" (excellent is) is a verb of praise that is not inflected, and its subject is a fa'il indicating the genus of the one praised. After it is mentioned another nominative called the "specified of praise" (al-makhsus bi'l-madh), which is either a mubtada' whose khabar is omitted or a khabar whose mubtada' is omitted. When something indicating the specified of praise has already preceded, it is not mentioned after that, as here, since the prior mention of "and the abode of the Hereafter" indicates that the specified of praise is the abode of the Hereafter. The meaning: "and excellent is the abode of the mindful: the abode of the Hereafter."

"Gardens of perpetual residence" (jannatu 'adn) is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, from among those whose subject is omitted in accordance with usage when the subject has already been discussed earlier, as mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, "Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves" [al-Nahl: 28]. The estimated form is: "It is the gardens of perpetual residence," i.e., the abode of the mindful is the gardens of perpetual residence.

The clause "which they will enter" (yadkhulunaha) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the mindful." Its purpose is to evoke that wondrous state, the state of their entering the abode of good, the best outcome, and the gardens.

The clause "they will have therein whatever they wish" (lahum fiha ma yasha'un) is a circumstantial clause of a pronoun, from the pronoun of subject in (yadkhuluna ha), and its content completes what is in the clause "which they will enter" of evoking that wondrous state.

The clause "Thus does God reward the mindful" is a new resumptive sentence. The use of the demonstrative (dhalika) serves to distinguish the reward and to draw attention to it, and to make the reward so distinguished and complete that the reward of the mindful is likened to it: the estimated meaning is "God rewards the mindful with a reward like that reward which you have known." It is a concluding sentence (tadhyil), because the definiteness in "the mindful" is for generality.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 32:

Page 144
﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, "Peace be upon you. Enter Paradise for what you used to do."﴾

This is the counterpart of His saying concerning their opposites: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 28]. Whatever is said in the counterpart is said in this one as well.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "tatawaffahum" with two taa' (fawqiyyatayn), like its parallel, while Hamzah and Khalaf read it with a single initial yaa' (tahtiyyah uula) in the same manner.

Al-tayyib (the good) is on the pattern fay'il, like qayyim and mayyit, and it is an intensive form denoting the attribute of goodness. Its basic meaning is pleasant fragrance, but it is applied, by the well-known figurative usage (al-majaz al-mashhur), to noble character and the perfection of the soul. Thus it is predicated of tangible things, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿halalan tayyiban﴾ (lawful and good), and of abstract and inner matters, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Peace be upon you, you are good﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and the saying of people, "Tibta nafsan" (you are good of soul). From it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes out by the permission of its Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. In the hadith, "Indeed Allah is Good (tayyib) and accepts only what is good (tayyib)," meaning good, lawful wealth.

So His saying here, ﴿tayyibin﴾ (good), gathers all these meanings: that is, the angels take them in death purified from shirk, with tranquil souls. This is the counterpart of His saying concerning their opposites: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 28].

The clause ﴿yaqulun salamun 'alaykum﴾ (saying, "Peace be upon you") is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the angels, a clause of concomitance with "tatawaffahum." That is, they take them in death while greeting them with peace. It is a peace of reassurance and honour at the time of their coming to take them in death, because the act of "tatawaffahum" begins from the moment the angels arrive until the souls are extracted, and this is a short portion of time.

Their saying, ﴿Enter Paradise for what you used to do﴾, is the counterpart of their saying to their opposites: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what you used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 28], ﴿So enter the gates of Hell﴾ [al-Nahl: 29]. What is said about the command to enter Paradise at the time of death is like what is said about its opposite mentioned just before, and it here refers to the bliss of unveiling (ni'im al-mukashafah).

﴿Are they waiting for anything but that the angels should come to them, or that your Lord's command should come? Thus did those before them act. And Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ ﴿So the evil consequences of what they had done befell them, and what they used to mock enveloped them.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), arising from the phrase ﴿Those before them had already schemed﴾ [al-Nahl: 26], because it raises the question of someone asking when the punishment would descend upon these people as it descended upon those before them. So it is said: They are waiting for nothing but one of two matters: the coming of the angels to seize their souls, whereupon the threat already mentioned is realised for them, or that the command of Allah should come. What is meant by this is the total destruction (istisal) alluded to by way of threat in His words ﴿Then Allah came at their structure from its foundations﴾ [al-Nahl: 26].

The interrogative is a denial (istifham inkari) in the sense of negation; therefore the exception (istithna') follows it.

Here (yanzurun) means waiting (intizar), which is the same as "nazra" (respite). The address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ, as a reminder of the certainty of the threat and of not being impatient for it, and as an allusion to the polytheists, warning them against being deceived by the delay of the threat and urging them to hasten to faith.

The attribution of the aforementioned waiting to them is contrary to what the apparent sense requires, by placing them in the position of one who waits for one of the two matters, because their state of turning away from the threat and not reflecting upon the evidences of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ, despite the manifestness of those evidences and their conveying certainty, is like the state of one who is certain that one of the two matters will befall him, so he awaits one of them. As you say to one who does not take precaution against his enemy: "You are awaiting nothing but to be taken captive." From this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then do they await anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them?﴾ [Yunus: 102], and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You want only to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not want to be among the reformers﴾ [al-Qasas: 19]. This is close to affirming a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, while it is not that.

[Page 146]

The clause ﴿Thus did those before them act﴾ [al-Nahl: 35] is an analogy with the states of the earlier nations, to establish both purposes.

The reference to the waiting derived from (yanzurun) is intended to denote turning away and delay; that is, like their delay, the action of those before them: that the punishment seized them suddenly, as it seized those before them. This warning to them is given although Allah has lifted the punishment of total destruction from the community of Muhammad ﷺ, by his blessing and by His will for the spread of his religion.

﴿Those before them﴾ [al-Nahl: 35] are those mentioned in His words ﴿Those before them had already schemed﴾ [al-Nahl: 26].

The clause ﴿And Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾ is an intervening parenthetical (i'tiradh) between the clause ﴿Thus did those before them act﴾ [al-Nahl: 35] and the clause ﴿So the evil consequences of what they had done befell them﴾.

The purpose of this parenthetical is that the mention of what those before them did points to what their outcome was, namely their total destruction, so it is followed by His words, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah did not wrong them﴾, that is, in what befell them.

Since this parenthetical includes that they wronged themselves, the connection of ﴿So the evil consequences of what they had done befell them﴾ to it, or to what precedes it, is a rare stylistic arrangement in speech. Its underlying structure may be estimated as: "Thus did those before them act and wronged themselves, so the evil consequences of what they had done befell them, and Allah did not wrong them." In changing the customary style there is an arousing of curiosity about the report, and an emphasis on its gravity, by stating that it is their self-wronging and that Allah did not wrong them. Thus the listener awaits a dreadful report, which is ﴿So the evil consequences of what they had done befell them﴾.

The befalling of evil consequences is either by an omitted genitive construction, that is, what befell them was the requital of them, or their evil deeds are treated as if they were what befell them, since they are the cause of what befell them; so this is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli).

Hāqa means "to encompass" (ahata), and al-hayq is encompassing. Then usage restricted hayq to the encompassing of evil. The discussion of this has already preceded at His words, exalted is He, ﴿So there encompassed those who mocked them what they used to mock﴾ [al-An'am: 10], at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

[Page 147]

The word (ma) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), whose referent is the punishment they were threatened with. The preposition (ba') in (bihi) is causal, and it is a stationary adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqarr) which is a qualifier of an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). The sense is: "what they used to mock with a mockery caused by it," that is, because of their denial of its occurrence. This usage is found in such a construction, and it has been repeated in the Qur'an, among which is what occurs in Surat al-Ahqaf. The ba' is not for transitivising the verb (yastahzi'un). The prepositional phrase was placed before the governing verb of its qualified noun for the sake of preserving the rhyme (ri'ayah 'ala al-fasilah).

﴿And those who associated others with God said: "Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything without His (leave)." Likewise did those before them act. So, is there upon the messengers anything but clear conveyance?﴾ This is the conjunction (ʿaṭf) of one narrative upon another, to relate one of the circumstances of their doubts and obstinacy, and a door of their denial.

That is because they were trying to confound the Messenger ﷺ by saying: God knows what they conceal and what they disclose; He is capable over them and over their gods; He does not approve that anything other than Him be worshipped; and He forbids them the baḥīra, the sāʾiba and the like. So they reckoned that they had defeated the Prophet ﷺ and overcome him in argument, and they said to him: "Had God willed that we not worship idols, He would not have enabled us to worship them; and had He willed that we not prohibit what we have prohibited, such as the baḥīra and the sāʾiba, He would not have allowed us to maintain that prohibition." This was an aim at confounding and denial.

God answered this by comparing their deeds with the deeds of the nations whom God destroyed. For had God been pleased with what they did, He would not have punished them with annihilation. Their outcome was the descent of the punishment, by His saying, ﴿Likewise did those before them act,﴾ and then the cutting off of the argument by His saying, ﴿So, is there upon the messengers anything but clear conveyance?﴾ That is: it is not the duty of the messengers, peace be upon them, to debate with the community.

Page 148

He said in Sūrat al-Anʿām: ﴿Those who associated others with God will say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated anything with Him, nor would our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything." Likewise did those before them deny, until they tasted Our might.﴾ [al-Anʿām: 148]. Here He called their statement a denial, like the denial of those before them, because its purpose was denial, and it reinforced their denial with an argument whose meaning they misunderstood. They supposed that God Himself moves people to their deeds, as the shadow-play operator and the puppeteer move their figures and images. That is ignorance on their part of the difference between the creation of beings and what people acquire through their own selves, and of the difference between the matter of denial and the matter of obligation (taklīf), and a confusion between approval (riḍā) and will (irāda). Had it not been for this confusion, their statement would have been faith.

The demonstrative ﴿kadhālika﴾ ("likewise") refers to associating partners and prohibiting things of their own accord; that is, as these did, so did those who were before them, namely those mentioned earlier in God's saying, ﴿Those before them had already schemed﴾ [al-Naḥl: 26], and His saying, ﴿Likewise did those before them act, and God did not wrong them﴾ [al-Naḥl: 33]. The intent is: they acted as these did, so their outcome was what you know. Had their deed been pleasing to God, He would not have destroyed them. Why then did they not take the destruction of those as evidence that God is not pleased with their deed? For the indication of punishment is more manifest than the indication of respite, since the indication of punishment is positive (wujūdiyya) and the indication of respite is negative (ʿadamiyya).

The pronoun ﴿naḥnu﴾ ("we") is an emphasis of the attached pronoun in ﴿ʿabadnā﴾ ("we worshipped"), and by it the conjunction upon the attached nominative pronoun is made valid. The repetition of the negative particle in His saying ﴿wa-lā ābāʾunā﴾ ("nor our fathers") is to emphasise the negating ﴿mā﴾.

Upon this was built the cutting off of the argument with them, and the informing of them that the messengers, peace be upon them, have no duty except conveyance, and among them is Muḥammad ﷺ. So beware lest your outcome be the outcome of the nations of the earlier messengers. The messengers are not charged with compelling people to faith, so that you should pursue with them the tactic of harassing them and enraging them.

Al-balāgh (conveyance) is a verbal noun of al-iblāgh, and al-mubīn means the clarifying, plain one.

The interrogation with ﴿hal﴾ ("is there?") is a denial, in the sense of negation; for this reason the exception came after it.

Page 149

The restriction (qaṣr) derived from the negation and the exception is a relative restriction (qaṣr idāfī), to reverse the belief of the polytheists, who, in their treatment of the Messenger ﷺ, held that the Messenger had a personal aim in what he called to.

The ruling is affirmed for all messengers, peace be upon them, although those being refuted had not thought of the matter of the earlier messengers, so that the sentence is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) for the argument, and so it conveys what is more general than the one refuted.

The speech is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ as instruction and consolation, and it implicitly includes a hint toward conveying (the message) to the polytheists.

﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, (saying): "Worship God and avoid ṭāghūt." Then among them were those whom God guided, and among them were those upon whom error was decreed. So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾ This is a conjunction upon the sentence ﴿Likewise did those before them act,﴾ and it completes the refutation of the polytheists' doubt, by way of detail after summary, to increase the establishment of the proof. So His saying, ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger,﴾ is an explanation of the content of the sentence ﴿So, is there upon the messengers anything but clear conveyance?﴾

The sentence ﴿Then among them were those whom God guided﴾ to its end is an explanation of the content of the sentence ﴿Likewise did those before them act.﴾

The meaning: God made clear to the nations, through the tongues of the messengers, peace be upon them, that He commands them to worship Him and to avoid the worship of idols. So from every nation there were groups whom God guided, and they affirmed and believed; and among them were groups in whom error had taken hold, so they perished. Whoever travels the earth sees the evidence of their annihilation.

Page 150

The ﴿an﴾ here is explanatory (tafsīriyya) for the clause ﴿fa-baʿathnā﴾ ("and We sent"), because sending (baʿth) includes the sense of saying, since it is a sending for conveyance.

Al-ṭāghūt is the genus of what is worshipped besides God, of idols; and they may mention it in the plural form, so it is said al-ṭawāghīt, which are the idols. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿They believe in jibt and ṭāghūt﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 51], in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.

The guidance of some of them was attributed to God, although He commanded all of them to guidance, as an alert to the polytheists concerning the removal of their doubt in their saying, ﴿Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾: God made guidance clear to them, so the guidance of those who are guided is by means of His clarification; He is therefore the Guider of them.

The expression concerning error, "﴿ḥaqqat ʿalayhim﴾" ("upon them was decreed"), rather than attributing the misguidance to God, is an indication that since God forbade them from error, their persistence in it was a sustaining of their earlier error, so "upon them was decreed the error," that is, it was established and did not lift.

In this there is a hint that the persistence of error is from the acquisition of their own selves. But it has come in other verses that God misguides the misguided, as in His saying, ﴿And whoever God wills to lead astray, He makes his breast constricted and tight﴾ [al-Anʿām: 125], and His saying after this, ﴿Indeed, God does not guide those who misguide﴾ [al-Naḥl: 37] according to the reading of the majority. So that from the totality of this there may result knowledge that God established many causes, some of which came from the propagation of minds and temperaments and the borrowing of some from others, and some of which follow misguided calls, in such a way that from the gathering of diverse matters, which none but God can number, there came complete causes that stand between the misguided and guidance. Therefore those causes were indeed the cause of error being decreed upon them. Thus, in terms of the immediate causes, their error was from the One who created those causes and created their laws throughout the ages. So understand.

Therefore the inference from them depends on travelling the earth; and had the intended meaning been mere perishing, He would have commanded them to observe graveyards and recall the earlier predecessors.
