Why then did they not take the destruction of those as evidence that God is not pleased with their deed? For the indication of punishment is more manifest than the indication of respite, since the indication of punishment is positive (wujūdiyya) and the indication of respite is negative (ʿadamiyya).

The pronoun ﴿naḥnu﴾ ("we") is an emphasis of the attached pronoun in ﴿ʿabadnā﴾ ("we worshipped"), and by it the conjunction upon the attached nominative pronoun is made valid. The repetition of the negative particle in His saying ﴿wa-lā ābāʾunā﴾ ("nor our fathers") is to emphasise the negating ﴿mā﴾.

Upon this was built the cutting off of the argument with them, and the informing of them that the messengers, peace be upon them, have no duty except conveyance, and among them is Muḥammad ﷺ. So beware lest your outcome be the outcome of the nations of the earlier messengers. The messengers are not charged with compelling people to faith, so that you should pursue with them the tactic of harassing them and enraging them.

Al-balāgh (conveyance) is a verbal noun of al-iblāgh, and al-mubīn means the clarifying, plain one.

The interrogation with ﴿hal﴾ ("is there?") is a denial, in the sense of negation; for this reason the exception came after it.

Page 149

The restriction (qaṣr) derived from the negation and the exception is a relative restriction (qaṣr idāfī), to reverse the belief of the polytheists, who, in their treatment of the Messenger ﷺ, held that the Messenger had a personal aim in what he called to.

The ruling is affirmed for all messengers, peace be upon them, although those being refuted had not thought of the matter of the earlier messengers, so that the sentence is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) for the argument, and so it conveys what is more general than the one refuted.

The speech is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ as instruction and consolation, and it implicitly includes a hint toward conveying (the message) to the polytheists.

* * *

﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, (saying): "Worship God and avoid ṭāghūt." Then among them were those whom God guided, and among them were those upon whom error was decreed. So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾ This is a conjunction upon the sentence ﴿Likewise did those before them act,﴾ and it completes the refutation of the polytheists' doubt, by way of detail after summary, to increase the establishment of the proof. So His saying, ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger,﴾ is an explanation of the content of the sentence ﴿So, is there upon the messengers anything but clear conveyance?﴾

The sentence ﴿Then among them were those whom God guided﴾ to its end is an explanation of the content of the sentence ﴿Likewise did those before them act.﴾

The meaning: God made clear to the nations, through the tongues of the messengers, peace be upon them, that He commands them to worship Him and to avoid the worship of idols. So from every nation there were groups whom God guided, and they affirmed and believed; and among them were groups in whom error had taken hold, so they perished. Whoever travels the earth sees the evidence of their annihilation.

Page 150

The ﴿an﴾ here is explanatory (tafsīriyya) for the clause ﴿fa-baʿathnā﴾ ("and We sent"), because sending (baʿth) includes the sense of saying, since it is a sending for conveyance.

Al-ṭāghūt is the genus of what is worshipped besides God, of idols; and they may mention it in the plural form, so it is said al-ṭawāghīt, which are the idols. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿They believe in jibt and ṭāghūt﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 51], in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.

The guidance of some of them was attributed to God, although He commanded all of them to guidance, as an alert to the polytheists concerning the removal of their doubt in their saying, ﴿Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾: God made guidance clear to them, so the guidance of those who are guided is by means of His clarification; He is therefore the Guider of them.

The expression concerning error, "﴿ḥaqqat ʿalayhim﴾" ("upon them was decreed"), rather than attributing the misguidance to God, is an indication that since God forbade them from error, their persistence in it was a sustaining of their earlier error, so "upon them was decreed the error," that is, it was established and did not lift.

In this there is a hint that the persistence of error is from the acquisition of their own selves. But it has come in other verses that God misguides the misguided, as in His saying, ﴿And whoever God wills to lead astray, He makes his breast constricted and tight﴾ [al-Anʿām: 125], and His saying after this, ﴿Indeed, God does not guide those who misguide﴾ [al-Naḥl: 37] according to the reading of the majority. So that from the totality of this there may result knowledge that God established many causes, some of which came from the propagation of minds and temperaments and the borrowing of some from others, and some of which follow misguided calls, in such a way that from the gathering of diverse matters, which none but God can number, there came complete causes that stand between the misguided and guidance. Therefore those causes were indeed the cause of error being decreed upon them. Thus, in terms of the immediate causes, their error was from the One who created those causes and created their laws throughout the ages. So understand.

Page 151

Then He drew from this the command to travel the earth, that they might look at the traces of the nations and see from them traces of annihilation different from the states of ordinary perishing. Therefore the inference from them depends on travelling the earth; and had the intended meaning been mere perishing, He would have commanded them to observe graveyards and recall the earlier predecessors.

**[Page 152]**

﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those whom He leads astray, and they will have no helpers﴾. This is an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a new sentence that answers an unstated question). The division of every misguided nation into those among them who are guided and those who remain in error raises a question in the mind of the Prophet ﷺ about the condition of this nation. Is it following the condition of the nations before it, or will Allah guide them all? That question would come from his eagerness for their good and his compassion for them. So Allah informed him that, despite his eagerness for their guidance, a group among them will remain in misguidance.

The verse contains two subtle points:

The first: an allusion in praise of the Prophet ﷺ for his eagerness for their good, despite the harm he suffered from them. Such harm is of the kind that tends to stir resentment in the one who suffers it. But the soul of Muhammad ﷺ is purified from every deficiency that arises from animal character traits.

The second subtle point: an indication that most of the nation of the Muhammadan call will be guided, and that those who go astray among them are a small group. They are those whom Allah did not decree to be guided, in His eternal knowledge, by the causes that arose from His creation and power, which prepared for them the continuation in misguidance.

*Al-hirs* (eagerness): an intense, pressing desire to attain what is desired, by striving through its means.

The conditional particle here does not make the occurrence of the content of the answer depend on the occurrence of the content of the condition. This is because the content of the condition is already known to occur, since its signs are apparent such that people know it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿[He is] ardently concerned for you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128]. Rather, it makes the knowledge of the content of the answer depend on the continuous occurrence of the content of the condition. The meaning is: if you are eager for their guidance with a continuous eagerness, then know that whomever Allah has led astray, you cannot guide him, you find no means to guide him, and no one can guide him. Thus the present tense (*al-mudari'*) is used here only to express renewal, like the saying of 'Antarah:

*If you are ready to fight me, behind the veil,*
*I am a physician in seizing the armored knight.*

Even clearer in this sense is his other saying:

*If you have resolved upon separation, then indeed*
*your camels were saddled in the dark night.*

In both verses, the verb of the condition carries the sense of "if that is a firm resolve," and the answer of the condition carries the sense of conveying knowledge.

The subject in the sentence reporting the continuation of their misguidance is the Divine Name (*ism al-jalala*, "Allah"), used to inspire awe, which arouses the desire to learn the news. The news is that their guidance will not occur except if Allah wills it, and no one can achieve it, neither you nor anyone else. So whoever Allah has decreed to continue in misguidance has no guide. Were it not for this subtle point, the apparent requirement would be that the subject be a pronoun referring to those spoken of, so that it would say: "indeed no one but Allah guides them."

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿لا يُهْدى﴾ (*la yuhda*) with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *dal*, in the passive form (*mabni lil-na'ib*, the form with a deputy subject). The agent is omitted to generalize: that is, no guide guides him.

The word ﴿مَن﴾ (*man*, "whom") is the deputy subject. The pronoun in ﴿يُضِلُّ﴾ (*yudill*) refers to Allah. That is, indeed Allah does not guide the one who is led astray, the *mudallal* (with a *fatha* on the *lam* from it). The predicate is causal (*sababi*), and the causal pronoun in the object position has been omitted because it is apparent. This has the same meaning as His saying: ﴿Whomever Allah leads astray, he has no guide﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whomever Allah leads astray, there is no guide for him﴾ [al-A'raf: 186].

'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿لا يَهْدِي﴾ (*la yahdi*) with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, in the active form (*mabni lil-fa'il*). The pronoun of the Divine Name is the subject, and ﴿مَن﴾ (*man*) is the object of ﴿يَهْدِي﴾ (*yahdi*). The pronoun in ﴿يُضِلُّ﴾ (*yudill*) refers to Allah. The causal pronoun is also omitted here. The meaning is: indeed Allah does not guide whoever He has decreed to continue in misguidance. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has led him astray knowingly﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23], up to His saying: ﴿So who will guide him after Allah?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23].

The meaning of ﴿وما لَهم مِن ناصِرِينَ﴾ (*and they will have no helpers*) is: they have no helper who saves them from the punishment. That is, just as they have no rescuer from the misguidance into which they have fallen, they likewise have no helper who averts from them the consequences of misguidance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 38:

﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths: God will not raise up those who die. Yes indeed! It is a promise binding upon Him, true; but most people do not know.﴾

This is a transition to relating another of their monstrous sayings in their disbelief, and it is an argument from the proofs of their denial of the Messenger ﷺ in what he reports. It displays his call in the guise of the impossible, and that is their denial of the second life and the resurrection after death. No mention of this had preceded in this surah except the digression in His words, ﴿But those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Nahl: 22]. Their oath upon the negation of resurrection was intended to show their certainty of its non-occurrence. The discussion of ﴿jahda aymanihim﴾ (with their most emphatic oaths) has already occurred at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Are these the ones who swore by God with their most emphatic oaths?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 53] in Surah al-'Uqud (al-Ma'idah).

They were certain of this and swore to it because they imagined that the soundness of bodies and the non-disintegration of them is a condition for their receiving life, and they saw the bodies of the dead exposed to dissolution, so how could they be restored as they were?

The clause ﴿God will not raise up those who die﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to the clause "they swore," being the content of what they swore to.

The resurrection (al-baʿth) was previously mentioned just now in His words, ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be raised up﴾ [al-Nahl: 21].

The shift from "the dead" (al-mawta) to "those who die" (man yamutu) is intended to signal that the relative clause gives the reason for the negation of resurrection, since the relative clause is more forceful in indicating causation than the derived noun (mushtaqq) is in indicating the causal link of the derivation. Thus they made dissolution incompatible with the restoration of life, as is reported of them: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "When we are dust, and our fathers, shall we indeed be brought forth?"﴾ [al-Naml: 67].

And "bala" (Yes indeed) is a particle that annuls a negation in a statement and in a question, i.e., "rather, God will raise them." "Wa'dan" (a promise) is in the accusative as an absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq), emphasizing what the particle of annulment indicates of the occurrence of resurrection after death. This type of absolute object is called an emphasis of itself (mu'akkidan li-nafsihi), i.e., emphasizing the meaning of a verb which is itself the same meaning as the absolute object.

"ʿAlayhi" (binding upon Him) is an attribute of "wa'dan," meaning: a promise like what is binding upon Him in that it does not admit of breach. So there is a metaphor by implication (isti'arah makniyyah): the promise God made by His pure will and choice is likened to a binding right upon Him, and it is hinted at by the particle of elevation (ḥarf al-isti'la').

"Ḥaqqan" (true) is a second attribute of "wa'dan," and "al-ḥaqq" here means the truthfulness that cannot be contravened. Its counterpart has already occurred in His words, exalted is He, ﴿A promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111] in Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah).

By "most people" is meant the polytheists, who were then the majority of people. "They do not know" means they do not know the manner of this, so they draw from their deeming it remote a proof of the impossibility of resurrection after annihilation.

The corrective particle (al-istidrak) arises from making it "a promise binding upon God, true," since the hearer might suppose that no one could be ignorant of such a matter; so the istidrak came to remove this supposition. Also, the clause ﴿a promise binding upon Him, true﴾ implies that its occurrence is possible, while people deem this remote.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 39:

Page 155
﴿That He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars.﴾

(Li-yubayyina) is a causal clause (ta'lil) for His words, may He be exalted, ﴿a promise binding upon Him, a truth﴾ [al-Nahl: 38], for the purpose of explaining the wisdom behind making it a binding promise that does not fail; for it is tied to wisdom, and God, may He be exalted, is Wise, and His acts do not run contrary to perfect wisdom. That is, He made the resurrection (al-ba'th) so that He might make clear to people the matter about which they differ, of truth and falsehood; thus the right of the one who is right becomes manifest, and the falsehood of the one who falsifies becomes manifest, in the creeds (al-'aqa'id) and the like, among the fundamentals of religion (usul al-din) and what is attached to them.

His words (yakhtalifun) encompass all the meanings of accountability for rights, for distinguishing rights from wrongs is entirely a place of people's disagreement and dispute.

He joined to this general wisdom a particular, subsidiary wisdom specific to those who are refuted here, namely that those who disbelieved come to know that they were liars in what they invented of polytheism, of declaring things forbidden, and of denying the resurrection.

In their coming to know this on the Day of Resurrection there is a source of remorse and regret over what they neglected of their denial. The explanation of the wisdom of recompense on the Day of Resurrection has already been given at the beginning of Surah Yunus.

(Kanu kadhibin) is stronger in describing them with lying than (kadhdhabu aw kadhibun), because of what (kana) indicates of existence, in addition to what the active participle (ism al-fa'il) requires of attribution. It is as if it were said: their lying came into being and they were described by it. And their lying necessitates that they are punished for their lying, so in it there is clear reproach and an allusion to punishment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 40:

﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ This sentence is connected to the sentence ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 38]; it clarifies that their ignorance of the extent of God the Exalted's power is what emboldened them to deny resurrection and to deem it impossible

صفحة ١٥٦
in their view. Thus it is an elucidation of the sentence that precedes it, and that is why it is separated from it. The sentence ﴿so that He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and so that those who disbelieved may know﴾ [al-Nahl: 39] to its end comes as a parenthetical insertion between the elucidation and that which is elucidated.

The meaning is that the bringing into being of any thing, when God wills it, depends only upon His power being related to its bringing into being. The revival of the dead is only one of the things, and resurrection is nothing but a bringing into being; so the raising of the dead is only one part of the bringing into being of existent things, and it does not fall outside His power.

The particle (innama) indicates a restriction, namely the restriction of the occurrence of bringing into being to the issuing of the command for it. This is a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb), to nullify the belief of the polytheists that the revival of the dead is impossible, thinking that it can only occur if the bodies are preserved from decay, as was mentioned just before. Thus by ﴿Our word to a thing﴾ is meant Our bringing a thing into being, that is, the relation of power to the creation of a thing; and by His saying ﴿when We intend it﴾ is meant when the divine will is related to it with an immediate relation. Since the cause of bringing into being is nothing more than the saying "Be," the claim that the revival of the dead is impossible is nullified; and for this reason this is a restriction of reversal to nullify the belief of the polytheists.

The word "thing" (shay') is here applied to the non-existent with regard to the intention of its existence, so it is of the type of applying the name of what something will become; or the intended meaning of "thing" is the absolute reality that is known, even if it is non-existent, and applying "thing" to the non-existent is an established usage.

And ﴿that We say to it, "Be"﴾ is the predicate of "Our word."

The intended meaning of the saying "Be" is the direction of power toward bringing the thing willed into being; He expressed that direction by means of speech, just as He expressed it by command in His saying ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82]. The thing whose coming into being is possible is likened to a person who is commanded, and the thing's responsiveness to the command of bringing into being is likened to the compliance of the one commanded with the order of the one who commands. All of this is a bringing-near to people by means of what they can understand; it is not an address to the non-existent, nor does the non-existent have a hearing by which it understands speech and thereby complies with the one who commands.

صفحة ١٥٧
And (kana) is complete (tammah).

The majority of readers recite (fa-yakunu) with the nominative (raf'), meaning (fa-huwa yakunu), coordinating it with the predicate, which is the clause (an naqula); and Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i recite it with the accusative (nasb), coordinating it with (naqula), meaning: that We say to it "Be" and that it come to be.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 16, verses 41–42:**

﴿Those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them in this world in a good place. But the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew. Those who were patient and upon their Lord they rely.﴾

When the wisdom of the Resurrection was established, namely that it clarifies that about which people differed, between guidance and misguidance, and among that is that it becomes clear that those who disbelieved were liars, it is known from it, through the clarification by the Resurrection, that those who believed were truthful, by the indication of opposition (tibaq, antithesis), and that they are rewarded and honoured. When this was known from the context, it was explicitly stated in this verse.

Along with this, their promise of a good outcome in this world was incorporated (idmaj, embedding of one theme within another), as a counterpart to the threat to the disbelievers of an evil outcome in it, which is implied by allusion (ta'ridh) in His saying, ﴿So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers﴾ [An-Nahl: 36]. The sentence is therefore conjoined (ma'tufah) to the sentence ﴿and that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars﴾ [An-Nahl: 39].

Al-muhajarah (emigration) is leaving one's dwellings for some purpose. The particle (fi) is used in the sense of causation (ta'lil), i.e., for the sake of Allah, and the speech is according to an elided genitive (mudaf) that is evident from the context; its implied form is: they emigrated seeking the pleasure of Allah.

The verb ﴿wronged﴾ is in the passive voice because the agent is evident from the context, and he is the polytheists. Wrongdoing (zulm) encompasses the various kinds of aggression, including harm and torture.

Al-tabwi'ah (settling) means lodging. Here it is applied to the reward with good, in return for emigration, by way of antithesis with emigration, since emigration is leaving one's dwellings, and so settling is its opposite.

In combining (hajarū) and (lanubawwi'annahum) there is the embellishment of antithesis (tibaq). The meaning is: We will surely reward them with a good reward, so He expressed the reward by settling, since it is a reward for abandoning a dwelling-place.

(Hasanah, good) is an adjective of an elided verbal noun (masdar) that follows (nubawwi'annahum), i.e., a good settling.

This reward compensates for all the harms that emigration entailed, the losses the emigrants suffered in leaving their homes and their wealth, and what they endured of the harm that compelled them to emigrate: torture, mockery, humiliation and persecution. Thus the "good" includes compensating them with better dwellings than their own and a homeland better than their homeland, namely Medina, and wealth better than their wealth, which is what they gained of spoils and tribute (kharaj). It is narrated that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he gave a man among the emigrants a gift, would say to him: "This is what your Lord promised you in this world, and what He has stored up for you in the Hereafter is greater." And (the good settling includes) victory over their enemies in the conquests, the most important of which was the conquest of Mecca; and security in their lives through the authority they attained. He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And He will surely change their fear into security﴾ [An-Nur: 55]. The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) concerns those Muslims who emigrated to the land of Abyssinia, without doubt, or those who emigrated to Medina in the first emigration before the emigration of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the remaining companions of his (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them, such as Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr and his companions, if this verse was revealed after the first emigration to Medina. Both possibilities do not contradict the Surah being Meccan, nor do they require restricting this promise to those people.

Then He followed this promise with the great promise intended, which is His saying, ﴿but the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾. The meaning of (greater) is that it is more important and more beneficial. Its attribution to the Hereafter is in the sense of (fi), i.e., the matter that is in the Hereafter.

The clause ﴿if only they knew﴾ is parenthetical (mu'taridah), and it is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) arising from the whole promise sentence, because that great promise of the good of this world and the Hereafter stirs in the souls of the listeners the question of how those who remained upon disbelief did not follow them. So the clause ﴿if only they knew﴾ comes as an explanation of what was unclear to the questioner. The implied meaning is: if they knew that, they would have followed them, but they do not know. So the pronoun in (they know) refers to those who disbelieved.

It is also possible that the question raised is: how do the emigrants grieve over what they left of their dwellings, wealth and families? Then the meaning would be: if the emigrants knew by direct witnessing what was prepared for them, they would not have grieved over parting from their homes, and their emigration would have been out of longing for what they would encounter after emigrating, because the effect of sensory knowledge upon human temperament is stronger than the effect of rational knowledge upon the details of conditions that souls love and towards which desires incline, as His saying, the Exalted, indicates: ﴿if only they knew﴾, i.e., if only they believed and had faith, because that is already present, and it does not suit the position of the counterfactual particle (law).

So the pronoun in (they know) according to this view refers to ﴿those who emigrated﴾ [An-Nahl: 110]. In this view the pronouns are consistent.

﴿Those who were patient﴾ is an adjective of ﴿those who emigrated﴾ [An-Nahl: 110]. Patience (sabr) is enduring hardships, and reliance (tawakkul) is depending upon.

Patience was discussed at His saying, ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 45], at the beginning of Al-Baqarah, and reliance at His saying, ﴿So when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159], in Al 'Imran.

The expression regarding patience is in the past tense, and regarding reliance in the present tense, as an indication that their patience had announced its end because its causes had ended, and that Allah had made relief for them through the emigration that had occurred and the emigration that was awaited. This is a glad tiding to them.

And that reliance is their habit, because they face great undertakings that are accomplished for them through relying upon Allah in their affairs, so they repeat it. In this there is a glad tiding of the guarantee of success.

In the meaning of this verse is His saying, the Exalted, ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good, and the earth of Allah is spacious. Only the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [Az-Zumar: 10].

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying, ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾, is for restriction (qasr), i.e., they rely only upon their Lord, not upon reliance on the chiefs of the polytheists and their allies.

(Hasanah, good) is an adjective of an elided verbal noun (masdar) that follows (nubawwi'annahum), i.e., a good settling.

This reward compensates for all the harms that emigration entailed, the losses the emigrants suffered in leaving their homes and their wealth, and what they endured of the harm that compelled them to emigrate: torture, mockery, humiliation and persecution. Thus the "good" includes compensating them with better dwellings than their own and a homeland better than their homeland, namely Medina, and wealth better than their wealth, which is what they gained of spoils and tribute (kharaj). It is narrated that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he gave a man among the emigrants a gift, would say to him: "This is what your Lord promised you in this world, and what He has stored up for you in the Hereafter is greater." And (the good settling includes) victory over their enemies in the conquests, the most important of which was the conquest of Mecca; and security in their lives through the authority they attained. He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And He will surely change their fear into security﴾ [An-Nur: 55]. The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) concerns those Muslims who emigrated to the land of Abyssinia, without doubt, or those who emigrated to Medina in the first emigration before the emigration of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the remaining companions of his (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them, such as Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr and his companions, if this verse was revealed after the first emigration to Medina. Both possibilities do not contradict the Surah being Meccan, nor do they require restricting this promise to those people.

Then He followed this promise with the great promise intended, which is His saying, ﴿but the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾. The meaning of (greater) is that it is more important and more beneficial. Its attribution to the Hereafter is in the sense of (fi), i.e., the matter that is in the Hereafter.

The clause ﴿if only they knew﴾ is parenthetical (mu'taridah), and it is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) arising from the whole promise sentence, because that great promise of the good of this world and the Hereafter stirs in the souls of the listeners the question of how those who remained upon disbelief did not follow them. So the clause ﴿if only they knew﴾ comes as an explanation of what was unclear to the questioner. The implied meaning is: if they knew that, they would have followed them, but they do not know. So the pronoun in (they know) refers to those who disbelieved.

It is also possible that the question raised is: how do the emigrants grieve over what they left of their dwellings, wealth and families? Then the meaning would be: if the emigrants knew by direct witnessing what was prepared for them, they would not have grieved over parting from their homes, and their emigration would have been out of longing for what they would encounter after emigrating, because the effect of sensory knowledge upon human temperament is stronger than the effect of rational knowledge upon the details of conditions that souls love and towards which desires incline, as His saying, the Exalted, indicates: ﴿if only they knew﴾, i.e., if only they believed and had faith, because that is already present, and it does not suit the position of the counterfactual particle (law).

So the pronoun in (they know) according to this view refers to ﴿those who emigrated﴾ [An-Nahl: 110]. In this view the pronouns are consistent.

﴿Those who were patient﴾ is an adjective of ﴿those who emigrated﴾ [An-Nahl: 110]. Patience (sabr) is enduring hardships, and reliance (tawakkul) is depending upon.

Patience was discussed at His saying, ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 45], at the beginning of Al-Baqarah, and reliance at His saying, ﴿So when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159], in Al 'Imran.

The expression regarding patience is in the past tense, and regarding reliance in the present tense, as an indication that their patience had announced its end because its causes had ended, and that Allah had made relief for them through the emigration that had occurred and the emigration that was awaited. This is a glad tiding to them.

And that reliance is their habit, because they face great undertakings that are accomplished for them through relying upon Allah in their affairs, so they repeat it. In this there is a glad tiding of the guarantee of success.

In the meaning of this verse is His saying, the Exalted, ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good, and the earth of Allah is spacious. Only the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [Az-Zumar: 10].

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying, ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾, is for restriction (qasr), i.e., they rely only upon their Lord, not upon reliance on the chiefs of the polytheists and their allies.

[p. 161]

The preceding verses were concerned with narrating the polytheists' denial of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), their rejection that he is a messenger sent by God, and their rejection that the Qur'an is revelation from God to him. This began with His saying ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Tales of the ancients"﴾ [An-Nahl: 24], and continued with the refutation of their false claims by decisive proofs, interspersed with other meanings that were woven into that discussion. Here, then, it returns to nullifying their doubt about his prophethood, namely that he is a human who is not fit to be an envoy between God and people. It nullifies this by analogical reasoning (qiyas al-tamthil, reasoning by comparison) with the earlier messengers whose missions Quraysh do not deny, such as Noah and Abraham, peace be upon them both. This looks back to His saying at the beginning of the surah ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [An-Nahl: 2].

The style of the composition has been changed here by directing the address to the Prophet (ﷺ), after it had been proceeding in the third-person style (al-ghaybah, speaking about them in the third person). This began from His saying ﴿But those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying﴾ [An-Nahl: 22] and His saying ﴿And those who associated said﴾ [An-Nahl: 35], and so on. This is to console the Prophet (ﷺ), because what preceded in the speech was the narration of their denial of him, both explicitly and allusively. So God turned to the Messenger (ﷺ) with direct address, because of what this speech contains of elevating his station by placing him in the rank of the earlier messengers, upon them be prayer and peace.

In this address there is an allusion (taʿrid) to the polytheists, and for this reason He turned to addressing them with His saying ﴿so ask the people of remembrance﴾.

The restrictive construction (qasr) reverses the belief of the polytheists and their saying ﴿Has God sent a human as a messenger?﴾ [Al-Isra: 94]. Thus sending is restricted to being connected to men who are described as those to whom revelation is given.

Then He called the polytheists to witness through the testimony of past nations, and turned to address them directly in rebuke, because direct address suits rebuke, as it has greater impact on the one being rebuked. So He argued against them with His saying ﴿so ask the people of remembrance, if you do not know﴾, and so on. This is an argument from the people of earlier religions, the People of the Scriptures: the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians.

Al-dhikr (the Reminder) is the book of the sharia (sacred law). It was previously discussed at His saying ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down"﴾ [Al-Hijr: 6] at the beginning of al-Hijr.

In His saying ﴿if you do not know﴾ there is an implication that they do know this, but they intended obstinacy and deception in order to mislead the common folk. For this reason the particle "in" is used in the conditional, since it is used for a condition whose fulfilment is presumed to be unlikely.

The clause ﴿so ask the people of remembrance﴾ is a parenthetical clause (jumla iʿtiradiyya) placed between the clause "And We did not send" and His saying ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾ [An-Nahl: 44].

A parenthetical clause is joined with the particle fa' when its meaning is a consequence of what precedes it. In al-Kashshaf, he treated it as a parenthetical clause on the basis of aspects he mentioned regarding what the phrase "with the clear proofs" is connected to.

It is transmitted from him, in the commentary on surah al-Insan at His saying ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way﴾ [Al-Insan: 29], that a parenthetical clause is not joined with fa'. The author of al-Kashshaf expressed doubt about the soundness of that transmission from him, because it contradicts what he said in the verse of surah al-Nahl.

His saying "with the clear proofs" (bi'l-bayyinat) is connected either to a stable predicate (mustaqarr sifah, a descriptive complement) or as a circumstantial clause (hal) of "men." He mentioned other possibilities for its connection in al-Kashshaf. The ba' (bi-) here denotes accompaniment, meaning "accompanied by the clear proofs and the scriptures." The clear proofs are indications of truthfulness, whether miracles or rational arguments. These were combined in the Qur'an, and they were distributed among the earlier messengers, just as much of them was divided and given to our Messenger (ﷺ).

[p. 162]

Zubur is the plural of zabur, which is derived from zabr, meaning writing. So the form fa'ul is in the sense of maf'ul (passive participle, "written"). The zubur are the books in which what was revealed to the messengers was written, such as the scrolls of Abraham, the Torah, and what the disciples (al-hawariyyun) wrote of the revelation to Jesus, peace be upon him, even if Jesus himself did not write it.

Perhaps the conjunction of "and the scriptures" (wa'l-zubur) upon "the clear proofs" is a conjunction of division (ʿatf taqsim), intended for distribution. That is, some of them came accompanied by the clear proofs, and some by both. This is because messengers may come without books, such as Handhala ibn Safwan, messenger of the people of al-Rass, and Khalid ibn Sinan, messenger of 'Abs. God did not mention a book for Noah, peace be upon him.

It may also be that al-zubur is taken specifically to mean concise books that do not contain an extensive body of law, such as the scrolls of Abraham, the Psalms of David (Zabur Dawud), and the Gospel, as they explained it in the commentary on surah Fatir, peace be upon them both.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 44:

﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder, that you may explain to the people what has been sent down to them, and that they may give thought.﴾

When the proof had become clear through the evidence of history, which cannot be denied, the intended conclusion was stated, namely that what was sent down to Muhammad ﷺ is nothing but a Reminder, and not "the fables of the ancients."

صفحة ١٦٣
Al-dhikr (the Reminder): speech that is meant to be remembered, i.e., recited and repeated. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down..."﴾ [al-Hijr: 6] in Surat al-Hijr. That is, you were not an innovation among the Messengers, for We have indeed revealed the Reminder to you. The Reminder is that which was sent down so that people would read it and recite it repeatedly, so that they might be reminded by what it contains. The placing of the prepositional complement before the object is for emphasis, with the second-person pronoun.

Regarding the restriction to the sending down of the Reminder immediately after His saying ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾: it indicates that the Book revealed to Muhammad ﷺ is both a clear proof (bayyinah) and a scripture (zabur) together, i.e., it is both a miracle and a book of legislation. This is among the distinctive features of the Qur'an in which no other book shares, nor any other miracle. Allah, Exalted is He, has said, ﴿And they say, "Why have no signs been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "The signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner."﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 50] ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them? Indeed, in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe.﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51].

In a hadith: the Prophet ﷺ said, "There is no prophet among the prophets except that he was given signs such that people believed in the like of them; but what I was given is a revelation which Allah revealed to me, so I hope to be the one with the most followers on the Day of Resurrection."

Al-tabyin (explanation): clarifying the meaning.

The definite article in al-nas (the people) is for generality.

The explicit noun in His saying ﴿what has been sent down to them﴾ implies that what the relative pronoun refers to is other than the Reminder mentioned earlier; for had it been the same, the apparent expression would have been to say "to explain it to the people." Therefore, the better view is that what was sent down to them refers to the laws (shara'i') with which Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ; the Qur'an comprises them and explains them through its eloquent composition and abundance of meanings. This is in the sense of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [al-Nahl: 89].

The attribution of the explaining to the Prophet ﹘ peace be upon him ﹘ is because he is the one who conveys this explanation to the people and to the nations in this manner, in view of mentioning the original purpose behind the sending down of the Qur'an.

صفحة ١٦٤
Some have interpreted ﴿what has been sent down to them﴾ as being the very same as the Reminder that was sent down, i.e., "We have sent down to you the Reminder that you may explain it to the people." In this case, the explicit noun is used in place of the pronoun, to convey that sending the Reminder down to the Prophet ﷺ is the same as sending it down to the people, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 10].
It is only expressed with the same wording twice to indicate the difference between the two sendings down: its sending down to the Prophet ﷺ directly, and its sending down to his conveying it to them.

So the explanation here means the clarifying of the meanings contained in the Qur'an, and the lam (in "li-tubayyin") denotes the cause of some of the wisdoms attached to the sending down of the Qur'an, for they are many. Among them is that the Prophet ﷺ explains it, so that the benefits of knowledge and clarity are achieved, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187].

There is no evidence in this verse for the issues of specifying the Qur'an by the Sunnah, explaining the general (mujmal) of the Qur'an by the Sunnah, or preferring the evidence of the mutawatir Sunnah over the evidence of the Book when they conflict, which are assumed matters in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), since both the Book and the Sunnah are the Prophet's explanation ﷺ, as he is the intermediary for both.

The conjunction of ﴿that they may give thought﴾ is another of the wisdoms of sending down the Qur'an, namely preparing people to reflect upon it and to ponder what brings them closer to the pleasure of Allah, Exalted is He. Thus, according to the first interpretation of ﴿that you may explain to the people﴾, the meaning is that they reflect on the meanings of the Qur'an by themselves and understand its benefits; and according to the second interpretation, that they reflect on your explanation and grasp it with their understanding.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 45:

﴿Do those who devised evil plots feel secure that Allah will cause the earth to swallow them, or that the punishment will come upon them from where they do not perceive?﴾ After their evil deeds and schemes had been mentioned, and after they had been threatened with the punishment of the Day of Resurrection explicitly and with the punishment of this world by implication, he followed this with an explicit threat of the punishment of this world, in the form of a rhetorical question expressing wonder at their persistence in obstinacy, while they did not expect that what Allah threatened them with through His Messenger ﷺ would come to pass. Thus they do not desist from plotting against the Prophet ﷺ. Their persistence was like the state of those who feel secure from the might of Allah. So the interrogative is used for wonder mixed with reproach.

"Those who devised" (alladhina makaru): they are the polytheists.

Makr (plotting) has already been mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Those before them had already plotted﴾ [al-Nahl: 26] in this surah.

His saying, Exalted is He, "evil" (al-sayyi'at) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar) of "they plotted" (makaru), which is estimated to suit the feminine form of its adjective. The meaning is: they plotted evil plots (al-makarat al-sayyi'at), just as plotting was described as evil in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the evil plot encompasses only its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43]. The feminine form in such cases is intended to indicate the sense of a trait or a deed, like "ghadrah" (a single act of treachery) for "ghadr" (treachery).

It is also permissible that "they plotted" (makaru) be construed with the sense of "they committed" (iqtarafu), so that "evil deeds" (al-sayyi'at) is in the accusative as its direct object. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative by omitting the preposition, which is the bi of instrument.

Khasf (sinking/swallowing) is a severe earthquake by which the earth splits, so that by its splitting a great chasm occurs into which dwellings and people fall, and then the earth closes over what has entered it. This befell the people of Babylon, and their place is called the Sinking of Babylon. It also befell the people of Lot when Allah turned its upper part to its lower part, and their lands are sunk today in the Lake of Lot in Palestine.

Khasafa is of the pattern of daraba, and it is used both intransitively and transitively. One says: "The earth sank" (khasafat al-ardu), and one says: "Allah sank the earth" (khasafa Allahu al-arda). He, Exalted is He, said, ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾ [al-Qasas: 81]. It does not take a further object beyond the direct object except with a transitivity particle, and most often it is transitive with bi, as here and in His saying ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾ [al-Qasas: 81], meaning: We made the earth swallow him, so the bi is for transitivity, as one says: "He took him away" (dhahaba bihi).

Adhab (punishment) encompasses everything that involves pain lasting for a period of time; therefore it is conjoined to khasf. The arrival of punishment upon them means its striking them, and this is likened to "coming."

"From where they do not perceive" (min haythu la yash'urun): from a place they do not expect harm to come from. So the meaning of "from where they do not perceive" is that it comes upon them suddenly, which they cannot repel, because, due to their might and strength, what they fear does not catch them unawares, since they have prepared its means. Thus the one coming from where they do not perceive is a punishment not known to them. The phrase "from where they do not perceive" is therefore a metonymy for a punishment they cannot withstand, by customary implication. Otherwise, the punishment of 'Ad came from a place they were aware of, as He, Exalted is He, said, ﴿But when they saw it as a cloud coming towards their valleys, they said: This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24]. The punishment of the Flood befell the people of Noah while they were looking on, and likewise the punishment of drowning befell Pharaoh and his people.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verses 46–47:

﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro, and they cannot escape.﴾ ﴿Or He seizes them through gradual wasting. Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ The seizing (al-akhdh) is used metaphorically for destruction. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We seized them with an overwhelming seizure﴾ [al-Haqqah: 10], and it has already been discussed at His saying ﴿We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair﴾ [al-An'am: 44] in Surat al-An'am.

Al-taqallub (going to and fro) is striving in the affairs of life: through trade, dealing, travel, conversation and competition. Its root meaning is movement forward and backward. The meaning is that Allah destroys them while they are unaware of the arrival of the punishment.

This is the counterpart (qasim) of His saying ﴿or the punishment comes upon them from where they do not perceive﴾ [al-Nahl: 45]. Similar in meaning is His saying ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our might will come upon them by night while they sleep?﴾ [al-A'raf: 97] ﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our might will come upon them in the morning while they play?﴾ [al-A'raf: 98].

The clause ﴿then they cannot escape﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh), meaning that their going to and fro does not prevent Him from seizing them, since their gathering together and mutual cooperation cannot overpower Him.

The particle (fi) is for figurative containment, that is, being involved in something, and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the object pronoun in (ya'khudhahum).

Page 167

Linguistically, al-takhawwuf has two verbal nouns: that of takhawwafa when intransitive, meaning "feared", and that of takhawwafa when transitive, meaning "diminished". The second usage is the dialect of Hudhayl, which is one of the eloquent dialects in which the Qur'an was revealed.

So the verse has two meanings. Either the meaning is that He seizes them while they are in a state of expecting the punishment to descend, by showing them its preliminaries, like thunder before lightning. Or the meaning is that He seizes them while they are in a state of diminishing, before He seizes them, by multiplying among them death, poverty and famine.

The preposition (ʿala) is used for control in both meanings, and the phrase it governs is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the object pronoun in (ya'khudhahum). It is like their saying: "He seized him unawares" (akhadhahu ʿala ghirrah).

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah narrated, one of them adding to the other, that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, did not understand the meaning of al-takhawwuf in this verse, and he wanted to write to the regions. He asked the people while he was on the pulpit: "What do you say about it?" A shaykh from Hudhayl stood up and said: "This is our dialect. Al-takhawwuf means al-tanaqqus (diminishing)." He said: "Do the Arabs know that in their poetry?" He said: "Yes. Our poet said:

The saddle shrank from her, high-humped and worn,
as the wood of the nab'a bow is worn down by the plane."

'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O people, hold to your diwan, it will not mislead you." They said: "And what is our diwan?" He said: "The poetry of the Jahiliyyah, for in it is the explanation of your Book."

The clause ﴿indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾ follows the preceding sentences as a causal consequence (tafri' al-'illah) of what was stated. The particle (inna) here conveys causation and does without the consequential fa'. As 'Abd al-Qahir (al-Jurjani) explained,

Page 168

it reinforces what the fa' would have conveyed. The causation here applies to what is understood from the whole of what was mentioned in the verse: that He, exalted is He, is able to hasten their destruction, and that He gave them respite until they forgot the might of Allah, so they became like those secure from it, to the point that He asks about them: are they secure from that or not?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 48:

﴿Have they not seen that everything which Allah has created casts shadows, turning from the right and the left, prostrating to Allah while they are humbled?﴾ After the proofs of His sole creation were established by the enumeration of His great creatures that He mentioned, the discourse moved to an indication from the state of the bodies that are upon the whole earth, signifying their submission to Allah, Exalted, a submission concurrent with their existence and with their turning from moment to moment. Whoever knows this knows it, and whoever is ignorant of it is ignorant; and the tongue of state (lisan al-hal) informs of it with respect to what has no knowledge. This is what Allah has established upon the earthly order, a creation whose state speaks of servitude to Allah, Exalted. This occurs in the accident most constantly attached to essences and most congruent with their forms, which is the shadow (zill).

The detailed explanation of this argument has already passed at His saying, Exalted, ﴿And their shadows in the mornings and the evenings﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15], in Surat al-Ra'd.

So the sentence is conjoined to the sentences before it, as the conjunction of one narrative to another.

The interrogation is denunciatory (istifham inkari), meaning: they have indeed seen, and the seeing is visual (basariyyah).

Al-Jumhur read ﴿أوَلَمْ يَرَوْا﴾ with a third-person yā', while Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (أوَلَمْ تَرَوْا) with a second-person tā', in the mode of address according to the manner of iltifat (shift of person).

And ﴿مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ is an explanation of the vagueness contained in the relative (ma), and it is an explanation in view of the description that is applied to it by the clause ﴿يَتَفَيَّأُ ظِلالُهُ﴾ and so on.

The tafayyu' is a tafa"ul form from fa'a al-zill fay'an, meaning it returned after the light of the sun had removed it. Perhaps its root is from (faa) when one returns after leaving a place. The tafayyu' of shadows is their moving from directions after the sunrise and after its decline.

The mention of shadows has already preceded at His saying ﴿وظِلالُهم بِالغُدُوِّ والآصالِ﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15] in Surat al-Ra'd.

His saying ﴿عَنِ اليَمِينِ والشَّمائِلِ﴾, meaning from the directions of the right and the directions of the left, is intended to clarify the marvelous state of the shadow, since it is at the right of the person at one time and at his left at another, that is, when he faces a direction and then turns his back to it.

The intended meaning is not specifically the right and the left, but likewise the front and the back, so the speech was abbreviated.

The word "right" (al-yamin) is given in the singular because it is meant as the genus of direction, as one says "al-mashriq." The plural "al-shama'il" is meant to denote the multiplicity of the genus of the left direction according to the multiplicity of its possessors, as He said ﴿فَلا أُقْسِمُ بِرَبِّ المَشارِقِ﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 40]. Thus the difference between singular and plural is stylistic variation (tafannun).

The coming of the verb yatafayya' with a yā' at its beginning in the singular form follows one of two possibilities for the verb when its subject is a plural that is not a sound plural; and with this Al-Jumhur read. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read (tatafayya') with two tā's, according to the other possibility.

The pronoun attached to (zilal) is given in the singular in consideration of the wording of (shay') though in meaning it is multiple, and in consideration of meaning the plural was attached to it.

(Sujjadan) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of (zilalihi) which refers back to (min shay'), so it is a qualifier of the tafayyu'; that is, this tafayyu' is accompanied by prostration, a concomitance of occurrence within it. The explanation of this has already passed at His saying, Exalted, ﴿وظِلالُهم بِالغُدُوِّ والآصالِ﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15] in Surat al-Ra'd.

The clause ﴿وهم داخِرُونَ﴾ stands in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (zilalihi); because it carries the meaning of the plural, by its referring back to ﴿ما خَلَقَ اللَّهُ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾. It was given the plural form specific to rational beings by way of predominance (taghlib), because among the totality of creatures are rational beings, who are the most important genus.

Al-dakhir: the submissive, humbled one, meaning (dakhirun) before the majesty of Allah, Exalted.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 16, verses 49–50:**

﴿To Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.﴾

When the preceding verse mentioned compelled prostration (al-sujud al-qasri), another kind of prostration was mentioned after it here, part of which is by choice and part of which is like choice.

Placing the prepositional phrase before its verb indicates restriction (al-hasr), meaning: what is in the heavens and what is on the earth prostrates to Allah and not to anyone else. This is an allusion to the polytheists, who prostrate to idols.

The relative pronoun (ما) was preferred over (مَن) to give precedence to the greater number of non-rational beings.

The phrase (مِن دابَّةٍ) is an explanation of (ما في الأرْضِ), since the dabbah (creature that crawls on the earth) is whatever crawls on the earth other than humans.

The meaning of the prostration of creatures to Allah is that Allah placed in their inspired (ilhami) perception the enjoyment of their existence, and of what they are in of playfulness, eating and drinking, and seeking to ward off from themselves whoever overpowers them, and from accidents, by defending or by avoiding, and similar pleasant things. Their state in this is like the state of a thankful one for whom those pleasant things are made easy, and their being made easy for them comes only from the One who originated them. Their states of enjoyment may be accompanied by movements resembling the gesture of a thankful one that approaches prostration. Perhaps some of their movements are not perceived by people, because they are subtle and people are unaware of their times. The application of the word "prostration" to this is a metaphor (majaz).

The phrase (ما في السَّماواتِ) includes created beings other than angels, such as spirits. Or "the heavens" may mean the atmosphere (al-ajwa'), so that what is in it is meant to be birds and moths.

Page 171

In mentioning the most noble of creatures and the least of them together, there is an allusion that blames those among humans who fall below the rank of creatures in denying the Creator, and that praises those among humans who resemble the state of the angels.

In making the creatures and the angels objects of (يَسْجُدُ), there is a use of one word in both its literal and metaphorical senses.

Describing the angels as ﴿they are not arrogant﴾ is an allusion to how far the polytheists are from the peak of that angelic rank. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the angels.

The clause ﴿they fear their Lord﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿and they are not arrogant﴾.

The "above" in His saying ﴿above them﴾ is a height of control, dominion and honor, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am: 18], and His saying ﴿and indeed We are above them, subduers﴾ [al-A'raf: 127].

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾ means they obey, and no disobedience issues from them.

Here is a place of prostration for the reciter by consensus. Its wisdom here is that the believer shows that he is among the praised group, those who resemble the angels in prostrating to Allah, Exalted is He.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 51:**

﴿And God said, "Do not take two gods. He is only one God, so fear Me alone."﴾

When the discussion of refuting the multiplicity of gods, which was common among all the Arab tribes, had been fully extended, and it was followed by the refutation of fabricating lies against the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Qur'an, the discourse turned to refuting another type of polytheism followed among some Arab tribes. This is the association of two independent divine principles, one of good and one of evil. The tribes of Arabs neighboring the lands of Persia adopted it, and the authority of Kisra (the Persian king) and their customs prevailed over them, such as the tribes of Bakr ibn Wa'il and Banu Tamim. Many of them adhered to Magianism (al-majusiyya), namely Mazdakism (al-mazdakiyya) and Manichaeism (al-manawiyya), in the time of Kisra Abarwiz and in the time of Kisra Anushirwan. Magianism affirms a doctrine of two gods:

(Page 172)

A god of good, who is Light, and a god of evil, who is Darkness. The god of good produces nothing but good and benefaction, and the god of evil produces nothing but evil and pains. They named the god of good "Yazdan" and the god of evil "Ahriman." They claimed that Yazdan was alone in divinity, and that he created only good, so there was nothing in the world but good. Then a thought of evil once occurred to his mind, and from it another god was produced, a partner to him, who is the god of evil. Al-Ma'arri related this in his Luzumiyyat with his saying:

*Yazdan thought in heedlessness, and from his thinking Ahriman was fashioned.*

They did not make these two principles into embodied images. Therefore, their religion is not counted among the worship of idols (al-taghut), because the name "taghut" is specific to worshipped images and bodies. In this respect, this religion resembles the religions that do not worship perceptible images. The discussion of Magianism will come when interpreting His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews﴾ [al-Hajj: 17] up to His saying "and the Magians" in Surah al-Hajj.

That this is the religion intended is indicated by the consequence in the verse ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from God; then when harm touches you, to Him you cry out﴾ [al-Nahl: 53], as will come.

So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And God said, "Do not take two gods"﴾ is a conjunction of one narrative to another, and it is connected to the sentence ﴿And We sent in every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship God and shun the taghut"﴾ [al-Nahl: 36].

The meaning of ﴿And God said, "Do not take two gods"﴾ is that He called people and set up the proofs for the invalidity of their belief. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They want to change the words of God﴾ [al-Fath: 15], and His saying ﴿Thus has God said before﴾ [al-Fath: 15].

The dual form in His saying "two gods" (ilahayn) is emphasized by the word "two" (ithnayn), to indicate that duality itself is intended by the prohibition, as a refutation of a specific kind of the polytheism of the polytheists. The prohibition is not merely against plurality of gods in general; rather, the intended prohibition is against this specific plurality, which is the saying of the Magians about two gods. In the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary), the mention of "two" is explained as serving to block the possibility that the word be understood as a genus in its literal sense rather than metaphorically.

Since they were prohibited from taking two gods, it follows by implication (dalalat al-iqtida', implication necessitated by the sense) that the taking of many gods is refuted.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is only one God﴾ may be an explanatory apposition (bayan) to the sentence ﴿Do not take two gods, two﴾. In that case, the sentence is a continuation of the saying of the verb ﴿And God said﴾, because explicative apposition (ʿatf al-bayan) follows what it explains, like the position of the second sentence in the verse of the poet:

*I say to him: "Depart, do not stay with us."*

For this reason it is separated (fasl) without conjunction, and by this, what was indicated before by implication is stated explicitly. The pronoun in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, He is only one God﴾ refers to the proper name of majesty (Allah) in His saying ﴿And God said﴾. That is, God said: indeed, God is only one God. This follows one of two ways of reporting speech, and what has the same meaning, in terms of sense, as it is here. His saying, exalted is He, quoting Jesus, peace be upon him, ﴿"Worship God, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117], where ﴿"Worship God"﴾ [al-Nahl: 36] explains the verb "You commanded me" (amartani), and the verb "You commanded me" carries the meaning of speech. God said to him: "Say to them: worship God, your Lord and their Lord," so he reported it in sense, and said: "my Lord."

The restriction (qasr) in His saying ﴿Indeed, He is only one God﴾ is a restriction of an attributed subject to an attribute (qasr mawsuf ʿala sifa), that is, God is specifically characterized by the attribute of the unity of divinity. This is a restriction of correction (qasr qalb, restriction that corrects a false belief), to refute the claim of the plurality of God.

It is also possible that the sentence ﴿Indeed, He is only one God﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraד) occurring as a reason (taʿlil) for the sentence ﴿Do not take two gods, two﴾, meaning: God forbade taking two gods because God is one; that is, God is the named referent of "god" (ilah), so taking two gods is an inversion (qalb) of the reality of divinity.

The restriction of the attribute of oneness to the proper name of majesty is in view of the fact that the referent of that proper name is equal to the referent of "god" (ilah), since the meaning of "god" is confined to the referent of that proper name.

The branching (tafriʿ) of ﴿So fear Me alone﴾ may be a consequence of the sentence ﴿Do not take two gods, two﴾, so that ﴿So fear Me alone﴾ is part of the speech that was said. In that case, there is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person in the first-person pronoun in His saying "fear Me" (farhabun).

It is also possible that it is a consequence of the verb "And God said," and then it is not part of the speech said, meaning: God said, "Do not take two gods, so do not fear other than Me." In this reading there is no shift (iltifat) in the discourse.

On this, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So fear Me alone﴾ branches off in the form of restriction, that is, a restriction of relative correction, meaning: complete dread is restricted to Him, so no account is given to the power of any other to harm anyone. This is a refutation of those who fear the god of evil, so the intended one is the one who is feared.

The restriction of the command to dread, and limiting it to being from God, implies a command to restrict hope to Him, because the restriction of dread indicates the belief that absolute power belongs to Him, exalted is He. Thus it refutes, a fortiori, those who hope in the god of good. The reason the verse limits itself to dread is that the nature of the Magians is that their worship is out of fear of the god of evil, since the god of good is safe from them, for he is naturally disposed to good.

In the pronoun of ﴿So fear Me alone﴾ (fa-iyyaya) there is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the first person, to match the transition of the discourse from establishing the proof of God's oneness in a general way to specifying this one as being God, the sender of the Qur'an, in order to confirm the establishment of the original belief. In this shift there is emphasis on dread, because of what the shift contains in terms of jolting the understanding of the addressees. A similar construction without a shift was mentioned earlier in Surah al-Baqarah.

The conjunction of the verb "fear Me" (farhabun) with the fa' (the particle of consequence) is so that it is a consequence of a consequence, which conveys the meaning of emphasis, because the connection of the verb "fear" with the object explicitly stated makes the separate pronoun mentioned before it, in estimation, the object of another verb. So the estimated sense is: "So Me, fear" (fa-iyyaya irhabu), "so fear Me," that is, I have commanded you to restrict your dread to Me, so fear Me, in compliance with the command.

﴿Wa lahu ma fi as-samawati wal-ard wa lahu ad-din wasiban afaghayra Allahi tattaqun﴾ (Qur'an 16:52)

The placement of the clause ﴿Wa lahu ma fi as-samawati wal-ard﴾ after the clause ﴿Wa qala Allahu la tattakhidhu ilahayni ithnayn﴾ (16:51) is appropriate because those who made two gods made them light and darkness. Since light and darkness are two manifestations of the phenomena of the heavens and the earth, the meaning is: what you claim as a god of good and a god of evil are among His creatures.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-majrur) gives restriction (hasr), so everything in the heavens and the earth falls under the scope of the lam of ownership (lam al-milk). This indicates that nothing among the creatures, whether good or evil, belongs to anyone other than Him. Thus it is ruled out that there could be another god with Him, because if there were another god with Him, some of the creatures would belong to him, since a god cannot be conceived without creatures.

The pronoun in (lahu) refers to the Name of Majesty (Allah) in the phrase ﴿Wa qala Allahu la tattakhidhu ilahayn﴾ (16:51).

So its conjunction to the clause ﴿Innama huwa ilahun wahid﴾ (16:51) is because the greatness of divinity requires awe of Him and restricting that awe to Him alone. It is therefore fitting to point out that the attribute of ownership (malikiyya) requires that worship be directed to Him alone.

As for His words ﴿Wa lahu ad-din wasiban﴾, the word ad-din (religion, obedience) may mean obedience, from the saying of the people: "The tribe obeyed (dānat) the king," meaning it obeyed him. In this case, it is among the completions of the clause ﴿Wa lahu ma fi as-samawati wal-ard﴾, because when He restricted existing things to being in His dominion, it was fitting to restrict obedience to Him. For this reason He placed the prepositional phrase before its verb in this clause, as occurred in the preceding one.

It is also permissible that ad-din means worship (diyana), in which case it is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) to the clause ﴿Wa qala Allahu la tattakhidhu ilahayn ithnayn﴾ (16:51). This is because the invalidation of the religion of polytheism is suited to the fact that people should not follow any religion except what Allah has legislated for them. That is, He is the One who legislates for you the religion, not anyone else among the leaders of misguidance, such as Amr ibn Luhayy, Zarathustra (Zaradasht), Mazdak, and Mani. The Exalted said: ﴿Am lahum shurakau shara'u lahum minad-din ma lam ya'dhan bihi Allah﴾ (42:21).

It is also permissible that ad-din means recompense, as in His words ﴿Maliki yawmi ad-din﴾ (1:4). In that case it is an incorporation (idmaj) to establish the Resurrection, which those people also deny. The meaning is: to Him belongs what is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him return all who are in the heavens and the earth. They do not return to other than Him, and no one will benefit them on that Day.

Wasib means firm and lasting. It is suitable for all three possibilities, but it adds to the third possibility, because it is an emphasis refuting their denial of the Resurrection.

On these two clauses is based the rebuke for their fearing other than Him. They used to fear the god of evil and draw near to him in order to be safe from his evil.

*Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 16 (al-Nahl), verses 53–54:*

﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah. Then when adversity touches you, to Him you cry for help. Then when He removes the adversity from you, behold, a group of you associate others with their Lord.﴾

This is a conjunction of one statement with another (*'atf khabar 'ala khabar*). It is a shift from reasoning by the created things of God that exist within the human being and what surrounds him of existing things, to reasoning by the blessings God has bestowed. Among people there are those who turn away from reflecting on them and from giving thanks for them, and they are the disbelievers. So in the earlier proofs the aim was to argue from the outset, followed by the reminder of favour (*imtinan*).

[Page 177 continues]

The style changes here, so that the primary aim becomes the reminder of blessings, with the consideration of creation incorporated into it. The address is directed to the whole community, and therefore the words of the Exalted that follow are: ﴿then when a group of you associate others with their Lord﴾.

It begins with blessings in a general way, in summary, and then certain important ones are mentioned.

The address is directed to the polytheists, as a reminder to them that Allah is their Lord and no other, because He is the Bestower of blessing.

The placement of the words of the Exalted ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ here is this: when in the preceding verse he had refuted the existence of two gods, one of whose action is good and the other whose action is evil, he followed it here by stating that good and harm are among the dispositions of Allah the Exalted. He gives blessing, and He is the one who removes harm.

The *ba'* (بِ) indicates accompaniment: what accompanies you and is established with you. And ﴿from blessing﴾ explains the vagueness of the relative *ma* (مَا).

The *min* (مِنْ) in the words of the Exalted ﴿then it is from Allah﴾ is for origin (*ibtida'iyyah*), meaning: reaching you from Allah, that is, from the bounty of Allah. This is because blessing does not proceed from the essence of Allah, but from an attribute of His power or an attribute of His action, according to those who affirm attributes of action. And since ﴿whatever blessing you have﴾ indicates generality, the statement that it is from Allah suffices without the use of a form of restriction (*qasr*).

The *thumma* (ثُمَّ) in the words of the Exalted ﴿then when adversity touches you﴾ indicates a sequence of rank (*tarakhi al-rutbi*), as is its usual function when it conjoins sentences; because turning to Allah at the occurrence of adversity is more remarkable as information than the information that all blessings are from Allah, and the content of the conjoined sentence is further from consideration than the content of the sentence it is conjoined to.

The aim is to establish that Allah the Exalted is the one who manages the causes of what they have of good and evil, that no god creates except Him, and that they do not turn to anyone but Him when harm befalls them, and harm is the opposite of blessing.

[Page 178]

The touching of harm means its arrival. The verb "touch" (*mass*) is used metaphorically for a light occurrence, to indicate the human being's impatience, such that he cries out to Allah upon the occurrence of even the least harm to him. The use of *mass* for a light affliction has already occurred in the words of the Exalted ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it except Him﴾ [al-An'am: 17] in Surat al-An'am.

*Tajaruna* (تَجْأرُونَ) means you cry out in supplication, and the verbal noun is *al-ju'ar*, in the pattern of names of sounds.

He follows this with another blessing, namely the blessing of removing harm from people, in the words of the Exalted ﴿Then when He removes the harm from you﴾, the verse.

The *thumma* (ثُمَّ) here indicates sequence of rank, as is its function in conjoining sentences, and the particle *thumma* is used because the content of the conjoined sentence is further from consideration than the content of the sentence it is conjoined to. For turning away from the Benefactor when harm is removed, and associating another with Him in worship, is more remarkable in state and further in occurrence than turning to Him at a time of hardship.

The aim is to record the ingratitude of the polytheists, and to show God's compassion towards creation in removing harm from them when they turn to Him, while He knows that among them are those who associate others with Him and persist in their polytheism after the harm has been removed from them.

The first *idha* (إذا) is implicitly conditional and is a temporal adverb. The second *idha* is sudden (*fuja'iyyah*), and the use of the particle of suddenness indicates the speed with which this group returns to polytheism, and that it does not delay until the memory of the blessing of the removal of harm from it has grown distant, so that they are caught by disbelief at once without anyone expecting it from them. Thus the group meant in the words of the Exalted ﴿then when a group of you﴾ is the group of polytheists.
