The aim is to establish that Allah the Exalted is the one who manages the causes of what they have of good and evil, that no god creates except Him, and that they do not turn to anyone but Him when harm befalls them, and harm is the opposite of blessing.

[Page 178]

The touching of harm means its arrival. The verb "touch" (*mass*) is used metaphorically for a light occurrence, to indicate the human being's impatience, such that he cries out to Allah upon the occurrence of even the least harm to him. The use of *mass* for a light affliction has already occurred in the words of the Exalted ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it except Him﴾ [al-An'am: 17] in Surat al-An'am.

*Tajaruna* (تَجْأرُونَ) means you cry out in supplication, and the verbal noun is *al-ju'ar*, in the pattern of names of sounds.

He follows this with another blessing, namely the blessing of removing harm from people, in the words of the Exalted ﴿Then when He removes the harm from you﴾, the verse.

The *thumma* (ثُمَّ) here indicates sequence of rank, as is its function in conjoining sentences, and the particle *thumma* is used because the content of the conjoined sentence is further from consideration than the content of the sentence it is conjoined to. For turning away from the Benefactor when harm is removed, and associating another with Him in worship, is more remarkable in state and further in occurrence than turning to Him at a time of hardship.

The aim is to record the ingratitude of the polytheists, and to show God's compassion towards creation in removing harm from them when they turn to Him, while He knows that among them are those who associate others with Him and persist in their polytheism after the harm has been removed from them.

The first *idha* (إذا) is implicitly conditional and is a temporal adverb. The second *idha* is sudden (*fuja'iyyah*), and the use of the particle of suddenness indicates the speed with which this group returns to polytheism, and that it does not delay until the memory of the blessing of the removal of harm from it has grown distant, so that they are caught by disbelief at once without anyone expecting it from them. Thus the group meant in the words of the Exalted ﴿then when a group of you﴾ is the group of polytheists.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 16, verse 55:**

﴿So that they may deny what We have given them. Then enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾

The *lām al-ta'līl* (the lām of causation) is connected to the verb (yushrikūn, "they associate partners"), which is part of the answer to His statement, exalted is He, ﴿When He removes the harm from you﴾ [al-Nahl: 54]. The *kufr* (ingratitude) here is *kufr al-ni'mah* (ingratitude for blessings), and for this reason His statement is linked to it:

Page 179

﴿what We have given them﴾, meaning of the blessings. The ingratitude for blessings is not what motivated them to associate partners, for their association was earlier than that and they had kept it up after the harm was removed from them. Rather, the coincidence of their return to association after the removal of harm was likened to the coincidence of a motive with the action it produces, and so the lām of causation was used for it. The point of resemblance is their hastening to ingratitude for blessings without delay.

Thus the lām of causation is metaphorically borrowed for this coincidence. This is a *istiʿārah tabaʿiyyah tamlīḥiyyah tahakkumiyyah* (a derivative, witty, and sarcastic metaphor). Its like occurs frequently in the Qur'an. Many grammarians have named this lām the *lām al-'āqibah* (the lām of consequence), and their example for it is His statement, exalted is He, ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. We have explained this in several places, the last of which is at His statement, exalted is He, ﴿that they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Nahl: 25], in this surah.

The pronoun in (liyakfurū) refers to *farīq* (a group), in consideration of its indication of a plurality of people.

*Al-iytā'* (giving) means bestowing, and it is used metaphorically for bestowing a beneficial state, because the nature of giving is to establish one in possession of something desired.

The relative construction ﴿what We have given them﴾ is used because of what the relative clause indicates, namely that it is a blessing, in order to make their ingratitude for it appear abominable, since ingratitude for blessings is ugly in the judgment of all rational people.

Following this, the address to them with the command to enjoy themselves is a command of respite and of little concern for them, and it has the meaning of leaving them alone.

*Al-tamatru'* (enjoyment) is benefiting from *matā'* (provision), and *matā'* is a thing that is benefited from in a desired way and that brings pleasure. One says *tamatta'a bi-kadhā* and *istamta'a* (he enjoyed such-and-such). The word *matā'* was discussed at the end of Surah Bara'ah.

The address is to the group who associate partners with their Lord, by way of *al-iltifāt* (shift of person). The more apparent view is that it is spoken as the saying of an omitted utterance, because it comes as a consequence of a statement addressed to all people, as has preceded. So what follows is a part of what it follows, and this conflicts with *al-iltifāt*, which requires that the referent of the pronoun be the referent of what precedes it.

The meaning is: "Say: Enjoy the blessings in which you are, until a term."

Page 180

What follows from this is a threat, that they will come to know the consequence of ingratitude for blessings after the enjoyment has ended. The object of (ta'lamūn) is omitted because it is clear from His statement, exalted is He, ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them﴾; that is, "you will know the recompense of your disbelief."

﴿Yet they assign to what they do not know a share of what We have provided for them. By God, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) of a state (ḥāl) among their states of disbelief that is connected with the blessing God bestowed upon them. It is therefore conjoined to the clause ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from God﴾ [al-Naḥl: 53]. It may also be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in the genitive in His words ﴿whatever blessing you have﴾ [al-Naḥl: 53], by way of iltifāt (shift in grammatical person). It may also be conjoined to (yushrikūna) in His words ﴿then, when a party of you ascribe partners to their Lord﴾ [al-Naḥl: 54].

What is related here is the set of ramifications (tafārīʿ) of their religion, arising from their associating partners with God, and which are themselves among the ramifications of their ingratitude for their Lord's blessing. For they assigned in their wealth a right to the idols, which had provided them with nothing. This has already occurred in Surat al-Anʿam at His words ﴿And they assign to God a share of what He has produced of crops and livestock, and they say: "This is for God," by their claim, and "this is for our partners."﴾ [al-Anʿam: 136].

However, here it is restricted to mentioning what they assigned to their partners, without what they assigned to God, because the context here is detailing their ingratitude for the blessing, unlike in Surat al-Anʿam, where the context is enumerating the states of their pre-Islamic ignorance (jāhiliyya). Although all of this is denounced against them, some disbelief is worse than other.

Al-jaʿl (assigning) means to make or to place. You say: "I have made for you in my wealth such-and-such." The present tense is used here to indicate that this occurs from them repeatedly and continuously, unlike His words ﴿And they swore by God﴾ [al-Naḥl: 38], which is a narration of an event that occurred in the past of their obstinacy and their disputation concerning the resurrection.

The object of yaʿlamūna is omitted because it is evident; it is the pronoun referring to (mā), meaning "they do not know it." The omission of this pronoun is common in speech.

The referent of the relative clause of mā lā yaʿlamūna is the idols. This relative clause is used to intensify the reproach of the absurdity of their opinions, since they set aside in their wealth a portion they give to things whose realities they do not know, let alone the extent of benefit they might obtain from them, and to fancies they imagine that have no existence in reality, nor in perception, nor any capacity for benefit, as He said: ﴿They are only names you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority. They follow only conjecture and what the souls desire.﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. The pronoun in taʿlamūna refers back to the implied subject of yajʿalūna.

Describing the share as ﴿from what We have provided them﴾ is to censure their wrongdoing, for they abandoned the Benefactor and did not draw near to Him by what pleases Him from their wealth, such as giving to the needy, which He commanded them to spend upon. Instead they spent that on drawing near to things imagined that never provided them with anything.

Then the address was turned toward them by way of iltifāt, for the purpose of threat. There is no obstacle to iltifāt here, since there is no particle of consequence (fāʾ al-tafrīʿ) as in His words ﴿so enjoy yourselves﴾.

The opening of the threat and warning with an oath is for its confirmation, since the questioning promised will take place on the Day of Resurrection, which they deny; thus it was appropriate to emphasize it.

The oath with the particle tāʾ (tā) is specific to cases where the matter sworn to is strange and remarkable, as was mentioned previously at His words ﴿They said: "By God, you know well that we did not come to cause corruption in the land."﴾ [Yūsuf: 73] in Surat Yūsuf, and it will come at His words ﴿And by God, I will surely plot against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 57] in Surat al-Anbiyāʾ. Thus the use of the particle tāʾ in the oath here signals that they will be questioned with a questioning as strange as the gravity of the offence about which they are questioned.

The questioning is a metonymy (kināya) for the punishment that follows from it, because in custom the punishment of a just ruler comes right after questioning the offender about what he committed, since perhaps he has something by which to defend himself.

[p. 182] Thus God applied the matter of reckoning on the Day of Resurrection according to that noble custom. The expression ﴿you used to fabricate﴾ is a metonymy for their deserving punishment, because lying against God is a grave crime.

The use of the verb of being (kāna) and the present tense indicates that fabrication was part of their character, and that it was repeated and continuous from them. Thus it is more eloquent than saying "what you fabricate" or "what you have fabricated."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 57:

﴿And they assign to Allah daughters—glory be to Him—while for themselves is what they desire.﴾ This is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿And they assign to that which they do not know a share of what We have provided for them﴾ [al-Nahl: 56].

This is an argument based on the blessing of Allah upon them in sons and daughters, which is the blessing of offspring, as indicated by His saying ﴿while for themselves is what they desire﴾, meaning: what they desire of the offspring from what We have provided them.

Incorporated within this argument and this reminder of favour is the mention of a monstrous form of their disbelief, namely their fabrication: that they claimed the angels to be daughters of Allah, from among the chieftains of the jinn, as indicated by His saying ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. This was the belief of the tribes of Kinanah and Khuza'ah.

Here, "jaʿl" (assigning) means attributing by speech.

And "(subhanahu)" (glory be to Him) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) standing in place of the verb, in the accusative of absolute object (mafʿul muṭlaq). It occupies the position of an interposed clause (jumla iʿtirasiyya) which functions as a response to their evil statement contained in the report ﴿And they assign to Allah daughters﴾, since "jaʿl" in it means the making of a statement. Thus his saying "(subhanahu)" is like their saying: "ḥāsha lillāh" (far be it from Allah) and "maʿādh Allāh" (God forbid), meaning: exalting Him above having such a thing.

"(Subhanahu)" was placed before His saying ﴿while for themselves is what they desire﴾ so that it would be an explicit statement that the declaration of His transcendence above this assigning concerns the very essence of it, namely the attribution of offspring to Allah, and not merely their assigning to Him specifically daughters rather than sons, which is more atrocious, as indicated by His saying ﴿while for themselves is what they desire﴾; because that would add to the aggravation. Thus His saying ﴿while for themselves is what they desire﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), and the fronting of the predicate in the clause is for the emphasis on them in that matter, in the manner of mockery (tahakkum).

The referent (māṣadaq) of ﴿what they desire﴾ is the male sons, by the context of its contrast with the daughters. And His saying ﴿And when one of them is given good tidings of a female﴾ [al-Nahl: 58], meaning: while they have males among their children, so why did they not assign to Allah sons and daughters? This is an escalation in refuting their beliefs according to their own customs. Otherwise, with respect to Allah, it is the same, due to equality in begetting, which is a requirement of origination (ḥudūth), from which the Necessarily Existent (wājib al-wujūd) is exalted.

This will be specifically refuted in His saying ﴿And they assign to Allah what they dislike﴾ [al-Nahl: 62]. For this reason, only the word "daughters," which indicates the females themselves, is mentioned here, and it is stated only that they desire sons, without addressing their dislike of daughters—though this is understood by implication—because that is another degree of their disbelief, which will be singled out for mention.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verses 58–59:**

﴿When one of them is given the good news of a female, his face darkens and he is filled with suppressed rage.﴾ ﴿He hides himself from the people because of the evil of the news he has been given. Shall he keep it despite contempt, or bury it in the dust? Evil is what they judge.﴾

The wāw in His words ﴿When one of them is given the good news of a female﴾ may be the circumstantial wāw (wāw al-ḥāl), and it may be that the clause is parenthetical (jumla mu'taridah), with the wāw being parenthetical (i'tiraḍiyyah). The lengthy treatment of it is warranted because it belongs to the branches of their polytheism. This is preferable to making it coordinated with the clause ﴿and theirs is what they desire﴾ [al-Nahl: 57], which occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), because that would defeat its purpose of enumeration. This purpose is among the requirements of the context, although the outcome of the two considerations is one in the essential meaning.

[p. 184]

The expression of the announcement of the birth of a female with the verb (bushshira, was given good news) in two places is because it is so in reality. The birth of a child is a blessing for the father, because of what he anticipates of companionship, of playfulness, of benefit from its service, and of its help when he needs it. It also increases the offspring of the tribe, which brings it honour, and it creates the bond of marriage-kinship (āṣirat al-ṣihr). Then, although this is good news in reality, the expression with it conveys an allusion (ta'rīḍ) with mockery (tahakkum) directed at them, since they consider the good news a calamity. This is from their distortion of realities. Allusion is one of the types of metonymy (kināyah), and metonymy is compatible with the literal meaning.

The bāʾ in (bi-l-unthā, with a female) marks the transitive complement of the verb of good news. It is attached to the female herself, but what is meant is her birth, so it is an elision of a known modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf maʿlūm).

The verb (ẓalla, remained/became) is one of the verbs of being (afʿāl al-kawn), the sisters of (kāna, was). These indicate that their subject is characterised by a lasting state. Therefore they require a subject in the nominative, called the ism, and a predicate in the accusative, called the khabar, which resembles the predicate of the subject of a nominal sentence. The grammarians called them (nawāsikh, abrogators) for this reason: they operate on what, were they absent, would be a subject and predicate, and since the status of the predicate changes with them, they are called abrogators because they nullify its nominative case. The same is true of (inna, indeed) and its sisters and (ẓanna, thought) and its sisters. This terminology is approximate and not elegant.

[p. 185]

Ẓalla is also used in the sense of (ṣāra, became), and this is what is meant here.

The blackening of the face is used for the colour of the face of one who is grieved, when dust overcomes it, so it is likened to blackness as an intensification (mubālaghah).

Al-kaẓīm is the angry one filled with rage. It was mentioned earlier in His words (fa-huwa kaẓīm, and he was filled with suppressed grief) in Surat Yusuf, meaning that he became filled with rage against his wife. This is from their ignorant and oppressive ignorance (jāhiliyyah), for they treat the woman as though the birth of males were in her choice. And why would he not be angry with himself, when he impregnates his wife with a female? One of their women said, recited by al-Asma'i, lamenting her husband, who had abandoned her because she bore daughters:

He becomes angry if we do not bear sons,
and we only give what we have been given.

The (tawārī, hiding) is concealment, the present tense of (wārāhu, concealed him), derived from (al-warāʾ, behind), which is the direction of the rear. The (min, from) in His words ﴿because of the evil of the news he has been given﴾ is the figurative source (ibtidāʾ majāzī), which conveys the sense of causation, since it is said, "I did such and such because of such and such." He, the Exalted, said ﴿and do not kill your children out of poverty﴾ [al-An'am: 151], meaning he hides because of that news.

The clause (ayumsikuhu, shall he keep it) is an inclusive apposition (badal ishtimāl) of the clause (yatawārā, he hides himself), because he hides out of shame before the people, and so he remains hidden from his people until his affair is forgotten. This is the meaning of His words (ayumsikuhu, etc.): he hesitates between these two matters, saying to himself, "Shall I keep it in contempt, or bury it in the dust?" What is meant is the hesitation over the answer to this question.

Al-hūn is humiliation. It was mentioned at His words ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20], in Surat al-An'am.

Al-dass is concealing a thing among the parts of another thing, like burial. What is meant is burial in the earth, which is infanticide (al-wa'd). They used to bury their daughters alive: some buried them right after birth, and some buried a female once she had grown, walked, and spoken, that is, when she had become visible to people and could no longer be hidden. This is among the most heinous deeds of the Jahiliyyah. They were in agreement upon it, and they regarded it as a right of the father, so the group would not denounce the perpetrator.

For this reason God called it a judgement in His words ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾, and He declared its condemnation with the particle (alā, indeed/unquestionably), because it is a great injustice upon which they had colluded, and they made it lawful for the people as an oppression against created beings. It is attributed to the plural pronoun, although the speech was about a singular unspecified act, in order to fulfil the right of this subtle point.

[Page 186]

﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil likeness, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness. And He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ This sentence is an interjection, answering their statement that is implied in His words, ﴿And when one of them is given good tidings of a female﴾ [al-Nahl: 58]. Its connection to the sentence ﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters — exalted is He!﴾ [al-Nahl: 57], as mentioned earlier, makes it equivalent to the sentence "exalted is He" (subhanahu). The difference is that "exalted is He" is an answer affirming Allah's transcendence above what they attribute to Him, whereas this sentence is an answer belittling them for how they treat daughters while attributing to Allah this category which they themselves hold in contempt.

The answer follows the Arab custom: when they hear a statement that is disliked or objectionable, they say to its speaker: "Into your mouth goes the kathkath" (a term for dry earth or crumbs, used as a curse), and they say: "May your hands be dusted (tariba yadaka)," "May your right hand be dusted (tariba yaminuka)," and "Be gone (ukhsa')."

Likewise, His words ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil likeness﴾ came as an insult to them.

The "likeness" (mathal) is a strange state in goodness or ugliness, and its being annexed to "evil" (al-su') is for clarification.

They are identified by "those who do not believe in the Hereafter" because they were known among the Muslims by this attribute, as in His words ﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts deny, and they are arrogant﴾ [al-Nahl: 22], and His words ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far error﴾ [Saba': 8].

The sentence ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest likeness﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil likeness﴾, because with it is completed the refutation of their statement and the censure of their opinion, since they attributed offspring to Allah, which is one of the necessary consequences of need and incapacity. When they attributed that to Him, they assigned to Him the lowest of the two categories in their own estimation, as He said: ﴿And they assign to Allah what they dislike﴾ [al-Nahl: 62]. This was not so in reality, but it went according to their belief, and as a charge against them by their own opinion.

[Page 187]

And "the highest" (al-a'la) is a superlative, and the object of comparison has been omitted for the purpose of generality, meaning: higher than every likeness in loftiness, by the indication of the context.

And "al-su'" (with a fatha on the sin) is the verbal noun of sa'ahu, when one does to him what he dislikes, while "al-su'" (with a damma on the sin) is the noun. It was mentioned in His words ﴿They afflict you with the worst punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meanings of "mathal" were detailed earlier at His words ﴿Their likeness is like the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] in al-Baqarah.

"Al-'Aziz al-Hakim" was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿And know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209] in Surat al-Baqarah.

This is a commentary on the verse, and the translation follows the Arabic faithfully.

This is an interjection in the midst of the reproach against their disbelief, of which one of the practices is the burying of daughters alive. As for the description of their attributing to God the daughters of whom they themselves are averse, and describing that as an unjust judgment (ḥukm sū'), and describing their condition as an evil likeness (mathal sū'), and informing them of the most distinctive of their beliefs, that they do not believe in the Hereafter, he follows that with a warning concerning their statements and actions.

And injustice (ẓulm) is transgression against right (al-ḥaqq), and the greatest of it is the transgression of the Creator's right over His creatures, which is the right of singling Him out for worship. For this reason, when injustice in the Qur'an is not attached to an object, as in ﴿they wronged themselves﴾ (ẓalamū anfusahum), what is intended by it is the greatest injustice, which is shirk, until this became a conventional reality in the terminology of the Qur'an. This is what is meant here by this warning. As for the injustice that is less than associating partners with God, it is not intended here, because it consists of graded degrees, as will come shortly, so it does not require the punishment of annihilation in its generality.

The definite article in "the people" (al-nās) is taken to be the generic definite (ta'rīf al-jins), so as to include all people, since that is more suitable to the context of warning. Thus the phrase ﴿al-nās﴾ is not intended to refer specifically to the idolaters of Makkah whom the preceding pronouns in His saying "that they may disbelieve in what We have given them" and what follows of pronouns refer to, and by this the word "al-nās" does not become an explicit noun in place of a pronoun.

The pronoun in ﴿ʿalayhā﴾ refers to the earth, even though no mention of it has occurred in the speech, since the context indicates it. This is a well-known usage in their speech, as in His saying ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Ṣ: 32], meaning the sun; and they say "it has become cold" meaning the morning; and the people of Madinah say "there is no one between its two lava-fields (labatayhā) who does such-and-such", meaning the two lava-fields of Madinah.

The word dābba is a name for what crawls on the earth, that is, walks, and its feminine form is according to the interpretation of "thing" (dhāt). The term dābba has come to be specifically used for what is other than man among what walks on the earth.

The particle law (lau) is a particle of conditional negation for negation, that is, a conditional particle indicating the non-occurrence of its consequent due to the non-occurrence of its condition. The condition after law is necessarily related to past time, so if a present-tense verb occurs after law, it generally shifts to past meaning.

So the meaning is: had God been punishing creation for their shirk, He would have annihilated them from the earth, and annihilated the beasts along with them; but He did not punish them.

The evidence for the negation of the condition of law is the negation of its consequent, and the evidence for the negation of its consequent is observation, since people and beasts have continued to exist upon the earth.

The connection between punishing the wrongdoers for their sins and annihilating the non-wrongdoing people and the beasts is that God created people to worship Him, that is, to acknowledge for Him divinity and oneness within it, according to His saying ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 56], and that this is deposited in the natural disposition (fiṭra), according to His saying (﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify"﴾ [al-A'rāf: 172]).

So the blessing of existence obliges the rational person to thank the One who brought him into existence. If he denies His existence or denies His singularity in divinity, he has broken the covenant that was established upon its condition, and so he deserves to be erased from existence through extermination and annihilation.

By this it is determined that what is meant by injustice in His saying ﴿by their injustice﴾ is shirk or ta'ṭīl (denial of the Creator). As for what is less than that of transgression against God's right by disobeying His command, or against the rights of creatures by seizing them, these are many degrees. Among them is one person's transgression against the existence of another human being whose life is protected, so that he deliberately kills him; his recompense is annihilation, because he annihilated his like, and it does not extend to the annihilation of those with him. What is less than that of injustice towards him has a punishment less than that, so nothing deserves destruction except shirk; but the nature of punishment is that it is restricted to the one who commits the offence.

The reason that punishment for shirk requires the annihilation of all the idolaters and their beasts is that the destruction of wrongdoers does not occur except through great events that are not limited to the extent of their dwellings, because the causes of destruction are not limited within the customary order of this world. Therefore the destruction encompasses the non-wrongdoing people and encompasses their beasts.

Since injustice, that is shirk, has not been absent from the earth, it follows that from the destruction of the people of injustice there spreads the destruction to all regions of the earth, so people and beasts perish. The annihilation comes over successive generations, for example from the time of Noah, so no beast is found on the earth at the time of the revelation of this verse.

As for those among the idolatrous community who may be righteous, God decrees for the righteous the causes of salvation through states that are beyond the ordinary, as He said ﴿And God will save those who feared Him by their achievement; no evil will touch them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Zumar: 61]. God has informed us that He saved Hūd and those who believed with him, and He informed us that He saved other prophets; and sufficient for you is the salvation of Noah, peace be upon him, and those who believed with him from the flood in the ark.

His saying ﴿But He delays them until a specified term﴾ indicates that their delay varies in its terms, so during the duration of those terms there remain many peoples by whom the earth is populated; and that is the cause of the survival of many nations of idolaters and those around them.

His saying ﴿from a beast﴾ implies the destruction of the beasts of people along with them, were God to will that; because the extermination of a nation includes the extermination of its beasts, since beasts were created for the benefit of people, so it is no wonder that God would exterminate them when He exterminates their owners.

Restricting the mention to "a beast" in this verse is a concision, because when the injustice of people leads to the extermination of beasts, the knowledge that it leads to the extermination of the wrongdoers is obtained by the indication of implication (dalālat al-iqtiḍā').

This is regarding the punishment of extermination. As for what befalls people of calamities and trials, of which His saying is relevant ﴿And guard against a trial that will not afflict exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾ [al-Anfāl: 25], that is tied to customary causes, so the exception of the righteous requires the suspension of many of the gears of the general natural order, and God does not desire its suspension because of what that entails of suspending great interests; and God knows best.

It has come in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim on the authority of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "When God intends a punishment for a people, the punishment strikes whoever is among them, then they will be resurrected according to their intentions." That is, the good person who is struck by the punishment, as a follower, receives a reward for what befalls him of the calamity of others; and what does not touch the innocent is only the punishment of the Hereafter, which God made as a recompense for the obligation, and this is the meaning of His saying "no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another."

In this verse there is an indication that the beasts that are on the earth were created for the benefit of man, so man's use of them for what they are suited for is not an injustice to them, nor is killing them for eating an injustice to them.

The word al-mu'ākhadhah (punishment) means a seizing whose purpose is recompense, so it is a severe seizing; and for this reason it is formed in the pattern mufā'alah, which indicates multiplicity. This indicates that the punishment negated by law is the immediate seizing appropriate to requital, because the custom in what is customary regarding requital is that it does not delay from the time of the occurrence of the sin.

For this reason the adversative came with His saying ﴿But He delays them until a specified term﴾, so the position of the adversative here is that it is a sequel to His saying ﴿He has left upon it no creature﴾.

The term ajal means the appointed period for a particular act, and musammā means the specified; because naming (tasmiyah) is the specification and distinguishing of a thing, and naming the terms is determining them.

A parallel to this has preceded at His saying ﴿And for every nation is a term; when their term comes, they will not remain behind it an hour, nor will they precede it﴾ [al-A'rāf: 34], in Sūrat al-A'rāf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 62:

﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues describe the lie that the best (reward) is theirs. Without doubt, for them is the Fire, and they will be hastened into it.﴾

This is a handful added to a bundle of their conditions in their polytheism, and it resembles the account of His saying, ﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters﴾ [al-Nahl: 57], with regard to what is specific to this account: their ascribing to Allah the things they find hateful, which is what their dislike of daughters required, by His saying, ﴿And for them is what they desire﴾ [al-Nahl: 57]. Thus that attribution comprised two features of the religion of polytheism: attributing offspring to Allah, and attributing to Him the lowest kinds of offspring in their own view. The first was singled out for mention in His saying, ﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters﴾ [al-Nahl: 57], with an allusion to their dislike of daughters as already mentioned, while this (verse) was singled out by explicit mention of dislike. For this reason the use of the relative pronoun and its clause, "what they dislike," fits the context, which is the denunciation of their saying and the condemnation of their selfishness. The relative pronoun may also be general, indicating that they attributed to Allah things they dislike for themselves, such as a partner in disposal, and things they do not accept for their gods, which they ascribed to Allah, as indicated by His saying, ﴿So what belongs to their partners does not reach Allah, but what belongs to Allah reaches their partners. Evil is what they judge﴾ [al-An'am: 136].

In al-Kashshaf: (They attribute to Allah the worst of their wealth and to their idols the best of it). So this is the intended generality of the relative pronoun, and this account is thus more general than the account of His saying, ﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters﴾ [al-Nahl: 57]. Its singling out for mention has two aspects: the difference in the consideration, and the addition of kinds of this attribution.

Page 192

The clause ﴿and their tongues describe the lie﴾ is a conjunction of one account to another account of their conditions of disbelief.

The meaning of "tasif" (describe) is to mention with explanation, clarification and detail, as if one were mentioning the attributes of a thing. The real meaning of description (wasf) is mentioning attributes and adornments, and then it was applied to clear, detailed speech. In al-Kashshaf, on the verse that comes later at the end of this surah, he said: This is from eloquent and fluent speech: it made speech as though it were the very substance of lying; so when their tongues utter it, they have depicted the lie in its own form, like their saying: "Her face describes beauty, and her eye describes magic." End of quote.

This has been mentioned before in His saying, ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted above what they describe﴾ [al-An'am: 100] in Surah al-An'am, and it will come at the end of this surah: ﴿And do not say, for what your tongues describe falsely: "This is lawful and this is unlawful"﴾ [al-Nahl: 116]. From this is the saying of al-Ma'arri:

The lightning of al-Ma'arra passed after weariness, then it spent the night at Rama describing exhaustion.

That is, it complains of fatigue from covering a long distance in a short time, and it is one of his fine metaphors.

What is meant by this lie is everything they say of the sayings of their elite and their common folk, whether by belief or by mockery. Of the first is the saying of al-As ibn Wa'il, related in His saying, ﴿And he said: "I will surely be given wealth and children"﴾ [Maryam: 77], and in His saying, ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, surely I will have with Him the best (reward)﴾ [Fussilat: 50]. Of the second is their saying about the calamity: that its bearer will ride it on the Day of Resurrection so that he will not tire.

"Al-kadhib" (the lie) is in the accusative as the object of "tasif" (describe).

And ﴿that for them is the best (reward)﴾ is either a substitute for "al-kadhib" or "al-husna" is an adjective of an omitted noun, that is, "the state that is the best."

Page 193

The clause ﴿Without doubt, for them is the Fire﴾ is a reply to their stated saying. The meaning of "la jaram" is "without doubt," that is, truly; it was mentioned in Surah Hud.

"Mufritun" with a light ra' vowelled with kasra, in the reading of Nafi', is an active participle of afrata, when something reaches its utmost limit, that is, "those who go to excess in taking from the punishment of the Fire."

Abu Ja'far read it with a kasra on the ra' and doubled, from farrata (doubled form), and the rest read it with a fatha on the ra' and lightened, in the pattern of the passive participle, that is, "those who are made to precede (fara), " with two fathas, which is the one sent ahead to the water to draw for others.

What is meant is that they will be those who precede to the Fire, hastened toward it, because they are the most deserving of the people of the Fire. On this interpretation, the use of "al-ifrat" for this meaning is a sarcastic metaphor, like the saying of Amr ibn Kulthum:

"We hastened the hospitality, lest you insult us"
He meant: we hastened to fight you when you descended upon us as raiders.
Together with the mention of the Fire in contrast to it, there is the figure of antithesis (tibaq). Moreover, Nafi's reading allows an interpretation in this sense too, since one may say: "afrata ila al-ma'" when he went ahead to it.

[Page 194]

This is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf ibtidāʾī*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic), and it falls within a parenthetical statement (*kalām iʿtirāḍī*, an interjected remark). Its purpose is to draw a comparison (*tanẓīr*) between the state of the polytheists being discussed, and their disbelief and bad deeds and judgments, and the state of the misguided nations before them, whom Satan led astray. These include the extinct nations such as ʿĀd and Thamūd, and the present-day communities such as the Jews and Christians.

The address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ in order to convey the message to the ears of the people, since the Qur'an was sent down to guide mankind. Therefore, the emphasis of the statement through the oath is directed at those for whom the statement is intended, not at the one addressed, because the Prophet ﷺ has no doubt about this.

The object of the oath (*maṣabb al-qasam*) is the consequence expressed in the words of God, Exalted be He, ﴿So Satan made their deeds appear fair to them﴾.

As for sending messengers to nations before them, the polytheists do not doubt this. The particle of oath *tāʾ* (*tāʾ al-qasam*, the "t" of oath) is usually used with something surprising, and the object of the oath here is the singular clause in the words of God, Exalted be He, ﴿So Satan made their deeds appear fair to them﴾. This is because the effect of Satan making their deeds appear fair to them, after guidance had come to them from their messengers, is a remarkable matter. The discussion of the particle of oath *tāʾ* has already been covered just above, in the words of God, Exalted be He, ﴿By God, you will certainly be questioned about what you used to fabricate﴾ [al-Naḥl: 56].

The clause ﴿So Satan made their deeds appear fair to them﴾ is conjoined (*maʿṭūfa*) to the clause of the oath, and the implied sense is: "We sent [messengers], so Satan made their deeds appear fair to them."

Satan making their deeds appear fair is a metonymy (*kināya*) for sins. Among these is the non-belief in the messengers, which is the full extent of the comparison, and among them are the innovations (*ibtidāʿāt*) that contradict what the messengers, peace be upon them, brought, such as the innovations of the polytheists regarding the *baḥīra* and the *sāʾiba*. The intended meaning is that the polytheists followed the path of those before them from the nations whose deeds Satan made appear fair to them.

The clause ﴿so he is their ally today﴾ may be consequent upon the whole clause of the oath, with the consequence being the intended purpose of the resumptive sentence for the comparison. In that case, the pronoun in (*waliyyuhum*, "their ally") refers back to those being compared, by the indication of the context. There is no objection to the two closely related pronouns having different referents when the context makes this clear, as in the words of God, Exalted be He, ﴿and they cultivated it more than they cultivated it﴾ [al-Rūm: 9].

The meaning is: so Satan is the ally of the polytheists today, that is, the one who manages their affairs, just as he was the ally of the nations before them when he made their deeds appear fair to them. That is, there is no ally for them today other than him, in response to their claim that they will have the best (*al-ḥusnā*). There is in the statement something resembling *iḥtibāk* (an interlocking ellipsis, where each part of a comparison omits what the other part mentions), and the implied sense is: "We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you, so Satan made their deeds appear fair to them, and he was then their ally. He is the ally of the polytheists today, making their deeds appear fair to them, just as he was the ally of those before them."

[Page 195]

His saying "today" (*al-yawm*) is used for a time that is known by the presence of the speaker, that is, "he is their ally now." The word "he" (*huwa*) is a metonymy for the continuation of his allegiance to them up to the time of the speaker, absolutely and without intending any particular restriction, by reason of what the word itself indicates of the period from the break of dawn until sunset.

It is in the accusative as an adverb of time for the present time. Its origin is "the present day," which is the day in which you are. This was discussed earlier, at the words of God, Exalted be He, ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾ [al-Māʾida: 3], in the Sūrat al-ʿUqūd (the Chapter of Contracts).

It is not used for a past day when it is defined with the definite article (*alif-lām*) except after a demonstrative (*ism al-ishāra*), as in: "that day" (*dhālika al-yawm*), or like "on that day" (*yawmaʾidhin*).

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 16, verse 64:**

﴿We did not send down to you the Book except that you might make clear to them that over which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence of the oath (qasam), and the connection (munāsabah, the thematic link between passages) is that the Qur'an was sent down to complete guidance and to remove the doubts (shubuhat) that had come upon past and present nations, so their like were left among the Arabs and others.

When their misguidance and doubts were mentioned, this was followed by an explanation of the wisdom behind sending Muhammad (ﷺ) and sending the Qur'an down to him. The Qur'an came to make clear to the polytheists their misguidance, with a clarity that leaves falsehood no path into souls, and to make guidance manifest with a clarity that leaves no room for bewilderment in minds, and as mercy for the believers, through what He rewarded them for their faith of the good of this world and the Hereafter.

[p. 196]
He expressed misguidance by the relative construction (ṭarīqat al-mawṣūliyyah) "that over which they differ" to indicate that the cause of misguidance is their disagreement regarding their prophets. The Arabs' misguidance differed: each tribe worshipped an idol, some of them worshipped the sun and the stars, and each tribe adopted for itself practices which they claimed to be a correct religion. They also disagreed with the Muslims about all of that religion.

The use of the restrictive form (ṣīghat al-qaṣr, restriction) in His words ﴿We did not send down to you the Book except that you might make clear﴾ is for the purpose of encompassing the most important aim and benefit of the Qur'an, for which it was sent down. It is thus a claimed restriction (qaṣr idaʿāʾī, a restriction by rhetorical claim), so that listeners would be eager to receive it and reflect upon it, whether believer or unbeliever, each according to his condition, until they are equal in being guided.

Furthermore, the restriction alludes to refuting the claims of those among the polytheists who supposed that the Qur'an was sent down to narrate stories to entertain souls in evening gatherings and the like, until their misleader said: "I will bring you something better than what Muhammad brought: I will bring you the story of Rustam and Isfandiyar." The most important purposes of the Qur'an are these comprehensive benefits that gather the roots of good, namely the removal of ignorance and guidance to true knowledge, and the attainment of the effect of those two matters, which is the mercy arising from keeping away from misguidance and following guidance.

The lam of causation (lām al-taʿlīl) was attached to the verb (tabayyana, "to make clear") occupying the position of an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi). This is because it is an action of the addressee (the Prophet), not of the subject of "We sent down" (ʾanzalnā). The Prophet is the one who directly performs the clarification through the Qur'an, by conveying and explaining it. Thus, in Arabic it is not correct to render the clarification as a verbal noun (taby īn) in the accusative as an object of purpose, since it is not one with the agent of the governing verb in its subject. For this reason, the coordinated items were changed and put in the accusative: "guidance and mercy" (hudan wa raḥmah), because they are actions of the one who sent down the Qur'an. God is the Guide and the Merciful through the Qur'an. Each of clarification, guidance and mercy is achieved through the Qur'an, so the three attributes ultimately become attributes of the Qur'an as well.

[p. 197]
The expression ﴿for a people who believe﴾ (li-qawmin yuʾminūn) rather than "for the believers" or "for those who have believed" indicates that they are a people for whom faith is like a disposition and a firmly established habit, by which their collective identity (qawmiyyah) is constituted, as previously mentioned in His words ﴿signs for a people who reason﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

This verse serves as a concluding appendix (tadhyīl, a closing statement that sums up and reinforces) for the lessons and proofs arising from the description of the states of created beings and the blessings of the Creator upon people, beginning from His words ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Naḥl: 17].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 65:

﴿And Allah sends down water from the sky, and by it gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen.﴾

The interjected speech has ended, and the discourse has returned to the proofs that creation belongs to Allah alone, together with what is incorporated in it of reminders of blessings. Thus this is one of the favours, a lesson among lessons, and a proof among proofs, branching off from the reminder of Allah's blessings and from taking heed of His wondrous workmanship.

The discourse has returned to enumerating abundant blessings, together with what they contain of lessons, in a wondrous combination of reasoning (istidlal) and a connection to the digression (al-kalam al-mu'tariḍ, the interjected speech) at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and by the stars they are guided﴾ [al-Nahl: 16], as you have known from what preceded. So the mention of the sending down of water in the previous verse was brought in the manner of reasoning, whereas here it is brought in the manner of bestowing favour (imtinan) by the blessing of giving life to the earth after its death by the water that descends from the sky.

On this basis, this blessing differs from the blessing mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿It is He who sends down water from the sky; from it you have drink, and from it are trees﴾ [al-Nahl: 10], by the difference in the primary purpose: there it is reasoning from the creation of water, whereas here it is bestowing favour.

The construction of the sentence on the verbal predicate (al-musnad al-fi'li) serves to convey restriction (takhsis), i.e., Allah, and none other, sends down water from the sky. This is in the sense of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Is there any of your partners who does anything of that?﴾ [al-Rum: 40]. The use of the proper name Allah (ism al-jalalah) instead of the pronoun, which is what the context would normally require, serves to draw attention to the report, since the sentence opens with this name, and because the proper noun's indication is clearer and more explicit. This is what the context of establishing that creation and bestowal belong to Allah alone, to the exclusion of His partners, requires, since the polytheists acknowledge that Allah is the doer of these things.

The giving of life to the earth is the bringing forth of what contains life, namely pasture and trees, and its death is the opposite of that. Thus the transitivity of the verb (aḥyā, "gave life to") to the earth is figurative (ta'diyah majaziyyah, metaphorical transitivity). This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿and by it gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] in Surat al-Baqarah, and the aspect of lesson in the verse about the descent of rain was explained there.

The clause (inna fi dhalika la-ayah, "indeed, in that is a sign") is a resumptive clause (mustan'afah). The emphasis with (inna) and the lam of initiation is because those who are not guided by this to the oneness (of Allah) deny that the people who hear this have known its indication of oneness; that is, they deny that this is suitable as a basis for reasoning.

The use of the demonstrative (ism al-ishārah, "that") instead of a pronoun is so that the sign encompasses all that has been mentioned: the sending down of rain, the giving of life to the earth by it, and its death before the giving of life.

The discussion of (qawmin yasma'un, "a people who listen") is like the discussion of His earlier saying (liqawmin yu'minun, "a people who believe").

Hearing (al-sam') is used here in a necessary meaning of its sense, by way of metonymy (kinayah), namely the hearing of reflection and fairness toward what they reflect upon. It is also an allusion (ta'ridh) against the polytheists who did not understand the indication of this toward oneness. For this reason the attribute of hearing was chosen here, the intended meaning being fairness and compliance, because the indication of rain and the life of the earth by it is well known and widely recognised, and its indication of the oneness of Allah, exalted is He, is manifest, and nothing turns away from it except obstinacy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 66:

Page 199
﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink of what is in their bellies, from between digestive contents and blood, pure milk, palatable to those who drink.﴾ This is another proof and one of the favours arising from the benefits of the creation of livestock, into whose favour the lesson has been incorporated by way of what it indicates of the wondrous craftsmanship of God, following His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the livestock—He created them for you; in them is warmth﴾ [al-Nahl: 5] up to His saying, ﴿Indeed, Lord of kindness, Most Merciful﴾.
The occasion for mentioning this blessing here is that by the milk of livestock is the life of man, just as the earth lives by the water of the sky, and that the effects of the water of the sky have an effect in the formation of the milk of animals through pasture.

This lesson is specific to what it draws attention to of the wondrous craftsmanship and wisdom in the creation of milk, through His saying, ﴿from between digestive contents and blood, pure milk, palatable﴾, then by reminding of the blessing to people in that, incorporating the lesson with the favour.

The sentence ﴿And indeed, for you in the livestock there is a lesson﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who hear﴾ [al-Nahl: 65], meaning: just as there was a lesson for a people who hear in the sending down of water from the sky, for you in the livestock there is also a lesson, since those addressed, who are the believers, are the people who hear.

The pronoun of address is a shift from the third person. Its emphasis with ﴿inna﴾ and the lam of initiation is like the emphasis of the sentence before it.

Al-an'am (livestock): a collective noun for every group of one of the kinds of camels, cattle, sheep and goats.

Al-'ibrah (lesson): that by which one is admonished and takes heed. It has been discussed at the end of Surah Yusuf. The clause ﴿We give you to drink of what is in their bellies﴾ stands in the position of explanation for the clause ﴿And indeed, for you in the livestock there is a lesson﴾.

Al-buṭūn (bellies): plural of baṭn, a name for the cavity containing the entire digestive system, from stomach, liver and intestines.

Page 200
The "min" (from) in His saying, ﴿mimma fi buṭūnihi﴾ ("of what is in their bellies") is for origin (ibtida'iyyah), because the milk is secreted from the fodder that is in the bellies; and the referent of "what is in their bellies" is the fodder. It is also permissible to make it partitive (tab'īḍiyyah), and then the referent of "what is in their bellies" is the milk, reckoning by its state of passing through the digestive apparatus before descending into the udder.
The "min" in His saying, ﴿min bayni farthin﴾ ("from between digestive contents") is superfluous, for emphasis of intermediacy, meaning: it is secreted in a state between the state of digestive contents and the state of blood.

The explanation came with ﴿nusqīkum﴾ rather than saying "you drink" or the like, by way of incorporating the favour with the lesson.

The aspect of the lesson in this is that what the bellies of livestock contain of fodder and pasture, through digestion in the stomach, then the liver, then the glands of the udder, is transformed into a liquid that is given to drink, and it is secreted from between the secretion of digestive contents and blood.

Al-farth (digestive contents): the residues left by the digestion of the stomach, which descend to the intestines and become digestive contents; and al-dam (blood): a secretion that the liver produces from the nourishment descending to it, which rises to the heart, and the mechanical movement of the heart drives it into the arteries and veins, and it continues circulating thus by means of the heart. Its mention has already been made at His saying, ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], in Surah al-'Uqud.

The meaning of the milk being "from between digestive contents and blood" is that it is a secretion occurring at the same time as the secretion of blood and the secretion of digestive contents. Its connection to digestive contents is that the blood that descends in the veins of the udder passes through the passage of the urinary and fecal wastes, and the glands of the udder secrete it as milk, just as the glands of the kidneys secrete it as urine without additional processing, and just as the intestinal crypts secrete fecal matter without processing—unlike the secretion of the prostate glands of semen, which depends on a processing toward which the blood descends.

It is not meant that milk trickles out from between two layers of digestive contents and blood; rather, what led to this notion among those who imagined it is taking "bayn" in its literal sense of a spatial location, whereas it is used much in a figurative sense for the middle between two ranks, as when they say: "Courage is a quality between recklessness and cowardice." Among the eloquence of the Qur'an is this expression, close to the understanding of every class of people according to the extent of their knowledge, while being consistent with the reality.

Page 201
The meaning: a secretion that is not blood, because it is smoother than blood, and because it does not remain in the veins of the udder as blood remains in the veins; it resembles the wastes in the necessity of its secretion, but it is not a waste, because it is a pure, beneficial, nourishing secretion, not a filthy harmful substance unfit for nutrition like urine and fecal matter.

The position of "from between digestive contents and blood" is the position of a descriptive qualifier of "milk"; it was placed before it for emphasis on it, because it is the locus of the lesson, so it received added emphasis; and by being placed first, it became a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl).

Since milk is produced in the udder and not in the belly, it was made the object of "nusqīkum," and "mimma fi buṭūnihi" was made an explanation of its source, not of its place of deposit. So the milk is not "of what is in the bellies"; for this reason "mimma fi buṭūnihi" was mentioned first, to show that it is connected to the verb "nusqīkum" and is not a description of "laban."

The attributes we have mentioned for milk are encompassed by His saying, ﴿pure, palatable to those who drink﴾. Its purity (khulūṣ) is its freedom from what urine and fecal matter contain, and its palatability (sawgh) to drinkers is its safety from what blood contains of harms to the one who drinks it; therefore the drinker does not find it hard to swallow nor finds it repugnant.

This marvellous description is among the scientific miracles of the Qur'an, for it is a description that none of the Arabs of that day could know the fine details of its formation, nor could they describe it with anything which, if a natural scientist described it, he could not describe it more concisely or comprehensively than this.

The singular pronoun of "al-an'am" in His saying, ﴿mimma fi buṭūnihi﴾ is in observance of the wording being singular, since a collective noun is a singular word, not among the forms of plurals; the wording may be observed, so its pronoun comes singular, and its meaning may be observed, so it is treated as plural, as in the verse of Surah al-Mu'minun: ﴿We give you to drink of what is in their bellies﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 21].

Page 202
Al-khalis (pure): what is stripped of what would cloud its clarity, so it is the clear one; and al-sa'igh (palatable): what passes easily down the throat.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim and Ya'qub read "nusqīkum" with a fatḥah on the nūn, the imperfect of saqā; Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs from 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a ḍammah on the nūn, as the imperfect of asqā; both are two dialects. Abu Ja'far read it with a feminine second-person prefix in place of the nūn, taking the pronoun as referring to al-an'am.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 67:

﴿And from the fruits of the date-palms and the grapes, you take from them intoxicant and good provision. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿And indeed for you in the livestock is a lesson﴾ [al-Nahl: 66].

The presence of "min" (from) at the beginning of the speech indicates the implied presence of a verb, indicated by the verb in the clause before it, which is (we give you to drink). So the sense is: and We give you to drink from the fruits of the date-palms and the grapes. It is not connected to (you take), as the second "min" in His saying (you take from it intoxicant) indicates. The arrangement of the speech points to the speaker's intent, and it is not valid to make it connected to (you take) placed before it, because that would move the meaning away from the favour of Allah's subtle kindness, since He made Himself the one who gives drink to people. This is a coordination from Him upon a favour, because (We give you to drink) came as an explanation of the clause ﴿And indeed for you in the livestock is a lesson﴾ [al-Nahl: 66]. The import of the verb (We give you to drink) is the import of favour, because drink is a excellence, and both lessons concern drink, and the connection is that both are water, and that both are pressed by the hand. The Arabs have used the word "milking" (ḥalb) for the pressing of wine and nabidh (date-wine). Ḥassān said, describing wine, both mixed and pure:

Both have milked the juice, so pour for me in a glass whose sealing is loosest.

It indicates that they are two lessons of a close kind that the concluding phrase in His saying (indeed in that is a sign) was placed after the mention of the two drinks, rather than concluding the drink of milk with it being a sign. The lesson in the creation of fruits is that they are suitable for pressing and fermentation, and comprise benefits for people and pleasures, and His saying ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason﴾ indicates that. This is connected to what preceded of the lesson in the creation of plants and fruits from His saying ﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops, the olives, the date-palms﴾ [al-Nahl: 11], and so on.

The clause (you take from it intoxicant) etc. is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

The "min" in both places is for origin (ibtidāʾiyyah). The first is connected to the implied verb (we give you to drink), and the second is connected to the verb (you take). The second is not partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah), because intoxicant is not part of the fruits, so the sense of origin encompasses both particles.

Sakar (intoxicant), with two fatḥahs, is the intoxicating drink.

This is a favour through what contains their desired pleasure, which is widespread among them, and that was before the prohibition of wine, because this verse is Meccan and the prohibition of wine was revealed in Medina, so the favour at that time was with what is permissible.

Rizq (provision) is food, and it is described as ﴿good﴾ (ḥasan) because of the benefits in it, and that is dates and grapes, because they are two sweet, delicious things that are eaten fresh and dried, and are suitable for storage, and among the conditions of grape juice is that it becomes vinegar and grape molasses.

The clause ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason﴾ is a repetition for enumerating the sign, because it is an independent sign.

The discussion of the clause ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason﴾ is like his saying a moment ago ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who hear﴾ [al-Nahl: 65], and the reference is to all that was mentioned of the blessing of giving milk to drink, giving intoxicant to drink, and the taste of the fruit.

The description of reason was chosen here, because the indication of the creation of the milk of livestock as evidence of Allah's wisdom requires reflection on what this verse describes here, and it is not self-evident like the indication of rain, as was previously mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verses 68–69 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And your Lord inspired the bee: "Take for yourself houses in the mountains, and in the trees, and in what they build."﴾ ﴿"Then eat of all the fruits and follow the ways of your Lord, made easy." From their bellies comes out a drink of varying colours, in which there is healing for mankind. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reflect.﴾

A lesson (ʿibrah) appended to a lesson, and a favour (minnah) appended to a favour. He changed the mode of expression for reflection (iʿtibar) because this lesson contains an alert to the great wisdom of God Most High, in that He deposited in the make-up of this weak insect this marvellous craftsmanship and placed in it this benefit. Just as He deposited in livestock their milk, and deposited in the fruits of the date palm and the grapevine a drink, what is in the bellies of bees is midway between what is in the bellies of livestock and what is in the heart of fruits. For the bee sucks from the fruits and the blossoms the sugary, honey-forming substances, then brings them out as honey, just as milk comes out from the essence of pasture.

There is another lesson in it: God deposited in the bee an awareness of a precise, well-regulated craft that produces a beneficial drink without needing the hand of a milker.

The sentence therefore opens with the verb "inspired" (awḥā) rather than with the Divine Name, as in the sentence "and God sent down" (wa-llāhu anzala), because the verb "inspired" carries an allusion to the inspiring (ilhām) of that weak insect with a wondrous management, a perfected action and an engineering in its nature.

That inspiration in itself is a proof of the great wisdom of God Most High, in addition to what follows it of indication of the power of God Most High, and a favour from Him.

Waḥy (inspiration) is a hidden speech and a sign indicating a verbal meaning. From this, what the angel conveys to the Messenger is called waḥy, because it is hidden from people's ears.

Here the term waḥy is applied to the hidden disposition that God deposited in the nature of the bee, by which it is driven to an organised action, arranged one part after another, in which its members do not differ. This is a likening of the inspiration to a hidden speech that contains that ordering, resembling the action of a learner by the teaching of a teacher, or of one who is commanded by the instruction of one who orders, which he received in secret. Thus the application of waḥy is a metaphorical allegory (istiʿārah tamthīliyyah).

Al-naḥl (the bee) is a collective noun of genus, its singular being naḥlah. It is an insect whose body is about twice the size of the common fly, with four wings, and the colour of its belly is dark, tending to red. In its proboscis is a fine sting, like the thorn in the fruit of the prickly pear (known in Indian usage as the Hindi fig), hidden beneath its proboscis, with which it stings what it fears among animals, poisoning the place with a poison that is not strong. But if the bee's sting is detached, it dies. The bees are of three kinds: male, female and sexless. The males are those that guard the hives, and for this reason they hover in flight in front of the hive with a buzzing. They fertilise the females, and by this fertilisation the females give birth to females.

The females are those called the yaʿāsīb (queen bees). They are larger in body than the males. The one that lays eggs in the hives is only a single female, and she may lay without the fertilisation of a male, but in this case she only produces males, so there is no benefit in her offspring for the production of the mothers.

As for the sexless ones, they are those that secrete honey, and they are the ʿawāsil (worker bees). They are smaller in body than the males, and they are the majority of the inhabitants of the beehive.

The particle "an" (that) is explanatory (tafsīriyyah), and it is a reinforcement (tarshīḥ) of the metaphorical allegory, because the explanatory "an" is among the companions of verbs that signify the sense of saying without its letters.

The taking of houses is the first stage of the precise craft that God deposited in the natures of bees. For they build houses with a precise order, then divide their parts into equal compartments with hexagonal shapes, so that no gap remains between them through which insects may slip. For the properties of hexagonal shapes, when some of them are joined to others, are that they connect and become like a single piece, whereas the other shapes, from the triangle to the decagon, when each one is joined to its like, do not connect, and gaps remain between them. Then they coat the surfaces of the hexagons with wax, a fatty substance that is pliable and closer to hardness, formed in a very fine sac beneath the belly of the working bee. The bee lifts it with her legs to her mouth, chews it, and places some of it beside some other to build the hexagon called the honeycomb (shahd), so as to prevent the honey from leaking out of it.

Since the bee-hives were well known to those addressed, the lesson was sufficed by alerting to them and reminding of them.

It is indicated that they are made in the best places, whether in the mountains, the trees or the trellises, and not like the dwellings of other insects. This is because of the nobility of the bee by what it contains of benefits and by what it comprises of subtle craftsmanship. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He, about their opposite: ﴿Indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾ [Al-ʿAnkabut: 41].

The discussion of the mountains has already been given at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then place upon every mountain a part of them﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 260], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The "min" (from/in) that governs "the mountains" and what is conjoined to it has the sense of "in", and its original meaning is the "min" of origin (ibtidāʾiyyah). The expression is therefore used with "min" rather than with the locative "fī", because the bees build houses for themselves, and they do not make their houses the crevices of mountains, nor the branches of trees, nor the sticks of the trellis.

This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And take from the station of Ibrahim a place of prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 125], and it is not like the "min" in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He has made for you from the mountains shelters﴾ [Al-Nahl: 81].

"What they build" (mā yaʿrishūn) means what they make into trellises (ʿurūsh), the plural of ʿarīsh. The ʿarīsh is a raised seat above the ground, in a vineyard or a field, made from sticks and roofed at its top with leaves or the like, so that it has shade, and its owner sits in it overlooking what is around him.

It is said: ʿarrasha, when he built and raised. From this, the couch that rises above the ground on which the great sit is called ʿarsh (throne).

This was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾ [Al-Anʿam: 141], in Surat al-Anʿam, and at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what they used to trellis﴾ [Al-Aʿraf: 137], in Surat al-Aʿraf.

The majority of the reciters read the vowel of the "rāʾ" in "yaʿrishūn" with a kasra, while Ibn ʿAmir read it with a ḍamma.

The "thumma" (then) is for ordering by rank (tartīb rutbī), because the inspiration of the bee to eat from the fruits results in the forming of honey in its bellies, and that is higher in rank than the taking of houses, because it is distinguished by honey over other insects that build houses, and because it is of greater benefit to humankind, and because from it comes its food by which it survives. The bee's sucking was called eating (akl) because it feeds on it, so it is not drinking.

The "thamarāt" (fruits) is the plural of thamarah. The original meaning of thamarah is what a tree brings forth as produce, such as dates and grapes, while the bee sucks from the blossoms before they become fruits. Thus the word "fruits" in the verse is applied to the blossoms by way of the figurative sense of the sent (al-majāz al-mursal), by the relation of what was (to what it becomes).

The clause "fa-slukī" (then follow) is conjoined with the particle of consequence (fāʾ al-tafrīʿ), to indicate that God deposited in the nature of the bee, at the time of grazing, the moving from flower to flower and from garden to garden. If it does not find a flower, it goes further afield in search of food. Then, when it is satisfied, it hastens to fly back right after being sated, so as to return to its hives and expel from its bellies the honey that exceeds its food. That course is a consequence of the nature of its eating.

[Page 208]

The explanation of this is that the blossoms and fruits have fine glands that secrete a sugary liquid, which the bee sucks, and it fills with it what resembles storage sacs in its bellies. It becomes sweeter in the bellies of the bees by mixing with chemical substances deposited in the bellies of the bees. When it goes back from its pasture to its hives, it expels from its mouth what has accumulated in its bellies after its body has taken what it needs for its food. This resembles the rumination of ruminant animals. That is honey.

When honey is expelled into the cells of the honeycomb it is liquid and thin. Then it begins to dry out the moisture of the flower waters that is in it, because of the warmth of the wax from which the honeycomb is built and the warmth of the hive, until it becomes thick. It is white in spring and dark in summer.

Al-suluk (the course) is passing through the middle of a thing by a path or the like. It was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus We cause it to enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾ [Al-Hijr: 12], in Surat al-Hijr.

It is mostly used transitively, as in the verse of al-Hijr, meaning "I cause it to enter". It is used intransitively, meaning "to pass", as here, because the paths cannot be the object of the transitive verb "salaka". Thus the accusative of "subul" (paths) here is by the elision of the preposition, as a broadening of usage.

The annexing of "subul" (paths) to "your Lord" is an indication that the bee is made subservient to following those paths, and nothing turns it away from them, because if it did not follow them the system of producing honey from it would be disrupted.

"Dhululan" (made easy) is the plural of dhalūl, meaning made tractable and subservient to that course. It was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Not a tractable beast that ploughs the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 71], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿From their bellies comes out a drink﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (istiʾnāf bayānī), because the report of the bee's inspiration to those actions prompts in the hearer's mind the question of the purpose of this wondrous creation. So the content of the clause "from their bellies comes out a drink" is an explanation of what was asked about. It is also the place of the favour, just as it was the completion of the lesson.

[Page 209]

The verb is in the present tense to indicate the renewal and repetition of the coming out.

Honey is referred to by the name "drink" rather than "honey", because of what the generic noun implies of benefit from it, and that is the locus of the favour, and so that it may be followed by the clause ﴿in it is healing for mankind﴾. It was named "drink" because it is a liquid that is drunk, not chewed. The drink was mentioned at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From it you have drink﴾ [Al-Nahl: 10], at the beginning of this surah.

Its description as ﴿of varying colours﴾ is because it has a part in the lesson, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾ [Al-Raʿd: 4]. This is among the signs of great power and subtle wisdom.

Honey has many properties of great benefit, which are explained in the science of medicine.

Healing is placed as contained within honey by way of figurative containment (al-ẓarfiyyah al-majāziyyah), namely association (mulābasah), to indicate the firm connection of healing with it, and as an indication that it does not necessarily follow that healing by it is constant in every state of temperaments. Conditions may arise for temperaments that make drinking honey unsuitable for them. Containment is suitable for indicating that the contained is not present in some parts of the container, because the container is generally wider than the contained. The occurrence of the non-concomitance in some states is likened to the scarcity of the quantity of the contained relative to the breadth of the container in some states of containers and their contents. By this, the description of mankind remains general, and the non-occurrence is only in some incidental states. Were it not for the incidental, all temperaments would be suitable for healing by honey.

The indefinite form of "healing" (shifāʾ) in an affirmative context does not require generality, so it does not require that it is a healing from every disease, just as the sense of "in" in figurative containment does not require the generality of all states.

The generality of the definite form in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for mankind﴾ does not require comprehensive generality for each individual. Rather the generality of the word "mankind" is generality by substitution (ʿumūm badalī), and healing is established for honey in individuals of mankind according to the differences in the needs of temperaments for healing. On this consideration is to be understood what came in the hadith in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri: that a man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "My brother's bowels have been loosened." He said: "Give him honey to drink." So he went and gave him honey to drink, then came back and said: "O Messenger of God, I gave him honey to drink and it only increased his looseness." He said: "Go and give him honey to drink." So he went and gave him honey to drink, then came back and said: "O Messenger of God, it has only increased his looseness." The Messenger of God said: "God has spoken the truth, and the belly of your brother has lied." So he went and gave him honey to drink, and he was cured.

For the meaning is that the healing which God informed of being present in honey is established, and that my brother the questioner's temperament has not developed anything that opposes it. This is indicated by the Prophet's ﷺ command to him to drink honey, for his report implies that honey, with respect to him, remains as God placed healing in it.

Among the delightful rarities is what is in al-Kashshaf: that among the interpretations of the Rafidah (a term for the Shi'i extremists) is that the intended meaning of "the bee" in the verse is 'Ali and his household. It is reported from one of them that he said in the presence of al-Mahdi: "The bees are only the Banu Hashim, from whose bellies knowledge comes forth." A man said to him: "May God make your food and drink a joke among their jests."

I say: The man who answered the Rafidi is Bashshar ibn Burd, and this story is mentioned in the reports about Bashshar.

The clause ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reflect﴾ is like the two similar clauses preceding it; it is a repetition to enumerate the proofs. The attribute of reflection was chosen here because drawing lessons (i'tibar) from the detailed explanation of what the verse stated in summary, concerning the organization of the bee's system, requires the exercise of precise thought and deep consideration.
