This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And take from the station of Ibrahim a place of prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 125], and it is not like the "min" in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He has made for you from the mountains shelters﴾ [Al-Nahl: 81].

"What they build" (mā yaʿrishūn) means what they make into trellises (ʿurūsh), the plural of ʿarīsh. The ʿarīsh is a raised seat above the ground, in a vineyard or a field, made from sticks and roofed at its top with leaves or the like, so that it has shade, and its owner sits in it overlooking what is around him.

It is said: ʿarrasha, when he built and raised. From this, the couch that rises above the ground on which the great sit is called ʿarsh (throne).

This was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾ [Al-Anʿam: 141], in Surat al-Anʿam, and at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what they used to trellis﴾ [Al-Aʿraf: 137], in Surat al-Aʿraf.

The majority of the reciters read the vowel of the "rāʾ" in "yaʿrishūn" with a kasra, while Ibn ʿAmir read it with a ḍamma.

The "thumma" (then) is for ordering by rank (tartīb rutbī), because the inspiration of the bee to eat from the fruits results in the forming of honey in its bellies, and that is higher in rank than the taking of houses, because it is distinguished by honey over other insects that build houses, and because it is of greater benefit to humankind, and because from it comes its food by which it survives. The bee's sucking was called eating (akl) because it feeds on it, so it is not drinking.

The "thamarāt" (fruits) is the plural of thamarah. The original meaning of thamarah is what a tree brings forth as produce, such as dates and grapes, while the bee sucks from the blossoms before they become fruits. Thus the word "fruits" in the verse is applied to the blossoms by way of the figurative sense of the sent (al-majāz al-mursal), by the relation of what was (to what it becomes).

The clause "fa-slukī" (then follow) is conjoined with the particle of consequence (fāʾ al-tafrīʿ), to indicate that God deposited in the nature of the bee, at the time of grazing, the moving from flower to flower and from garden to garden. If it does not find a flower, it goes further afield in search of food. Then, when it is satisfied, it hastens to fly back right after being sated, so as to return to its hives and expel from its bellies the honey that exceeds its food. That course is a consequence of the nature of its eating.

[Page 208]

The explanation of this is that the blossoms and fruits have fine glands that secrete a sugary liquid, which the bee sucks, and it fills with it what resembles storage sacs in its bellies. It becomes sweeter in the bellies of the bees by mixing with chemical substances deposited in the bellies of the bees. When it goes back from its pasture to its hives, it expels from its mouth what has accumulated in its bellies after its body has taken what it needs for its food. This resembles the rumination of ruminant animals. That is honey.

When honey is expelled into the cells of the honeycomb it is liquid and thin. Then it begins to dry out the moisture of the flower waters that is in it, because of the warmth of the wax from which the honeycomb is built and the warmth of the hive, until it becomes thick. It is white in spring and dark in summer.

Al-suluk (the course) is passing through the middle of a thing by a path or the like. It was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus We cause it to enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾ [Al-Hijr: 12], in Surat al-Hijr.

It is mostly used transitively, as in the verse of al-Hijr, meaning "I cause it to enter". It is used intransitively, meaning "to pass", as here, because the paths cannot be the object of the transitive verb "salaka". Thus the accusative of "subul" (paths) here is by the elision of the preposition, as a broadening of usage.

The annexing of "subul" (paths) to "your Lord" is an indication that the bee is made subservient to following those paths, and nothing turns it away from them, because if it did not follow them the system of producing honey from it would be disrupted.

"Dhululan" (made easy) is the plural of dhalūl, meaning made tractable and subservient to that course. It was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Not a tractable beast that ploughs the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 71], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿From their bellies comes out a drink﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (istiʾnāf bayānī), because the report of the bee's inspiration to those actions prompts in the hearer's mind the question of the purpose of this wondrous creation. So the content of the clause "from their bellies comes out a drink" is an explanation of what was asked about. It is also the place of the favour, just as it was the completion of the lesson.

[Page 209]

The verb is in the present tense to indicate the renewal and repetition of the coming out.

Honey is referred to by the name "drink" rather than "honey", because of what the generic noun implies of benefit from it, and that is the locus of the favour, and so that it may be followed by the clause ﴿in it is healing for mankind﴾. It was named "drink" because it is a liquid that is drunk, not chewed. The drink was mentioned at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From it you have drink﴾ [Al-Nahl: 10], at the beginning of this surah.

Its description as ﴿of varying colours﴾ is because it has a part in the lesson, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾ [Al-Raʿd: 4]. This is among the signs of great power and subtle wisdom.

Honey has many properties of great benefit, which are explained in the science of medicine.

Healing is placed as contained within honey by way of figurative containment (al-ẓarfiyyah al-majāziyyah), namely association (mulābasah), to indicate the firm connection of healing with it, and as an indication that it does not necessarily follow that healing by it is constant in every state of temperaments. Conditions may arise for temperaments that make drinking honey unsuitable for them. Containment is suitable for indicating that the contained is not present in some parts of the container, because the container is generally wider than the contained. The occurrence of the non-concomitance in some states is likened to the scarcity of the quantity of the contained relative to the breadth of the container in some states of containers and their contents. By this, the description of mankind remains general, and the non-occurrence is only in some incidental states. Were it not for the incidental, all temperaments would be suitable for healing by honey.

The indefinite form of "healing" (shifāʾ) in an affirmative context does not require generality, so it does not require that it is a healing from every disease, just as the sense of "in" in figurative containment does not require the generality of all states.

The generality of the definite form in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for mankind﴾ does not require comprehensive generality for each individual. Rather the generality of the word "mankind" is generality by substitution (ʿumūm badalī), and healing is established for honey in individuals of mankind according to the differences in the needs of temperaments for healing. On this consideration is to be understood what came in the hadith in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri: that a man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "My brother's bowels have been loosened." He said: "Give him honey to drink." So he went and gave him honey to drink, then came back and said: "O Messenger of God, I gave him honey to drink and it only increased his looseness." He said: "Go and give him honey to drink." So he went and gave him honey to drink, then came back and said: "O Messenger of God, it has only increased his looseness." The Messenger of God said: "God has spoken the truth, and the belly of your brother has lied." So he went and gave him honey to drink, and he was cured.

For the meaning is that the healing which God informed of being present in honey is established, and that my brother the questioner's temperament has not developed anything that opposes it. This is indicated by the Prophet's ﷺ command to him to drink honey, for his report implies that honey, with respect to him, remains as God placed healing in it.

Among the delightful rarities is what is in al-Kashshaf: that among the interpretations of the Rafidah (a term for the Shi'i extremists) is that the intended meaning of "the bee" in the verse is 'Ali and his household. It is reported from one of them that he said in the presence of al-Mahdi: "The bees are only the Banu Hashim, from whose bellies knowledge comes forth." A man said to him: "May God make your food and drink a joke among their jests."

I say: The man who answered the Rafidi is Bashshar ibn Burd, and this story is mentioned in the reports about Bashshar.

The clause ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reflect﴾ is like the two similar clauses preceding it; it is a repetition to enumerate the proofs. The attribute of reflection was chosen here because drawing lessons (i'tibar) from the detailed explanation of what the verse stated in summary, concerning the organization of the bee's system, requires the exercise of precise thought and deep consideration.

[Page 211]

[Qur'an 16:70] "And Allah created you, then He causes you to die, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that after knowledge he knows nothing. Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful."

This is a transition from argument based on the subtle workmanship of Allah as evidence of His oneness, to argument based on His dominion over creation, a dominion that is overwhelming and that they cannot repel, and which proves His sole lordship over them and the greatness of His power. This is indicated by the concluding phrase "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful." He created them without any choice on their part, then He causes them to die against their will, or returns them to a state they dislike, so they cannot resist it or escape from it. Through this, the meaning of servitude (ʿubudiyyah) is realised in its clearest manifestation.

The sentence begins with the Name Allah for the purpose explained when discussing His words [Qur'an 16:65] "Allah sends down water from the sky." As for repeating the Name Allah here instead of using a pronoun, it is because the context of argumentation (al-istidlal) requires repeating the name of the one whose existence is being established, with its letter *dal* having a fatḥah, in order to affirm His attributes with clear explicitness.

The predicate is given as a verbal sentence (fiʿliyyan) to convey restriction of the subject to the verbal predicate in affirmation, as in the example: *anā saʿaytu fī ḥājatika* ("I strove on your behalf" / أنا سَعَيْتُ في حاجَتِكَ). Its parallel has already occurred in His words [Qur'an 16:65] "Allah sends down water from the sky." This is a lesson, and it is also a favour. Creation, which is bringing into existence, is a blessing because of the nobility of existence and humanity. Causing to die also contains blessings for the one who dies, since by it the pains of decrepitude are removed, and blessings for his kind, since by it the condition of the remaining members of the kind is ordered after those before them have passed away. All of this is according to what is generally the case, individually and as a kind, and Allah specifies His blessing and its measure for whomever He wills.

When "then He causes you to die" (ثُمَّ يَتَوَفّاكم) is set against His words [Qur'an 16:70] "and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age," it is understood that the meaning of "then He causes you to die" is at the time of death, which is the customary and usual age, since reaching the most abject age is rare.

Al-arḏal (الأرْذَل, "most abject") is the superlative of *al-radhālah* (الرَّذالَة), which is inferiority in qualities that cause displeasure.

Al-ʿumr (العُمُر, "age/lifespan") is the duration of remaining in life, because it is derived from *al-ʿumr* (العُمُر), which means occupying a place, i.e., the population of the earth. He, the Exalted, said [Qur'an 30:9] "They tilled the earth and populated it." Therefore the construction "most abject of age" (أرْذَلِ العُمُرِ) is an idāfah of an attribute to the thing it qualifies, in the manner of the rational metaphor (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī, مجاز عقلي), because what is truly described as most abject is the state of the human being in his age, not the age itself. So "the most abject age" is the state of bodily decrepitude and weakness of intellect, which occurs within the duration of life. As for the duration of life itself, it is what it is; it is not described as inferior or noble.

Decrepitude (al-haram) does not have a fixed occurrence by a number of years, since it differs according to bodies, lands, health and sickness, and the variation of temperaments within the moderate range. This inferiority is an inferiority of health with no connection to the state of the soul. Thus it befalls both the Muslim and the disbeliever, and it is called "most abject age" for both of them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "sought refuge from being returned to the most abject age."

The lām of causation (lām al-taʿlīl) that enters upon *kay* (كَيْ, "so that") as a verbal particle (maṣdariyyah) is used with the meaning of outcome and consequence, by likening the outcome to the cause, as a metaphor (isti'ārah) which indicates that there is no goal for a person in that prolongation of life. This is an implicit rebuke of people, since they desire long life, and an alert to the necessity of refraining from that desire. It is as if it were said: among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he becomes unable to know what he did not know, because he is slow to accept knowledge, and perhaps he does not conceive of what he receives, and then forgetfulness quickly comes upon him. A person dislikes the state of the decline of his knowledge, because he becomes like the dumb animals.

The use of the causal particle with the meaning of consequence is common in eloquent speech in contexts of reproach, correction, or the like. It was discussed earlier in His words [Qur'an 3:178] "We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin," in Surat Āl ʿImrān. The matter was also discussed shortly before, in His words [Qur'an 16:54] "when a group of you associate partners with their Lord, so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them," in this surah.

The indefinite form of "knowledge" (ʿilm, عِلْمٍ) is the indefinite of genus (tankīr al-jins), and the meaning is: "so that he knows nothing after he had knowledge," i.e., so that the acceptance of knowledge may depart from him.

The phrase "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful" (إنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ قَدِيرٌ) is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl, تَذْيِيل), alerting that the purpose of the sentence is to show the greatness of Allah's power and the greatness of His knowledge. The attribute of All-Knowing is mentioned first, because power operates in accordance with knowledge, and the greatness of power corresponds to the breadth of knowledge. The one of weak power is afflicted with exhaustion from the strength of his knowledge, because his aspiration calls him to what he cannot attain, as Abū al-Ṭayyib said:

*"When souls are great, the bodies grow weary in pursuing their aims."*

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 71:

﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. Yet those who are favoured do not give their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they become equal in it. Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?﴾

This is an argument for the overpowering control (al-tasarruf al-qahir) of God, the Exalted. It follows the argument from giving life and causing death, and what lies between them of decrepitude, with an argument from provision.

Since provision is granted to every existing thing, the argument is built on the inequality within it, unlike the argument in His saying, ﴿And Allah created you, then He causes you to die﴾ [al-Nahl: 70].

The way this verse serves as proof of overpowering control is that provision is granted to all creation, and the distribution of provision among people does not follow their desires or their deserts. You find the shrewdest and most intelligent and most understanding of people restricted in provision, and conversely you see the most ignorant and least capable of planning granted abundance in provision. Both men have had what they have received compelled upon them. The one who is restricted does not know the causes of his restriction, and the one who is granted abundance does not know the causes of the facilitation of his provision. This is because the causes are many, generating one another, linked in a chain, and deeply hidden, to the point that one thinks the causes of both matters are absent, when in fact they are not absent, but they are not encompassed by human knowledge. Among what is attributed to al-Shafi'i:

*And among the proof of destiny and its being
is the misery of the intelligent and the good life of the fool.*

Page 214

For this reason the distribution of provision is ascribed to God, the Exalted, because its causes lie beyond the grasp of human minds. The wise person is not disturbed by this, unlike the saying of Ibn al-Rawandi:

*How many an intelligent person whose doctrines have failed him,
and how many a fool whom you find provided for.*

*This is the one who left thoughts bewildered,
and turned the learned expert into a heretic.*

This judgment indicates the weakness of its author in the reality of knowledge, so how much more so in mastery. Beyond the argument, the verse conveys the sense of a favour, since the statement implies that provision is granted to all.

So the clause ﴿Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision﴾ serves as an introduction to the proof and is one of the favours, because favouring in provision implies bestowing the basic provision itself.

The clause is not the locus of the argument; rather the argument lies in the illustration in His saying ﴿Then those who are favoured do not give their provision...﴾ and so on.

The treatment of the subject being the Name of Majesty (Allah) and the predicate being a verbal sentence built upon it is like the discussion of His saying ﴿And Allah created you, then He causes you to die﴾ [al-Nahl: 70]. The meaning is: Allah, not other than Him, provided for you all and favoured some of you over others in provision, and you cannot but acknowledge this for Him.

The argument was completed at His saying ﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision﴾ through the method of brevity, as it is said: a suggestive flash.

Following this clause, by way of a consequence introduced by "fa" as an incorporation (idmaj), comes His saying ﴿Then those who are favoured do not give their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they become equal in it﴾. This incorporation came in the form of an illustration to demonstrate the error of the people of polytheism when they made some created things equal to the Creator, associating them with Him in divinity, which is corruption in their thinking. This is like what they used to say in the talbiyah of the pilgrimage: "Here I am, no partner is Yours, except a partner who belongs to You, You own him and what he owns." Thus the illustration exposed the falsehood of the belief in associating others with Allah by comparing it with the condition of those blessed with provision, who do not consent to share the surplus of their provision with their slaves; so how can they make His slaves equal to Allah in His supreme attribute, which is divinity?

Page 215

The elegance of this argument is that the two compared conditions and the thing compared to them are the conditions of master and slave, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He has set forth for you an example from yourselves: Do you have among what your right hands possess any partners in what We have provided you, so that you are equal in it, fearing them as you fear one another?﴾ [al-Rum: 28].

The purpose of the illustration is to make their statement appear abhorrent and to show that it is impossible to be true by customary standards, and then to increase the abhorrence by pointing out that they accept for Allah what they would not accept for themselves, as in His saying ﴿And they assign to Allah daughters—glory be to Him—while for themselves they have what they desire﴾ [al-Nahl: 57], up to His saying ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾ [al-Nahl: 60].

The indication of the illustration and its intended purpose is the context.

His saying ﴿Then those who are favoured﴾ is a negation, with "ma" as the negative particle, and the "ba'" in "bi-radddi rizqihim" is the "ba'" that is added to the predicate of a negation introduced by "ma" and "laysa".

Al-radd: the one who gives. As in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "and the fifth is returned to you," meaning: they do not give their provision to their slaves as a sharing, such that they would make them equal to themselves; that is, that does not happen.

Attributing ownership to the right hand is a metaphorical attribution in the intellectual sense (majaz 'aqli), because the right hand is an imagined cause of ownership: the cause of ownership is either capture, which is the result of fighting with the sword held by the right hand, or purchase and payment of the price, which by custom is made with the right hand. So it is an imagined cause arising from custom.

The clause ﴿so that they become equal in it﴾ is connected to the clause ﴿Then those who are favoured do not give their provision﴾; that is, they do not share with their slaves their provision so that they would be equal in it. That is, this does not occur, so that this does not happen. Thus the position of this nominal clause is similar to the position of the verb after the causal "fa" in response to a negation.

As for the clause ﴿Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?﴾, it is suitable to be a consequence of the clause ﴿Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision﴾ in view of what it contains of favour, that is: Allah has bestowed upon you all provision; then do you deny the blessing of Allah? This is an interrogative used for reproach, in that they associated with the One who bestowed favour upon them deities who have no share in bestowing favour upon them,

Page 216

and this is the denial of blessing, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, those you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision; so seek provision from Allah, and worship Him, and be grateful to Him﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 17]. The clause ﴿Then those who are favoured...﴾ up to His saying ﴿so that they become equal in it﴾ is parenthetical between the two clauses.

On this view, "yajhadun" in the reading of the majority with the yā' is a shift (iltifat) from address to third person; its point is that since the intended subject of the argument was the polytheists, and they were the object of reproach, it was fitting to turn away from addressing them and let the aim of reproach reach them by allusion, like the saying of the poet:

*A shallow opinion refused you the gaining of praise,
and a soul whose price God has narrowed from good.*

*When it urges him to good once,
it disobeys him, and if it intends evil, it obeys it.*

Then he states explicitly what was alluded to in His saying ﴿Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?﴾

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, and Ruways, from Ya'qub, read "tajhadun" with the tā' (second person), in accordance with the apparent sense, and the interrogative is then used for warning.

The clause ﴿Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?﴾ may also be a consequence of the clause "Then those who are favoured do not give their provision," so that the reproach is directed at a group among the polytheists, namely those who were favoured with provision, who are the people of abundance among them and their chiefs, and who were most intense in disbelief in the religion and most united against the Muslims. That is: Do those who were favoured deny the blessing of Allah, when He poured the blessing upon them, so that they become even more polytheistic? Like His saying ﴿And leave Me with the deniers, possessors of luxury, and give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11].

On this view, "yajhadun" in the majority reading with the yā' follows the apparent sense, while in Abu Bakr's reading from 'Asim with the tā' it is a shift from third person to address, turning to them directly in order to instil dread into their souls.

Page 217

The verb "yajhadun" has been given a complement by the "bi" because it includes the meaning of "yakfurun" (they disbelieve), and the "bi" is for emphasising the connection of the verb to its object, like "wamsahu bi-ru'usikum" (and wipe your heads). The placing of "bi-ni'mati Allah" before its governing verb "yajhadun" is for the sake of the rhyme of the verse-ending (fasila).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 72:

﴿And Allah has made for you spouses from among yourselves, and made for you, from your spouses, sons and grandchildren, and provided you with good things. Will they then believe in falsehood and deny the blessing of Allah?﴾

It is a conjunction with what precedes it, and it is an argument from the wondrous craftsmanship in the creation of offspring, since it was made to accompany the companionship between the two spouses, in that He made the offspring from both of them, and did not make it separate from one of the two parents or from both of them.

He made offspring known and connected to their origins through the instinct for preserving lineage which man was inspired with. Thus it is among the signs of His oneness, as He said in Surat al-Rum: ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought.﴾ [al-Rum: 21]. So He made it a sign that contains signs, and this craftsmanship includes many blessings, as indicated by His saying ﴿and with the blessing of Allah they deny﴾.

The discussion of the phrase ﴿And Allah has made for you﴾ is like the discussion of its two preceding counterparts, and the lam in ﴿has made for you﴾ serves to transitive the verb (ja'ala) to a second object.

The meaning of ﴿from among yourselves﴾ is "from your own kind," like His saying ﴿so when you enter houses, greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61], meaning "upon the people who are in the houses," and His saying ﴿a messenger from among themselves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164], and His saying ﴿then you are those who kill your own selves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85].

The address with the plural pronoun of the addressees is directed to all people, and the masculine pronoun predominates.

This is a blessing, in that He made the companion of man formed from his own kind. Had He not done so, man would have been compelled to seek companionship with another species, and the companionship between the spouses would not have been attained. This state — although it exists in most kinds of animals — is a blessing that man perceives and that other species do not perceive, and it is not part of the essence of a blessing that the one who is blessed be alone in possessing it.

Al-azwaj (the spouses) is the plural of zawj, which is that thing which becomes two together with another thing; for this reason the word zawj is described by the meaning of "second." The discussion of it has already passed in His saying ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Description by "zawj" indicates its constant association with another, for this reason the female's partner and the male's partner are called zawj. This is a blessing peculiar to man, since Allah inspired him to make a partner for himself, and created him upon a system of love and other such feelings, which do not permit him to neglect his spouse as the dumb animals neglect their females, and their females turn away from their males.

The (min) that enters upon ﴿from among yourselves﴾ is partitive.

He made children a blessing for man, and made their being from a wife another blessing; because through her the children's being his sons is realized in relation to the male, and their continued connection to him in relation to [the mother], and the existence of a partner for him in bearing the responsibility of managing their affairs in their state of weakness.

The (min) that enters upon ﴿from your spouses﴾ is for origination, meaning: He made for you sons descending from your spouses.

The hafadah (grandchildren) is the plural of hafid, like kamalah, the plural of kamil. The hafid originally means one who hastens in service, and it was applied to a son's son, because he often serves his grandfather on account of the grandfather's weakness due to old age. Thus Allah blessed man by preserving the chain of his lineage through the regulation of the first link in it,

that is, that his sons are from his wife, then that the sons of his sons are from their wives. Thus the chain of lineages is regulated by this firm and wondrous system. Other animals do not perceive their grandchildren at all, and they perceive filiation only in the case of the female of the animal for a short period close to nursing. The grandchildren are for man an increase in the family's joy. He said, Exalted is He, ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hud: 71]. The initial (min) has operated upon (hafadah) by means of the conjunction particle, because origination occurs directly and through an intermediary.

The clause ﴿and provided you with good things﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿has made for you from among yourselves spouses﴾ and what follows it, owing to the correspondence with what is in the clauses conjoined to it of including the favour of the blessings of the family members, for its complements are abundant provision, as He said in Al 'Imran: ﴿Adorned for people is the love of desires: women and children, and heaped-up piles of gold and silver﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14], etc.

Tarafa said:

So I have become one of great wealth, and noble sons surround me, lords of the lordly.

Wealth and family do not please one without the other.

Then "provision" may be intended to mean wealth, as in His saying in the story of Qarun: ﴿And those who had desired his place the day before began to say, "Woe to us! Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it"﴾ [al-Qasas: 82]. This is the apparent meaning, and it accords with what is in the verse mentioned just above. It is also possible that what is intended is giving edible good food, as in His saying ﴿and found with her provision﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37].

The (min) is partitive.

The "good things" (al-tayyibat) is an adjective of a deleted noun indicated by the verb (razaqakum), that is, "the good provisions," and the feminine form is for the sake of the plural. Al-tayyib is an intensive adjective pattern (fay'il) describing goodness; its original meaning is purity and pleasant scent, then it was used for what is agreeable and pure of hardship, as He said: ﴿So We will surely give him a good life﴾ [al-Nahl: 97], and it is used for what is wholesome of its kind, as in His saying ﴿And the good land — its vegetation comes out by the permission of its Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 58], in Surat al-A'raf, and from it His saying ﴿those whom the angels take in death while they are good﴾ [al-Nahl: 32], which has been mentioned just above.

So the "good things" here are the abundant provisions that are beloved, as mentioned in the verse in Surat Al 'Imran, or the pleasant and wholesome foods and drinks. The mention of the good things has already occurred at His saying ﴿This day the good things have been made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5] in Surat al-Ma'idah, and the word "good" was mentioned in His saying ﴿Eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Upon this argument and favour there follows a rhetorical question of reproach concerning their belief in manifest falsehood, so the consequence of reproach following it is clearly oriented.

Falsehood (al-batil) is the opposite of truth, because that which does not create is not worshipped in truth. The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿bi-l-batil﴾ before its complement serves to emphasise the identification of their falsehood.

The shift from the preceding address to the third person in His saying ﴿Will they then believe in falsehood?﴾ proceeds in the same manner as what preceded in His saying ﴿Will they then deny the blessing of Allah?﴾ [al-Nahl: 71].

His saying ﴿and with the blessing of Allah they deny﴾ is conjoined to the clause of reproach, and it is a reproach directed at what His saying ﴿And Allah has made for you from among yourselves spouses﴾ up to His saying ﴿and provided you with good things﴾ contains, of the favour of that creation and provision, after both being evidence of Allah's sole divinity.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿and with the blessing of Allah they deny﴾ before its governing verb is for emphasis.

The pronoun of the third person in His saying ﴿they deny﴾ is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), to confirm the judgment of their ingratitude for the blessing, because ingratitude for blessing is more hidden than belief in falsehood, since ingratitude relates to states of the heart. Thus two emphases are gathered in the clause: the emphasis conveyed by the fronting, and the emphasis conveyed by the pronoun of separation.

The use of the present tense in (yu'minun) and (yakfurun) indicates renewal and repetition.

In the combination of yu'minun and yakfurun there is an elegant rhetorical embellishment: antithesis (tibaq).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 73:

﴿And they worship, besides Allah, that which possesses for them no provision from the heavens and the earth at all, and they are not able [to do so].﴾ This is a conjunction with the two sentences of rebuke, and it is an addition to the rebuke, for the two sentences that it is conjoined to convey rebuke for their belief in false deities and their ingratitude for the blessing of the true object of worship.

This conjoined sentence conveys rebuke for giving thanks to one who does not deserve thanks, for worship is a form of thanks. Thus they worshipped what does not deserve worship and has no hand in any blessing, namely the idols, because they do not possess the provision that comes to them, being themselves in need, and they cannot provide them with sustenance, being powerless. So the meaning of this sentence reinforces the meaning of what precedes it, with a difference in the aspect of the rebuke entailed in each of them.

Possession of provision means the capacity to give it. And "possession" (al-mulk) is used for capacity, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Who then can avail anything against Allah if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17] in Surah al-'Uqud. And "provision" (al-rizq) here is a verbal noun in the accusative of the object, meaning: they do not have the capacity to provide.

The "min" (from) in ﴿from the heavens and the earth﴾ is for the starting point, meaning: provision described as coming from the heavens and the earth.

And "shay'an" (anything) is an intensification in the negated, meaning: they do not possess even a small portion of provision. It is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "rizqan" (provision), so it has the sense of a direct object, as if it were said: He does not possess for them anything of provision.

Page 222
﴿And they are not able﴾ is a conjunction with "yamliku" (possesses), so it belongs to the relative clause of "ma" (that which). The plural pronoun refers back to "ma" (that which) in view of its indication of the group of idols worshipped by them, and the plural form used for rational beings was applied to it, in conformity with their belief that they understand, intercede and respond.

The omission of the object of "yasta'ina" (they are able) is for the purpose of generality, meaning: they are not able to do anything, because those idols are stones that are capable of nothing. And "al-istita'ah" (ability) means capability.

So do not strike similitudes for God. Indeed God knows, and you do not know. This is a consequence (*tafri'*) drawn from everything that preceded it of signs, lessons, and favors. From all of these it has been established that God alone is divine, that He has no partner in what He created and bestowed, and, a fortiori, that He has no offspring and is not to be likened to created things. Therefore it is fitting for the context that a prohibition follow: the polytheists are to be restrained from likening anyone other than God to God in any of these respects, and from likening Him to existent things.

This follows the manner of God's words: ﴿O people, worship your Lord who created you﴾ up to His words ﴿So do not set up rivals to God while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:21-22], and His words ﴿And he struck for Us a similitude and forgot his own creation, saying: "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:78].

The word *al-amthal* here is the plural of *mathal* (with two fatha vowels), meaning "the like" (*al-mumathil*), as in the expression *shabah*, meaning "similar" (*mushabih*). The phrase *darb al-amthal* (striking similitudes) has commonly been used for likening one state to another, or one condition to another. Here, however, it is used in a different sense.

The meaning of "striking" (*al-darb*) in the expression "he struck such-and-such as a similitude" has been explained at His words ﴿Indeed God is not ashamed to strike any similitude﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:26] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The lām in *Allah* is connected to *al-amthal*, not to *tadribu*, since the intended meaning is not that they strike the similitude of the idols with God in the way that one strikes an example for people, as in His words ﴿He has struck for you a similitude from yourselves﴾ [al-Rum 30:28].

The reason that polytheism is described as striking a similitude for God is that they attributed to the idols the attributes of divinity and likened them to the Creator. Thus applying the striking of a similitude to it is like His words ﴿And they said, "Are our gods better, or is He?" They did not strike it for you except as a dispute﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:58]. They used to say of these idols, "These are our intercessors with God," and they said the angels are "the daughters of God," being among the nobles of the jinn. This is the striking of a similitude and the likening of God to created beings in being influenced by the intercession of equals and notables, and in being proud of having sons.

The clause ﴿Indeed God knows﴾ gives the reason for the prohibition against likening God to created things, and it alerts the reader that their ignorance is what led them into those absurd beliefs. It also indicates that God, when He forbade them and restrained them from likening Him to what they had likened Him to, forbade them only because He knows the falsehood of their belief.

In His words ﴿and you do not know﴾ there is an invitation to exercise sound reasoning, so that they may reach knowledge free of illusions.

Page 223

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 75:

﴿Allah sets forth an example: a slave owned, who has no power over anything; and one whom We have provided with a goodly provision from Us, so he spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal? Praise be to Allah. But most of them do not know.﴾

It follows their rebuke for likening Allah to His creation, or likening the creation to their Lord, by depicting their situation in this matter as the situation of one who compares a slave with his master in spending. The clause ﴿Allah sets forth an example: a slave﴾ and so on is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani, a new sentence that answers an implied question) arising from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they worship, besides Allah, that which possesses for them no provision from the heavens or the earth at all, and they are not able﴾ [al-Nahl: 73].

He compares the state of their idols in their inability to provide for them with the state of a slave who has no power to act on his own behalf and owns no property. And He compares Allah's state in providing for them with the state of a wealthy owner who disposes of his affairs as he wills, including spending. Knowing the two states being compared is indicated by the context. The intended purpose is to deny equivalence between the two states, so how can they claim that their idols are equal to Allah in divinity? For this reason the clause ﴿Are they equal?﴾ follows.

[p. 224]
He concluded this parable with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, as in Surah Ibrahim: ﴿Have you not considered how Allah sets forth an example: a good word﴾ [Ibrahim: 24] up to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the example of an evil word is like an evil tree﴾ [Ibrahim: 26], and so on. The intended purpose in both contexts is one, and the difference in style only points to the distinction between what is intended first and what is intended second, as we indicated there.

And the 'abd (slave) is a human being whom another human being owns by capture, by purchase, or by inheritance.

The word (slave) is described here by His saying (owned) to emphasize the intended meaning, and to indicate what is implied in the word 'abd of the meaning of ownership, which requires that he does not act with his work in the manner of one who is free.

(Slave) is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for His saying (an example), and this is with an elided noun, i.e. the state of a slave, because the mathal (parable, example) is the form derived from the totality of these attributes. The clause ﴿who has no power over anything﴾ is an attribute of 'abd, i.e. incapable of everything people are capable of, such as being blind, disabled, or deaf, such that he is the least useful of slaves.

This is an example for their idols, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those you invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are created﴾ [al-Nahl: 20], ﴿dead, not alive﴾ [al-Nahl: 21], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 17].

And (min, "who") is a relative pronoun whose referent is free, by the indication that it stands in contrast to an owned slave, and that it is described as having goodly provision: ﴿so he spends from it secretly and openly﴾, i.e. as he wills. This is one of the dispositions of free people, because slaves do not own provision according to the custom of the Arabs. As for the ruling on a slave owning property in Islam, that is referred to other evidences from the foundations of the Islamic Law, and this verse has no connection to it.

Al-rizq (provision) here is a name for the thing by which one is provided.

Al-hasan (goodly) is that which is not marred by any defect in its kind, such as scarcity of availability at the time of need, or quick spoilage like the weevil in wheat, or inferiority like rotten dates. The point of resemblance is the meaning present in the state of the one compared to, namely baseness, lack of fitness to act, and inability to do any work; and in the state of freedom, wealth, and disposing as one wishes.

The clause ﴿so he spends from it﴾ is made a consequence (mufarra'ah) of the preceding one, rather than being made an attribute of provision, to indicate that the content of both clauses is intended for its own sake as a perfection in the one described: his being the possessor of goodly provision is a perfection, and his disposing of his provision by giving is another perfection. Both are the opposite of the deficiencies of the owned slave, who has no power over anything of spending, nor over what he might spend.

He made the predicate a verb to indicate firmness, i.e. he spends with firm spending, and he made the verb present (mudari') to indicate renewal and recurrence, i.e. he continually spends and increases.

(Secretly) and (openly) are two circumstantial accusatives (hal) from the pronoun in yunfiqu, and they are two verbal nouns (masdar) interpreted as an adjective, i.e. secretly and openly in his spending. The purpose of mentioning them is to generalize spending, as a metonymy for the independence of disposal and the absence of any obstacle preventing him from spending.

This is an example for the self-sufficiency of Allah, exalted is He, and His generosity toward people.

The clause ﴿Are they equal?﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿Allah sets forth an example﴾. It clarifies the purpose of the comparison: the parable intends the non-equivalence of the two states, so that from it one may infer the non-equivalence of the people of the first state with the one described by the second state. The interrogative is used for denial.

As for the clause ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾, it is a parenthetical clause between the interrogative that implies negation and the transitional (intiqali) turn introduced by (but). The purpose of this clause is that it has become clear from the parable that Allah alone bestows favor, and therefore He alone deserves thanks, and that their idols do not deserve to be thanked.

Since praise is one of the manifestations of gratitude in the form of speech, it is here used as a metonymy for gratitude, since the discourse concerns the polytheists' failure in the obligation of gratitude, as they praised the idols and abandoned praising Allah. And in the hadith: "Praise is the head of gratitude."

This eloquent clause is brought to indicate the restriction of praise to the dominion of Allah, exalted is He. This is either a restriction claimed (qasr ida'i), because praise is only for a favor, and whoever other than Allah bestows a favor, his bestowal is only a manifestation of the favor of Allah, exalted is He, which flowed through his hands, as was mentioned at the beginning of Surah al-Fatihah; or it is a restriction relative to a particular (qasr idafi, qasr ifrad), to refute the polytheists, since they divided their praise between Allah and their gods.

The reason for this parenthetical clause here is the preceding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And with the favor of Allah they disbelieve﴾ [al-Nahl: 72], ﴿and they worship, besides Allah, that which possesses for them no provision﴾ [al-Nahl: 73]. So when He set forth for them the example that makes clear their error, and followed it with the clause ﴿they are not equal﴾ [al-Tawbah: 19], the reins of discourse were turned to praise belonging to Allah, not to the idols.

The clause ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ is a turn (idrab) for the transition from arguing against them to declaring them ignorant regarding their belief.

He attributed the negation of knowledge to most of them, because among them are those who know the truth but deny it, in order to preserve leadership and to win the obedience of their common folk. So this is a direct censure of most of them, and it is a censure of the few among them by the brand of obstinacy and stubbornness through allusion.

This is similar to His saying, exalted is He, in Surah al-Zumar: ﴿Allah sets forth an example: a man in whom are partners disputing with one another, and a man belonging wholly to one man. Are the two equal in comparison? Praise be to Allah. But most of them do not know﴾ [al-Zumar: 29].

The plural form in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Are they equal?﴾ came out of consideration for the owners of the compared likeness, since they are many idols, each one of which is compared to an owned slave who has no power over anything. So the plural form here is an abstraction of the parable (tajrid lil-tamthiliyyah), i.e. are those equal with the true God, the Powerful, the Disposer? And the plural pronoun of their group was treated as the plural of rational beings (ism jam' al-'alim), by giving precedence (taghlib) to one side of the two parables, which is the side of the powerful God.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 76:

﴿And Allah presents an example: two men, one of them mute, unable to do anything, and a burden upon his master; wherever he directs him, he brings no good. Is he equal to one who commands justice and is on a straight path?﴾

This is a second parable of two states with two states, the aspect of comparison being different. Here what is taken into account is the meaning resulting from the state of the mute man, which is incapacity to perceive and to act, and the impossibility of benefit from him in all his conditions. And the meaning resulting from the state of the man complete in intellect and speech, in his perception of good, his being guided to it, his perfection of his action and the action of the one he guides, is what Allah presented as an example of his perfection and of his guiding people to the truth, and as an example of the lifeless idols which neither benefit nor harm.

In this parable he joined the states of the two men at the outset, then elaborated at the end of the statement, while mentioning the non-equivalence between them, in a style of composition of wondrous concision. For he omitted from the opening of the parable the mention of the second man, confining the mention of him to the conclusion of non-equivalence, as a variation in the contrast between the style of this parable and the style of the preceding one, which is in the words of the Exalted ﴿Allah presents an example: a slave owned, who has no power over anything﴾ [al-Nahl: 75]. Such variation is among the aims of eloquent speakers, out of dislike for repetition, since repeating a style is equivalent to repeating words.

Al-abkam (the mute): the one described as bakam, with a fatha on the ba' and the kaf, which is dumbness from birth at the time of delivery, such that he neither understands nor makes himself understood. Added to his description is that he is a burden who has no power over anything; and this was discussed at the words of the Exalted ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18] at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Page 228.

Al-kall (burden): with a fatha on the kaf, meaning a dependent on people. In the hadith: "Whoever leaves behind a kall, it is upon us" — i.e., whoever leaves behind dependants, we shall provide for them. The root meaning of kall is heaviness, and from it arose figurative meanings that became well known and equal the literal meaning.

Al-mawla (master): the one who takes charge of another's affairs. The meaning is: he is a dependant upon his guardian, not managing his own affairs. This was discussed at the words of the Exalted ﴿Nay, Allah is your Mawla﴾ [Al 'Imran: 150] in Surat Al 'Imran, and at the words of the Exalted ﴿and they are returned to Allah, their true Mawla﴾ [Yunus: 30] in Surat Yunus.

Then his description of little benefit increases with the words of the Exalted ﴿wherever he directs him﴾. That is, his master directs him to a task that he should do or bring about, ﴿he brings no good﴾, that is, he is not guided to what he was directed to; for good is that in which the purpose of the act is achieved and its benefit realised.

The relative clause ﴿who commands justice﴾ indicates that he is wise, knowing the realities, and a sincere adviser to people, commanding them to justice; for he commands this only when he has known it and considered it carefully.

Al-'adl (justice): the truth and the correct, that which accords with reality.

Al-sirat al-mustaqim (the straight path): the way with no crookedness in it. It is applied here to righteous action, since action is likened to conduct and behaviour; when it is righteous, it is like travelling on a path that leads clearly to the intended goal. He is therefore not equal to one who knows no guidance and cannot give direction, but is rather in need of one who supports him.

The first is like the lifeless idols which do not comprehend, and which need someone to guard them and to wipe the dust and dirt from them. The second is an example of His perfection, exalted be He, in His essence and in His overflowing of good upon His servants.

[Page 229]

﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and the matter of the Hour is not but like the blink of an eye or closer. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾ This was among the statements of their disbelief that were related: they swore by Allah that Allah would not resurrect whoever dies. This was because they imagined that the annihilation of this great world and the restoration of bones that have become decayed were something impossible. Allah refuted that immediately by saying that Allah is capable of everything He wills.

Then the discourse moved on from this to the presentation of proofs for the Oneness (of Allah) and His power. The explanation followed in sequence, and the aims varied according to the occasions. Among this was their threat that, if Allah were to seize people for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon the earth a single living creature. But He grants them respite and delays them until a term that He determined in His knowledge, according to His wisdom. And He warned them against being overtaken by it. Then the discourse turned aside into an interjection, reminding them that Allah does not remove from His power any act greater than what is hidden from their perception. The matter of the Hour, whose possibility they denied, and whose delayed arrival deceived them, is something that does not escape the disposal of Allah and His will, whenever He wills it. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, to such an extent that He has left nothing of what was related about them of their disbelief and disputation without making it clear to them, in order to exhaust every excuse for them.

Among the implications of this delay is that its explicit wording includes instruction, and its allusion includes threat and warning.

The lam in His saying ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ is the lam of ownership (lam al-milk). "Al-ghayb" is a verbal noun used in the sense of an active participle, meaning "the things that are absent," and it was discussed in His saying ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. It is what is absent from people's eyes, among hidden things and realms that the senses of earthly creatures cannot reach to witness.

The statement that they belong to Allah also implies, by way of kinayah (metonymy), that He knows them.

[Page 230]

The fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-majrur) conveys exclusivity (hasr), meaning that it belongs to Him and not to another. The lam of ownership also conveys exclusivity, so the fronting serves to emphasize the exclusivity, or it is for emphasis of importance.

"Amr al-sa'ah" means its great matter. Thus "al-amr" is an important matter, as in His saying ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1], and as in the words of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "Nothing came with it at this hour except a matter," meaning a concern and a grave affair.

"Al-sa'ah" is a term that has become predominantly applied to the time of the annihilation of the world, and it is among the unseen matters of the heavens and the earth.

"Lamh al-basar" is the directing of the sight toward the thing seen, since "al-lamh" is looking. The aspect of comparison is that it is something achieved without effort, because the blink of the eye is the easiest and swiftest of the movements of the limbs. It is easier and swifter than moving the feet in walking, and than signalling with the hand.

This comparison is more eloquent than the one in the saying of Zuhayr:

*"So they and the valley of al-Rass are like the hand to the mouth."*

The aspect of comparison may be that the occurrence is certain without hardship, and without delay when Allah wills it and it takes place. On this basis, the statement affirms the possibility of its occurrence and warns against being deceived by its delay.

The aspect of comparison may also be swiftness, meaning the speed of its coming when Allah wills it. That is, it occurs suddenly, without signs, as in His saying ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾ [al-A'raf: 187].

The purpose is to warn them and caution them against being overtaken by the Hour, so that they might desist from what they are engaged in at the time of the warning. It should not be supposed that the blink of the eye is a comparison in the swiftness of its occurrence, for that possibility is void, since the actual occurrence is protected from it.

The "aw" in ﴿or it is closer﴾ is for transitional idrab (a shift in statement, idrab intiqali), a turning away from the first comparison, on the ground that the thing compared is stronger in the aspect of comparison than the thing it is compared to. The speaker gives the listener the impression that he intends to bring the meaning closer to him by way of comparison, then turns away from the comparison, on the ground that what is compared is stronger in the aspect of comparison, and that he finds no likeness for it. So he states this explicitly, and thus the bringing near takes place initially, followed by the expression of the reality secondarily.

[Page 231]

Then, the nearness in His saying ﴿or it is closer﴾ is, according to the first interpretation of "the blink of the eye," spatial nearness, a metonymy for its being within the realm of what is capable, like a thing close at hand to be taken, as in His saying ﴿And We are closer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16].

According to the second interpretation, the nearness is nearness in time, meaning closer in duration to the blink of the eye, that is, swifter in occurrence.

The concluding statement (al-tadhyil) with His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ is suitable for both interpretations.

﴿It is Allah who brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing, and made for you hearing, sight and hearts, that perhaps you may be grateful.﴾ This is a return to the abundant proofs of Allah's sole control over affairs and to the enumeration of blessings upon mankind, linked by conjunction to the clause ﴿And Allah made for you spouses from yourselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 72], after he had interrupted the enumeration of blessings with what the context required of admonition and warning.

In these blessings he has considered the subtle kindness of Allah the Exalted toward people, so that this may serve as a transition to the call to Islam and a statement of the foundations of the call of Islam in His words, the Exalted, ﴿Thus He completes His favour upon you, that perhaps you may submit [to Him]﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], and so on to the end of the passage.

The meaning is: just as He brought you forth from non-existence and placed in you perception and what perception depends upon, namely life, so likewise He will bring you into being on the Day of Resurrection after non-existence.

Since this act is a proof of the possibility of resurrection, it is also a motive to thank Allah by affirming His oneness and rejecting association with Him, for a favour moves the intelligent person to gratitude.

[p. 232]

The opening of the statement with the Name of Majesty (Allah), and making the predicate about Him a verb, has been explained earlier at His words, the Exalted, ﴿And Allah sent down water from the sky﴾ [al-Nahl: 65] and the verses after it.

Ikhraj (bringing forth) means making something appear from one place to another.

Ummahat (mothers) is the plural of umm (mother), and it was discussed earlier at His words, the Exalted, ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], in Surat al-Nisa'.

Batn (belly/womb) is what lies between the ribs of the chest down to the pubic region, and it contains the intestines, the stomach, the liver and the womb.

The clause ﴿knowing nothing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in akhrajakum, because a child at birth has no knowledge of anything. Then his senses gradually convey things to him, so Allah placed in the child the instruments of perception and the roots of thought.

Thus His words, the Exalted, ﴿And made for you hearing, sight and hearts﴾ are explained as meaning that He brought into existence in you the perception of hearing, sight and intellect; that is, their existence in people, until they reach the degree of perfection by which they lead to knowledge of many things, as indicated by its contrast with His words, the Exalted, ﴿knowing nothing﴾, meaning, so you came to know things.

The reason for using the singular for hearing (sam') and the plural for sight (absar) was discussed earlier at His words, the Exalted, ﴿Or who controls hearing and sight﴾ [Yunus: 31] in Surat Yunus, and at His words, the Exalted, ﴿Say: Tell me, if Allah took away your hearing and your sight﴾ [al-An'am: 46] in Surat al-An'am.

Af'idah (hearts) is the plural of fu'ad, whose root meaning is the heart, but it is often used for the intellect, and this is what is meant here. Hearing and sight are the greatest instruments of perception, since through them one perceives the most important particulars, and they are the strongest means of perceiving the necessary sciences.

So what is meant by hearing is the sense by which sounds are perceived, whose instrument is the ear canal; and by sight is the sense that perceives individual entities, whose instrument is the pupil. He mentioned only these two among the senses because they are the most important, and because through them one perceives the evidences for correct belief.

[p. 233]

Then after these two he mentioned the hearts, that is, the intellect, the seat of all perception. The senses convey their perceived objects to it, and this is knowledge of simple concepts (tasawwurat mufradah).

The intellect has another kind of perception, which is the perception of the connection of one of two known things with the other, and this is the assents (tasdiqat), which are divided into self-evident truths (badihiyyat), such as the fact that the negation and affirmation of a thing in every respect cannot coexist, and that the whole is greater than the part;

and into theoretical truths (nazariyyat), also called acquired truths (kasbiyyat), which is knowledge of the attribution of one of two known things to the other after the intellect has moved to join or separate them. For example, the mind may grasp what a body is and what a thing that is newly originated (muhdath, with the d vowelled with fatha) is, but the mere presence of these two concepts in the mind is not enough for the intellect to affirm that the body is newly originated. Rather, there must be other prior knowledge, which indicates the comparison between the quiddity of corporeality and the attribute of origination.

Thus acquired sciences cannot be acquired except through self-evident sciences, and the occurrence of these self-evident sciences happens only when the concepts of their subjects and predicates arise, and the arising of these concepts is only through the aid of the senses in their particulars. Therefore the five senses are the original cause of the arising of these sciences, and hearing and sight were the first of the senses in acquiring concepts and the most important of them.

These sciences are a blessing from Allah the Exalted and a kindness, because through them a person perceives what benefits him and applies his intellect to what guides him to realities, so that he is saved from error that leads to destruction and great calamities. They are therefore a great blessing. For this reason, after mentioning them, He the Exalted said, ﴿that perhaps you may be grateful﴾, meaning that they are a cause for hoping for their gratitude to the One who bestowed them, glorified be He.

The discussion of the meaning of ﴿that perhaps you may be grateful﴾ has passed more than once in its like and parallels.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 79:

Page 234
﴿Have they not seen the birds, made subservient in the air of the sky? None holds them up except Allah. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ The position of this sentence is that of giving the reason for, and providing evidence of, the great power of Allah and the wondrous perfection of His workmanship, and of His kindness toward creatures. When He mentioned the gift of reason and the senses, by which benefits are acquired and harms averted, He drew people's attention to a kindness that they witness most plainly in the weakest of animals: the subjugation of the air to birds, and their creation fit to flutter in it without any teaching, is a kindness toward them, required by the weakness of their constitutions, since they lack the means of defending their lives. So Allah gave them swiftness of movement together with the ability to keep away from whatever humans and beasts might attack them.

Because of this position, the sentence was not joined by conjunction (ʿaṭf) to the one before it, since its content contains no blessing upon humans; rather it is a sign of the power and knowledge of Allah, Exalted. This is unlike its counterpart in Surah al-Mulk, ﴿Have they not seen the birds above them, spreading their wings?﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], which was joined by conjunction to signs indicating the power of Allah, the Exalted, from His saying ﴿And We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5], then He said ﴿And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾ [al-Mulk: 6], then He said ﴿Are you secure that He who is in the heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you?﴾ [al-Mulk: 16], then He said ﴿Have they not seen the birds﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], and so on. For this meaning, this verse alone was followed by the sentence ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

Taskhir (subjugation) means making something submissive to work. It was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subservient by His command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], in Surah al-A'raf.

Al-jaw (the air) is the open space between the earth and the sky; its being attributed to the sky is because it appears, to the observer's eye, joined to the blue dome.

Al-imsak (holding) is firm restraint against escaping. It was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then retain in kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], in Surah al-Baqarah.

Page 235
What is meant here is what holds them back from falling to the earth against their will. Allah's holding them up consists of His creating wings and tails for them, and making the wings and tails capable of spreading, and creating their bones lighter than the bones of other animals, such that when they spread their wings and tails and rise up with their muscles, they become extremely light; so they swim in the air, and their weight is not sufficient to pierce the air beneath them, except when they draw in their wings and tails and bend the sinews of their backbones at the moment they wish to descend to the earth or to lower themselves in the air. Thus they hover in the air however they wish, then they land whenever they wish or when they tire. Had Allah not created them in that state, they would not have been able to stay aloft. So that is called holding, in the manner of metaphor (istiʿarah), and it is a kindness toward them.

The seeing (ruʾyah) is visual, and its verb is transitive by itself; its being followed by the preposition (ilā) is because the verb is construed with the sense of (yanẓurū) (look).

﴿Subservient⦆ (musakhkharāt) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), and the clause ﴿None holds them up except Allah﴾ is a second circumstantial clause.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ألَمْ يَرَوْا﴾ with the third-person masculine yāʾ, following the shift of style (iltifāt) away from addressing the polytheists, as in His saying ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers﴾ [al-Nahl: 78].

Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, Yaʿqub and Khalaf read ﴿ألَمْ تَرَوْا﴾ with the second-person tāʾ of address, following the address mentioned earlier.

The interrogation is one of denial (istifham inkari), its meaning being the denial that they have seen the birds subservient in the air, by treating their seeing them as the equivalent of not seeing them, because the benefit of seeing, namely perceiving what the seen thing indicates about Allah's exclusive divinity, is absent.

The sentence ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ is a resumptive sentence of explanatory resumption (istiʾnaf bayani), because the denial directed at the polytheists for not benefiting from the proofs they see raises a question in the listener's mind: was the failure to benefit from the indication of seeing the birds general among humans? It is answered that the believers derive many indications from that.

Page 236
The emphasis with ﴿inna﴾ (indeed) suits the interrogation of denial directed at those who did not see those signs; so the sentence that indicates the believers' benefit from that indication was emphasized, because the speech is addressed to those who were not guided by that indication, and so they are like one who denies that there is any indication in that for the believers, since the polytheists look through the mirror of their own selves.

Between the denial directed at them for not seeing the subjugation of the birds, and the affirmation of the believers' seeing, there is the figure of antithesis (ṭibāq) as an embellishment. Between the negation of the polytheists' not-seeing and the emphatic affirmation of the believers' seeing, there is likewise the figure of antithesis as an embellishment. And between the pronoun in ﴿yarawā﴾ and the phrase ﴿qawmin yu'minun﴾ there is also opposition, so antithesis occurs three times, and this is the most eloquent antithesis that has come embedded within an explanation.

The plural ﴿āyāt﴾ (signs) is because the birds contain various indications: from the creation of the air, and the creation of the bodies of birds fitted for flight in the air, and the creation of the inspiration in birds to swim in the air, and that they do not fall to the earth except by His will. The signs are specified for the believers because, through the disposition of faith, they have become accustomed to employing their reflection in deducing the realities of things, unlike the people of disbelief, whose disposition of disbelief is naturally inclined to aversion from following those who advise, and to obstinate rejection of the truth.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 80:**

﴿And Allah has made for you from your homes a place of rest, and He has made for you from the hides of livestock tents that you find light (to carry) on the day you travel and the day you settle; and from their wool, their fur, and their hair, furnishings and provision for a time.﴾ This is among the enumeration of the blessings to which Allah inspired humankind, namely the blessing of thought in making dwellings that protect and provide comfort, and what resembles them of clothing and furnishings. It is coordinated (ʿaṭfan) with the sentence ﴿And Allah brought you out from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾ [al-Nahl: 78]. All of these are among the subtle kindnesses for which Allah prepared human intellect and facilitated its means.

Page 237

This is the blessing of the inspiration to take dwellings, and it is the foundation of preserving the species from the calamities of atmospheric events, such as severe cold or heat, and from the dangers of predators and vermin. It is also the foundation of civilization and urban life, because towns and the dwelling places of tribes are established through the gathering of houses, and likewise through the gathering of tents and pavilions.

The discussion of the construction of the sentence ﴿And Allah has made for you﴾ [al-Nahl: 72] is like the discussion of the one before it.

**Wa-buyūt** (houses): the second letter (the bāʾ) may be pronounced with a *ḍamma* or a *kasra*. It is the plural of *bayt*. The *ḍamma* is the regular form, since it follows the pattern *fuʿūl*, which is consistent for the plural of *faʿl* with a fatḥa on the first radical and sukūn on the second. As for the *kasra* on the bāʾ, it is due to the proximity of the *yāʾ* after the bāʾ, since moving from a *ḍamma* to pronouncing a *yāʾ* is heavy. Al-Zajjāj said: "Most grammarians do not know the *kasra*" (i.e., they do not know it as a dialectal form), while Abū ʿAlī demonstrated its permissibility. This was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The *kasra* reading is that of the majority (al-Jumhūr). The *ḍamma* reading is that of Abū ʿAmr, Warsh from Nāfiʿ, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim.

**Al-bayt** (the house) is a place to which a structure is assigned, and a tent that surrounds it, which determines its location so that its builder may take it as a residence to which he returns and in which he shelters from heat and cold. Its enclosure may be of stone and clay, and is called a wall (*jidār*), or of wood, reeds, or other materials, and it is also called *al-akhṣāṣ*. Above its enclosure is placed a covering that shelters it from above, called the roof (*al-saqf*), made of beams and plastered over. These are the houses of the people of cities and villages.

The enclosure of the house may also be made of tanned leather, and is called the dome (*al-qubbah*), or of cloth woven from fur, hair, or wool, and is called the tent (*al-khaymah*) or the pavilion (*al-khibāʾ*). All of these take a shape close to the pyramidal, whose two sides or sections meet at the top, resting on a pole, and extend downward widening in the shape of a cone. These are the houses of the Bedouins in the deserts, the people of camels and sheep, who make them because they are most suitable for their seeking of pasture, so they carry them with them when they move,

Page 238

following the places of grazing for their livestock and the truffles for their sustenance. The house has already been mentioned in the verse ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125] in Surat al-Baqarah.

**Jaʿala** (made) here means "brought into existence," so it takes one object only.

**Al-sakan** is a noun meaning "that which is inhabited," while **al-suknā** is the verbal noun of *sakana fulānun al-bayt*, meaning when someone takes the house as his residence. It derives from *al-sukūn*, meaning "settling."

The word **sakanan** is in the accusative as the object of **jaʿala**.

The phrase ﴿min buyūtikum﴾ ("from your houses") explains *sakanan*, so **min** is explanatory (*bayāniyyah*). Alternatively, it may be taken as indicating origin (*ibtidāʾiyyah*), and the statement then falls under *tajrīd* (a rhetorical device of abstraction), by treating the houses as though they were something other than the residence itself, like the saying: "If you meet so-and-so, you will surely meet from him a sea." The underlying structure is: "And Allah has made your houses for you a residence."

It has also been said that *sakanan* is a verbal noun, but this view is weak. On that reading, the favour refers to the inspiration indicated by the settling, and **min** is of origin, since the beginning of settling occurs in houses.

The word "houses" here includes all their types.

Specifically mentioned are the domes and tents in the words ﴿And He has made for you from the hides of livestock houses﴾, because the domes are made of leather and the tents of woven fur, wool and hair; and these arise from the skin, since the hide is the raw skin with what is on it. When it is tanned and its hair removed, it becomes *al-adīm* (tanned leather).

This is a favour specific to houses that are movable and portable. All of humankind are either people of villages or tribes, or nomads.

**Al-sīn** and **al-tāʾ** in **tastakhiffūnahā** are for finding (*lil-wijdān*), meaning you find them light, i.e., light to carry when you travel, since they are easy to take down from their places, fold, and load onto mounts; and when you dismount to settle in the place you have moved to, they are easy to pitch and secure in the ground.

Page 239

**Al-ẓaʿn** (travel) with a fatḥa on the ẓāʾ and the ʿayn, or with the ʿayn made sukūn. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Abū Jaʿfar, and Yaʿqūb read it with the first form, and the rest read it with the second. It means journeying.

**Al-yawm** (the day) is used for a period and a time, meaning the time of your journey.

**Al-athāth** (furnishings), with a fatḥa on the hamzah, is a collective noun for the things spread out in houses, such as cushions, rugs, and carpets, all of which are woven or stuffed with wool, hair, or fur.

**Al-matāʿ** (provision) is more general than *al-athāth*, and includes sacks, halters, saddles, felt, and hobbles.

**Al-matāʿ** is that by which one enjoys benefit and profit. It derives from *al-mataʿ*, which means "to take something away." Because of attention to its derivation, it is connected with ﴿for a time﴾ (*ilā ḥīn*). The purpose of this connection is an admonition: that these things are or that they are destined for a cessation that prevents their benefit, so that people may be prepared and ready for the Hereafter, and follow what pleases Allah, as He said: ﴿You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 20].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 81:

﴿And Allah has made for you shade from what He has created, and made for you shelters in the mountains, and made for you garments that protect you from the heat, and garments that protect you from your violence. Thus does He complete His favour upon you, that you may submit.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with its counterparts.

The discussion of the composition (naẓm) of "And Allah has made for you" [an-Nahl: 80] is like the discussion of its preceding counterparts.

This is a reminder of the blessing of inspiration toward protecting oneself from the harms of heat and cold while travelling, following on from the favour of the same kind in the state of residence and settlement. It also mentions the blessing of creating the things by which such protection is achieved through the use of what exists, and the making of what a person needs of clothing. God created shade fit for protection from the heat of the sun. He created caves in the mountains so that they could be taken as refuge. He created the materials of clothing, along with the inspiration to the craft of weaving them, and He created iron for making armour for fighting.

The "min" in ﴿mimmā khalaqa﴾ is for the beginning of the extent (ibtidāʾiyyah).

The discussion of "ẓilāl" (shades) has already been covered just above, at His words ﴿Whose shadows incline from the right and the left﴾ [an-Nahl: 48], because shadows are the traces of bodies blocking the light of the sun from falling upon the earth.

"Akhnān" is the plural of "kinn", with the kāf vowelled with a kasra. It is a noun of the form fiʿl in the sense of maf'ūl, meaning "that in which one is sheltered", and these are the caves and the hollows.
