The "min" in His words ﴿mimmā khalaqa﴾ and ﴿min al-jibāl﴾ is partitive (tabʿīḍ). People used to take refuge in the caves at the intense heat of midday or when the rain was heavy, as is recorded in the hadith of the three men who asked Allah by their best deeds, in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī.

"Sarābīl" is the plural of "sirbāl", which is the shirt that protects the body from the heat of the sun, just as it protects it from the cold.

He specified heat here because it was the most common condition in the lands of those addressed at the time of its revelation. Moreover, when He mentioned warmth in His words ﴿And the cattle — He created them for you; in them is warmth﴾ [an-Nahl: 5], He mentioned its opposite here.

The "sarābīl" that protect from violence are iron armour. Among the names of the shirt is "al-dirʿ" (coat of mail), "al-sirbāl", and "al-badan".

"Ba's" means severity in war. Its attribution to the pronoun is in the sense of distribution, meaning that some of you protect others from one another's violence, as He explained with His words ﴿and makes some of you taste the violence of others﴾ [al-Anʿām: 65]. He also said ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great violence﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 25], which is the violence of swords, and His words ﴿And We taught him the craft of making armour for you, to protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 80].

[Page 241]

The clause ﴿Thus does He complete His favour upon you﴾ is a concluding summary (tadhyīl) of the blessings mentioned. The thing referred to is the completion found in the blessings mentioned, or the completion derived from "yutimmu" (He completes).

"La'alla" is for hope, used in the sense of desire: a desire that you submit, that is, that you follow the religion of Islam, which calls you to what results in thanking Allah for His blessings.

The interpretation of the meaning of hope in the words of Allah the Exalted has already been discussed in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿But if they turn away, then upon you is only the clear conveyance [of the message]﴾. This is a consequence (tafri') of the clause ﴿so that you may submit﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], and it comes as an interjection (i'tiraD) between the clause ﴿Thus He completes His favour upon you﴾ [al-Nahl: 81] and the clause ﴿And on the Day We raise up from every nation a witness﴾ [al-Nahl: 84].

He has turned the address away from them to the address of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is a type of iltifat (a shift in style, the turning of discourse from one mode of expression to another) and a turning from the one to whom the speech was directed to addressing another person.

The meaning is: Thus He completes His favour upon you, so that you may submit. But if they do not submit, then upon you is only the conveyance.

The purpose is to console the Prophet (ﷺ) over their failure to respond.

Al-tawalli means al-i'rad (turning away). The verb (tawallaw) here is in the past tense form, meaning: if they turn away from the call, then there is no shortcoming on your part and no blame upon you, for you have indeed conveyed the clear conveyance that makes the way plain.

The restriction (qasr) is relative (qasr idafi, a restriction relative to a particular context). That is: upon you is nothing but the conveyance, not the turning of their hearts to Islam; or, you are not responsible for their recompense for turning away, rather their recompense is upon Us, as in His saying, ﴿But upon you is only the conveyance, and upon Us is the reckoning﴾ [al-Ra'd: 40].

He has made this an answer to the clause (fa-in tawallaw), by placing the cause and reason in the position of the effect and result. The sense of the speech is: if they turn away, then there is no shortcoming and no accountability upon you, [page 242] because upon you is nothing but the conveyance. A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 92].

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 16, verse 83:

﴿They recognise the blessing of Allah, then they deny it, and most of them are disbelievers.﴾ This is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), because their turning away from Islam, despite the abundance of reasons to follow it, raises a question in the mind of the listener: how were the proofs of Islam hidden from them? The answer is that they recognised the blessing of Allah, but they turned away from it out of denial and obstinacy. It is also permissible to make it a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in (*tawallaw*, "they turned away"), and it is also permissible for it to be a comprehensive apposition (*badal al-ishtimal*) for the clause (*tawallaw*).

All of these aspects require that it not be conjoined to what precedes it. The meaning is: they know the blessing of Allah that is counted for them, since they benefit from it. And while they are certain that it is a blessing from Allah, they deny it, that is, they deny its thankfulness. A blessing requires that the one who receives it give thanks to the one who bestowed it. When they worshipped that which does not bestow blessings upon them, it is as if they denied it. The verb (*yunkiruna*, "they deny") has therefore been used in the sense of denying the due right of the blessing. The attribution of the denial of the blessing to them is either a linguistic metaphor (*majaz lughawi*), or a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), meaning that they deny what it is associated with, which is thankfulness.

The (*thumma*, "then") here denotes sequence in rank (*al-tarakhi al-rutbi*), as is its usual function in conjoining sentences. It is therefore a conjunction to the clause (*ya'rifuna ni'mata Allah*, "they recognise the blessing of Allah"), as if it were said: "and they deny it." Because (*thumma*) is used for conjunction, it requires sharing in the ruling, and because it denotes sequence in rank, the meaning of temporal delay for which it is originally designed has been removed from it. Thus it retains the meaning of sharing, and the delay becomes a delay in rank, because denying the blessing of Allah is a strange matter.

The denial of the blessing is shared by all the polytheists, their leaders and their common folk. A group among the polytheists, who are the leaders of disbelief and whose character is reasoning and reflection, recognised the blessing through their affirmation of the Bestower, and through what they heard of the proofs of the Qur'an, to the point that they wavered and doubted the religion of polytheism. Then they stubbornly persisted and insisted upon polytheism. For this reason, that is expressed by denial, which is the opposite of affirmation.

As for His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and most of them are disbelievers﴾, the apparent meaning of the word (*aktharu*, "most") and the word (*al-kafirun*, "the disbelievers") is that those who are described as disbelievers are the majority of the polytheists, not all of them. Therefore the intended meaning of "the majority" is understood as referring to the common folk among the polytheists, for most of them are simple-minded and remote from reflection. They do not perceive the blessing of Allah, since the blessing of Allah requires that He alone be worshipped, so their polytheism was firmly rooted. This contrasts with their intellectuals and people of reflection, for they have hesitation in their souls. However, the love of leadership among their people drives them to disbelief. His statement, exalted is He, about them has already been mentioned in Surah al-'Uqud (Surah 5): ﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against Allah, and most of them do not reason﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103]. They are also those about whom Allah, exalted is He, said in another verse: ﴿It is not you they deny, but it is the wrongdoers who reject the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 33].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 84:

﴿And [mention] the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness, then permission will not be given to those who disbelieved, nor will they be asked to make amends.﴾

The waw (wa) is conjunctive, joining the clause "wa-yawma nab'athu" etc. to the clause ﴿Then if they turn away, your duty is only the clear conveyance﴾ [al-Nahl: 82], with the implied meaning: "And mention the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness." Thus the reminder of that Day is part of the clear conveyance. The meaning is: "If they turn away, your duty is only the clear conveyance; and We will requite them on the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness against them." That is because the description "shahid" (witness) implies that he is a witness over those who believed in him and over the disbelievers, i.e., a shahid, since he conveyed to them the message of Allah.

The raising of a witness from every nation indicates that Muhammad (ﷺ) is a witness over these disbelievers, as the words of the Most High that follow shortly indicate: ﴿And We bring you as a witness over these people﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]. By this, the matter of the conjunction is brought into order, and so is the transition to describing the Day of Reckoning and drawing attention to its importance.

Page 244
"Yawma nab'athu" is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bihi) of a verb that is implied. You may also take "yawma" as accusative in the sense of a circumstantial adverb (zarfiyyah) governed by a deleted operator that is indicated by the preceding speech, estimated in whatever the meaning allows, such as: "We will call them to account with a reckoning from which they will not be asked to make amends," or "they fell into what they fell into of the great calamity."

What prompted this deletion is that what should govern the adverb, namely "la yu'dhanu lilladhina kafaru" ("permission will not be given to those who disbelieved"), has been turned into a clause coordinated to the adverbial clause by the particle "thumma" (then), which indicates a graded (rutbi) sequence, since the original is: "wa-yawma nab'athu min kulli ummatin shahidan thumma la yu'dhanu lilladhina..." to its end. So the adverb remained without a complement, and the hearer had no choice but to estimate it by what his mind inclined to, and this conveys awe and dread, and it is of the marvels of concision (ijaz).

Al-shahid: the witness, al-shahid being the same as al-shahid; its counterpart has already been discussed at the words of the Most High ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ [al-Nisa': 41] in Surat al-Nisa'.

Al-ba'th: bringing him forward to the place of standing.

"Thumma" is for graded sequence (al-tartib al-rutbi), because their being silenced from speech, with the impossibility of making amends, is more severe in dread than the bringing of a witness against them. "Thumma" is not for temporal succession, because the non-granting of permission to them is simultaneous with the raising of the witness against them. The meaning is: they will not be given permission to argue on their own behalf, so the complement of "yu'dhanu" is deleted because it is evident from the words of the Most High ﴿nor will they be asked to make amends﴾.

It is also possible that the negation of permission is a metonymy (kinayah) for expulsion, just as permission was a metonymy for honour, as in the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah: "I have not asked permission of the Messenger of Allah since I embraced Islam except that he granted it to me." In that case no complement is estimated for it. Or it means: they will not be given permission to leave Jahannam when they ask Him, saying ﴿Call upon your Lord that He may lighten for us a day of the punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 49]. So it is like His words ﴿Today they will not be brought out from it, nor will they be asked to make amends﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 35].

Al-isti'tab: its root is seeking al-'utba, and al-'utba is contentment after anger. It is said: "Fulan asta'tabahu fa-a'tabahu," when he pleased him. The Most High said ﴿And if they seek to make amends, they will not be of those who are granted amends﴾ [Fussilat: 24].

Page 245
When it is put in the passive, the original is that its deputy subject (na'ib al-fa'il) is the one from whom contentment is sought. You say: "Fulan asta'taba fa-lam ya'tab." As for what occurs in the Qur'an in the passive, its deputy subject has come as the pronoun of those seeking amends, as in this verse, and as in His words in Surat al-Rum ﴿So on that Day the excuse of those who did wrong will not benefit them, nor will they be asked to make amends﴾ [al-Rum: 57], and in Surat al-Jathiyah ﴿Today they will not be brought out from it, nor will they be asked to make amends﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 35]. Al-Raghib explained it, saying: "Al-isti'tab is that it is sought from a person that he seek contentment." End of quotation.

Upon this, one says: "ista'taba fa-lam yusta'tab." And it is said, according to the original: "ista'taba fulan fa-lam yu'tab," and this usage arose from deletion, its original being "ista'taba lahu," meaning he asked him to make amends; it became so common in usage that the passive of ista'taba has become rare in any meaning other than this one.

"Wa-la hum yusta'tabun" is coordinated to "la yu'dhanu lilladhina kafaru," although it is more specific than it. It is a specific coordinated to a general, for the sake of giving attention to its particularity, to indicate that they are despaired of obtaining contentment from them by all the people of the place of standing, such that they know there is no benefit in asking them to make amends; therefore no one among them advises them to make amends. If "la yu'dhanu" is taken as a metonymy for expulsion, then the meaning is: they will be expelled and will not find anyone who advises them to make amends.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 85:

﴿When those who did wrong see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be given respite.﴾ This is conjoined (ʿatf) to the clause ﴿Then they will not be permitted [to make excuses], those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Nahl: 84]. The word (idhā) is a conditional particle of time (ẓarfiyyah).

The clause (fa-lā yukhaffafu) is the response (jawāb) of (idhā), and the particle (fa) is attached to it to emphasize the sense of conditionality and responsiveness, to remove the possibility that it is a fresh sentence (istiʾnāf).

Page 246.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) took (idhā) to be a pure time-adverb (ẓarf) stripped of the sense of conditionality, governed (manṣūb) by a deleted verb, for the purpose of intensifying the terror. Such an assumption requires that the adverb have no complement (mutaʿallaq), so a complement is supposed for it that suits the context, as was supposed in the words of God Most High ﴿and the day We raise up﴾ [al-Nahl: 84]. The estimate is: when those who did wrong see the punishment, it will weigh heavily upon them and overtake them. On this view, the (fa) in His words ﴿fa-lā yukhaffafu﴾ is explanatory (faṣīḥah), and is not a connective particle for the response.

The phrase (alladhīna ẓalamū) refers to the same people as (alladhīna kafarū), so the use of this designation in place of a pronoun is an explicit mention in place of the implicit (iẓhār fī maqām al-iḍmār). The purpose is to bring the attributes that they have taken on upon them. The meaning is: they will not be permitted [to make excuses], those who disbelieved, nor will they be asked to make amends (yustaʿtabūn). Then they will be driven to the punishment, and when they see it, it will not be lightened for them, that is, they will ask for its lightening, or for the postponement of their being thrust into it, and none of that will be granted to them. The word "punishment" is used to denote its instruments and its place.

The predicate is stated as a verbal clause (jumlah fiʿliyyah) about the subject, because a verbal clause predicated of a noun conveys the strengthening of the judgment. Thus the intention is to strengthen the judgment of negation: that the non-lightening of the punishment for them is certain to occur, with no hope of its being reversed. Thus this clause is emphasized in the same way that the preceding clause is emphasized by (fa). That is, they will be cast swiftly into the punishment.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (*al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*) on Surah 16, verses 86–87:**

﴿When those who associated partners with God see their partners, they will say, "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to invoke besides You." But they will throw the word back at them: "You are indeed liars."﴾ ﴿And they will submit to God on that Day, and what they used to fabricate will vanish from them.﴾

"Those who associated partners" are the same as "those who did wrong," "those who see the punishment," "those who disbelieved," and "those who will not be given leave." Using these three relative clauses (*ṣilāt*, the clauses that follow a relative pronoun) together for them adds to the record against them, showing the various kinds of their crime, which goes back to their denial of what God called them to. This is the reason for using the overt noun in place of a pronoun here, as was mentioned earlier in God's words, ﴿When those who did wrong see the punishment﴾ [an-Naḥl: 85].

The association meant here is their associating the idols with God in the attribute of divinity. So "the partners" must refer to the idols, that is, the partners of God according to their belief. In this sense, the word "partners" is attached to a pronoun referring to "those who did wrong" in God's words, "their partners." This is like the saying of Khālid ibn al-Ṣaqʿab al-Nahdī to ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib. When ʿAmr spoke in a gathering of people, claiming that he had raided Banū Nahd and killed Khālid, and Khālid was present at that gathering, Khālid called out to him: "Easy, Abū Thawr, your slain man is listening," meaning, "your supposed slain man." The attribution here is for mockery. The meaning is: when those who associated partners see the partners they consider to be with them, that is, in their assumption.

You may also take the word "partners" as a title that has lost the sense of being described as a partner and has become a title for the idols. Then the attribution stays in its original sense.

The meaning is that they see the idols when they are thrown with them into the Fire. God said, ﴿Its fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24].

Their saying, ﴿Our Lord, these are our partners﴾, is either a kind of confession made unintentionally, as a disgrace for them, like God's words, ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them﴾ [an-Nūr: 24]. Or it is a kind of disowning responsibility and shifting the blame onto the objects of worship, as if they were saying that these incited them to worship them. This is like God's words, ﴿Those who followed will say, "If only we had another chance, we would disown them as they have disowned us"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167].

The *fā'* in *fa-alqaw* (﴿they threw﴾) indicates immediate sequence, to show the prompt denial of what their statement contained. God made those idols speak, and they denied what their statement contained: that the idols were partners with God, or that their worship was incited by them. This was done to expose them and to cause them regret.

The plural used in the demonstrative and the relative pronoun is the plural of rational beings, in keeping with their belief in the divinity of the idols.

Since the speech of the idols is not something customary, it is expressed by the word "throwing" (*ilqāʾ*), which indicates that God caused the speech to pass over the mouths of the idols without their being speakers, as if it had fallen from them.

Attributing "throwing" to the pronoun of the partners is a rational metaphor (*majāz ʿaqlī*), because the partners are only its place of manifestation.

He used the plural pronoun for rational beings in the verb *alqaw* ("they threw") to harmonize it with the demonstrative and the relative pronoun, which refer to rational beings (*mushākala*).

Describing them as liars relates to what their speech implied: that those are gods invoked besides God. This is like what occurred in the hadith, where it is said to the Christians, "What were you worshipping?" and they reply, "We worshipped the Messiah, the son of God." Then it is said to them, "You have lied; God did not take any son." As for the explicit content of their speech, namely their saying, ﴿These are our partners whom we used to invoke besides You﴾, they are truthful in it.

The clause ﴿You are indeed liars﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for "the word." The verb *alqaw* is repeated in His words, ﴿And they will submit to God on that Day﴾, because the agent of the throwing is different. So the pronoun of the second "word" refers back to those who associated partners.

You may also take the second verb *alqaw* as similar to the earlier verb *alqaw*. You may also take the throwing as an image representing their state in relation to a fighter who is defeated, who throws down his weapon before his conqueror. So in His words *alqaw* there is an implicit metaphorical image (*makniyya tamthīliyya*), together with the harmony of expression (*mushākala*) found in the word *alqaw*. "Salm" with a fathah on the *lām* means submission, that is, obedience and abandoning obstinacy.

﴿And what they used to fabricate will vanish from them﴾ means: what they used to fabricate in the world of the idols, such as their claims that the idols hear them and similar things, will be gone from them and will part from them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 88:

Page 249
﴿Those who disbelieve and bar (others) from the way of Allah — We shall increase them in punishment upon punishment because of what they used to spread corruption.﴾

When he had mentioned the punishment that those who disbelieve in them will face, he here resumed with mention of an increase in punishment for them, in addition to the increase in their disbelief, because they bar people from following Islam. This is what is meant by "barring from the way of Allah" (al-sadd 'an sabil Allah), namely the way that leads to Allah, that is, to being among His allies and His party. The purpose is to alert the Muslims to their scheming and corruption, and to hint at a warning against falling into their snares.

The "increase" of punishment (ziyadat al-'adhab) means doubling it.

The definite article in His saying, ﴿upon the punishment﴾ (fawqa al-'adhab), is the definite article of the known kind (ta'rif al-jins al-ma'hud), since it was previously mentioned in His saying, ﴿And when those who did wrong see the punishment﴾ (Surah al-Nahl: 85). Because the punishment of their disbelief had become known through frequent mention of it, it became like something already known. As for the punishment of their barring people, it does not come to mind; it was therefore unknown, and so indefiniteness (al-tankir) suits it.

The "ba'" in ﴿because of what they used to spread corruption﴾ (bima kanu yufsidun) indicates causation. The meaning is their corrupting of those inclined toward Islam by enticing them to remain in disbelief, as they did with al-A'sha when he came to Makkah desiring Islam, praising the Messenger ﷺ with his ode:

"Did your eyes sleep the night, sleepless?"

His story is in the books of biography (sirah) and literature (adab). And as they did with 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl al-Dawsi: when he came to Makkah, men of Quraysh approached him and said: "O Tufayl, you have come to our land, and this man who is among us has troubled us greatly. He has divided our community and scattered our affair, and his speech is like sorcery. We fear for you and for your people what has befallen us. So do not speak with him and do not listen to anything from him." The account of the conversion of Abu Dharr also mentions how they confronted him with harm in the Sacred Mosque when they learned of his conversion.

[p. 250]

﴿And on the Day We raise up from every nation a witness against them from among themselves, and We bring you as a witness against these people﴾ repeats the sentence ﴿And on the Day We raise up from every nation a witness, then it will not be permitted for those who disbelieved﴾ (16:84). This repetition is what allows the clause ﴿and We bring you as a witness against these people﴾ to be joined by conjunction (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿And on the Day We raise up in every nation a witness against them﴾.

Since it is a repetition, the sentence is restated in the form of an emphatic clause linked by the conjunction "wa" (and). Also, this sentence adds the description ﴿from among themselves﴾, so a difference arises from the previous sentence, and difference itself calls for conjunction.

One of the reasons for repeating the content of the earlier sentence is that there is a long gap between the two sentences, filled by what intervenes between them, from God's words ﴿Then it will not be permitted for those who disbelieved﴾ (16:84) up to His words ﴿for what they used to corrupt﴾ (16:88). So it is like the repetition in the verse of Labid:

*So the two of them contended over a long shadow that flutters, like the smoke of a kindled fire whose flame is ignited,*

*Fed with the growth of arfaj shrubs, its smoke like the smoke of a rising fire, its peaks высоко ...*

Yet the repetition is more fitting here, because the separation is longer.

From this repetition there results the emphasis of the threat and of recording (the matter as a fixed decree).

The verb *nabʿathu* (We raise up) is construed here with the preposition *fī* (in), while its counterpart in the previous sentence is construed with *min* (from). This is done so that variety arises between the two repeated expressions, renewing the attentiveness of the listeners.

In this sentence it is added that the witness is from among themselves, as an increase in reminder that the testimony of the messengers against the nations is a testimony with which they have no grounds for objection, because it is the witness of people from their own folk, and the witnessed-against cannot find in it any room for criticism.

[p. 251]

Also, after the allusion warning against those who bar the disbelievers from the way of God, there is a fitting place for reminding the Muslims of God's blessing upon them, since He has sent among them a witness who testifies for them to what benefits them and to what harms their enemies.

The discussion of the rest of this sentence is the same as what preceded in its counterpart.

Since the witnesses for the past nations were raised, with the meaning of their being raised on the Day of Resurrection, the expression is given in the present tense.

The clause ﴿and We bring you as a witness against these people﴾ may be conjoined to the whole clause ﴿And on the Day We raise up﴾, so the meaning is: "and We bring you, when We sent you to your community, as a witness against them", that is, destined to be a witness against them on the Day of Resurrection. This is because the Prophet ﷺ, at the time this verse was revealed, was alive, and he was a witness in the present and the future. So the past tense was chosen in *jiʾnā* (We brought) to indicate that it is a coming that occurred from the day of his mission.

From this it is known that he will also witness on the Day of Resurrection on equal footing with the rest of his fellow witnesses over the nations, since the purpose of all of that is to threaten his people and warn them. This aspect is highly appropriate for the conjunction to it of His words ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾ (16:89), and so on.

You have learned from this that the clause ﴿and We bring you as a witness﴾ is not conjoined to (*nabʿathu*) in such a way that it enters into the scope of the adverbial phrase, which is *yawma* (the Day); rather it is conjoined to the entire clause *yawma nabʿathu*, because the intended meaning is: "and We bring you as a witness from the time of sending you." On this basis the speech is complete at His words ﴿from among themselves﴾, so it is fitting to pause there for this reason.

It is also permissible that it be conjoined to the clause ﴿We raise up from every nation a witness﴾ (16:84), so that it enters into the scope of the adverbial phrase, and the past tense is used with the meaning of the future figuratively, because its occurrence is certain, so it resembles what has occurred and passed. In that case the pause falls at His words *shahīdan* (a witness), and there results from changing the form of the present verb to the past a preparation for the conjunction of ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾.

The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was not described as being "from among themselves", because he was sent to all nations and is a witness over all of them. As for his being described in that way in God's words ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ (9:128) in Surat al-Tawba, that is a clarifying description required by the context of reminding the addressees among the hypocrites, who, in addition to disbelief in God, added the ingratitude for the blessing of sending a messenger to them from their own people.

There is nothing in His words ﴿against these people﴾ that requires restricting his testimony to being a testimony against those among the polytheists who are being spoken about; rather, He limited it to them because the discourse is about threatening and warning them.

*Hā'ulāʾ* (these) is a pointer to someone present in mind, namely the polytheists about whom the discourse has been extensive. I have traced the occurrences of this demonstrative (*hāʾulāʾ*) in the Qur'an and found that it refers to the polytheists of Mecca. Its explanation has been given before at His words ﴿And We bring you as a witness against these people﴾ (4:41) in Surat al-Nisa', and His words ﴿If these people disbelieve in them﴾ (6:89) in Surat al-Anʿam.

* * *

﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things, and as guidance, mercy and good tidings for the Muslims﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿and We bring you as a witness﴾, meaning: "We sent you as a witness against the polytheists, and We sent down to you the Qur'an so that the Muslims might benefit from it. So the Messenger of God ﷺ is a witness against the deniers and a guide for the believers."

This is a transition (*takhalluṣ*) to beginning the enumeration of the blessings upon the believers: blessings of guidance and blessings of reward for good deeds, and an explanation of the blessings of this Book sent down to them.

[p. 253]

The definiteness of *al-kitāb* (the Book) is for prior reference, and it is the Qur'an.

*Tibyānan* (as an explanation) is an object of purpose (*mafʿūl li-ajlihi*). *Tibyān* is a verbal noun that indicates emphasis in the verbal-noun sense, then it is used with the meaning of the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*), so two intensifications result. It is pronounced with a kasra on the *tāʾ*, and there is no verbal noun of the pattern *tifʿāl* with a kasra on the *tāʾ* except *tibyān* meaning explanation, as here, and *tilqāʾ* meaning encounter, not meaning a place. All other verbal nouns following this pattern have a fatha on the *tāʾ*.

As for the names of entities and attributes following this pattern, they have a kasra on the *tāʾ*, and they are few. Among them are *timthāl* (image) and *tinbāl* (a short person). Ibn Malik, in his poem *Naẓm al-Fawāʾid*, counted them up to fourteen words.

Every "all things" (*kulla shayʾ*) implies generality, except that it is a customary generality, within the sphere of what the religions and laws come for: the reform of souls, the perfection of morals, the rectification of civil society, the clarification of rights, and what the call depends upon of argumentation for divine unity and the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ, and what comes through all that of scientific truths and cosmic subtleties, the description of the conditions of nations, the causes of their success and failure, the admonition drawn from their traces through the evidence of history, and what runs through that of their laws, civilizations and crafts.

Within all of that there are secrets and insights from the foundations of the sciences and knowledge, suitable to be an explanation of all things in the true sense of generality, if the way of detailed explanation is followed in clarifying them, and one is guided in them by what the Messenger ﷺ explained, and what his companions and the scholars of his community followed after him. Then there is what returns to encouragement and warning, from describing what has been prepared for the obedient and what has been prepared for those who turn away, and describing the unseen world and the Afterlife. So in all of that there is an explanation of every thing whose explanation is intended, for the sake of insight into this great purpose. Thus that customary generality is, in its explicit sense, referred back to a true generality by its implications and necessary consequences. This is among the most wondrous aspects of the inimitability (*iʿjāz*) of the Qur'an.

[p. 254]

The guidance, mercy and good tidings are singled out for mention because of their importance. Guidance is what the explanation includes concerning the rectification of beliefs and understandings and the rescue from error. Mercy is what it includes concerning the happiness of both lives, the worldly and the otherworldly. Good tidings are what it contains of the promise of both the worldly and the otherworldly good outcomes.

All of this is for the Muslims and not for others, because when others turned away from it, they deprived themselves of benefiting from all its distinctive qualities.

So the *lām* in *li-kulli shayʾ* (for all things) is connected to *tibyānan* (as an explanation), and it is the *lām* of reinforcement (*lām al-taqwiya*), because *kulla shayʾ* has the sense of a direct object of *tibyānan*. And the *lām* in *lil-muslimīn* (for the Muslims) is the *lām* of purpose (*lām al-ʿilla*), connected by dispute (*tanāzuʿ*) to *tibyānan wa-hudan wa-raḥmatan wa-bushrā* (as explanation, guidance, mercy and good tidings). This is the preferred view.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 90 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice, excellence, and giving to kinsfolk, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing, and oppression. He admonishes you that you may be reminded.﴾ When it was stated that this Qur'an is an exposition of all things, and a guidance, a mercy, and good tidings for the Muslims, it became fitting to transition to the explanation of the foundations of guidance in the legislation of the Islamic religion, which return to the matter of commanding and forbidding, since the whole of the Shari'ah is commanding and forbidding, and God-consciousness (taqwa) is confined to compliance and avoidance. Thus this verse is a resumption to explain that the Book is an exposition of all things, for it comprises the foundations of legislation.

The opening of the sentence with the emphatic particle (inna) is for attentiveness to the matter it contains, and its beginning with the Name of Majesty (Allah) is for honor. The verbs (yamuru, "commands") and (yanha, "forbids") are mentioned rather than saying "be just" and "avoid immorality," for the sake of arousing interest. A parallel to this is the hadith: "Indeed Allah is pleased with three things for you and displeased with three things for you," and so on.

Justice ('adl) is giving the right to its rightful owner. It is the comprehensive principle for the rights that return to the necessary (darury) and the needed (hajiy) of rights, both personal rights and rights of transactions, since the Muslim is commanded to be just in his own self, as He, Exalted, says: ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195], and he is commanded to be just in dealing, and this dealing is of two kinds: dealing with his Creator, by acknowledging His attributes and fulfilling His rights; and dealing with the creatures, which is among the foundations of familial companionship and social association, and this is in words and deeds. He, Exalted, says: ﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative﴾ [al-An'am: 152], and He, Exalted, says: ﴿And when you judge between people, judge with justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 58], and this has preceded in Surat al-Nisa'.

From this branch out the divisions of the system of social transactions: of etiquettes, rights, judicial rulings, testimonies, and dealings with nations. He, Exalted, says: ﴿And let not the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to God-consciousness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8].

The details of justice return to the evidences of the Shari'ah, so justice here is a concise and comprehensive word. With its generality, it suits the circumstances of the Muslims when they were in Makkah, so one resorts to what is established among people in the principles of the laws, and to what the Shari'ah has laid down of clarification in matters of obscurity. Thus the rights of Muslims over one another, of brotherhood and sincere counsel, have become part of justice by the design of the Islamic Shari'ah.

As for excellence (ihsan), it is dealing with goodness from one who is not obliged to one who deserves it. Goodness (husn) is what is beloved to the one who receives it and was not obligatory upon the doer. Its highest level is what is in regard to God, Exalted, which the Prophet ﷺ explained with his saying: "Excellence is that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." Below that is drawing near to Allah through voluntary acts. Then excellence in dealing, in what exceeds obligatory justice, and it enters all words and deeds and with all categories, except what the Shari'ah has forbidden as excellence.

Among the lowest levels of excellence is what is in the hadith of the Muwatta': "A prostitute saw a dog panting from thirst, eating the moist earth, so she took off her shoe, tied it to a rope, drew water for it in a well, and gave it to drink, and Allah forgave her."

And in a hadith: "Indeed Allah has prescribed excellence in all things. So when you kill, kill well, and when you slaughter, slaughter well."

Among excellence is that the one who is benefited repays the benefactor for his kindness, since repayment is not obligatory.

To the reality of excellence return the roots and branches of all the etiquettes of companionship, in the family and in friendship, and pardoning rights that are obligatory is part of excellence, for His saying: ﴿And those who pardon people, and Allah loves the good-doers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134]. And this has preceded at His saying: ﴿And to parents, excellence﴾ [al-Isra': 23] in Surat al-An'am.

Allah singled out for mention, from the genus of types of justice and excellence, a significant type that people often neglect and are negligent of its right or its merit, which is giving to kinsfolk (iytaa dhi al-qurba). For it is established in people's souls to care about attracting the distant and guarding against his evil, just as it is established in them to be heedless of the near and to feel secure on his side, and to become accustomed to laxity regarding his rights. For this reason they commonly took the wealth of orphans from their guardians. He, Exalted, says: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [al-Nisa': 2], and He says: ﴿And give the near relative his right﴾ [al-Isra': 26], and He says: ﴿And what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women﴾ [al-Nisa': 127], and so on. For this reason they directed most of their excellence to the distant, to attract praise and good remembrance among people. This custom remained widespread among people, even in Islam, until now, and they are not concerned about the nearest.

In the Jahiliyyah they used to direct the bequests of their wealth to their companions from the notables of the people. For this reason He, Exalted, says: ﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, that he make a bequest to parents and near relatives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180]. So Allah singled out from among the genus of justice and the genus of excellence the giving of wealth to the kinsman, as an alert to the believers of that day that the relative has more right to fairness than others, and more right to excellence than others, because he is the locus of heedlessness, and because his benefit is more fruitful than the benefit of many other types.

This refers to the reform of the system of family and tribe, preparing people's souls for the rulings of inheritance that were legislated afterward.

The mention of the particular after the general is frequent in speech, for its importance. So giving to kinsfolk has two rulings: obligation for some of it and recommendation for some of it. This was before the prescription of the bequest, and then the prescription of inheritance.

Dhu al-qurba is the possessor of kinship, i.e., of the giver. This has preceded at His saying: ﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative﴾ [al-An'am: 152] in Surat al-An'am.

Iytaa' (giving) is bestowing, and what is meant is giving wealth. He, Exalted, says: ﴿He said: Will you supply me with wealth? What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾ [al-Naml: 36], and He says: ﴿And gives wealth out of love for it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177].

Allah forbade immorality (fahsha'), wrongdoing (munkar), and oppression (baghy), and these are the foundations of corruption.

As for immorality (fahsha'), it is a comprehensive term for every deed or word that souls find abhorrent because of its corruption, from sins that corrupt a person's soul: from false belief, or a deed that corrupts creation, and those that harm individuals, such that they spread corruption among them, through killing, theft, slander, or seizing property; or that harm the condition of society and introduce disorder into it, through armed robbery, adultery, gambling, or drinking wine. Thus everything that causes the disruption of the necessary (darury) interests enters into immorality, and Allah has called them the grave sins (fawahish). The mention of immorality has preceded at His saying: ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden the grave sins﴾ [al-A'raf: 33] in Surat al-A'raf, which is Makkan.

As for wrongdoing (munkar), it is what upright souls reject and what the Shari'ah dislikes, in deed or word. He, Exalted, says: ﴿And indeed, they utter a wrong word and falsehood﴾ [al-Mujadila: 2], and He says: ﴿And you commit wrongdoing in your gatherings﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29]. Rejection has degrees: among them is the degree of the forbidden, and among them is the degree of the disliked, for it is forbidden as well. Wrongdoing includes everything that leads to the disruption of the needed (hajiy) interests, and likewise what nullifies the embellishing (tahsiniy) interests without leading to harm.

Allah singled out for mention a type of immorality and wrongdoing, which is oppression (baghy), out of concern for prohibiting it, and as a blocking of the means to its occurrence, because souls are drawn to it by the impulse of anger, and they are heedless of what it encompasses of the prohibition within the generality of immorality, because of its prevalence among people. The Arabs were people of valor, bravery, and pride, so oppression against others was common among them when a self-admiring person encountered from someone something he disliked, or a treatment he considered humiliating and a lack of honoring him. Thus for the one seeking oppression there would become confused the goodness of defending against what he calls honor, and the ugliness of exceeding the limit of retribution.

So oppression (baghy) is transgression in dealing, either without a corresponding wrong, like the raid that was a means of livelihood in the Jahiliyyah, or by exceeding the limit in response to a wrong, like excessive punishment. For this reason He, Exalted, says: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you, and fear Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194], and He says: ﴿That, and whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with, and then is oppressed, Allah will surely help him﴾ [al-Hajj: 60]. This has preceded at His saying: ﴿And sin and oppression without right﴾ [al-A'raf: 33] in Surat al-A'raf.

This verse has gathered the foundations of the Shari'ah in the command of three things and the prohibition of three things; rather, in the command of two things and a supplement, and the prohibition of two things and a supplement.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated that this verse was the cause of the firm establishment of faith in 'Uthman ibn Maz'un, for when it was revealed, 'Uthman ibn Maz'un was beside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he was newly Muslim, and his Islam was out of shyness before the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet recited it to him. 'Uthman said: "That was when faith settled in my heart." And from 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As: "I was sitting with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when his gaze became fixed, and he said: Jibril came to me and commanded me to place this verse in this position: ﴿Indeed Allah commands justice﴾ the verse." End of quotation. This indicates that this verse was not revealed connected to the verses before it, so its placement in this position is suitable both as an explanation of the verse ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an exposition of all things﴾ [al-Nahl: 89], etc., and as an introduction to what follows: ﴿And fulfill the covenant of Allah when you have made it﴾ [al-Nahl: 91].

And from Ibn Mas'ud: this verse is the most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an.

And from Qatadah: There is no good character that the people of the Jahiliyyah practiced and considered good except that Allah commanded it in this verse, and there is no character that they used to reproach among themselves except that Allah forbade it and disparaged it, and He only forbade the base and blameworthy morals.

Ibn Majah narrated from 'Ali: "Allah commanded His Prophet to present himself to the tribes of the Arabs. So he went out and stopped at a gathering of people from Shayban ibn Tha'labah during the season, and invited them to Islam and to support him. Mafruq ibn 'Amr among them said: To what do you invite us, brother of Quraysh? Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited to them: ﴿Indeed Allah commands justice and excellence﴾ the verse. He said: By Allah, you have invited to the noble morals and the best deeds, and indeed a people have lied about you, and conspired against you."

It is also narrated that the famous words in which al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah testified to the Qur'an, from his saying: "Indeed it has sweetness, and indeed upon it is radiance, indeed its upper part is fruitful, and indeed its lower part is abundant, and it is not the speech of a human being," were said upon hearing this verse.

And the Caliph 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him, was guided to what this verse gathers of meanings of goodness. When he was appointed caliph in the year 99, he wrote commanding the preachers to recite this verse in the sermon on Friday, and its recitation was to replace what they used to say in the Friday sermon of cursing 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. In the recitation of this verse in place of that cursing there is a subtle point: that it requires the prohibition of that cursing, since it is among immorality, wrongdoing, and oppression.

I have not found the time when this cursing was innovated, but it did not occur in the caliphate of Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him.

In al-Sirah al-Halabiyyah it is related that Shaykh 'Izz al-Din ibn 'Abd al-Salam composed a book called (al-Shajarah), in which he explained that this verse includes all the legal rulings in all the chapters of jurisprudence, and al-Subki named it in the Tabaqat (Shajarat al-Ma'arif).

The clause ﴿He admonishes you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the Name of Majesty.

The exhortation (al-wa'z): speech intended to keep the one addressed away from corruption and to urge him toward righteousness. It was discussed earlier at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿So turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [An-Nisa': 63], in Surah An-Nisa'.

The address is to the Muslims, because exhortation is the concern of one who is in need of perfection of the soul; for this reason He paired it with hope, saying ﴿that you may remember﴾.

Remembrance (at-tadhakkur): returning to what was created and forgotten, that is, in hope that you will remember, meaning that you will remember through this exhortation what it comprises; for it is comprehensive and lasting in your souls.

[Page 261]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 91:

﴿And fulfil the covenant of God when you have made it, and do not break oaths after their confirmation, when you have made God your surety. Indeed, God knows what you do.﴾ When God commanded the believers with the essence of benefits (milak al-maslahah), and forbade them from the essence of harms (milak al-mafasid), by what His words indicated, ﴿He admonishes you that you may remember﴾ (An-Nahl: 90), this was a fine connection (munasabah) for this transition, which is among the purposes of the varied style of the Qur'an. He also made clear to them that they had reached perfection and good through that Book which explains everything. Indeed, He reminded them of fulfilling the covenant by which they had pledged to God when they embraced Islam, which is what they had pledged to the Prophet ﷺ, namely: "that they would not disobey him in what is good." The Prophet ﷺ used to take the pledge (bay'ah) from everyone who embraced Islam from the beginning of Islam in Makkah.

The pledge was repeated before the Hijrah and after it, concerning other matters, such as the support (nusrah) that the Ansar pledged on the night of al-'Aqabah, and like the pledge of al-Hudaybiyah.

[Page 261 continues]

The address is to the Muslims concerning the preservation of their covenant by preserving the Sharia. The attribution of the covenant to God (idafat al-'ahd ila Allah) is because they had pledged to the Prophet ﷺ upon Islam, which God had called them to. Thus they had pledged to God, as He said: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to God﴾ (Al-Fath: 10), and He said: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they pledged to God﴾ (Al-Ahzab: 23). The intended meaning is a warning to those who were recent in their acceptance of Islam (hadithu 'ahd bi-al-Islam) against breaking the covenant of God. The word ﴿إذا﴾ (idha, "when") here is merely temporal (li-mujarrad al-zarfiyyah), because the addressees had pledged to God to believe and obey. So the use of the temporal particle is to emphasise the fulfilment. The meaning is: whoever makes a covenant, fulfilling it becomes obligatory for him. The indication of this is His words: ﴿and do not break oaths after their confirmation, when you have made God your surety﴾.

The ﴿عهد﴾ ('ahd, covenant) is an oath (halif), and it was discussed earlier in His words, ﴿those who break the covenant of God after its ratification﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 27), in Surah al-Baqarah. Likewise, breaking (naqd) was discussed in that verse. Breaking oaths (naqd al-ayman) means nullifying that for which they were made. So breaking refers to nullifying what is sworn to, not nullifying the oath itself. He made the nullifying of what is sworn to as the breaking of the oath in His words, ﴿and do not break oaths﴾, to magnify and intensify the seriousness of breaking, because it is a violation of the sanctity of the oath.

And ﴿after their confirmation﴾ is an addition for the sake of warning, and it is not a restriction on the prohibition by a condition of "after," since the intended meaning is known oaths, namely the oaths of the covenant and the pledge, and there is no "after" in them.

And ﴿بعد﴾ (ba'da, "after") here has the meaning of ﴿مع﴾ (ma'a, "with"), since the sense of "after" and the sense of "with" have one effect here, which is the occurrence of the solidifying and confirming of the oaths. Like the saying of al-Shumaydhar al-Harithi:

"O sons of our paternal uncle, do not mention poetry, after you buried the rhymes in the desert of al-Ghumayr."

That is: do not mention that you are poets, and that you have poetry, or do not utter poetry while there are reasons for refraining from it, in the event of the desert of al-Ghumayr. And His words: ﴿Wickedness is a bad name after faith﴾ (Al-Hujurat: 11), and His words, ﴿those who break the covenant of God after its ratification﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 27).

[Page 262]

The ﴿توكيد﴾ (tawkid) is the solidifying (tawthiq) and the repeated twisting (takrir al-fatl). It is not the emphasis of the wording (tawkid al-lafz), as some have mistakenly thought. Rather, it is the opposite of breaking. Its attribution to the pronoun of the oaths is not an attribution of a verbal noun to its subject, nor to its object, since the verbal noun is not intended to express renewal but the noun itself. So it is the original attribution (al-idafah al-asliyyah) in the sense of the lam (of possession), meaning the solidifying that is established for them and specific to them. The meaning is: after what is in them of confirmation. His words, ﴿when you have made God your surety﴾, clarify this.

The meaning is: and do not break the oaths after swearing them. There is no indication in the verse that some oaths are such that breaking them carries no blame, which is what they called the oath of idle swearing (yamin al-laghw). That is a slip away from the course of the Qur'anic composition (mahay' al-nazm al-qur'ani).

What we have explained is supported by His words, ﴿and you have made God your surety over yourselves﴾, which occurs in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (la tanqudu, "do not break"). That is: do not break the oaths while you have made God a surety over yourselves when you swear by His name. The meaning of an oath is calling God as a witness to the truth of what the swearer says. So one brings the name of God as one brings the person of a witness. For this reason the oath is called testimony (shahadah) in many places, as in His words: ﴿so the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by God that he is indeed among the truthful﴾ (An-Nur: 6). The meaning is that this situation is more evident in deserving the prohibition against it.

The kafil (surety) is the witness, the guarantor, and the watcher over a thing, who is concerned with achieving its purpose.

The meaning is that swearing by the name of God is calling God as witness and entrusting oneself to Him. At the time of covenants they used to swear and call sureties to enforce them. Al-Harith ibn Hillizah said:

"And remember the alliance of Dhu al-Majaz, in which covenants and sureties were put forward."

[Page 263 begins]

The phrase ﴿عليكم﴾ ('alaykum, "over you") is connected to ﴿جعلتم﴾ (ja'altum, "you have made"), not to ﴿كفيلا﴾ (kafilan, "surety"). That is: you have placed Him in your own place as surety, so He is the surety and also the one to whom surety is owed (al-makfulu lahu), in the manner of their saying, "you are the adversary and the judge," and His words: ﴿and they thought that there is no refuge from God except in Him﴾ (At-Tawbah: 118).

The clause ﴿إن الله يعلم ما تفعلون﴾ (Indeed God knows what you do) is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah), and it is a statement intended to warn against negligence in holding fast to faith and Islam, by reminding them that God is aware of what they do. So the emphasis with ﴿إن﴾ (inna) is for the sake of giving importance to the statement.

Likewise, the emphasis is by constructing the sentence with a verbal predicate, rather than saying, "Indeed God is All-Knowing," or "God may know."

The present tense was chosen in ﴿يعلم﴾ (ya'lamu, "knows") and in ﴿تفعلون﴾ (taf'alun, "you do"), because it indicates renewal, meaning: whenever they do an action, God knows it.

The purpose of all these sentences, from His words ﴿And fulfil the covenant of God﴾ up to here, is the emphasis of the instruction to preserve the covenant of faith, and to avoid apostasy into disbelief, and to block the entrances of the temptation of the polytheists into the souls of the Muslims. For they turn them away from the path of Islam with various kinds of obstruction, such as their saying: ﴿We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished﴾ (Saba': 35), as His words indicate: ﴿And thus We tested some of them by means of others, that they might say: "Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour from among us?"﴾ (Al-An'am: 53), up to ﴿Is not God most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾ (Al-An'am: 53). This has already been discussed in Surah al-An'am.

The commentators did not mention a cause of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) for this verse, and it does not need one. They mentioned, regarding the following verse, His words ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his faith﴾ (An-Nahl: 106), that the verse ﴿And fulfil the covenant of God when you have made it﴾ up to its end was revealed concerning those who returned to disbelief after faith when the polytheists tempted them, as will come. Thus they made a connection between the two verses.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "It is as if a group among those who had embraced Islam in Makkah was adorned by Satan, due to their anxiety over what they saw of the dominance of Quraysh, and their weakening of the Muslims, and their harming of them. And since they were promising them that if they returned they would break what they had pledged to the Messenger of God ﷺ, God strengthened them." End of quotation. He means that the tone of warning in this speech, up to His words ﴿God only tests you thereby﴾ (An-Nahl: 92), reveals a state of whispering that entered the hearts of some recent converts to Islam, so God informed them of it, warned them against it, and they were safe.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 92:

[Page 264]
﴿And do not be like her who unravels her thread after it has been made strong, into fragments, taking your oaths as deceit between you, lest one community be more numerous than another. Allah only tests you thereby; and He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that about which you used to differ.﴾ This is an admonition regarding the state of those who break the covenant.

It is an continuation (ʿaṭf) on the sentence ﴿And do not break your oaths after their confirmation﴾ [al-Nahl: 91]. The conjunction was chosen because of the difference in meaning between the two sentences, since this second one contains an illustration (tamthīl). Although in terms of its position it is like an emphasis (tawkīd) of the sentence ﴿And do not break your oaths﴾ [al-Nahl: 91], they were forbidden to become a well-known example among the Arabs used for mockery: the woman who unravels her yarn after twisting it firmly. The one who unravelled her yarn was a woman named Rayṭah bint Saʿd al-Tamīmiyyah, from the Banu Tamim, of the Quraysh. She is referred to by means of a relative clause (mawṣūl), because she is famous for the content of the relative clause; and because the content of the relative clause is the state being compared in this illustration; and because the Qur'an does not mention by proper name anyone except those famous for a great matter, such as Jalut (Goliath) and Qarun (Korah).

It is mentioned about her story that she was a foolish woman of disordered mind, who had maidservants. She had made a spindle the length of an arm, a spindle-whorl like a finger, and a large whorl proportionate to that. She and her maidservants would spin from morning until noon, then she would order them and they would unravel what they had spun. She did this every day. Thus her condition was the ruin of what had been beneficial and firm of her work, and returning it to a state of unfitness. So they were forbidden to be in a state like hers in breaking the covenant of Allah, which is the covenant of faith, by returning to disbelief and the deeds of the Jahiliyyah. The point of resemblance is the return to corruption after being clothed in righteousness.

[Page 265]
Al-Ghazl here is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., that which is spun, because it is what accepts unravelling. Al-ghazl (spinning) is the twisting of tufts of wool or hair so that they become threads whose parts are firmly joined, by means of turning the spinning tool, such that the twisted tufts are wound by hand, becoming a thick, long thread of the needed length to serve as warp (suda) or weft (luḥma) for weaving.

Al-quwwah (strength) means the firmness of the spinning, i.e., she unravelled it although it was firmly twisted, with no cause for unravelling it. For if its twisting had not been firm, there would have been an excuse for unravelling it.

Al-ankath, with a fatḥah on the hamzah, is the plural of nikth (with a kasrah on the nūn and sukūn on the kāf), meaning mankūth, i.e., unravelled. Its parallel is naqḍ and anqāḍ. The intention of the plural form is that what was one thread she made unravelled, i.e., into many threads, by reducing it to the state it was in before spinning, namely being threads in number.

Ankathan is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of her thread, i.e., she unravelled it so that it became fragments.

The clause ﴿tattakhidhūna aymānakum﴾ (taking your oaths) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿wa lā tanquḍū al-aymān﴾ [al-Nahl: 91].

Al-dakhal, with two fatḥahs, means corruption, i.e., you make your oaths, which you swore... Al-dakhal also means a corrupt thing. From the speech of the Arabs: "You see the youths like palm trees, and what do you know of the dakhl?" (the khāʾ is sukūn in language, or for metrical necessity if it is verse, or for rhyme if it is prose), i.e., what do you know of the corruption among them? The meaning: you make your oaths, which are the reality by being honoured and sound, corrupt and false, so the description of oaths as dakhal is a rational metaphor (ḥaqīqah ʿaqliyyah); or you make them a cause of corruption among you, as you make them a means of treachery and deceit, so the description of oaths as dakhal is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī).

The aspect of corruption is that oaths require the reassurance of those who swear to each other; when one of the two sides breaks them, he has caused enmity and rancour. This is a warning to them and a frightening of the evil consequence of breaking an oath; it does not imply that a breaking had occurred among them.

[Page 266]
﴿an takūna ummah﴾ (that one community be) is the object of an elided preposition lām, as is most common with ʾan, and the meaning is causal (taʿlīl). It is the cause for the prohibited breaking of oaths, i.e., you break oaths because one community is more numerous than another, i.e., stronger and greater in number.

Ummah means a group and a tribe, and the intended meaning is the group of polytheists and their allies. Arbā means more, and it is the superlative from al-rubuww, on the pattern of al-ʿulūw, i.e., increase. It admits both the literal sense, namely the abundance of number, and the figurative sense, namely comfort of condition and goodness of life. The word arbā gives all these meanings, so no other word can substitute for it in covering all these meanings; its placement here is therefore a requirement of inimitability (iʿjāz). The meaning: let the fact that one community is better than another not move you to break the oaths.

It is known that the community that is better is the one for whose sake the oath is broken, and the less-favoured community is the one separated from; i.e., let the fact that the polytheists are greater in number and wealth than the Muslims not move you to break the oath, so as to separate from the community of the Muslims and return to the disbelievers.

The sentence ﴿innamā yablūkumu Allāh bih﴾ (Allah only tests you thereby) is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf bayānī) answering the causal clause with what the wisdom requires: that by this Allah tests the sincerity of faith, as in His saying ﴿And He raised some of you above others in degrees, that He may test you in what He has given you﴾ [al-Anʿam: 165].

The restriction derived from ﴿innamā yablūkumu Allāh bih﴾ is a restriction of a described thing to an attribute (qaṣr mawṣūf ʿalā ṣifah), and the implied meaning is: that increase is nothing but a trial for you. Al-balw means testing; its attribution to Allah means a metaphor for displaying the condition of the Muslims, and it has parallels in the Qur'an. The pronoun in (bih) refers to the verbal noun derived from the phrase ﴿an takūna ummah hiya arbā min ummah﴾.

Then the emphasis is conjoined to it: that He will certainly make clear to them on the Day of Resurrection what they used to differ about of states, so the realities will appear as they are, not veiled by the adornments of desires nor by the disliked things contrary to natures; for the Hereafter is the abode of realities, with no confusion in it. On that day you will know that Islam is pure good, and that disbelief is pure evil.

[Page 267]
He confirmed this promise with two emphases: the oath indicated by the lām, and the nūn of emphasis. This is further shown in the consequences that follow: bliss comes as a result of faith, and punishment comes as a result of polytheism. All of that is an explanation of what they used to differ about in this world.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 93:

﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one community. But He sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do.﴾

When He deferred the clarification until the Day of Resurrection, He added further information about the wisdom of this deferral. He informed them that He is able to make the truth clear to them in this world, and so make them one community. However, He sent astray whom He willed, meaning He created in him the motive toward misguidance (da'iyat al-dalal), and He guided whom He willed, meaning He created in him the motive toward guidance (da'iyat al-huda). Here He referred the matter to His will in summary, because it is impossible to unfold the secrets of wisdom behind that.

Its reference is to the will of Allah the Exalted that He creates people upon this difference, which arises from differences in states of thought, in levels of perception and intellects. This comes about through great transformations that befall the human being in his procreation, his civilization, and other matters, which His saying the Exalted summarized: ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4] ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 5] ﴿Except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds; for them is a reward uninterrupted﴾ [al-Tin: 6]. This will is not known in its reality except by Allah the Exalted, and its effects appear in the group of those who are guided and the group of those who are astray.

Since His saying ﴿But He sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ may deceive those of short vision, so that they reckon that the misguided and the guided are equal before Allah, and that the misguided are excused in their misguidance because it is an effect of the will of Allah, He followed that with His saying

Page 268
﴿And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do﴾, emphasized with two emphatics, as its counterpart was mentioned just before, meaning: about what you do of deeds of misguidance or deeds of guidance.

And the question (al-su'al) is a metaphor for accountability (al-muhasaba), because it is a wise question upon which illumination (al-inara) is based, and it is not a question of inquiry (su'al istitla'),

[Page 269]

**Surah 16, verse 94:** *"And do not take your oaths as means of deceit among you, lest a foot slip after it was firmly planted, and you taste evil for what you hindered from the way of Allah, and for you is a great punishment."*

When He warned them against the breaking of oaths, which leads to their oaths becoming a means of deceit (*dakhal*) among them, and alluded in general terms to the corruption this causes among them, He returned to explaining the outcome of that action. This return serves to state explicitly the prohibition against it, to emphasize the warning, and to detail the corruption in this world and the evil outcome in the Hereafter. Thus His saying, "*And do not take*" (*wa-la tattakhidhu*), is an explicit prohibition. His saying, "*take your oaths as a means of deceit among you*" (*tattakhidhuna aymanakum dakhalan baynakum*), is an emphasis of His earlier saying, "*take your oaths as a means of deceit among you*" (An-Nahl 16:92). The branching of His saying, "*lest a foot slip*," up to His saying, "*from the way of Allah*," is a detailing of what was summarized in the meaning of *dakhal*.

His saying, "*And for you is a great punishment*," which is conjoined to the branching clause, is a threat of the punishment of the Hereafter. With this introduction and this branching that arises from the clause "*And do not take your oaths as a means of deceit among you*," this verse has become distinct from its earlier counterpart through detail and addition. It is therefore fitting that it be conjoined to it because of this difference, although the norm for an emphatic clause is that it not be conjoined.

*Al-zallal* (slipping) is the slipping of the foot and its moving from its place against the will of its owner, due to the smoothness of the ground caused by wet mud, or the displacement of pebbles or a stone beneath the foot, so that the walker falls to the ground. It was discussed earlier at His saying, "*Then Satan caused them to slip from it*" (Al-Baqarah 2:36), in Surat al-Baqarah.

The slipping of the foot is a figure for the disruption of a condition and exposure to harm, since falling or breaking follows from it, just as the firmness of the foot (*thubut al-qadam*) is the foot's establishment upon the ground, and this is a figure for the uprightness of a condition and the continuation of progress.

Since the intended purpose is to depict what the breaking of oaths brings about of deceit, their condition is likened to the condition of a person walking on a path whose foot was firm, but then it slipped with him and he was thrown down. The thing being likened to is the condition of one man, and for this reason "*qadam*" (foot) is indefinite and singular, since the intention is not a specific foot, nor a number of feet. You say to a group who are hesitating over a matter: "I see you advancing one foot and delaying another," depicting their condition by the condition of a person hesitating in walking toward something.

The addition of "*after its firmness*" (*ba'da thubutiha*), although slipping cannot be conceived except after firmness, serves to depict the difference between the two states, and that it is a descent from a state of happiness to a state of misery, and from a state of safety to a state of trial.

*Al-thubut* is the verbal noun of *thabata*, like *al-thabat*, and it means steadfastness and the absence of movement. Later writers among the scholars of language distinguished *al-thubut* spelled with *waw* as the figurative meaning, namely established certainty, like the establishment of a witness's probity before a judge, and they reserved *al-thabat* spelled with *alif* for the literal meaning. This is a fine distinction.

*Al-dhawq* (tasting) is used figuratively for strong sensation, as in His saying, "*that he may taste the consequence of his affair*" (Al-Ma'idah 5:95), which was discussed in Surat al-'Uqud.

*Al-su'* is what causes pain. Its meaning here is the tasting of evil in this world through their being treated as those who break faith with the religion or as those who betray their covenants.

"*Sadadtum*" (you hindered) here is intransitive, meaning that they were turning away from the way of Allah, as was mentioned just before. This is because the verses came concerning the keeping of the covenant that they made with Allah, that is, adhering to Islam.

Thus, "*the way of Allah*" is the religion of Islam.

His saying, "*And for you is a great punishment*," is the punishment of the Hereafter for returning to disbelief, or for the sin of breaking a covenant.

Allah protected the Muslims from apostasy (*ridda*) throughout the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and no one apostatized except after the Hijrah (*hijra*), when hypocrisy (*nifaq*) appeared. The incident of 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh was a single lapse among the Emigrants. He repented, and the Prophet ﷺ accepted his repentance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 95–96:

﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price. Indeed, what is with Allah is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿What is with you will end, and what is with Allah remains. And We will surely reward those who were patient with their best reward for what they used to do.﴾

The "small price" is what the polytheists promise them, if they turn back from Islam, of wealth and a comfortable life. This is a prohibition against breaking the covenant of Islam, on account of what they would miss by entering Islam of benefits among the people of polytheism. On this basis, this sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And do not break oaths after their confirmation﴾ [al-Nahl: 91] and to the sentence ﴿And do not take your oaths as means of deception among yourselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 94], because each of these sentences addresses a specific aim among the things that may prompt breaking [the oath].

Al-thaman (the price) is the compensation that the one who engages in an exchange takes. The discussion of its counterpart was already presented at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price, and fear Me alone﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41], in Surat al-Baqarah, and we mentioned there that "qalilan" (small) is a descriptive (qualifying) adjective, not a restrictive one, meaning that every compensation taken in exchange for breaking the covenant of Allah is a small compensation, even if it is the greatest of gains.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, what is with Allah is better for you﴾ is a justification for the prohibition, based on describing the compensation of the forbidden exchange as small, for what is with Allah is better than every price, however great its value.

﴿What is with Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11] is what He has stored up for the Muslims of good in this world and in the Hereafter, as we will point out at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while being a believer﴾ [al-Nahl: 97], and so on. The good of this world that is promised is greater than what the polytheists offer them, and the good of the Hereafter is greater than all of it. Thus the "with-ness" here means storing up for them, as you say: "You have such-and-such with me," and it is not the with-ness of Allah's ownership as in His saying ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ [al-An'am: 59] and His saying ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures﴾ [al-Hijr: 21] and His saying ﴿And what is with Allah is enduring﴾.

And (wa-innama) here is composed of (inna) and the relative (ma). Its proper writing would be with (ma) separated from (inna), because it is not the restrictive (ma); but it was written in the Mushaf joined, in consideration of the state of pronunciation, and the joining of its like was not consistent in all places of the Mushaf.

The meaning of ﴿if you only knew﴾ is: if you know the reality of the consequences of things, and the immediate does not deceive you. It contains an exhortation to them toward reflection and knowledge.

The sentence ﴿What is with you will end, and what is with Allah remains﴾ is a concluding (tadhyil) and explanatory sentence for the content of the sentence ﴿Indeed, what is with Allah is better for you﴾, namely that what is with Allah for them is a renewed good that has no end, and that what the polytheists give them is limited and perishable, because the treasures of people are bound to be depleted by giving, while the treasures of Allah remain.

Nafad (ending) is extinction, and baqa' (remaining) is the absence of perishing.

That is, what is with Allah does not perish, so it is more fitting to rely on the gift of Allah promised for Islam rather than on the gifts of people, whose provision runs out, however abundant.

This statement functions as a concluding sentence for what precedes it and is sent forth as a proverb, so it is to be understood in its most general sense. For this reason the pronoun in (with you) refers to all people, by the indication of the concluding sentence and the proverb, and by the indication of the contrast with what is with Allah. That is: what is with you, O people, is what is with the one promised and what is with the one promising, because those forbidden from breaking the covenant have nothing in their own hand.

Since their prohibition from accepting what the polytheists promise them involved urging them to deprive themselves of that immediate benefit, they were promised the reward for their patience in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We will surely reward those who were patient with their reward﴾.

Al-Jumhur read (la-yajziyanna) with the yā' of the third person, and the pronoun refers to the Name of Majesty in His saying, exalted is He, "bi-'ahdi Allah" and what follows it, so He is the One who forbids and promises, and therefore He is the one who recompenses for obedience to His command and prohibition.

Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, and Ibn Dhakwan on the authority of Ibn 'Amir in one of his two narrations, and Abu Ja'far read it with the nun of majesty, so it is a shift (iltifat).

(Ajrahum) is in the accusative as the second object of (yajziyanna), with its being construed to carry the meaning of giving, which transitively takes two objects.

The (ba') is causal, and (ahsan) is a superlative form used for intensification in goodness, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He said: "My Lord, the prison is more beloved to me than what they invite me to"﴾ [Yusuf: 33], meaning: because of their deeds that reach the utmost in goodness, which is the deed of persisting in Islam while swallowing the pain of trial from the polytheists. The promise has been emphasized with the oath particle (lam of oath) and the emphatic nun.
