Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 97:

﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them with their best deeds for what they used to do.﴾ Since the promise mentioned earlier by His saying, ﴿And We will surely reward those who were patient with their best deeds for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 96], was specific to those who were forbidden from exchanging the covenant of Allah for a small price, He followed it with a generalization of it to everyone who equals them in steadfastness upon Islam and righteous action, along with clarification of the reward. Thus this sentence serves as a conclusion (tadhyil) to the one before it and an explanation of the general reward it contains. Both considerations necessitate separating it from what precedes it.

Page 273

His saying, ﴿male or female﴾, is a specification of the generality indicated by the relative pronoun (man). In this clarification there is an indication that the rulings of Islam apply equally to men and women, except for what the religion has restricted to one of the two categories. It also emphasizes this promise, just as it emphasized what it clarifies.

The phrase (la-nuhyiyannahu) is mentioned so that the description of the type of life may be built upon it, by His saying, ﴿a good life﴾, and that verbal noun is the intended object; that is, "We will surely make for him a good life." The promise begins by attributing the giving of life to the divine name (Allah), as an honor to him, as if it were said: "Then for him there is a good life from Us." Since the life of the individual has a specific duration, the term "life" was often applied to its duration, so it is described as "good" in this sense, meaning that what occurs during it is good. This description is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), meaning that what is in it is good, and what accompanies it of the circumstances that befall a person during his lifetime. Thus whoever of the Muslims who did righteousness dies, Allah compensates him for his deed with what he missed of His promise.

This meaning is explained by what is related in the Sahih from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, who said: "We emigrated with the Messenger of Allah seeking thereby the face of Allah, so our reward became due from Allah. Among us were those who passed away without consuming anything of their reward. Among them was Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who was killed on the day of Uhud and left nothing but a woolen cloak. When we covered his head with it, his feet would appear, and when we covered his feet with it, his head would appear. And among us were those whose fruit had ripened for them, so they were gathering it."

Al-tayyib (the good) is what is pleasant and fine; its opposite is al-khabith (the bad) and al-sayyi' (the evil). This is a promise of the goods of this world, the greatest of which is contentment with what Allah has apportioned to them, good hope in the outcome, health and well-being, and the dignity of Islam in their souls. This is a subtle station, in which conditions vary according to the variation of the inner states of souls, and Allah gives His believing servants according to the ranks of their resolves and hopes. Whoever watches over his own soul sees evidences of this.

He followed the promise of the reward of the Hereafter with His saying, ﴿And We will surely reward them with their best deeds for what they used to do﴾. This is therefore specific to the reward of the Hereafter by the contextual indication, unlike its counterpart mentioned just before, which is general in both rewards.

[Page 274]

﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord.﴾ ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him.﴾

The position of the *fa'* of consequence (*fa' al-tafri'*, the particle showing that what follows is a result of what precedes) here is subtle and fine. For this reason, some of the skilled exegetes undertook to investigate it. In *al-Kashshaf*, [al-Zamakhshari] said: "When He mentioned righteous deeds and promised a reward for them, He connected to this His words, ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God﴾, to indicate that seeking refuge is one of the deeds for which a great reward is given." End of quote.

This is the suggestion of a weak connection, which does not establish a firm link between the parts of the composition.

Fakhr al-Din [al-Razi] said: "When He said, ﴿And We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾ [An-Nahl: 97], He guided to the act by which deeds are freed from whisperings." End of quote.

This is more acceptable than the words of *al-Kashshaf*. Abu al-Su'ud added: "Since the basis of the reward is the goodness of the deed, He arranged upon it the guidance to that by which a righteous deed becomes good, namely by being freed from the taint of corruption." In the words of both of them there is a weakness: there is no reason to restrict seeking refuge to the intention of reciting the Qur'an.

As for the statement of Ibn 'Atiyya: "The *fa'* in *fa-idha* (so when) is a connecting particle between the two statements, and the Arabs use it in such a context. Thus the *fa'* in this case is merely for joining one statement to another." He supported this with usage, and the responsibility for it rests upon him.

Sharaf al-Din al-Tibi said: "His words, ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾, are connected by the *fa'* to what preceded, His words, ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation for all things, and as guidance, mercy, and good tidings for the Muslims﴾ [An-Nahl: 89]. This is because, when He bestowed upon the Prophet ﷺ the sending down of a Book comprising all the attributes of perfection, and that it is an explanation of everything, and drew attention to the fact that it explains everything through a comprehensive word, which is His words, ﴿Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct﴾ [An-Nahl: 90]—"

[Page 275]

—"...and the verse [continues], and He joined to it ﴿And fulfil the covenant of God when you have made it﴾ [An-Nahl: 91], and emphasized it with such emphasis, He then said, ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾, meaning: when you begin to recite this noble, comprehensive Book, of which you have drawn attention to some of what it contains, and when Satan contends with you by his prodding and his blowing, then seek refuge in God from him. The intention is to guide the community." End of quote.

This is the best of the interpretations. It had occurred to me before I read his words, and then I found it in his words, so I praised God and asked His mercy upon him. Accordingly, what lies between the clause ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation﴾ [An-Nahl: 89], etc., and the clause ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'taridha*), and the purpose of the consequential connection is the beginning of the praise of the Qur'an.

The name "the Qur'an" is stated explicitly rather than replaced with a pronoun referring to "the Book," in order to indicate the distance of the referent.

The more apparent view is that *qara'ta* ("you recite") is used to mean intending the act, like His words, ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 6], and His words, ﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾ [Al-Isra': 35], and His words, ﴿Those who divorce their wives by *zihar* and then retract what they said﴾ [Al-Mujadilah: 3], meaning: those who intend to return to their wives, by the indication of His words after it, ﴿before they touch each other﴾ [Al-Mujadilah: 3], in Surah al-Mujadilah; and His words, ﴿Let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them﴾ [An-Nisa': 9], in Surah al-Nisa', meaning: those who are about to leave behind after their death; and His words, ﴿And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a screen﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 53], meaning: when you intend to ask them. And in the hadith: "When you sell, say: No deception (*la khilaba*)."

A few scholars took it in its apparent sense of the act occurring, so they made the seeking of refuge to come after the recitation. This is attributed to Malik in *al-Mujma'a*, but the correct report from Malik is the opposite of this. It is attributed to al-Nakha'i, Ibn Sirin, and Dawud al-Zahiri, and it is narrated from Abu Hurayrah.

The *ba'* in *bi-Allah* serves to make the verb of seeking refuge transitive; one says: "he took refuge in a fortress" (*ʿaadha bi-hisnin*), and "he took refuge in the sanctuary" (*ʿaadha bi-l-haram*).

The *sin* in ﴿seek refuge in God﴾ (*fa-ista'idh*) is for requesting, meaning: so request refuge in God from Satan. And *al-'awdh* (refuge) is seeking shelter in that which protects and guards from a harmful matter.

[Page 276]

The meaning of requesting refuge in God is an attempt to take refuge in Him, and this cannot be conceived on God's part except by supplicating that He grant refuge. Among the best forms of compliance is to imitate the grammatical form of the command in what belongs to the category of speech, in such a way that nothing is changed except the change that is unavoidable. Thus the imitation is of the wording *ista'idh*, by what indicates the request for refuge, by saying *ista'idhu* or *a'udhu*; and the word *a'udhu* was chosen because it is one of the forms of performative speech (*insha'*), so that it contains the performance of the request—more hidden than the word *ista'idhu* in the performance of request. This follows the example of another verse: ﴿And say: My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the prompting of the devils﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 97]. And the rest of the wording of the verse of seeking refuge is left in its original form. This is the most excellent of examples. It has been related concerning the Prophet's ﷺ practice in this command that he used to say: "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan," imitating the wording of this verse. He did not say in the seeking of refuge ﴿I seek refuge in You from the prompting of the devils﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 97], because that is outside the recitation of the Qur'an, and the Prophet ﷺ did not imitate it in his seeking refuge for recitation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Nothing has been authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ beyond this wording. What is reported of additions to it has not been authentically transmitted from him at all. There is the hadith of al-Tirmidhi from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: 'When the Messenger of God ﷺ rose at night, he would say: I seek refuge in God, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan, from his prodding...'" and so on. That is a seeking of refuge for seeking protection, and not the seeking of refuge for the sake of reciting the Qur'an.

The name *al-shaytan* (Satan) was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿to their devils﴾ in Surah al-Baqarah, and *al-rajim* (the accursed) was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿and We guard it from every accursed devil﴾ [Al-Hijr: 17] in Surah al-Hijr.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the intended meaning is its generality to his community, by the indication of His words, ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾.

The seeking of refuge was legislated at the beginning of recitation to indicate the preciousness and purity of the Qur'an, since it descends from the holy angelic world. So the beginning of its recitation was made by being free from the psychological imperfections which are from the work of Satan. The servant has no ability to repel those imperfections from himself except by asking God to keep Satan far from him, by seeking refuge in God. For the side of God is holy, and devils do not approach whoever takes refuge in Him. So God guided His Messenger to request [that refuge]

[Page 277]

that, and guaranteed him that He would grant him refuge from it, and grant refuge to his community in a suitable manner, just as the invocation of the name (*tasmiyah*) was legislated for matters of importance, and just as purity was legislated for prayer.

The formula "in the name of God" (*bi-smi Allah*) was not legislated for this purpose because the situation is one of freeing oneself from imperfections, not one of seeking blessing and auspiciousness. For the Qur'an itself is blessing and auspiciousness and complete perfection. So the seeking of blessing is already attained, and it is only that Satan is feared to overshadow its blessings and introduce into them what diminishes them. The recitation of the Qur'an is an expression that includes pronouncing its words and understanding its meanings, and both are exposed to the whisperings of Satan: a whispering that relates to its words, such as forgetting, since forgetting causes the reciter to lose what the forgotten portion contains of guidance; and a whispering that relates to its meanings, such as misunderstanding it or turning its intended meaning upside down. The latter is more severe than the whispering of forgetting. This meaning suits the interpretation of the command to seek refuge at the beginning of recitation.

As for those who understood the command to seek refuge to mean that it is after finishing the recitation, they said: because the reciter is in an act of worship, perhaps conceit (*ujb*) or showing off (*riya'*) enters him, and these are from Satan; so he is commanded to seek refuge from him, for safety from his enticement toward that.

The interpretation of the command in this verse, according to the majority, is recommendation (*nadb*), for lack of indications of obligation (*ijab*). For it has not been established that the Prophet ﷺ made it explicit. Some scholars recommended it absolutely, in prayer and outside it, at every recitation. Some of them made all the recitation of prayer one recitation, so that one seeking of refuge at its beginning suffices, and this is the view of the majority of these. Some of them made the recitation of each rak'ah a separate recitation.

Among the scholars is one who made it recommended for recitation outside prayer, and this is the view of Malik. He disliked it in the recitation of obligatory prayer, and permitted it without recommendation in the recitation of supererogatory prayer.

Perhaps he saw that in prayer there is sufficiency for protection from Satan.

It was also said: the command is for obligation (*wujub*). It was said this is specific to the recitation of prayer, and this is attributed to 'Ata'. The Qur'an has applied the term "Qur'an" to the recitation of prayer in His words, ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is witnessed﴾ [Al-Isra': 78].

[Page 278]

Al-Thawri said it is obligatory in the recitation of prayer and other than it. It is narrated from Ibn Sirin that seeking refuge at recitation is obligatory once in a lifetime. Some people said: the obligation is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, and recommendation applies to the rest of his community.

The sources of these opinions all go back to the interpretation of the verb in His words, "you recite" (*qara'ta*), the interpretation of the command in His words, "so seek refuge" (*fa-ista'idh*), and the interpretation of the Qur'an together with what surrounds this of the Sunnah, both in practice and in abstention.

According to all the opinions: seeking refuge is prescribed for beginning recitation, or for intending it, and it is not prescribed at every utterance of Qur'anic words, such as pronouncing a verse or verses of the Qur'an in teaching, admonition, or the like. This is contrary to what some of the showy pretenders do: when they cite a verse of the Qur'an outside the context of recitation, they say, after "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan," something like "as His words, [the Exalted], say," and then cite a verse.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he has no authority﴾, etc., is an explanation of the command to seek refuge from Satan when intending to recite the Qur'an, and an explanation of the manner of seeking refuge.

As for its being an explanation (*ta'lil*, rationale), it is to increase the urging toward compliance with the command, by showing that seeking refuge prevents Satan's domination over the one who seeks refuge; for God has prevented him from dominating those who believe and rely upon Him. Seeking refuge from him is a branch of the branches of reliance upon God, since taking refuge in Him is reliance upon Him. And in informing of the reason there is an encouragement for the one commanded to act, so that he becomes knowledgeable of the wisdom behind it.

As for its being an explanation (*bayan*, clarification), it is because of what it includes of mention of reliance upon God, in order to clarify that seeking refuge is an expression of reliance upon God, Exalted, for repelling Satan, so that the one seeking refuge fixes his intention upon that. Seeking refuge is not merely a statement without bringing to mind the intention of taking refuge in God.

So the clause ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾ is a second attribute of the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*, i.e., "those who"). The prepositional phrase has been placed before the verb for restriction (*qasr*), meaning: they rely upon none but their Lord. And its verb was made in the present tense to convey the renewal and continuity of reliance. Thus the negation of Satan's authority is conditional upon two matters: faith (*iman*) and reliance (*tawakkul*). From this comes an interpretation of His words in another verse: ﴿Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them﴾ [Al-Isra': 65].

[Page 279]

*Al-sultan* (authority) is a verbal noun on the pattern of *al-ghufran*, and it means domination and firm control.

So the meaning is that faith is the origin of weakening Satan's authority over the soul of the believer; when reliance upon God is added to it, the authority of Satan is repelled from the believer who relies upon Him.

The clause ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) of the explanatory type (*isti'naf bayani*), because the content of the preceding clause raises the question of one who asks: "Then over whom is his authority?"

[Page 280]

The restriction (qasr) derived from *innama* ("only") is a relative restriction (*qasr idafi*), as shown by the contrast with the preceding clause. That is, it means "only" in the sense of excluding those who do not belong to the two groups mentioned, namely "those who believe and upon their Lord rely." Thus the restriction serves to affirm the statement ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe﴾, to heighten attention to establishing its meaning. Therefore, it should not be understood from the restriction that he has no authority over anyone other than these two groups: those believers who neglected reliance upon God, and those who were deceived by some of the whisperings of Satan.

The meaning of *yatawallawnahu* ("take him as a guardian") is that they take him as their ally (*waliyyan*). These are the people who persistently adhere to creeds (*milal*) founded on what opposes Divine guidance (*al-hady al-ilahi*), out of desire for them. There is no doubt that those who take him as a guardian constitute a group other than the polytheists, because the conjunction (*'atf*) by its apparent form requires difference, and they are many categories of the People of the Book. The repetition of the relative pronoun in His words ﴿and those who are polytheists through him﴾ is because their allegiance to Satan is stronger.

He used the present tense (*al-mudari'*) to indicate the renewal of taking him as a guardian, meaning those who renew their taking him as a guardian. This is to alert that whenever they take him as a guardian by inclining to obey him, his authority over them becomes established, and that when taking him as a guardian ceases by abandoning it or by repentance, his authority is stripped from them. The phrase ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾ is conjoined without repeating the relative pronoun, to indicate that the two attributes are like a single relative clause for a single relative pronoun, because the intended meaning is the combination of the two descriptions.

The *ba'* in ﴿through him﴾ (*bihi*) denotes causation, and the pronoun in the genitive refers back to Satan, meaning they became polytheists because of him. It is not like the *ba'* in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and that you associate with God that for which He has sent down no authority﴾ [al-A'raf: 33].

The predicate was made a nominal sentence (*jumla ismiyya*) because of its indication of permanence and stability, since associating partners (*al-shirk*) is a continuous attribute, for its seat is the heart, unlike sins, whose manifestations are the limbs (*al-jawarih*). This indicates that Satan's authority over the polytheists is stronger and more lasting, because its cause is fixed and enduring.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in ﴿through him they are polytheists﴾ serves to convey restriction, meaning they did not associate partners except through his cause, in refutation of their statement ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated [anything with Him]﴾ [al-An'am: 148], and their statement ﴿Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 35], and their statement ﴿We found our fathers upon it, and God has commanded us with it﴾ [al-A'raf: 28].

[Page 274]

﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord.﴾ ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him.﴾

The position of the *fa'* of consequence (*fa' al-tafri'*, the particle showing that what follows is a result of what precedes) here is subtle and fine. For this reason, some of the skilled exegetes undertook to investigate it. In *al-Kashshaf*, [al-Zamakhshari] said: "When He mentioned righteous deeds and promised a reward for them, He connected to this His words, ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God﴾, to indicate that seeking refuge is one of the deeds for which a great reward is given." End of quote.

This is the suggestion of a weak connection, which does not establish a firm link between the parts of the composition.

Fakhr al-Din [al-Razi] said: "When He said, ﴿And We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾ [An-Nahl: 97], He guided to the act by which deeds are freed from whisperings." End of quote.

This is more acceptable than the words of *al-Kashshaf*. Abu al-Su'ud added: "Since the basis of the reward is the goodness of the deed, He arranged upon it the guidance to that by which a righteous deed becomes good, namely by being freed from the taint of corruption." In the words of both of them there is a weakness: there is no reason to restrict seeking refuge to the intention of reciting the Qur'an.

As for the statement of Ibn 'Atiyya: "The *fa'* in *fa-idha* (so when) is a connecting particle between the two statements, and the Arabs use it in such a context. Thus the *fa'* in this case is merely for joining one statement to another." He supported this with usage, and the responsibility for it rests upon him.

Sharaf al-Din al-Tibi said: "His words, ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾, are connected by the *fa'* to what preceded, His words, ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation for all things, and as guidance, mercy, and good tidings for the Muslims﴾ [An-Nahl: 89]. This is because, when He bestowed upon the Prophet ﷺ the sending down of a Book comprising all the attributes of perfection, and that it is an explanation of everything, and drew attention to the fact that it explains everything through a comprehensive word, which is His words, ﴿Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct﴾ [An-Nahl: 90]—"

[Page 275]

—"...and the verse [continues], and He joined to it ﴿And fulfil the covenant of God when you have made it﴾ [An-Nahl: 91], and emphasized it with such emphasis, He then said, ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾, meaning: when you begin to recite this noble, comprehensive Book, of which you have drawn attention to some of what it contains, and when Satan contends with you by his prodding and his blowing, then seek refuge in God from him. The intention is to guide the community." End of quote.

This is the best of the interpretations. It had occurred to me before I read his words, and then I found it in his words, so I praised God and asked His mercy upon him. Accordingly, what lies between the clause ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation﴾ [An-Nahl: 89], etc., and the clause ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'taridha*), and the purpose of the consequential connection is the beginning of the praise of the Qur'an.

The name "the Qur'an" is stated explicitly rather than replaced with a pronoun referring to "the Book," in order to indicate the distance of the referent.

The more apparent view is that *qara'ta* ("you recite") is used to mean intending the act, like His words, ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 6], and His words, ﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾ [Al-Isra': 35], and His words, ﴿Those who divorce their wives by *zihar* and then retract what they said﴾ [Al-Mujadilah: 3], meaning: those who intend to return to their wives, by the indication of His words after it, ﴿before they touch each other﴾ [Al-Mujadilah: 3], in Surah al-Mujadilah; and His words, ﴿Let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them﴾ [An-Nisa': 9], in Surah al-Nisa', meaning: those who are about to leave behind after their death; and His words, ﴿And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a screen﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 53], meaning: when you intend to ask them. And in the hadith: "When you sell, say: No deception (*la khilaba*)."

A few scholars took it in its apparent sense of the act occurring, so they made the seeking of refuge to come after the recitation. This is attributed to Malik in *al-Mujma'a*, but the correct report from Malik is the opposite of this. It is attributed to al-Nakha'i, Ibn Sirin, and Dawud al-Zahiri, and it is narrated from Abu Hurayrah.

The *ba'* in *bi-Allah* serves to make the verb of seeking refuge transitive; one says: "he took refuge in a fortress" (*ʿaadha bi-hisnin*), and "he took refuge in the sanctuary" (*ʿaadha bi-l-haram*).

The *sin* in ﴿seek refuge in God﴾ (*fa-ista'idh*) is for requesting, meaning: so request refuge in God from Satan. And *al-'awdh* (refuge) is seeking shelter in that which protects and guards from a harmful matter.

[Page 276]

The meaning of requesting refuge in God is an attempt to take refuge in Him, and this cannot be conceived on God's part except by supplicating that He grant refuge. Among the best forms of compliance is to imitate the grammatical form of the command in what belongs to the category of speech, in such a way that nothing is changed except the change that is unavoidable. Thus the imitation is of the wording *ista'idh*, by what indicates the request for refuge, by saying *ista'idhu* or *a'udhu*; and the word *a'udhu* was chosen because it is one of the forms of performative speech (*insha'*), so that it contains the performance of the request—more hidden than the word *ista'idhu* in the performance of request. This follows the example of another verse: ﴿And say: My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the prompting of the devils﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 97]. And the rest of the wording of the verse of seeking refuge is left in its original form. This is the most excellent of examples. It has been related concerning the Prophet's ﷺ practice in this command that he used to say: "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan," imitating the wording of this verse. He did not say in the seeking of refuge ﴿I seek refuge in You from the prompting of the devils﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 97], because that is outside the recitation of the Qur'an, and the Prophet ﷺ did not imitate it in his seeking refuge for recitation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Nothing has been authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ beyond this wording. What is reported of additions to it has not been authentically transmitted from him at all. There is the hadith of al-Tirmidhi from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: 'When the Messenger of God ﷺ rose at night, he would say: I seek refuge in God, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan, from his prodding...'" and so on. That is a seeking of refuge for seeking protection, and not the seeking of refuge for the sake of reciting the Qur'an.

The name *al-shaytan* (Satan) was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿to their devils﴾ in Surah al-Baqarah, and *al-rajim* (the accursed) was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿and We guard it from every accursed devil﴾ [Al-Hijr: 17] in Surah al-Hijr.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the intended meaning is its generality to his community, by the indication of His words, ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾.

The seeking of refuge was legislated at the beginning of recitation to indicate the preciousness and purity of the Qur'an, since it descends from the holy angelic world. So the beginning of its recitation was made by being free from the psychological imperfections which are from the work of Satan. The servant has no ability to repel those imperfections from himself except by asking God to keep Satan far from him, by seeking refuge in God. For the side of God is holy, and devils do not approach whoever takes refuge in Him. So God guided His Messenger to request [that refuge]
