The *ba'* in *bi-Allah* serves to make the verb of seeking refuge transitive; one says: "he took refuge in a fortress" (*ʿaadha bi-hisnin*), and "he took refuge in the sanctuary" (*ʿaadha bi-l-haram*).

The *sin* in ﴿seek refuge in God﴾ (*fa-ista'idh*) is for requesting, meaning: so request refuge in God from Satan. And *al-'awdh* (refuge) is seeking shelter in that which protects and guards from a harmful matter.

[Page 276]

The meaning of requesting refuge in God is an attempt to take refuge in Him, and this cannot be conceived on God's part except by supplicating that He grant refuge. Among the best forms of compliance is to imitate the grammatical form of the command in what belongs to the category of speech, in such a way that nothing is changed except the change that is unavoidable. Thus the imitation is of the wording *ista'idh*, by what indicates the request for refuge, by saying *ista'idhu* or *a'udhu*; and the word *a'udhu* was chosen because it is one of the forms of performative speech (*insha'*), so that it contains the performance of the request—more hidden than the word *ista'idhu* in the performance of request. This follows the example of another verse: ﴿And say: My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the prompting of the devils﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 97]. And the rest of the wording of the verse of seeking refuge is left in its original form. This is the most excellent of examples. It has been related concerning the Prophet's ﷺ practice in this command that he used to say: "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan," imitating the wording of this verse. He did not say in the seeking of refuge ﴿I seek refuge in You from the prompting of the devils﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 97], because that is outside the recitation of the Qur'an, and the Prophet ﷺ did not imitate it in his seeking refuge for recitation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Nothing has been authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ beyond this wording. What is reported of additions to it has not been authentically transmitted from him at all. There is the hadith of al-Tirmidhi from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: 'When the Messenger of God ﷺ rose at night, he would say: I seek refuge in God, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan, from his prodding...'" and so on. That is a seeking of refuge for seeking protection, and not the seeking of refuge for the sake of reciting the Qur'an.

The name *al-shaytan* (Satan) was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿to their devils﴾ in Surah al-Baqarah, and *al-rajim* (the accursed) was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿and We guard it from every accursed devil﴾ [Al-Hijr: 17] in Surah al-Hijr.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the intended meaning is its generality to his community, by the indication of His words, ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾.

The seeking of refuge was legislated at the beginning of recitation to indicate the preciousness and purity of the Qur'an, since it descends from the holy angelic world. So the beginning of its recitation was made by being free from the psychological imperfections which are from the work of Satan. The servant has no ability to repel those imperfections from himself except by asking God to keep Satan far from him, by seeking refuge in God. For the side of God is holy, and devils do not approach whoever takes refuge in Him. So God guided His Messenger to request [that refuge]

[Page 277]

that, and guaranteed him that He would grant him refuge from it, and grant refuge to his community in a suitable manner, just as the invocation of the name (*tasmiyah*) was legislated for matters of importance, and just as purity was legislated for prayer.

The formula "in the name of God" (*bi-smi Allah*) was not legislated for this purpose because the situation is one of freeing oneself from imperfections, not one of seeking blessing and auspiciousness. For the Qur'an itself is blessing and auspiciousness and complete perfection. So the seeking of blessing is already attained, and it is only that Satan is feared to overshadow its blessings and introduce into them what diminishes them. The recitation of the Qur'an is an expression that includes pronouncing its words and understanding its meanings, and both are exposed to the whisperings of Satan: a whispering that relates to its words, such as forgetting, since forgetting causes the reciter to lose what the forgotten portion contains of guidance; and a whispering that relates to its meanings, such as misunderstanding it or turning its intended meaning upside down. The latter is more severe than the whispering of forgetting. This meaning suits the interpretation of the command to seek refuge at the beginning of recitation.

As for those who understood the command to seek refuge to mean that it is after finishing the recitation, they said: because the reciter is in an act of worship, perhaps conceit (*ujb*) or showing off (*riya'*) enters him, and these are from Satan; so he is commanded to seek refuge from him, for safety from his enticement toward that.

The interpretation of the command in this verse, according to the majority, is recommendation (*nadb*), for lack of indications of obligation (*ijab*). For it has not been established that the Prophet ﷺ made it explicit. Some scholars recommended it absolutely, in prayer and outside it, at every recitation. Some of them made all the recitation of prayer one recitation, so that one seeking of refuge at its beginning suffices, and this is the view of the majority of these. Some of them made the recitation of each rak'ah a separate recitation.

Among the scholars is one who made it recommended for recitation outside prayer, and this is the view of Malik. He disliked it in the recitation of obligatory prayer, and permitted it without recommendation in the recitation of supererogatory prayer.

Perhaps he saw that in prayer there is sufficiency for protection from Satan.

It was also said: the command is for obligation (*wujub*). It was said this is specific to the recitation of prayer, and this is attributed to 'Ata'. The Qur'an has applied the term "Qur'an" to the recitation of prayer in His words, ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is witnessed﴾ [Al-Isra': 78].

[Page 278]

Al-Thawri said it is obligatory in the recitation of prayer and other than it. It is narrated from Ibn Sirin that seeking refuge at recitation is obligatory once in a lifetime. Some people said: the obligation is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, and recommendation applies to the rest of his community.

The sources of these opinions all go back to the interpretation of the verb in His words, "you recite" (*qara'ta*), the interpretation of the command in His words, "so seek refuge" (*fa-ista'idh*), and the interpretation of the Qur'an together with what surrounds this of the Sunnah, both in practice and in abstention.

According to all the opinions: seeking refuge is prescribed for beginning recitation, or for intending it, and it is not prescribed at every utterance of Qur'anic words, such as pronouncing a verse or verses of the Qur'an in teaching, admonition, or the like. This is contrary to what some of the showy pretenders do: when they cite a verse of the Qur'an outside the context of recitation, they say, after "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan," something like "as His words, [the Exalted], say," and then cite a verse.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he has no authority﴾, etc., is an explanation of the command to seek refuge from Satan when intending to recite the Qur'an, and an explanation of the manner of seeking refuge.

As for its being an explanation (*ta'lil*, rationale), it is to increase the urging toward compliance with the command, by showing that seeking refuge prevents Satan's domination over the one who seeks refuge; for God has prevented him from dominating those who believe and rely upon Him. Seeking refuge from him is a branch of the branches of reliance upon God, since taking refuge in Him is reliance upon Him. And in informing of the reason there is an encouragement for the one commanded to act, so that he becomes knowledgeable of the wisdom behind it.

As for its being an explanation (*bayan*, clarification), it is because of what it includes of mention of reliance upon God, in order to clarify that seeking refuge is an expression of reliance upon God, Exalted, for repelling Satan, so that the one seeking refuge fixes his intention upon that. Seeking refuge is not merely a statement without bringing to mind the intention of taking refuge in God.

So the clause ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾ is a second attribute of the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*, i.e., "those who"). The prepositional phrase has been placed before the verb for restriction (*qasr*), meaning: they rely upon none but their Lord. And its verb was made in the present tense to convey the renewal and continuity of reliance. Thus the negation of Satan's authority is conditional upon two matters: faith (*iman*) and reliance (*tawakkul*). From this comes an interpretation of His words in another verse: ﴿Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them﴾ [Al-Isra': 65].

[Page 279]

*Al-sultan* (authority) is a verbal noun on the pattern of *al-ghufran*, and it means domination and firm control.

So the meaning is that faith is the origin of weakening Satan's authority over the soul of the believer; when reliance upon God is added to it, the authority of Satan is repelled from the believer who relies upon Him.

The clause ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) of the explanatory type (*isti'naf bayani*), because the content of the preceding clause raises the question of one who asks: "Then over whom is his authority?"

[Page 280]

The restriction (qasr) derived from *innama* ("only") is a relative restriction (*qasr idafi*), as shown by the contrast with the preceding clause. That is, it means "only" in the sense of excluding those who do not belong to the two groups mentioned, namely "those who believe and upon their Lord rely." Thus the restriction serves to affirm the statement ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe﴾, to heighten attention to establishing its meaning. Therefore, it should not be understood from the restriction that he has no authority over anyone other than these two groups: those believers who neglected reliance upon God, and those who were deceived by some of the whisperings of Satan.

The meaning of *yatawallawnahu* ("take him as a guardian") is that they take him as their ally (*waliyyan*). These are the people who persistently adhere to creeds (*milal*) founded on what opposes Divine guidance (*al-hady al-ilahi*), out of desire for them. There is no doubt that those who take him as a guardian constitute a group other than the polytheists, because the conjunction (*'atf*) by its apparent form requires difference, and they are many categories of the People of the Book. The repetition of the relative pronoun in His words ﴿and those who are polytheists through him﴾ is because their allegiance to Satan is stronger.

He used the present tense (*al-mudari'*) to indicate the renewal of taking him as a guardian, meaning those who renew their taking him as a guardian. This is to alert that whenever they take him as a guardian by inclining to obey him, his authority over them becomes established, and that when taking him as a guardian ceases by abandoning it or by repentance, his authority is stripped from them. The phrase ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾ is conjoined without repeating the relative pronoun, to indicate that the two attributes are like a single relative clause for a single relative pronoun, because the intended meaning is the combination of the two descriptions.

The *ba'* in ﴿through him﴾ (*bihi*) denotes causation, and the pronoun in the genitive refers back to Satan, meaning they became polytheists because of him. It is not like the *ba'* in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and that you associate with God that for which He has sent down no authority﴾ [al-A'raf: 33].

The predicate was made a nominal sentence (*jumla ismiyya*) because of its indication of permanence and stability, since associating partners (*al-shirk*) is a continuous attribute, for its seat is the heart, unlike sins, whose manifestations are the limbs (*al-jawarih*). This indicates that Satan's authority over the polytheists is stronger and more lasting, because its cause is fixed and enduring.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in ﴿through him they are polytheists﴾ serves to convey restriction, meaning they did not associate partners except through his cause, in refutation of their statement ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated [anything with Him]﴾ [al-An'am: 148], and their statement ﴿Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 35], and their statement ﴿We found our fathers upon it, and God has commanded us with it﴾ [al-A'raf: 28].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 101:

﴿When We substitute a verse in place of another verse—and Allah knows best what He sends down—they say, "You are only a fabricator." Rather, most of them do not know.﴾ The discourse has continued concerning the matter of the Qur'an, and its exoneration from what Satan whispers in order to turn people away from following it.

Since one of the greatest aims of this surah is to make clear that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah, and to make clear its excellence and guidance, the surah began with the verse ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command﴾ [al-Nahl: 2]. Then it was followed by what the polytheists fabricated of disparagement concerning it, after various transitions in which there came ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "The fables of the ancients"﴾ [al-Nahl: 24]. This was followed by wonderful transitions: so the discourse returns to the Qur'an and its virtues, from His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And We have not sent down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them that about which they differ﴾ [al-Nahl: 64], then His saying ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an exposition of all things﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]. Following that came a witness that gathers what the Qur'an brought, namely the verse ﴿Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct﴾ [al-Nahl: 90]. When what necessitates the establishment of the excellence of the Qur'an had settled in souls, He drew attention to its preciousness and blessing by His saying ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl: 98]. Inevitably, the context became prepared for nullifying another fabrication of theirs against the Qur'an, a fabrication disguised with doubts, like their earlier fabrication to which He alluded by His saying ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "The fables of the ancients"﴾ [al-Nahl: 24]. That fabrication is their deliberate deception concerning verses of the Qur'an that come differing from other verses, due to the difference of the requirement and the context, and the variation between gentleness and severity, or between generality and specificity, and the like of what is accompanied by the difference of contexts, the difference of aims, and the difference of the circumstances to which they are attached. So they take from the apparent sense of these, apart from placing them in their proper places and carrying them to their proper meanings, points of attack with which they boast in their assemblies, making that out to be incoherence of speech and claiming it as evidence that the speaker is following one of two statements or both. Part of this arises from the shortness of their faculties in grasping the aims of the Qur'an and the sublimity of its meanings, and part arises from deliberate feigning of ignorance, clinging to the surface of speech, by which they confuse the weak in understanding among their followers. For this reason He, may He be exalted, said ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾, meaning: and among them are those who know, but they are obstinate.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Whenever a verse containing severity was revealed, and then a verse gentler than it was revealed, the disbelievers of Quraysh would say: 'By Allah, Muhammad is only mocking his companions. Today he commands a matter, and tomorrow he forbids it, and he does not say these things except from himself.'" End of quote.

This statement is the best of what the exegetes have said regarding the essential meaning of this verse. The intended sense of the substitution in His saying ﴿We substitute﴾ (baddalna) is absolute variation between purposes and contexts, or variation in meanings and their differing according to the differing aims and contexts, while the combining of their possible senses is clear.

The intended sense of "verse" (ayah) here is a complete utterance of the Qur'an, and it is not intended to mean the sign of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ, i.e., the miracle, by the indication of His saying ﴿and Allah knows best what He sends down﴾.

So the substitution includes the abrogation of rulings, such as the abrogation of His saying ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud, nor be silent in it﴾ [al-Isra: 110] by His saying ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists﴾ [al-Hijr: 94]. This is rare in the Qur'an that is recited to the polytheists, because the abrogation of rulings became frequent only after the Hijrah, when the Islamic community was formed. As for the abrogation of recitation, there has not come from the reports what requires its occurrence in Makkah; so whoever interprets the verse with it, as is reported from Mujahid, his view is problematic.

It also includes apparent contradiction through generality and specificity, and the like of the contradiction that is resolved by one part being read in light of another, so that part explains part and interprets part, such as His saying ﴿And the angels glorify the praise of their Lord and seek forgiveness for whoever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5] in Surah al-Shura together with His saying ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify the praise of their Lord and believe in Him and seek forgiveness for those who believed﴾ [Ghafir: 7] in Surah al-Mu'min. They take the generality of ﴿and seek forgiveness for whoever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5] and make it contradict the specificity of ﴿and seek forgiveness for those who believed﴾ [Ghafir: 7], and they claim that it is a turning away from one of the two statements toward the latter of them.

Likewise His saying ﴿And be patient over what they say and part from them with gracious parting﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10]: they take from its apparent sense that it is a command to abandon them. Then when verses came afterward calling them and warning them, they claimed that his speech had been annulled and that something had appeared to him which had not appeared to him before.

Likewise His saying ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9] alongside verses describing the punishment of the polytheists and the reward of the believers.

Likewise His saying ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164] alongside His saying ﴿that they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾ [al-Nahl: 25].

Of this is what appears as contradiction at first sight, such as His saying after mentioning the creation of the earth ﴿Then He istawa to the heaven﴾ [Fussilat: 11] in Surah Fussilat, together with His saying ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30] in Surah al-Nazi'at. They suppose it to be a contradiction, through heedlessness of the interpretation that "after that" (ba'da dhalika) is taken to mean "with" (ma'a), which is a frequent usage. They imagine a contradiction while being ignorant of, or feigning ignorance of, the eight established units in logic.

So the substitution (tabdil) in His saying "We substitute" (baddalna) is the replacement of something with a substitute (badal), i.e., a replacement. Replacement does not require the annulment of what is replaced (the mu'awwad, with the letter waw fathah), but requires that one thing be made a substitute for another. It may appear to the hearer that a term like the replaced one was made a substitute for a term like the substitute (with the letter waw kasrah) in different verses according to the differences of aims—such as good tidings and warning, or encouragement and intimidation, or summary and explanation—so the detractors make it into incoherence, because the like of it had been substituted, and they do not reflect on the difference of aims. Something of this meaning has already been mentioned at His saying ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this or change it﴾ [Yunus: 15] in Surah Yunus.

And ﴿in place of a verse﴾ (makan ayah) is in the accusative as a locative adverb of place: meaning, a verse comes in a call and address in the place of another verse that came in a similar call. Thus "place" here is figurative, namely the state of the discourse and address, as it is also called a "station" (maqam), so one says: "This is the station of anger, so do not bring jesting into it." It is not intended to mean its place in the leaves of the mushaf, nor that substitution means erasing it from it.

The clause ﴿and Allah knows best what He sends down﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the conditional (idha) and its answer, and its purpose is to teach the Muslims, not to refute the polytheists; for if they knew that Allah is the one who sends down the Qur'an, the slander would have been removed. The meaning is: He knows best what He sends down of a verse in place of a verse; so He knows the place of the first, the place of the second, and the meaning of both, and each is according to a measure and a consideration in His sight.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿bima yunazzilu﴾ with a fatha on the nun and a shaddah on the zay, while Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a sukun on the nun and a light zay.

The narration of their slander against the Prophet ﷺ is in the form of restricting the described to the description: they made him to have no attribute except fabrication. This is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), i.e., you are not one sent by Allah. This is from their rashness and haste in an unjust judgment. They did not limit themselves to saying that his substitution is fabrication, but made the Messenger restricted to being a fabricator, to convey that the Qur'an that came is restricted to being fabrication.

The original sense of iftira' is invention, and it came to be predominantly applied to the invention of a report, i.e., its fabrication, so it equated falsehood in meaning. For this reason it may be used alone as here, and it may be used together with "kadhib" (lie), as in His coming saying ﴿Only those who do not believe fabricate lies﴾ [al-Nahl: 105], returning it to the original sense of invention; so an object is given to it which reverts to its meaning, and so it came to be in the sense of an absolute object. This was already discussed at His saying ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103] in Surah al-'Uqud.

And "bal" (rather) is for the refutative turning away from their statement, and it is of the method of general refutation in the science of debate.

The pronoun in "akthalso-hum" (most of them) refers to those who said "You are only a fabricator": meaning, it is not as they said, but most of those who say that do not know, i.e., do not understand the placing of speech in its proper places and carrying it to its proper meanings.

It is understood from the judgment upon most of them of not knowing that a few of them know that this is not fabrication, but they say it as confusion and slander, and they do not know that the descent from Allah does not contradict the annulment of some rulings when the benefits differ, or when gentleness is observed.

It is permissible to take the word "akthar" (most) as meaning all of them, as has preceded in this surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 102:

﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth, to make firm those who believe, and as guidance and good tidings for the Muslims.﴾ This is a response to their saying, ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [An-Nahl: 101]. Therefore the verb "say" (qul) is left unconjoined, because it occurs in the course of dialogue. The meaning is: say to them, "You are not a fabricator, and the Qur'an is not a fabrication. Rather, the Holy Spirit has brought it down from God." The command to say this to them strengthens his resolve, so that their excessive slander does not divert him from debating with them.

After God refuted their claim that he is a fabricator by way of counter-argument (naqd, a refutation that exposes the contradiction within the opponent's claim), He commanded His Messenger to explain to them the nature of the Qur'an. This is the subtle point of the shift (iltifat, a change in grammatical person within a single discourse) in His words "from your Lord," which departs from what the apparent form of the reported speech would require. The apparent form would be "from my Lord." The shift to direct address was made to comfort the Prophet (ﷺ) by intensifying the intimacy of the discourse with him in the mode of direct address.

The name "Lord" (al-Rabb) was chosen because it carries the sense of care and management.

"The Holy Spirit" (Ruh al-Qudus) is Gabriel. It was mentioned previously in His words, ﴿And We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 87], in Surat al-Baqarah. "The Spirit" (al-Ruh) means the angel, as in God's words, ﴿So We sent to her Our Spirit﴾ [Maryam: 17], that is, an angel from among Our angels.

[p. 285]

"Holiness" (al-Quds) means purity, and here it is intended in its literal and figurative sense, which is excellence and grandeur of rank.

The construction of "the Spirit" with "holiness" is an idafa (genitival construction) in which the qualified noun is joined to its qualifier, like the expressions "Hatim of generosity" and "Zayd of goodness," where the meaning is "Hatim the generous" and "Zayd the good." Thus the meaning is "the holy angel."

The "bi" in "in truth" (bi-al-haqq) indicates association (mulabasah). It is an adverbial phrase that is fixed in a position of ḥal (a circumstantial accusative), relating to the pronoun in the object of "brought it down," as in God's words, ﴿grows forth with oil﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 20]. That is, it is accompanied by truth, with no admixture of falsehood in it.

One of the reasons for the revelation of the Qur'an in the described manner is mentioned here. This is the substitution of one verse for another, since in this there is firmness for those who believe, as they understand the import of every verse and are guided by it. The verses of good tidings serve as glad tidings for them, while the verses of warning are applied to the people of disbelief.

Thus, in God's words, ﴿brought it down from your Lord﴾, there is a refutation of their saying, ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [An-Nahl: 101]. In His words "in truth" there is an alert to people to consider the wisdom behind the variety of its purposes, and that these are true.

In the explanation by the wisdom of firmness, guidance, and good tidings, there is a demonstration of the firmness of the faith of the believers and the soundness of their judgment in understanding this elevated speech. It is also a confirmation of their hearts with the truth of certainty, and guidance and good tidings for them.

In linking the relative clause and its complement to the verb of firming, there is an indication that the attainment of this for them is due to their faith. It thus implies, by way of allusion, that those who do not believe have perceptions too limited to grasp that truth, so their understanding becomes confused, they increase in disbelief, they go astray, and it becomes a warning to them.

By "the Muslims" is meant those who believe. The apparent form would have been "and guidance and good tidings for them," but he departed to the explicit noun in order to increase their praise by another noble attribute.

God's words, ﴿guidance and good tidings﴾ [An-Naml: 2], are conjoined to the prepositional phrase in His words "to make firm" (li-yuthabbita). Thus "guidance and good tidings" are two verbal nouns in the position of the accusative of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi, an object indicating the reason for the action). The reason is that "to make firm," although it is governed by "li" in form, cannot be put in the accusative as an object of purpose, because it is not a pure verbal noun.

As for "guidance and good tidings," since they are two verbal nouns, they are indeed properly in the accusative as objects of purpose. Had their case-endings been visible, they would be in the accusative, as in God's words, ﴿that you may ride them and as adornment﴾ [An-Nahl: 8].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 103:

﴿And indeed We know that they say, "It is only a human being who teaches him." The tongue of the one they point to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic speech.﴾ This is connected (ʿuṭifa) to the clause ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another﴾ (al-Nahl 16:101). It is a refutation of another deception with which they mislead their common people. They would say: "Muhammad receives the Qur'an from a man of Makkah." It was said that the one who made this claim was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and others. Concerning him, the Exalted said: ﴿This is only magic, transmitted (from others)﴾ (al-Muddaththir 74:24) and ﴿This is only the word of a human being﴾ (al-Muddaththir 74:25). That is, no angel is dictating it to him; rather a human being is teaching him. They had identified the man by what the Exalted's words indicate: ﴿The tongue of the one they point to is foreign.﴾

The opening of the sentence with the emphatic oath particle (lam al-qasam) and (qad) indicates that only the leaders of the polytheists said this to their common followers, and did not circulate it among the Muslims, because it was an obvious falsehood. It also indicates that God made the Muslims aware of it. In Makkah there was a Roman youth named (Jabr), who was a freedman of ʿAmir ibn al-Hadrami and made swords in Makkah. He would read from the Gospel what the ordinary Christians of his kind read of prayers. The leaders of the polytheists used this to create confusion among the common people, since most people of Makkah were unlettered (ummiyyun). They would assume that whoever recites words he has memorized, even if distorted, or writes letters he has learned, must be a person of knowledge. When his people shunned the Prophet ﷺ and boycotted him, he would sit with this youth. This youth had outwardly embraced Islam, so the Quraysh said: "This one teaches Muhammad what he says."

Page 287

It was also said that there was a Roman youth named (Bil'am), who was a slave in Makkah belonging to a man of the Quraysh. The Messenger of God ﷺ would stand by him and invite him to Islam. They said: "Muhammad learns from him." This slave would say: "He only stands by me to teach me Islam."

The singular form in ﴿to whom﴾ indicates that the intended person is one man. It has also been said that the intended persons are two slaves, (Jabr) and (Yasar), who were both bondsmen. In that case, the word (basharun, human being) is meant generically, and the singular pronoun agrees with the singular form of its referent.

The Qur'an resolved this confusion here with the clearest resolution, speaking a decisive word without lengthy dispute: ﴿The tongue of the one they point to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic speech.﴾ That is: how could he teach him when he is a foreigner who scarcely expresses himself clearly, while this Qur'an is eloquent, Arabic, and inimitable?

The sentence is a response to their statement, and so it is resumed (mustaʾnafa) as an explanatory resumption (istiʾnaf bayani), because their saying ﴿It is only a human being who teaches him﴾ implies that it is not sent down from God. A questioner may ask: "What is the answer to their statement?" and it is then said: ﴿The tongue of the one…﴾ and so on. This construction resembles the construction of the Exalted's words: ﴿They say: "We will not believe until we are given what the messengers of God were given." God knows best where to place His message﴾ (al-Anʿam 6:124).

Alhada (ilhad, deviation) is like lahada: it means to turn away from the straight path. It is one of the verbs with a hamza that carry the meaning of the unaugmented form, as when they say abana for bana. So the meaning of yulhidun is that they incline away from the truth, because fabricating excuses is what they do. They abandon the straight truth, that it is speech sent down from God, in favor of saying "a human being teaches him." That is a deviation from the truth, and it is ilhad.

It is also possible that ilhad refers to their inclining, with their vague speech, toward a specific intended person. They said "a human being teaches him" and kept silent about identifying him, to give themselves latitude in fabricating excuses. When they find a naive simpleton who asks who is meant by "human being," they say to him: "It is (Jabr) or (Bil'am)." When they sense the questioner's shrewdness, they feign ignorance and say: "He is a human being among people." So applying ilhad to this meaning is like applying "inclination" (mayl) to "choice."

Nafiʿ and the majority read yulhidun with a damma on the yaʾ, as the imperfect of alhada. Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read yalhadun with a fatha on the yaʾ, from lahada, which is synonymous with alhada. Ilhad has already been mentioned in the Exalted's words: ﴿And leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾ (al-Aʿraf 7:180), in surah al-Aʿraf. This hamza is not like the one in their saying alhada al-mayyit (he placed the dead in a lahd), because that one means "to make him one who has a lahd (niche)."

Al-lisan (tongue) means speech. The word for the instrument has been used for speech. Al-aʿjami is what is attributed to the aʿjam, meaning one who cannot clearly express his intended meaning, as opposed to every speaker whose meaning they do not understand. For this reason they called animals ʿajmawat (dumb creatures). The yaʾ in aʿjamiyy is the yaʾ of relation (yaʾ al-nisba). Since the thing attributed is itself a description, the relation serves to intensify the description.

Al-mubin is an active participle from abana, when something becomes possessed of clarity (ibana), meaning it increases in clarity, in the sense of eloquence and rhetorical excellence. Thus there is complete antithesis between it and the tongue of the one they point to.

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah, Allah will not guide them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ This is a parenthetical clause (*jumlah mu'tarida*). That this verse follows the mention of the fabrications of those who affected eloquence (*al-mutaqa'irin*), who spread rumors about the Qur'an among the common folk, indicates that those meant by "those who do not believe" are the people just referred to. They are a known group, marked by extreme enmity toward the Prophet ﷺ and by firm determination in obstructing people from him, to the point that they reached a degree of disbelief beyond which there is no further degree. Thus the word of Allah took effect against them, that they would not believe. These are therefore an unspecified group at that time, but they are indicated in general terms, and the outcomes of their conditions reveal their specific identities.

Among those who disbelieved in the Prophet ﷺ were Abu Jahl and Abu Sufyan. Abu Sufyan remained in disbelief longer than Abu Jahl did. But Abu Jahl mixed his disbelief with harming the Prophet ﷺ and seething rage against him, whereas Abu Sufyan confined himself to defending his religion and his people and to repelling the Muslims from defeating them. So Allah deprived Abu Jahl of guidance, and he died in disbelief, while He guided Abu Sufyan, and he became one of the best of the believers, and he was honored by the marriage relationship (*sihr*) with the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Umar ibn al-Khattab were both disbelievers, and each of them was pushing people away from following Islam. But al-Walid used to invent excuses and slanders against the Qur'an, and that was a form of scheming, whereas Umar used to turn people away openly with harshness, without fabrication. So Allah deprived al-Walid ibn al-Mughira of being guided, and He guided Umar to Islam, and through him Islam became strong. Thus it became clear to people that al-Walid was among those who do not believe in the signs of Allah, and that Umar was not among them. Both were disbelievers together at some time. What points to this meaning that we have mentioned is His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and a stubborn disbeliever﴾ [Az-Zumar: 3], where He described the one whom Allah does not guide with two attributes: lying and extreme disbelief.

Thus it becomes clear that the meaning of His saying, ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾, is one for whom belief is contrary to the natural disposition of his character, not merely to the inclinations of his desires. Allah knows that such a person will not believe, and that he is not open to belief. Therefore Allah does not guide him, meaning He does not create guidance in his heart.

This manner of expression is the reverse of His saying, ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the words of your Lord have been fulfilled will not believe﴾ [Yunus: 96]. Each points to a great meaning.

The position of this sentence relative to the one before it is that of a justification (*ta'lil*) for all of their reported statements, and a concluding summary (*tadhyil*) of the outcome of their conditions. For this reason it is separated without a conjunction.

The phrase ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [An-Nahl: 63] is conjoined to ﴿Allah will not guide them﴾ to indicate their deprivation of good and their being cast into evil, since when they are deprived of guidance they fall into error. ﴿And what is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Yunus: 32]. This is like His saying, ﴿It is decreed concerning him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [Al-Hajj: 4]. The punishment includes the punishment of this world, which is the punishment of killing, such as what befell Abu Jahl on the Day of Badr from the pain of wounds while he was in the agony of death, and then from the humiliation of being finished off after that.

[Page 289]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 105:

Page 290
﴿Only those fabricate lies who do not believe in the signs of Allah; and it is they who are the liars.﴾ This is a rebuttal of their saying ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl: 101], by reversing what they alleged against them (i.e., against the disbelievers), just as His saying ﴿The tongue of the one they refer to is foreign﴾ [al-Nahl: 103] was an answer to their saying ﴿Only a human teaches him﴾ [al-Nahl: 103]. Thus, after He had exonerated the Qur'an from being fabricated, and the one to whom it was sent down from being a fabricator, He turned the reins toward explaining who the fabricator really is, and this is from the method of reversal (qalb) in the situation.

The point of relevance of mentioning it here is that their saying ﴿Only a human teaches him﴾ [al-Nahl: 103] entails denying the Prophet ﷺ in that what he brought was sent down to him from Allah. So they, in this respect, were confirming by its content their saying ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl: 101]; each of the two statements confirms the other. When He rebutted their saying ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl: 101] with His saying ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 101], ﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has sent it down from your Lord with truth﴾ [al-Nahl: 102], their other statement was reported explicitly in His saying ﴿The tongue of the one they refer to is foreign﴾ [al-Nahl: 103], and its content was answered here with His saying ﴿Only those fabricate lies who do not believe﴾, and so on, thereby achieving a rebuttal of its counterpart, namely their saying ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl: 101], with a statement more eloquent than theirs. For they, in their saying ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl: 101], used a form of restriction (qasr) that is more emphatic than what they said; since their saying ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ restricts the addressee to the constant attribute of fabrication, the nominal sentence requiring permanence and continuity. So He answered them with a form that restricts them to repeated and renewed fabrication, since the present tense indicates renewal.

He emphasized the verb of fabrication with its object, which has the sense of the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq), because the meaning returns to it.

And "lie" (al-kadhib) was defined by the definite article of the genus, which indicates the distinction of the quiddity of the genus and its presence in the mind, for the definiteness of a generic noun is stronger than its indefiniteness, as was previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

Page 291
He expressed those restricted to it by the relative pronoun instead of mentioning their pronoun, so that one would not say: "Only you fabricate lies," in order to convey their notoriety for the content of the relative clause, and because the relative clause has an effect on their fabrication, owing to what the relative form conveys of an allusion to the reason for constructing the predicate.

Accordingly, whoever does not believe in the clear proofs, which are the signs of truth, cannot but fabricate, in order to promote his denial of the clear proofs. In this there is a kinaya (allusion) that their denial of the signs of Allah stems from obstinacy and not from doubt.

Then the restrictive clause was followed by another restrictive clause by way of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) and the definiteness of the predicate, namely the clause (and it is they who are the liars).

It was opened with the demonstrative noun, after mentioning the attribute of not believing in the signs of Allah; in order to alert that those indicated are deserving of what follows the demonstrative in the report, namely their restriction to lying, because whoever does not believe in the signs of Allah takes lying as a habitual and constantly renewed practice.

The predicate in this clause was made definite by the article al-, to convey that the genus of liars is united in them and is confined to them, i.e., those whom you know to be the group of liars are these. This amounts to restricting the genus of the predicate to the subject, so two restrictions occur in this clause: the restriction of a described subject to an attribute, and the restriction of that attribute to that subject. The first two restrictions, arising from His saying ﴿Only those fabricate﴾ and His saying (and it is they who), are relative (idafi), i.e., not others than them, whom they accused of fabrication while he (the Prophet) is exempt from it. The third, ﴿and it is they who are the liars﴾, is a real restriction, ideally asserted for emphasis, since the attainment of the genus in them reached a strong degree that made it equivalent to its being confined to them.

And in the relative clause the form "do not believe" was chosen rather than "did not believe," so that it would be in the same pattern as what they were characterized by previously in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 104], and because the present tense carries the indication that they are persistent in the absence of belief, so that its opposite is not established for them.

[p. 292]

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah al-Nahl, verse 106:

﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, except one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith, but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment.﴾ When the warning had already been given against breaking the covenant of Allah that they had made, and against being deceived by the abundance and prosperity of the polytheist nation, and when the warning against a foot slipping after it had been firmly planted had been given, and when they were given the good tidings of a good life, and the reward for their righteous deeds, which alludes to holding fast to the Qur'an and being guided by it, and when they were warned not to be deluded by the doubts of the polytheists and their temptation to deny the Qur'an, he followed this with a threat against disbelief after belief. Therefore the speech is an initial resumption (*istiʼnaf ibtidaʼi*, a new beginning of discourse, not linked grammatically to what precedes).

The reason for the transition is that the polytheists were trying to tempt those who inclined toward Islam and those who had embraced it. For this reason he answered them with His words, ﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has sent it down﴾ [An-Nahl: 102], up to His words, ﴿to strengthen those who believe﴾ [An-Nahl: 102]. They were saying, ﴿It is only a human being who teaches him﴾ [An-Nahl: 103], so He answered them with His words, ﴿The tongue of the one they point to is foreign﴾ [An-Nahl: 103].

The young man whom they meant by their saying, ﴿It is only a human being who teaches him﴾ [An-Nahl: 103], had embraced Islam, then the polytheists tempted him and he disbelieved. He was Jabr, the freed slave of 'Amir ibn al-Hadrami. The polytheists had also pressed a group of Muslims to apostatize, among them Bilal, Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, Yasir, and Sumayya, the parents of 'Ammar ibn Yasir, and 'Ammar, their son. They remained steadfast in Islam. But they tempted 'Ammar, so he outwardly showed them disbelief while his heart remained firm in faith. They also tempted other men, who disbelieved. Among these he mentioned al-Harith ibn Rabi'a ibn al-Aswad, Abu Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, 'Ali ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf, and al-'As ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj. I think these are the ones concerning whom the Exalted said: ﴿Among people is one who says, "We believe in Allah," but when he is harmed for Allah, he regards the trial of people as the punishment of Allah﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 10], in Surah al-'Ankabut. So from this occasion came a response that returns the end of the speech to its beginning.

[p. 293]

Moreover, the content of ﴿whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief﴾ is the counterpart of the content of ﴿whoever does righteousness, male or female, while being a believer﴾ [An-Nahl: 97]. Thus encouragement is followed by warning, just as the passage began with a warning, as a safeguard for what is good against corruption. Then the speech returned to the reform of those into whom corruption had crept, and the door of concession (*rukhsa*, a legal dispensation) was opened for those who preserve their goodness as far as possible.

Know that the verse, if it refers to a group who disbelieved after their Islam, then "whoever" (*man*) is a relative pronoun (*mawsula*), and it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and the predicate (*khabar*) is ﴿upon them is wrath from Allah﴾. The predicate is joined with "fa" (then), because the subject has a resemblance to a conditional particle, and the relative pronoun may be treated as a conditional. This occurs in the Qur'an in several places, among them His words: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and women and then did not repent, for them is the punishment of Hell﴾ [Al-Buruj: 10], and His words, ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾ [At-Tawba: 34], up to His words, ﴿so give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [At-Tawba: 34], in Surah Bara'a (At-Tawba). It has been said that a group disbelieved after their Islam, as has been reported concerning the case of Jabr, the slave of Ibn al-Hadrami. This interpretation is more fitting with His words, ﴿Those are the ones upon whose hearts Allah has set a seal﴾ [An-Nahl: 108], up to the end of the verse.

If that did not happen, then the verse is merely a warning to the Muslims against returning to disbelief. For this reason "whoever" (*man*) is a conditional particle (*shartiyya*), and the condition is not intended to refer to a specific person; rather it is a warning, meaning: whoever (of you) disbelieves in Allah. This is because the past tense in the condition turns into the meaning of the present tense, and ﴿upon them is wrath from Allah﴾ is the response (*jawab*).

The warning is present under both meanings.

As for His words, ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith﴾, it is a concession and an excuse for what proceeded from 'Ammar ibn Yasir and those like him, when the punishment of those who tempted them became severe.

His words, ﴿except one who is compelled﴾, are an exception from the generality of "whoever disbelieves." This is so that the ruling of the condition does not fall upon him. That is: except one whom the polytheists compelled to disbelief, that is, to express it. So he expressed it verbally, but his belief did not change. This is a group to whom Allah granted this concession, as will come later.

What makes the exception valid is that he who spoke the words of the disbelievers has indeed disbelieved by his words.

The corrective (*istidrak*) with His words, ﴿but whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾, is a corrective to the exception. It is a safeguard lest one understand that the one under compulsion is permitted to slip away from faith in his heart.

"Whoever" (*man*) is a clarifying apposition (*sharh ma'tuf*) connected by "but" (*lakin*) to ﴿one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith﴾. This is because it carries the meaning of a negative, since it follows an exception from an affirmative. So the particle "but" (*lakin*) is conjunctive, and the presence or absence of the "wa" (and) is not significant, according to the verified view.

"Upon them is wrath" was chosen instead of something like "Allah has become wrathful against them," because of what the nominal sentence indicates of permanence and stability, meaning wrath with which there is no forgiveness.

The fronting of the prepositional predicate before the subject is for the sake of concern for their matter, so it places first what points to them. It also allows the subject to be indefinite, since the indefiniteness is intended to express magnitude, meaning: a great wrath. Thus indefiniteness suffices in place of an adjective.

As for fronting ﴿for them﴾ before ﴿a great punishment﴾, it is for the sake of concern.

Compulsion (*ikrah*) is forcing someone to do what he hates to do. It occurs only by inflicting something that the human capacity cannot bear: severe pain, or imprisonment, or chains, or the like.

This verse grants concession to the one compelled to show disbelief, that he may display it through any of its outward forms that people in custom call disbelief, whether by speech or by action.

The scholars of Islam have agreed to apply this to utterances of disbelief. They said: whoever is compelled to disbelief, the rulings of disbelief do not apply to him, because the compulsion is an indication that his disbelief is dissimulation (*taqiyya*, concealment of faith under threat) and a placating conduct (*musana'a*), after he had been a Muslim. Allah has granted this concession out of kindness to His servants, and in consideration of things by their ends and purposes.

[p. 295] (Note: the printed sequence continues on p. 295 below.)

[p. 295]

In the hadith: that this occurred to 'Ammar ibn Yasir, and that he mentioned it to the Prophet (ﷺ), who approved of him and said to him: "If they return to you (with the same demand), then return (to the same concession)." The scholars agreed upon this. Only Muhammad ibn al-Hasan deviated: he applied to this outward display of disbelief the ruling of the disbelievers in outward appearance, as with an apostate, so he is asked to repent for as long as he is able to do so.

The majority of scholars equated utterances of disbelief with its actions, such as prostration to an idol. A group said that compulsion to actions of disbelief does not permit them. This was attributed to al-Awza'i, Sahnun, and al-Hasan al-Basri. But this distinction is not clear. Allah has tied the concession to the firmness of the heart in faith, and has forgiven what lies beyond the heart.

If compulsion is the cause of the concession for the outward display of disbelief, then it is even more so for other sins, such as drinking wine and fornication, and in lifting the causes of blame in matters other than wronging others, such as compulsion to divorce or to sell.

As for wronging people, and the liability for damages, there are degrees of compulsion and degrees of the wrong to which one is compelled. The highest is compulsion to kill a soul. This shows that it does not permit one to proceed to killing, because the threat may not be carried out, and the victim's soul is lost.

Moreover, some kinds of wrongdoing may make compulsion a pretext for committing them, through collusion between the one compelled and the one who compels. For this reason, the one who compels has a share of the consideration in assigning responsibility to him.

This verse has not addressed anything other than Allah's accountability regarding His pure right. What lies beyond that is a field for independent reasoning (*ijtihad*). The disagreement about the divorce of one under compulsion is well known, and its details and subsidiary branches are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (*furu'*) and in some works of tafsir.

[Page 296]

﴿That is because they preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter, and because Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ This sentence stands in the position of a causal explanation (ta'līl), which is why it is separated from the sentence before it. The demonstrative "that" (dhālika) refers to the content of His words, ﴿Upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a tremendous punishment﴾ [An-Nahl: 106].

The pronoun in (bi-annahum) refers to those who disbelieved in Allah, whether the referent of "those who" (man) is specific or hypothetical according to the two possibilities mentioned earlier.

The bā' (bi-) is causal (sababiyyah), so what follows it is a cause.

Istaḥabbū (اسْتَحَبُّوا) is an intensified form of aḥabbū (أحَبُّوا), like istākhara and istakāna. The verb istaḥabbū has been given the sense of faḍḍalū (فَضَّلُوا, "they preferred"), and so it takes the preposition ʿalā (عَلى, "over"). That is, because they put the benefit of this world before the benefit of the Hereafter. They had settled in their hearts the truth of Islam, and they only turned away from it out of fear of persecution, or out of desire for a comfortable life. Thus their disbelief is worse than the disbelief of those who remained in disbelief from before the prophetic mission (al-baʿthah).

﴿And that Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ is a second cause of the wrath and the punishment. That is: and because Allah has deprived them of guidance, so they will die upon disbelief. The explanation of this has already been given at His words, ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah – Allah will not guide them﴾ [An-Nahl: 104].

This is a concluding generalization (tadhyīl, تَذْيِيلٌ) for what is contained in the form "the disbelieving people" (al-qawm al-kāfirīn) of generality that includes those being spoken about and others. So this is not an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (iẓhār fī maqām al-iḍmār); rather, it is a generalization after specification (ʿumūm baʿda khuṣūs).

The insertion of the word "people" (qawm) indicates that whoever has this trait is known by it, it has taken hold of them, and it has become their settled nature, to the extent that it is as though this description unites them.

It has already been stated that when a description or predicate follows the word "people" (qawm), it indicates that it is one of the constituents of their peoplehood, as in His words, ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ [An-Nahl: 12] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His words, ﴿But signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus: 101] in Surat Yunus.

[Page 297]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verses 108–109:

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts, their hearing, and their sight; and those are the heedless.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the losers.﴾ This sentence explains the sentence ﴿And that Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ [al-Nahl: 107], in that their being deprived of guidance is due to their being deprived of benefiting from its means: from sound reflection on the proofs of God's oneness, from heeding the call of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Qur'an revealed to him, and from the steadfastness of the heart in preserving the faith that had entered it, since they stripped themselves of it after having been clothed in it.

The opening of the sentence with the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) serves to distinguish them with the utmost distinction, clarifying the meaning of the preceding relative clause, which is their attribution of apostasy into disbelief after faith, by speech and by belief.

He referred to the demonstrative with the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) because of what it implies regarding the reason for the ruling expressed by this sentence, namely the content of the sentence ﴿upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment﴾ [al-Nahl: 106].

Al-tab' (sealing): it is a metaphor for the prevention of faith and its proofs from reaching them, following the manner of likening the intelligible to the perceptible. It has been discussed in detail earlier, at His saying ﴿Allah has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and upon their sight is a covering﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The sentence ﴿And those are the heedless﴾ is a completion of the explanation, i.e., the heedless in the most complete degree of heedlessness; for the heedless who has reached the utmost extent contradicts the state of being guided.

The restriction here is a restriction of a described entity to a attribute (qasr mawsuf 'ala sifa), and it is real-claimed (haqiqi id'a'i), intended for emphasis, because the other heedless ones are not taken into account; for they have reached the extreme of heedlessness, such that every other heedless person is counted as one who is not heedless. From here comes the meaning of perfection in heedlessness, not from the definite article (lam al-ta'rif).

The sentence ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the losers﴾ is placed in the position of a consequence of what precedes it, because what precedes it has become like evidence for its content; therefore it is opened with the expression negating doubt.

Indeed (la jaram) carries the meaning of (la mahala, "without doubt") or (la budda, "necessarily"). It was mentioned earlier in this surah at His saying ﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ [al-Nahl: 23], and its detailed explanation was given at His saying ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers﴾ [Hud: 22] in Surat Hud. The meaning is: their loss is the (true) loss, because they squandered the bliss with an everlasting squandering.

This meaning applies to both of the aforementioned interpretations regarding the referent of (man) in His saying ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 106] and so on.

In Surat Hud the expression ﴿they are the greatest losers﴾ [Hud: 22] occurs, and here ﴿they are the losers﴾ occurs; because the verse in Surat Hud is preceded by ﴿Those are the ones who have lost themselves, and what they used to fabricate has strayed from them﴾ [Hud: 21], so the intended purpose there was to explain that their loss in the Hereafter is greater than their loss in this world,
