It has been discussed in detail earlier, at His saying ﴿Allah has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and upon their sight is a covering﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The sentence ﴿And those are the heedless﴾ is a completion of the explanation, i.e., the heedless in the most complete degree of heedlessness; for the heedless who has reached the utmost extent contradicts the state of being guided.

The restriction here is a restriction of a described entity to a attribute (qasr mawsuf 'ala sifa), and it is real-claimed (haqiqi id'a'i), intended for emphasis, because the other heedless ones are not taken into account; for they have reached the extreme of heedlessness, such that every other heedless person is counted as one who is not heedless. From here comes the meaning of perfection in heedlessness, not from the definite article (lam al-ta'rif).

The sentence ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the losers﴾ is placed in the position of a consequence of what precedes it, because what precedes it has become like evidence for its content; therefore it is opened with the expression negating doubt.

Indeed (la jaram) carries the meaning of (la mahala, "without doubt") or (la budda, "necessarily"). It was mentioned earlier in this surah at His saying ﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ [al-Nahl: 23], and its detailed explanation was given at His saying ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers﴾ [Hud: 22] in Surat Hud. The meaning is: their loss is the (true) loss, because they squandered the bliss with an everlasting squandering.

This meaning applies to both of the aforementioned interpretations regarding the referent of (man) in His saying ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 106] and so on.

In Surat Hud the expression ﴿they are the greatest losers﴾ [Hud: 22] occurs, and here ﴿they are the losers﴾ occurs; because the verse in Surat Hud is preceded by ﴿Those are the ones who have lost themselves, and what they used to fabricate has strayed from them﴾ [Hud: 21], so the intended purpose there was to explain that their loss in the Hereafter is greater than their loss in this world,

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 110:

﴿Then indeed your Lord—for those who emigrated after they had been tried, then strove and endured—indeed your Lord, after that, is surely All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿whoever disbelieves in God after his belief﴾ [al-Nahl: 106] up to His words ﴿they are the losers﴾.

Page 299

The particle ﴿thumma﴾ (then) here denotes sequence of rank (al-tartīb al-rutbiyy), as is its usual function when it conjoins clauses, because the content of this conjoined clause is greater in rank than the clause it is conjoined to, since there is nothing greater than the pleasure of God, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and the pleasure of God is greater﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72].

By ﴿those who emigrated﴾ is meant the emigrants to Abyssinia (al-Habasha) whom the Prophet ﷺ permitted to emigrate in order to escape the harm of the polytheists, and the meaning of emigration (hijrah) is not sound except for this emigration to the land of Abyssinia.

Ibn Ishaq said: When the Messenger of God ﷺ saw what his Companions were suffering of affliction, and what he himself was in of well-being because of his standing with God and his uncle Abu Talib, and that he was not able to prevent them from what they were in of affliction, he said to them: "If you were to go out to the land of Abyssinia, for there is a king there under whom no one is wronged, and it is a land of truthfulness, until God grants you relief from what you are in." So at that time the Muslims among the Companions of the Messenger of God went out to the land of Abyssinia, fearing trial and fleeing with their religion. End of quotation.

When God mentioned those who believed and endured harm, and excused those who feared the torment of trial by uttering words of disbelief with their mouths while their hearts were reassured in faith, He mentioned another group who achieved success by fleeing from trial. This was lest someone imagine that their separation from the Prophet ﷺ in that hardship would weaken the community of the Muslims. Thus He completed the mention of all the groups of Muslims, and He alluded to their share of excellence by His words ﴿who emigrated after they had been tried﴾, calling their action hijrah.

This term, in the terminology of the Qur'an, indicates leaving one's homeland for the sake of preserving the religion, as is related of Abraham, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord﴾, and as He said concerning the Ansar: ﴿They love those who emigrated to them﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], meaning the believers who had left Makkah.

He called what they encountered from the polytheists a trial (fitnah). Fitnah means torment and severe, repeated harm which leaves the one afflicted with neither patience nor judgement. God said: ﴿The day they will be tried over the Fire﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 13], ﴿Taste your trial﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 14], and He said: ﴿Indeed those who tried the believing men and women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10]. Its explanation was given earlier at His words ﴿and trial is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191] in Surat al-Baqarah. That is, harm befell them for the sake of God.

Al-mujahadah means resisting with effort (al-juhd), that is, with capacity.

By mujahadah here is meant their defending themselves against the polytheists so that they would not return them to disbelief.

These two verses are Meccan, revealed before the legislation of jihad, which in the sense of fighting the disbelievers to support the religion.

Al-sabr means steadfastness in bearing what is disliked and hardships. It was explained earlier at His words ﴿and seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45] in Surat al-Baqarah.

He emphasised the report with the verbal emphatic particle (in) to confirm the promise, and the concern (al-ihtimam) repels any deficiency in their excellence.

This is indicated by what is in Sahih al-Bukhari: "That Asma' bint 'Umays, who was among those who came from the land of Abyssinia, entered upon Hafsah, and 'Umar entered upon her and said to her: 'We preceded you in emigration, so we have more right to the Messenger of God than you.' Asma' became angry and said: 'No indeed, by God, you were with the Prophet, who fed your hungry and instructed your ignorant, while we were in a distant and hostile land in Abyssinia, and we were harmed and feared, and that was for the sake of God and His Messenger. By God, I will not eat any food or drink any drink until I mention what you said to the Messenger of God.' When the Prophet ﷺ came to Hafsah's house, Asma' said: 'O Messenger of God, 'Umar said such and such.' He said: 'What did you say to him?' She said: 'I said to him such and such.' He said: 'He is not more entitled to me than you. For him and his companions is one emigration, but for you, the People of the Ship, there are two emigrations.'"

The lam in His words ﴿for those who emigrated﴾ is related to ﴿Forgiving﴾, placed before it for emphasis. ﴿Indeed your Lord﴾ is repeated a second time because of the long separation between the name of (inna) and its predicate, which is linked to the lam of commencement, together with the benefit of verbal emphasis.

Page 301

The definiteness of the predicated subject, which is the name of (inna), is by way of the annexation (idafah) rather than by proper name, because of what the annexation of the word "Lord" to the pronoun of the Prophet alludes to: that forgiveness and mercy were for his Companions, because they were harmed for the sake of God and for the sake of the Prophet ﷺ. Thus the attribution of forgiveness to God under the title of being the Lord of Muhammad ﷺ is a style indicating the exalted Essence and the Muhammadan Essence.

This is among the finest subtleties of the Qur'an in joining the name of the Prophet with the name of God, in view of this particular attribution.

The pronoun in ﴿after that﴾ refers either to the emigration derived from ﴿those who emigrated﴾, or to what has been mentioned: emigration, trial, striving, and patience, or to the trial derived from ﴿they were tried﴾. All these possibilities indicate that forgiveness and mercy for them are a reward for some of those actions, or for all of them.

Ibn 'Amir read ﴿futinu﴾ with a fatha on the fa' and the ta', in the active form, and this is a dialect of iftatana, meaning "fell into trial."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 111:

﴿On the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself, and every soul will be paid in full for what it did, and they will not be wronged.﴾ It is possible that this is a fresh statement (isti'naf) and a concluding remark (tadhyil), with the implied sense: "Remember the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself." It came after the warning and the threat, as a threat to those who were warned and as a promise to those who were given glad tidings.

It is also possible that it is connected to His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord, after that, is surely Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 110]. In that case the accusative of ﴿the Day when every soul comes﴾ is by way of adverbial complement (zarfiyyah) to (Forgiving, Merciful), meaning: He will forgive them and show them mercy on the Day of Resurrection, such that they will find no trace of their sins, which most people are not free from, and they will find mercy from Allah towards them on that day. This meaning is what the use of this adverbial phrase requires.

Al-mujadalah (pleading/disputing) is defending oneself with speech in order to escape the consequence of an act. It has already been discussed at His saying ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who deceive themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 107] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The first "nafs" (soul) means the essence and the person, as in His saying "that the soul is for the soul" (al-nafs bi-l-nafs). The second "nafs" is that by which the person is a person. The difference between them is by consideration, like the saying of a Bedouin whose brother killed his son, recorded in al-Hamasah:

I say to the self, in consolation and solace: one of my two hands has struck me, and it did not intend (it).

It has already been discussed at His saying ﴿and you forget yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44] in Surat al-Baqarah. That is because the Arabs conceive of the human being as a composite of body and spirit, and they call this the nafs, i.e. the essence, which is what the speaker expresses by the pronoun "I". They also conceive of an inner power by which the human perceives, and they call this nafs too. From this the scholars of logic took the term "rational soul" (al-nafs al-natiqah).

The meaning is: every person comes defending his essence, i.e. defending himself with his words in order to ward off the consequences of his deeds. So the doer of the pleading and what is in the position of its object are one thing. This is close to the type in which the agent and the object are one thing in verbs of thinking and invoking frequently, such as "arani fa'ilan kadha" (I see myself doing such-and-such), and their saying "'adimtani" and "faqadtani" (you have lost me), and rarely with other verbs, as in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

I have spent the night guarding myself alone, and the cry of the beasts of prey, with their howling, and the owls, prevents me.

Tuwaffa (is paid in full): is given something complete, i.e. whole, not diminished. (Ma 'amilat) is the second object of tuwaffa, and it is by elision of a noun, its implied sense being: the recompense of what it did, i.e. of reward or punishment. Mentioning "every soul" in the place where a pronoun would stand makes the sentence self-standing so that it functions like a proverb.

Al-zulm (wronging) is transgression against what is right. It is applied here to exceeding the specified limit of the recompense in evil, and falling short of it in good, because when Allah specified the recompense for evil and promised recompense for good, that became, as it were, a right for each party. The knowledge of the degrees of this specification is entrusted to Allah the Exalted, and your Lord does not wrong anyone.

The pronoun in ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ refers to "every soul" according to meaning, because "every soul" denotes a collection of souls.

The addition of this clause is to make explicit the implication of "and every soul will be paid in full for what it did", because paying the recompense in full for the deed necessitates that such payment be just. So it states this necessary consequence by way of negating its opposite, which is wronging them, and also to draw attention to the fact that justice is one of the attributes of Allah the Exalted. At the same time, it emphasises the first meaning.

Ibn ʿAshur, *al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*, commentary on Surah 16, verse 112:

﴿Allah sets forth a parable: a town that was secure and at peace, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place. Then it denied the blessings of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they had been doing.﴾ This is a coordination (ʿaṭf) of one admonition upon another. What it is coordinated with is the sentences expressing Allah's favours upon them, beginning with His words ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ (an-Naḥl 16:53), and what is connected to them, up to His words ﴿They recognise the blessing of Allah, then deny it, and most of them are disbelievers﴾ (an-Naḥl 16:83). After that, the discourse moves to a threat, from His words ﴿And on the Day We raise up from every nation a witness﴾ (an-Naḥl 16:84).

After He had threatened them with dreadful warnings, through His words ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ (an-Naḥl 16:104) and His words ﴿Upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment﴾ (an-Naḥl 16:106), up to His words ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the losers﴾ (an-Naḥl 16:109), the discourse returns to threatening them with a punishment in this world. He makes them an example of a town that was punished with the punishment of this world, or He makes them a parable and an admonition for whoever commits the same kind of denial of Allah's blessings that they committed.

[p. 304]

It is also permissible that what is coordinated with it is the clause ﴿The Day every soul comes pleading for itself﴾ (an-Naḥl 16:111) and what follows, on the basis of the implied imperative "remember" (udhkur), meaning: remind them of the terror of the Day ﴿when every soul comes pleading for itself﴾ (an-Naḥl 16:111) and so on, and Allah sets forth a parable of their punishment in this world, in the manner of a town that was secure and so on.

*Ḍaraba* here means *jaʿala* (to make, to render). That is, He made the composed expression, which indicates its meaning, and He revealed it to His Messenger ﷺ, just as one says, "So-and-so sent a parable: his saying is such-and-such."

The expression of the setting forth of the parable, which took place at the time the verse was revealed, is in the past tense in order to arouse interest in listening to it. This is the use of the past tense for the present, to affirm that it is occurring, like ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ (an-Naḥl 16:1). Or it is to bring the past close to the present, like the phrase "the prayer has been established."

It is also permissible that *ḍaraba* is used in the sense of a command or request, meaning: "Set forth, O Muḥammad, for your people a parable: a town..." and so on, as will come under His words ﴿Allah sets forth a parable: a town that was secure﴾ in Surah az-Zumar. It was phrased in the form of a report in order to attribute it to Allah, honouring Him and drawing attention to Him. It is distinguished from what is phrased as a request, such as ﴿And set forth for them a parable: the companions of the town﴾ (Yā-Sīn 36:13), which will be mentioned in Surah az-Zumar, so refer to it. This has already been discussed under His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to set forth a parable﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:26) in Surah al-Baqarah, and under His words in Surah Ibrahim ﴿Have you not seen how Allah sets forth a parable: a good word﴾ (Ibrahim 14:24).

He made the parable a town described by attributes that clarify its condition, which is the intended purpose of the illustration. Thus, there was no need to specify which town it was.

The point in this is that this parable is suitable to allude to the polytheists, in the possibility that the town is their town, namely Makkah, by making them an example for the people after them. This possibility is strengthened if this verse was revealed after the people of Makkah were struck by the famine with which they had been warned in His words ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ (ad-Dukhān 44:10)

[p. 305]

﴿covering the people; this is a painful punishment﴾ (ad-Dukhān 44:11). This is the smoke that the people of Makkah saw during the years of drought that struck them through the supplication of the Prophet ﷺ.

This is supported by His words after it: ﴿And there had certainly come to them a Messenger from among them, but they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers﴾ (an-Naḥl 16:113).

Perhaps those addressed by this parable are the Muslims who emigrated after they had been tried, namely the companions of the migration to Abyssinia, as consolation for them over leaving their land, and as encouragement for them to thank Allah, since He brought them out of that town and they were spared what befell its people and what might yet befall them.

The meaning of "town" (qaryah) has already been discussed under His words ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:259) in Surah al-Baqarah.

By "the town" is meant its people, since they are the real object of the reference to the town, as in His words ﴿And ask the town﴾ (Yūsuf 12:82). *Al-amn* (security) means safety from the domination of an enemy.

*Al-iṭmi'nān* means ease and tranquillity of mind. It has already been discussed under His words ﴿But that my heart may be assured﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:260) in Surah al-Baqarah, and His words ﴿So when you are at ease, establish the prayer﴾ (an-Nisāʾ 4:103) in Surah an-Nisāʾ.

He placed security before tranquillity, since tranquillity is not attained without it, just as fear is caused by agitation and anxiety.

His words ﴿its provision coming to it abundantly﴾ refer to the ease of provision in it, which is one of the causes of a comfortable life. Makkah was indeed like this. Allah says: ﴿Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary to which the fruits of every thing are brought?﴾ (al-Qaṣaṣ 28:57). *Al-rizq* (provision) means foodstuffs. It has already been discussed under His words ﴿No food will come to you that you are provided with﴾ (Yūsuf 12:37) in Surah Yūsuf.

*Al-raghad* means abundant and pleasant. It has already been discussed under His words ﴿And eat from it in abundance wherever you wish﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:35) in Surah al-Baqarah.

[p. 306]

The phrase ﴿from every place﴾ means from many places, and *kull* (every) is used to express abundance, as already discussed under His words ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ (al-Anʿām 6:25) in Surah al-Anʿām.

*Al-anʿum* is the plural of *niʿmah* (blessing) in an irregular form.

The meaning of disbelief in "the blessings of Allah" is disbelief in the Benefactor, because they associated others with Him in worship, and so did not thank the true Benefactor. This points to His words ﴿They recognise the blessing of Allah, then deny it, and most of them are disbelievers﴾ (an-Naḥl 16:83).

The verb *kafarat* (it denied) is connected by the particle of sequence (fa) after ﴿was secure and at peace﴾ in terms of the disbelief occurring after the blessings they were enjoying when disbelief arose among them, which was at the time of the Messenger being sent to them.

As for the connection of ﴿so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear﴾ with the particle of sequence (fa), it is a sequence in the customary sense in this kind of case, because it occurred after a period had passed over them while they persisted in their disbelief, and the Messenger kept repeating the call and warning them about it. When it occurred some time afterwards, which was not long, and was a recompense for their disbelief, it was treated as though it were the thing sequenced after their disbelief.

*Al-idhāqah* (causing to taste) is literally the tongue's perception of the states of flavours. Here, and in several places in the Qur'an, it is used metaphorically for the firm perception of pain and harm, like the firm tasting of food by the one who tastes it, from which there is no escape. It has already been discussed under His words ﴿That he may taste the consequence of his affair﴾ (al-Māʾidah 5:95) in Surah al-Māʾidah.

*Al-libās* (garment) literally means the thing that is worn. Its being attributed to hunger and fear is evidence that it is used metaphorically for the state of a person that envelops him, which is constant with him as a garment is constant with the one who wears it, like His words ﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:187), by the common factor of enveloping and constancy.

[p. 307]

Of the same kind is the metaphor of *al-bilā* (wearing out) for the loss of a person's quality, likening the loss after firm establishment to the wearing out of a garment after it was new, in the verse of Abū al-Ghūl al-Ṭahawī:

"And their valour does not wear out, even if they have been burned in war, time after time."

And the metaphor of stripping off garments for the cessation of companionship, in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"So strip off your garments from your garments, and they will be stripped away."

Among the subtleties of eloquence is making the garment a garment of two things, because the complete wearing of a garment is for a man to wear a waist-wrapper and a tunic.

Since *libās* was used metaphorically for the enveloping of what had covered them of hunger and fear, and its constancy, it was intended to convey that this is firmly established in them and settled in their perception, like the settling of food in the belly, since it is tasted on the tongue and in the throat and felt in the abdomen and the intestines.

So the verb *idhāqah* (causing to taste) was borrowed for it, for embellishment and to combine food and garment, since the ultimate form of hospitality and honour is that a guest is served and clothed with a robe of a waist-wrapper and a cloak. So there were two sarcastic metaphors.

Thus the verse contains two metaphors: the first is the metaphor of *idhāqah*, which is a clear subordinate metaphor (*tabaʿiyyah muṣarraḥah*), and the second is *libās*, which is a clear primary metaphor (*aṣliyyah muṣarraḥah*).

Among the marvels of the composition is that the second was made to branch off from the first and to be built upon it, by making its wording the object of the verb of the first. Through this it is conveyed that hunger and fear encompass the people of the town in all their conditions, are constant with them, and reach them with a painful extent.

The phrase ﴿for what they had been doing﴾ is stated in summary, relying on what precedes it that explains it, namely His words ﴿so they denied the blessings of Allah﴾.

Qur'an 16:113: ﴿And indeed there came to them a Messenger from among themselves, but they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers.﴾

When He informed about them that they were made to taste the garment of hunger and fear because of what they used to do, and what He had mentioned of their conduct was that they disbelieved in the blessings of Allah, there is added here that what they used to do is general to every deed that does not please Allah, not restricted to their disbelief in the blessing of Allah. And among the most grievous of what they used to do was their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) even though he was from among them, and this is more evident in the sense of bestowing favour upon them and showing kindness to them. And there is no town that was destroyed without a messenger from among its own people having come to it, as in ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns until He sends in their mother-town a messenger reciting to them Our verses﴾ [al-Qasas: 59].

Al-akhdh (الأخذ, "seizing") means destruction (al-ihlak). It has been discussed earlier at His words ﴿So We seized them suddenly while they did not perceive﴾ [al-A'raf: 95] in Surat al-A'raf.

The sentence is emphasised with the lam of oath and the particle of confirmation (harf al-tahqiq), for attention to this report, as an alert to the listeners who are being addressed, because it is the locus of warning.

The definite form of "al-'adhab" (the punishment) is generic (li-l-jins), meaning: the punishment seized them, like His words ﴿And We did not send a prophet into any town without seizing its people with adversity and hardship, that perhaps they would humble themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 94] ﴿Then We replaced the bad with the good until they multiplied and said, "Indeed, adversity and ease touched our fathers," so We seized them suddenly while they did not perceive﴾ [al-A'raf: 95].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 114:

﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good; and be grateful for the favour of Allah, if it is Him that you worship.﴾ This is a consequence (tafri') of the admonition and the parable (darb al-mathal), and it was addressed to a group of the Muslims, as is indicated by His saying ﴿If it is Him that you worship﴾ and ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion﴾ [al-Nahl: 115] to the end of the verse.

Page 309
It may be that this is directed at the people of the migration to Abyssinia (Habasha), when they became secure under a just king in a land where they found lawful provision, which they were given and which they earned by their own labour. That is: if you know the condition of the town that is set forth as a parable, or alluded to, then be grateful to Allah, who saved you from the like of what befell that town. So be grateful to Allah and do not disbelieve in Him as the people of that town disbelieved in His blessing. His saying ﴿and be grateful for the favour of Allah﴾ thus corresponds to His saying in the parable ﴿but it denied the favours of Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 112], [meaning: if you do not worship other than Him], as is required by faith. The making of this conditional (ta'liq dhalika bi'l-shart) serves to urge obedience, to manifest the sincerity of their faith. The name of Allah (ism al-jalala) is stated in His saying ﴿and be grateful for the favour of Allah﴾, although the apparent requirement would be the pronoun, in order to add emphasis to the reminder, and so that this command stands independent in its indication, such that it may be used as a proverb.

It has been said: this verse was revealed at Madina, and the meaning is the same; but this is a distant opinion.

The imperative in His saying ﴿So eat﴾ is for the purpose of bestowing favour (imtinan). The introduction of the particle of consequence (harf al-tafri') upon it is because the command to eat is a preliminary to the command to give thanks, which is the intended object of the consequence. The intended meaning is: be grateful for the favour of Allah, and do not disbelieve in it, lest there befall you what befell the people of the town set forth as a parable.

Al-halal (the lawful) is that which is permitted by the Law (shar'an), and al-tayyib (the good) is that which is pleasant to people in taste and whose sustenance benefits them.

This sentence explains the content of the verse ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good﴾ [al-Nahl: 114], to distinguish the good from the foul. The things mentioned among the prohibited items are foul by their very nature (khubthan fitriyyan). Some of them are corrupting to the formation of nourishment because of the harm they contain, and these are the carrion, the blood, and the flesh of swine. Others are contrary to the natural disposition (munafin lil-fitrah), and this is what was dedicated to other than Allah, because it contradicts thanking the One who bestowed the favour. Allah created the livestock, yet the polytheists mention the name of other than Allah over them.

In order to convey the explanation of the lawful and good through this sentence, the particle of restriction (adat al-hasr) is used in it. That is, He prohibited for you only the four mentioned things, so whatever is other than them remains good.

This is with regard to goodness and foulness in their essence. Foulness may occasionally befall some foods incidentally (ardan).

The occasion for this limitation regarding the prohibited items is that some Muslims were in a land of strangeness, where the flesh of swine and what was dedicated to other than Allah may be eaten, and some of them were in a land where blood and what was dedicated to other than Allah may be eaten. The explanation of a similar verse has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah and al-An'am.

[Page 310]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verses 116–117:

﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe as falsehood, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to attribute falsehood to Allah. Indeed, those who attribute falsehood to Allah will not succeed.﴾ ﴿A little enjoyment, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

The address has returned to the polytheists, as indicated by His saying ﴿concerning what your tongues describe as falsehood﴾. So this sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And Allah presents an example: a town﴾ [al-Nahl: 112], and so on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 119:

﴿Then indeed your Lord — for those who did evil in ignorance and then repented after that and amended — indeed your Lord, after it, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ The placement of this verse relative to the verses before it is like the placement of His earlier saying ﴿Then indeed your Lord — for those who emigrated after they had been tested﴾ [al-Nahl: 110]. When the conditions of the people of polytheism were mentioned, and among them was what they had forbidden for themselves, and the Muslims had shared with them in that during the days of ignorance (jahiliyyah), and the stern rebukes for what they had done had come down, it was possible that there would occur to the minds of the Muslims that they might suppose some of what they had committed in the jahiliyyah would befall them. So Allah reassured their souls that when they repented by giving up that through Islam, and amended their conduct after they had corrupted it, then Allah had indeed forgiven them a great forgiveness and had shown them a vast mercy.

The address was directed to the Prophet ﷺ, indicating that this forgiveness is among the blessings of the religion with which he was sent.

Mentioning the name "Lord" (Rabb) in construct with the pronoun of the Prophet is for the subtle point mentioned just previously in His saying ﴿Then indeed your Lord — for those who emigrated﴾ [al-Nahl: 110].

Al-jahalah (ignorance): the absence of knowledge of what is obligatory; the intended meaning here is their ignorance of the evidences of Islam.

The particle ﴿thumma﴾ (then) indicates ranking sequence (al-tartib al-rutbi), because the clause introduced by "thumma" contains the ruling on repentance, and that forgiveness and mercy are among its effects; and that is more important to the addressees than the threat that preceded it. That is, those who did evil while ignorant of what indicates the corruption of what they had done, and that was before they responded to the call of the Messenger. For during the period of their delay in entering Islam they are described as people of ignorance and jahiliyyah, or as ignorant of the punishment awaiting disobedience to the Messenger and their obstinacy towards him.

Included in this ruling is whoever among the Muslims commits a forbidden act while ignorant that it is forbidden, provided he was not negligent in his ignorance. This was already discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah for those who do evil in ignorance﴾ [al-Nisa': 17] in Surat al-Nisa'.

His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord, after it﴾ is a verbal emphasis (ta'kid lafzi) of His saying ﴿Then indeed your Lord﴾, for increasing the attention given to the report beyond the attention already conveyed by the emphasizing particle and the lam of commencement. The predicate of "inna" is connected to its subject because of the distance between them.

The predicate came with describing Allah by the intensive forms of forgiveness and mercy, and this is a metonymy (kinayah) for His forgiving them and His mercy towards them, within the description of Allah with these two great attributes.

The "ba'" in ﴿bi-jahalah﴾ (in ignorance) is for accompaniment (al-mula-basah), and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿amilu﴾.

The pronoun in ﴿min ba'dihā﴾ refers either to ignorance (al-jahalah) or to repentance (al-tawbah).

The fundamental root from which this transition and its branches arise is what was mentioned in the verse before it, concerning the people of the Jahiliyyah forbidding for themselves much of what Allah had bestowed upon people.

Abraham (peace be upon him) was described as being "a community" (ummah). The ummah is a great group of people gathered by a unifying element. This was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The description of Abraham (peace be upon him) with this is a striking description, for two meanings:

The first: he was, in excellence, virtue and perfection, like a complete community. This is like the saying: "You are the man, the whole man." Al-Buhturi said:

"I have not seen men differ in excellence such that a thousand are counted as one."

And on the authority of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him): the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Mu'adh is a community, obedient to Allah."

**Page 316**

The second: he was a community by himself in religion, because at the time of his mission there was no other monotheist worshipping Allah. It has remained standing through the ages. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about Khaṭar ibn Mālik the soothsayer: "He will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection as a community by himself," narrated by al-Suhayli in al-Rawḍ al-Unuf. I have seen a report that the Prophet (ﷺ) said this statement about Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl.

Al-qānit: the obedient one. It was discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿Stand before Allah in devotion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The lām (in lahu, "for Allah") is the lām of reinforcement (lām al-taqwiyah), because the governing word is a branch in its action.

Al-ḥanīf: the one who keeps away from falsehood. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Say: rather, the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135], in Surat al-Baqarah. The three nouns are predicates of kāna (كان, "was"), and they are excellences.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) to refute the claims of the polytheists that their practice was the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him). They had depicted Abraham and Ishmael (peace be upon them both) casting divining arrows (yastaqsimān bil-azlām), and they placed the image inside the Ka'bah, as came in the ḥadīth about the conquest (Ghazwat al-Fatḥ). So His saying ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ is not offered as praise of Abraham, but as a declaration of his innocence from what the falsifiers invented about him. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Your companion is not mad﴾ [al-Takwir: 22]. It is like an emphasis of the description ḥanīf by negating its opposite, as in: ﴿Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide﴾ [Ṭaha: 79].

The negation of his being among the polytheists was with the particle (لَمْ, lam), because lam changes the tense of the present verb (al-fi'l al-muḍāri') into the past, so it expresses the negation of the verb's root in the past time, and it also expresses the renewal of that negation, which is a characteristic of the present verb. Thus two meanings arise: the negation of the signified of the verb by its root, and the renewal of the negation by its form. It means that Abraham (peace be upon him) was never afflicted with polytheism at all, for Abraham (peace be upon him) did not associate anything with Allah from the time he became discerning, and he will never be afflicted with polytheism.
