And the ḥanīfiyyah is what Islam brought: the permissibility of all good things on earth, except what Allah has explicitly declared forbidden, as in the verse: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 145], and so on.

Abraham (peace be upon him) was described as being "a community" (ummah). The ummah is a great group of people gathered by a unifying element. This was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The description of Abraham (peace be upon him) with this is a striking description, for two meanings:

The first: he was, in excellence, virtue and perfection, like a complete community. This is like the saying: "You are the man, the whole man." Al-Buhturi said:

"I have not seen men differ in excellence such that a thousand are counted as one."

And on the authority of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him): the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Mu'adh is a community, obedient to Allah."

**Page 316**

The second: he was a community by himself in religion, because at the time of his mission there was no other monotheist worshipping Allah. He is the one through whom Allah revived monotheism, spread it among the nations and regions, built for it a great landmark, which is the Ka'bah, and called people to its pilgrimage, to make His remembrance widespread among the nations. It has remained standing through the ages. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about Khaṭar ibn Mālik the soothsayer: "He will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection as a community by himself," narrated by al-Suhayli in al-Rawḍ al-Unuf. I have seen a report that the Prophet (ﷺ) said this statement about Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl.

Al-qānit: the obedient one. It was discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿Stand before Allah in devotion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The lām (in lahu, "for Allah") is the lām of reinforcement (lām al-taqwiyah), because the governing word is a branch in its action.

Al-ḥanīf: the one who keeps away from falsehood. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Say: rather, the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135], in Surat al-Baqarah. The three nouns are predicates of kāna (كان, "was"), and they are excellences.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) to refute the claims of the polytheists that their practice was the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him). They had depicted Abraham and Ishmael (peace be upon them both) casting divining arrows (yastaqsimān bil-azlām), and they placed the image inside the Ka'bah, as came in the ḥadīth about the conquest (Ghazwat al-Fatḥ). So His saying ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ is not offered as praise of Abraham, but as a declaration of his innocence from what the falsifiers invented about him. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Your companion is not mad﴾ [al-Takwir: 22]. It is like an emphasis of the description ḥanīf by negating its opposite, as in: ﴿Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide﴾ [Ṭaha: 79].

The negation of his being among the polytheists was with the particle (لَمْ, lam), because lam changes the tense of the present verb (al-fi'l al-muḍāri') into the past, so it expresses the negation of the verb's root in the past time, and it also expresses the renewal of that negation, which is a characteristic of the present verb. Thus two meanings arise: the negation of the signified of the verb by its root, and the renewal of the negation by its form. It means that Abraham (peace be upon him) was never afflicted with polytheism at all, for Abraham (peace be upon him) did not associate anything with Allah from the time he became discerning, and he will never be afflicted with polytheism.

**Page 317**

And ﴿grateful for His blessings﴾ is a fourth predicate of kāna, and it is praise of Abraham (peace be upon him), and an allusion to his descendants who associated partners with Allah and were ungrateful for Allah's blessing, in contrast to His saying: ﴿So it denied the blessings of Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 112]. The discussion of the blessings of Allah was mentioned shortly before.

The clause ijtabāhu (He chose him) is a resumption of an explanatory kind (istinaf bayani), because the preceding praise raises the question of a questioner about the cause of Abraham's achievement of these praiseworthy qualities, so it is answered that Allah chose him, as in His saying: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124].

Al-ijtibā' means choosing. It is the form ifti'āl from jabā, meaning he gathered. It was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And We chose them and guided them to a straight path﴾ [al-An'am: 87], in Surat al-An'am.

Guidance to the straight path: guidance to monotheism and the religion of the ḥanīfiyyah.

The pronoun in ﴿Âtaynāhu (We gave him)﴾ is an iltifāt (shift) from the third person to the first person, for stylistic variety, since three third-person pronouns follow one another.

Al-ḥasanah in this world is everything in which there is ease of life: tranquillity of the heart through religion, health, safety, long life, sufficient abundant provision, and good remembrance among people. It was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And among them is he who says: Our Lord, give us good in this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201].

Al-ṣalāḥ (righteousness) is the perfection of uprightness in the religion of truth. This description was chosen as a sign that Allah honoured him by answering his supplication, since He related that he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 83].

[Page 318]

﴿Then We revealed to you, "Follow the religion of Abraham, upright, and he was not among those who associated others with God."﴾ (Thumma) indicates ordering by rank (al-tartīb al-rutbī), pointing out that the content of the conjoined clause is far superior in rank to the content of what precedes it. This is a great honouring of the Prophet (ﷺ) and of the Islamic law (sharī'a), and an additional honouring of Abraham (peace be upon him). The meaning is: We made you follow the religion of Abraham. That is among the greatest of the honours We have bestowed upon you. I have already explained earlier that this clause is the intended one, and that the clause "Indeed Abraham was a community [ummah]" [An-Nahl: 120] and what follows it is a preface to it.

"We revealed to you" is added to draw attention to the fact that Muhammad's following the religion of Abraham was by revelation from God and by truthful guidance. It is an allusion that those among the Arabs who claimed to follow the religion of Abraham before this had strayed from it, either through a doubtful basis, such as Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt and Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, or without any doubtful basis, such as the claims of Quraysh about their religion.

The particle (an) is explanatory (tafsīriyya) for the verb "We revealed" (awḥaynā), because it carries the sense of saying without its letters, so it needed to be explained by the explanatory particle.

Al-ittibā' (following) means tracing a course along another course, and here it is used figuratively for acting in the manner of the other's action.

"Ḥanīfan" (upright; a ḥanīf is one who turns away from falsehood towards pure monotheism) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of Abraham, in which case it is an additional emphasis on its like before it; or it is a state of the pronoun in "ilayka" (to you) or of the pronoun in "ittabi'" (follow). That is: "Be, O Muhammad, upright as Abraham was upright." For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was sent with the easy, upright religion (al-ḥanīfiyya al-samḥa)."

Explaining the verb "We revealed" by the clause "to follow the religion of Abraham" is an explanation by a comprehensive statement of what God revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) of the laws of Islam,

[Page 319]

together with the information that these are established upon the foundations of the religion of Abraham. The intended meaning is not that what was revealed to him was the phrase "follow the religion of Abraham, upright", because the Prophet (ﷺ) did not know the details of the religion of Abraham. So it is established that the meaning is that what was revealed to him sprang from the law of Abraham (peace be upon him).

His saying "and he was not among those who associated others with God" is among what God revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), which is reported by His saying "Then We revealed to you". It is conjoined to "upright" on both of the two possibilities regarding the bearer of that state. On the first possibility the state is an additional emphasis for His earlier saying "and he was not among those who associated others with God" [An-Nahl: 120]. On the second possibility it is a declaration of the purity of the Islamic law, which follows the religion of Abraham, from any admixture of association with God.

The negation of his being among the associators here is by the negating particle "mā", because when "mā" negates the verb "kāna" (was) it conveys the strength of negation and the remoteness of what is negated. It is enough to note that denial (judḥūd) is built upon it, as in: "He was not such as to do such-and-such."

Thus three benefits are derived from His earlier saying "and he was not among those who associated others with God" [An-Nahl: 120] and from His saying here "and he was not among those who associated others with God": the negation of association from Abraham at all times of the past; the continuous renewal of the negation of association in a constant manner; and his complete freedom from association.

It is known from this that the religion of Islam is free from anything that might attach to it the taints of association, because it came just as Abraham came, proclaiming the divine oneness of God in divinity, and uprooting the roots of association. The divine laws, all of them, although they warn against association, the Qur'an is distinguished among them by blocking the avenues through which association might creep in, by the clarity of its statements and the eloquence of its exposition, and it has not left in this any ambiguous words, as may be found in some other books, such as what is found in the Torah describing the Jews as "sons of God", and what is in the Gospels of the notion of the sonship of Jesus (peace be upon him) to God, exalted is He above what they describe.

[Page 320]

This meaning has been indicated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "O people, indeed Satan has despaired of being worshipped in this land of yours, that is, the land of Islam, forever. But he has been content to be obeyed in other matters, of those deeds of yours that you consider trivial. So beware of him concerning your religion."

The meaning of Muhammad's following the religion of Abraham, which occurs in many verses of the Qur'an, is that the religion of Islam was built upon the foundations of the religion of Abraham, which are the foundations of the natural disposition (fiṭra), and moderation between severity and leniency, as He, exalted, said: "And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion, the religion of your father Abraham" [Al-Ḥajj: 78].

In the matter of God's command to Abraham to slaughter his son (peace be upon them both), and then his son's ransom by the slaughter of a sheep, is a symbol of the transition from the severity of the other religions in their sacrifices to the leniency of the religion of God, the upright one, in offering animals rather than human beings. For this reason He, exalted, said: "And We called to him: O Abraham! You have fulfilled the vision. Indeed, thus We reward the good-doers. Indeed, this is the manifest trial. And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice" [As-Saffat: 104–107].

Thus the law whose details and branches are built upon the foundations of a law is considered as if it were that law. For this reason the verifying scholars among our scholars said: the ruling established by analogy (qiyās) in Islam may rightly be said to be the religion of God, although it cannot rightly be said that God said it. It is not meant that all that Islam brought was brought by Abraham (peace be upon him), for that does not occur to the mind. Islam is a legal, governing law, while the law of Abraham was a tribal law particular to a people. Nor is it meant that God commanded the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to follow the religion of Abraham at the outset, before He revealed to him the laws of the religion of Islam, because that, although it is correct in meaning and admitted by the words of the verse, is not sound, since nothing in the Islamic legislation indicates that it abrogates (naskh) what the Prophet (ﷺ) had been upon before.

[Page 321]

So the Prophet's following of the religion of Abraham was, in word and deed, in the foundations of the law: in affirming monotheism and debating on its behalf, and following what the natural disposition requires. And in its branches: in what God revealed to him of the upright religion, such as circumcision, the characteristics of the natural disposition, and good conduct.

[p. 322]

The position of this verse indicates that it contains a meaning connected with the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham), and with the coming of Islam on its foundation.

When the preceding verse negated that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was among the polytheists, in response to the claims of the polytheistic Arabs that they were upon the religion of Ibrahim, the discourse moved, on this occasion, to refuting what resembles those claims. These are the claims of the Jews that the religion of Judaism is the religion of Ibrahim, a claim they invented at the time of the rise of Islam, denying a virtue that had escaped them, namely the virtue of having their religion founded upon the first religion of primordial, complete nature (al-fitrah). This was out of envy from their own selves. We have already explained this at the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham?﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 65] in Surat Ali 'Imran.

So this verse is like the verse of Ali 'Imran: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him? Will you not reason?﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 65] ﴿Here you are, those who argued about that of which you have knowledge; but why do you argue about that of which you have no knowledge? And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 66] ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a hanif, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 67] This indicates that these three groups differed concerning Abraham, and each of them claims that it is upon his religion. However, in this verse he limited himself to refuting the claims of the polytheists with the greatest proof, which is that their religion is association (of partners with Allah), while Abraham (peace be upon him) was not among the polytheists. He followed that with the refutation of the claims of the Jews, because these claims may be more widespread, since the Jews used to mix with the Arabs in their lands. The people of Makkah used to have contact with the Jews during their travels and in their markets, unlike the Christians.

Since this surah is Meccan, it did not address the Christians, whom it addressed in Surat Ali 'Imran.

For this reason, the clause ﴿Indeed, the Sabbath was only enjoined upon those who differed concerning it﴾ is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) arising from His words ﴿Then We revealed to you, [O Muhammad], to follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth﴾ [an-Nahl: 123], since it raises a question from the opponents: how can Islam be from the religion of Abraham? In it (Islam), the day of Friday was made the sacred day, whereas the Torah had made the day of sanctification for the Jews the Sabbath. Perhaps the Jews used this to create confusion against the Muslims, so His words ﴿Indeed, the Sabbath was only enjoined upon those who differed concerning it﴾ served as an answer to this question.

This clause came as an interjection between the clause ﴿Then We revealed to you, [O Muhammad], to follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth﴾ [an-Nahl: 123] and the clause ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom﴾ [an-Nahl: 125], etc.

For this reason the clause was opened with the particle of restriction, indicating that it is meant to reverse what the questioning, confusion-making opponents assumed.

This is a method well known in many of the replies given to refute a supposed opinion. The pronoun in His words ﴿concerning it﴾ refers to Abraham with an omitted modifier, meaning: they differed concerning his religion. It does not refer to the Sabbath, since there is no benefit in that meaning. Those who differed concerning Abraham, that is, concerning his religion, are the Jews, because they are the people of the Sabbath.

The meaning of (was enjoined, ju'ila, as-sabt) is: was obligated and specified upon them, that is, the rulings of the Sabbath were imposed upon them: among them the prohibition of work on it, and the prohibition of using servants and animals on the day of the Sabbath.

He turned away from mentioning the name of the Jews or the Children of Israel, even though that is more concise, to expressing them by the relative pronoun, because their being well known by the relative clause is sufficient to define them, along with what the relative pronoun and its clause contain of an indication of the reason for the predicate's construction. This indication is what is intended here, because the purpose is to establish that the Jews were not upon the hanifiyyah (pure monotheistic primordial faith), as you have just understood.

The meaning of the verb (differed, ikhtalafu) is not the occurrence of disagreement among them over the matter of the Sabbath. Rather, the verb (ikhtalafu) is meant to signify (khalafu), "they opposed," as in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "and their opposing their prophets," that is, their doing what is contrary to what their prophets commanded. So the summary of the meaning is as follows: the Sabbath was only imposed upon the people of the Sabbath because they were not upon the religion of Ibrahim, for it is undisputed among them that the prohibition of the Sabbath is not part of the religion of Ibrahim, nor is it one of its laws.

The sacred day among the Christians was not mentioned, because there was no call for that at the time this surah was revealed, as you have understood.

It should not be inferred from this that the sacred day in the religion of Ibrahim was Friday, since there is nothing that indicates this. What is sufficient to negate that the Jews were upon the religion of Ibrahim is that the day of the Sabbath's prohibition was not part of the religion of Ibrahim.

Then, the more apparent view is that the sanctity of Friday was reserved for the Islamic religion, based on the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "This is the day about which they differed, and Allah guided us to it. So people follow us in it: the Jews tomorrow and the Christians the day after tomorrow." His words, "and Allah guided us to it," indicate that this had not preceded in any other religion.

This is the way to interpret this verse, and the place of the verb and of the pronoun in the genitive in His words ﴿differed concerning it﴾.

What the commentators have mentioned of various views does not avoid being forced and being of no benefit. They made the pronoun in (concerning it, fihi) refer to the Sabbath, and they interpreted the meaning of disagreement concerning it in various ways. There is no connection between the predicate and what is supposed to be a cause for it, in the sense of the Sabbath being imposed upon them, because they differed with their prophet Musa (peace be upon him) on account of the Sabbath. Their prophet had commanded them to honor Friday, but they refused and asked that the Sabbath be the most excellent day of the week, on the grounds that Allah had decreed the creation of the heavens and the earths before the day of Sabbath, and no creation took place on the day of Sabbath. So Allah punished them by making the prohibition of the Sabbath strict upon them. This is what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, but it is not authentically transmitted from him. How could it be, when Allah, exalted is He, said ﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath"﴾ [an-Nisa: 154], and how could it be consistent for Musa (peace be upon him) to turn away from the day that Allah commanded him to honor to another day, for the desire of his people, when he was known for firmness in religion?

Among the commentators is one who claimed that the Torah commanded them with an unspecified day, so they specified it as the Sabbath. This is not consistent, because Musa (peace be upon him) lived among them for eighty years. How could it be correct that they did that out of misunderstanding of the Torah? Perhaps the perplexity of the commentators in reconciling the meanings of this verse will become apparent to you.

The (innama, "indeed... only") is for restriction, and it is a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb) intended to refute the Jews, by arguing against them that they are not upon the religion of Ibrahim, because Allah made the Sabbath for them a new legislation by the explicit statement of their own Book, since their predecessors were not upon it. The structure of the argument is: if the prohibition of the Sabbath was not from the religion of Ibrahim, then the people of that prohibition are not upon the religion of Ibrahim.

The meaning of (was made, ju'ila, as-sabt) is that it was made a venerated day on which there is no work. That is, Allah made the Sabbath venerated. The second object of the verb of making was omitted, because it was treated as intransitive, for brevity, so as to include all the states of the Sabbath mentioned in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath"﴾ [an-Nisa: 154] and His words ﴿when they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-A'raf: 163].

The verb (was made, ju'ila) was given the meaning of (was obligated, furida), so it takes the preposition (upon, 'ala).

Allah, exalted is He, reserved for Muhammad (ﷺ) that he would be the inheritor of the foundations of Ibrahim. So He made for the Jews and the Christians a religion that opposes the religion of Ibrahim, and He set a sign for that, which is the day by which the origin of that religion is recognized. The change of that day at the time of the mission of the Messiah (peace be upon him) is an indication of this, so that the Sabbath would not remain continuously among the Children of Israel, as a warning that they were subject to the abrogation (naskh) of their religion by the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him), and as a preparation for them to receive yet another abrogation afterward by another religion, whose sign would be a day other than the Sabbath and other than Sunday. This is the interpretation by which the coherence of the verses with one another becomes apparent.

The (between them, baynahum) is an adverbial complement of the judgment derived from (will judge, yahkumu), meaning a judgment among them, and (baynahum) is not for making (yahkumu) transitive, since there is no mention here of disagreement between two parties.

[Page 326]

﴿Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition, and argue with them in the best manner.﴾ The meaning of this verse serves as an explanation of His saying, ﴿Then We revealed to you: Follow the religion of Abraham, a man of pure faith (hanifan)﴾ [An-Nahl: 123]. The intended meaning of what was revealed to him concerning following the religion of Abraham is the religion of Islam, and the religion of Islam is founded on the principles of the hanifiyya (the pure monotheistic faith of Abraham). Therefore, the Messenger ﷺ, in calling people to Islam, was necessarily calling them to follow the religion of Abraham.

God's addressing His Messenger ﷺ with this command, while he was calling to Islam and in agreement with the foundations of the religion of Abraham, is evidence that the form of the imperative is used to request continuity in the Islamic call, together with what is added to that of guidance to the methods of calling to the religion.

This verse thus includes the reinforcement of the Messenger ﷺ in his call, and that the words of the polytheists to him, ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [An-Nahl: 101], and their saying, ﴿It is only a human who teaches him﴾ [An-Nahl: 103], should not make him despair, and that the fact that God does not guide those who do not believe in the signs of God should not turn him away from the call. This is because the polytheists did not leave any stratagem, which they thought would discourage the Prophet ﷺ from his call, without directing it at him: from explicit denial, mockery, threats, obscenity, fabrication, and slander, as is related in various places in the Qur'an, and in this surah. This is because they are ignorant of the ranks of the people of election, and they measure them by the standard of their own souls. So they supposed that what they brought of nonsense would discourage him and nearly cause him to turn away from their call.

The "way (sabil) of the Lord" means His path. It is used figuratively for every action that by its nature brings its doer to the good pleasure of God Most High, because the action which accrues to its doer as a goal resembles a road leading to an intended place. Therefore the name "way" is borrowed for the means of a thing.

Al-Qurtubi said: This verse was revealed in Mecca at the time when the command to make a truce with Quraysh was given, that is, during the period of the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya.

Al-Wahidi related from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed after the Battle of Uhud, when the sight of the mutilation of Hamza, may God be pleased with him, grieved the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "I will kill seventy men of them in his place." This implies that the verse is Medinan.

I do not think what the two of them mentioned is correct. Perhaps what deceived the one who narrated it is His saying, ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [An-Nahl: 126], as will come later. Rather, the placement of the verse is connected to what precedes it and does not need the invention of a occasion of revelation.

The idafa of "way" (sabil) to "your Lord" (rabbika) is on the basis that God guided to it and commanded adherence to it. This idafa is a tajrid (abstraction) of the metaphor, and this compound has become a proper name by predominance for the religion of Islam, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of God﴾ [Al-Anfal: 36]. This is the intended meaning here, and in His saying after it, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way﴾ [An-Nahl: 125].

"The way of God" is also used as a name by predominance for supporting the religion by fighting, as in His saying, ﴿And strive with your wealth and your selves in the way of God﴾ [At-Tawba: 41].

The "bi" in His saying "bil-hikmah" (with wisdom) is for accompaniment (mula'abah), like the "bi" in the Arab saying to the newlywed: "bil-rifa' wal-banin" (with felicity and sons), with the implied meaning "you have married (a'rasta)," which the context indicates. It is either related to "ud'u" (call), or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "ud'u."

[Page 327]

The object of "ud'u" is omitted for the purpose of generality, or because the verb has been treated as intransitive, since the intended meaning is continuity in the call, not the specification of those called, because that is a matter known from the state of the call.

The sense of accompaniment requires that his call to the way of God not be devoid of these two qualities: wisdom and good admonition.

So "wisdom" (hikmah) is firm knowledge, that is, correct and free of error. Thus "hikmah" is not applied except to pure knowledge free of the blemishes of errors and remnants of ignorance in teaching people and refining them. For this reason, they defined wisdom as: knowledge of the realities of things as they are, according to human capacity, such that the realities resembling one another do not become confused for their possessor, and he does not err regarding causes and reasons. It is a comprehensive term for every speech or knowledge in which the reform of people's condition is observed, and their belief is a continuous reform that does not change. The discussion of it has already been treated in detail under His saying, ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [Al-Baqara: 269] in Surat al-Baqara, so refer to it. "Hikmah" is also applied to the knowledge possessed by the prophets, and its synonym is "hukm."

"Good admonition" (mawiza) is speech that softens the soul of the one addressed toward doing good. It is more specific than wisdom, because it is wisdom in a particular style for its delivery. It has been discussed under His saying, ﴿So turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [An-Nisa': 63] in Surat an-Nisa', and under His saying, ﴿an admonition and a detailed explanation of all things﴾ [Al-A'raf: 145] in Surat al-A'raf.

Describing it as "good" (hasana) is an exhortation that it should be gentle and acceptable to people, meaning good in its kind, since kinds differ in excellence according to the differences in the desired qualities in them.

The conjunction of "admonition" to "wisdom" is because they differ with respect to generality and specificity in a particular aspect (wajhi). For admonition may take the path of persuasion, so among admonition is wisdom, and among it is oratory (khitaba), and among it is argumentation (jadal).

[Page 328]

In terms of their essence, there is a general and specific relation from one aspect between them. But what is intended by them is that which does not go beyond wisdom and good admonition, by the indication of the change in style, since he did not conjoin the verbal noun of argumentation to wisdom and admonition by saying, "and argumentation in the best manner," but rather brought its verb, and because the intended meaning is to restrict the permission for it to being like "that which is best," as He said, ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in the best manner﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 46].

"Mujadala" (argumentation) is arguing to correct an opinion and to refute what opposes it, or an action of that kind. Since what the Prophet ﷺ encountered from the harm of the polytheists could lead him to harshness in argumentation, God commanded him to argue with them in the best manner. It was discussed shortly before under His saying, "who argues on behalf of herself" [Al-Mujadila: 1], and earlier under His saying, ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who deceive themselves﴾ [An-Nisa': 107] in Surat an-Nisa'. The meaning is: when the call compels the disputing of the polytheists, then dispute with them in the best manner. The one preferred over is the argument coming from them, since argumentation requires the action to proceed from both sides. So it is understood that what is commanded is that the argument proceeding from him be better in goodness than the argument proceeding from them, like His saying, ﴿Repel with that which is better﴾ [Fussilat: 34].

Since argumentation only occurs with opponents, He explicitly used the pronoun of the absent plural in "argue with them," the intended referent being the polytheists, for the polytheists differ in the manner of their disputation. Among them is one who disputes gently, like what is in the hadith: "The Prophet ﷺ recited the Qur'an to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, then said to him: Do you see any harm in what I say? He said: No, by the water." And: "The Prophet ﷺ recited the Qur'an to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul in the assembly of his people, and 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said: O man, if what you say is true, then sit in your house, and whoever comes to you, speak to him, and whoever does not come to you, do not approach him, and do not come to him in his assembly with what he dislikes."

[Page 329]

The polytheists' challenging of the Prophet ﷺ in argumentation occurred more than once. Among that is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "When the saying of God Most High was revealed, ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 98], and the verse, 'Abd Allah al-Zib'ara said: I will certainly dispute with Muhammad. So he came to him and said: O Muhammad, 'Isa has been worshipped, and the angels have been worshipped; are they then fuel for Hell? The Prophet ﷺ said: Recite what follows: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us, they will be kept far from it﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 101]." Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Tabarani, and Abu Dawud in the book of Nasikh and Mansukh narrated it.

"Admonition" is qualified by "good," but "wisdom" is not qualified by the like of that, because since the purpose of admonition is mostly to restrain the soul of the one admonished from his evil deeds or from expectation of such from him, it is a likely occasion for harshness on the part of the admonisher, and for brokenness to arise in the soul of the admonished. God guided His Messenger to aim in admonition that it be good, that is, by softening speech and encouraging the one admonished toward good. God Most High said, addressing Moses and Aaron: ﴿Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 43], ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech; perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44].

In the hadith of al-Tirmidhi from al-'Irbad ibn Sariya, he said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ admonished us with an admonition from which hearts trembled and eyes overflowed with tears," the hadith.

As for wisdom, it is teaching for those seeking perfection from a teacher who is concerned with teaching his students, so it is only in a good state. Therefore there is no need to alert that it should be good.

Since argumentation is disputation over an action or an opinion with the aim of persuading with the aspect of truth in it, it cannot but be either of wisdom or of admonition. But it has been made a separate category alongside them here with regard to the purpose that calls to it.

Since the Prophet's ﷺ argumentation with them was among the aftermath of the call, it was described as "the best," just as admonition was described as "good."

[Page 330]

The polytheists used to argue with the Prophet intending to confound him and to deceive him by confusion. God directed attention to the manner of the Prophet's argument with them, to complete the etiquette of all the means of calling. So the pronoun in "wa-jadilhum" (and argue with them) refers to the polytheists by the indication of the context, since it is evident that the Muslims do not argue with the Prophet ﷺ, but receive from him as one who seeks benefit and guidance. This necessitates the change of style regarding argumentation, since He did not say "and the good argumentation," but rather said "and argue with them." God also said: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in the best manner﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 46].

Included in "that which is best" is the rejection of their denial with speech that is not explicit in refuting their claim, from the words addressed to them, such as His saying: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24], and His saying: ﴿And if they argue with you, say: God is most knowing of what you do. God will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which you used to differ﴾ [Al-Hajj: 68-69].

The verse implies that the Qur'an includes these three methods of the call, and that the Messenger ﷺ, when he calls people by means other than the Qur'an, such as his sermons, admonitions, and guidance, follows with them these three methods. All of that is according to what the context requires of the meanings of speech and the conditions of those addressed, whether elite or common.

The intention is not that a single speech must necessarily include these three conditions together. Rather, a speech may be wisdom while including harshness and warning and being free of argumentation, and it may be argumentation without being admonition, like His saying: ﴿Then you are those who kill yourselves and expel a group of you from their homes, supporting [their enemies] against them in sin and aggression. And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while their expulsion was forbidden to you. Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ [Al-Baqara: 85].

And like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to 'Adi ibn Hatim, who was a Christian before his conversion to Islam: "Indeed, you eat the mirba' (a tax on spoils), and it is forbidden in your religion."

[Page 331]

Among the scientific miracles of the Qur'an is that this verse gathered the principles of true rational reasoning: demonstration (burhan), rhetoric (khitaba), and dialectic (jadal), which in the science of logic are termed the "arts" (sina'at), and which are the accepted arts. As for sophistry (sophistry, sufsata) and poetry (shi'r), the wise who are truthful keep away from them, let alone the prophets and messengers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 125 (part 2 of 2):

Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi) said: Calling people to a doctrine or a position must necessarily be based on a proof (hujjah). The purpose of mentioning the proof is either to establish that doctrine and that belief in the hearts of the listeners, or to silence and confound the opponent.

As for the first purpose, it divides into two kinds. The proof is either a true, certain proof, free from the possibility of its opposite, or it is not so, but rather yields an apparent conjecture (zann) and persuasion (iqna'). Thus it becomes clear that proofs are confined to these three kinds. The first is the proof that yields certain beliefs, and this is what is called wisdom (hikmah). The second is the conjectural indicators, which is the good admonition (mawizah hasanah). The third is the arguments whose aim is to confound the opponent, and this is disputation (jidal).

Disputation itself is of two kinds. It is either composed of premises accepted by the majority, which is disputation conducted in the best manner, or it is composed of false premises which the speaker tries to pass off on the listeners by false stratagems, and this is unbecoming for people of virtue. End of quotation.

This is what logic calls sophistry (safsatah). Among it are the poetic premises (al-muqaddimat al-shi'riyyah), which are gilded sophistry.

The verse comprises all the kinds of true proof, by bringing together the places of each of their types among the methods of calling to the faith, but in a manner of overlapping (tadakhul), not in the manner of mutual exclusion and division as the terminology of the logicians has it. For the technical proofs of the logicians are, in their view, some of them coordinate (qasim) with others, so the relation between them is one of exclusion (tabayun). As for the methods of the Islamic call, the relation between them is one of general and specific, absolute or partial (al-'umum wa al-khusus al-mutlaq aw al-wajhi). Its detailed explanation would lead us into prolixity, and your mind is not dull in disentangling them.

To wisdom returns the discipline of demonstration (burhan), because it is composed of certain premises, which are established truths that necessitate the attainment of knowledge of things as they are.

To admonition returns the discipline of rhetoric (khitabah), because rhetoric is composed of conjectural premises, since what is taken into account in it is what prevails among people of ordinary reason, and accepted common assumptions suffice as admonition. An example of it from the Qur'an is His saying, ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an immorality and hateful and an evil way﴾ [an-Nisa': 22]. His saying "and hateful" (maqtan) points out that when they did it in the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah) they used to call it "the marriage of hatred" (nikah al-maqt), so this attribute was applied to it because it persuades that it is an immorality. This is therefore a rhetorical argument (istidlal khitabi).

As for disputation, it is what is put forward in debates and contention of proofs that are accepted between the disputants, or from proofs that are well-known. The name "disputation" is applied to the argument that circulates specifically in the context of debate, and does not attain the rank of wisdom. It may be of a kind that would be accepted as admonition if delivered outside the situation of debate. The sages of Islam called it jadal, bringing it close to the meaning it has in the Greek language.

* * *

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of the guided﴾

This sentence is a justification (ta'lil) for the command to persist in the call, after the announcement that those who do not believe in the signs of Allah will not be guided by Allah, and after describing the states of their denial and obstinacy.

When the exhortation after that to continue calling to the religion required an explanation of the wisdom in it, the wisdom was explained: that Allah is most knowing of the outcome of people, and this knowledge is not for anyone other than Allah among the people. So there is nothing for you but conveying the message. That is: do not despair of their guidance, and do not go to the extent of grief over their not being guided, because knowledge of who is guided and who is led astray is entrusted to Allah, and your only duty is to convey in every state. This is a decisive statement distinguishing the party of truth from the party of falsehood.

He placed the knowledge of who has strayed first, because it is the purpose of the justification, since their call is more emphatic, and guiding them to the right path through good admonition and the best disputation is more important. Then He followed this with knowledge of the guided, for the sake of completeness.

In it is an allusion that one does not know whether some of those who have despaired of their faith may have had Allah expand their breast to Islam after despair of them.

The emphasis of the predicate by the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) is for the sake of giving it importance. As for (inna), in a context of justification it is merely for the sake of emphasis, and it stands in the place of the conjunctive fa' (fa' al-tafri') as 'Abd al-Qahir clarified in Dala'il al-I'jaz. Its function of emphasis here is dispensed with, because of the presence of the pronoun of separation in the sentence, which conveys restriction (qasr) of the attribute to the one described, since restriction is emphasis upon emphasis.

The repetition of the pronoun of separation in His saying ﴿and He is most knowing of the guided﴾ serves to specify the strengthening of this statement. For if it were said, "and most knowing of the guided," it could be understood as coordinated with the sentence "He is most knowing of who has strayed," so that it would be a predicate of (inna) not included within the scope of strengthening by the pronoun of separation. Therefore the pronoun of separation was repeated to remove this possibility.

He did not say "and of the guided" (wa-bi-al-muhtadin), explicitly attaching knowledge to them, so that it would be explicit that knowledge pertains to it. These two restrictions are relative (idafi), meaning: your Lord is most knowing of the misguided and the guided, not those who think they are guided and that you are misguided.

The superlative in His saying "He is most knowing" is a comparison with the knowledge of others concerning this, since it is a knowledge that varies according to the variation of those who know in grasping realities.

In this superlative is an allusion to the obligation of seeking perfect knowledge of guidance, distinguishing truth from falsehood, probing deeply into that, avoiding haste in judgment without a strong conjecture regarding the truth, and beware of the currents of desires overwhelming one, so that realities are not reversed and minds do not wander down crooked paths. For the truth endures through time, and falsehood is refuted by proof and demonstration.

To acquire the character of this verse is that everyone who occupies a station of the stations of the Messenger (ﷺ) in guiding the Muslims or governing them must be following the three methods: wisdom, good admonition, and disputation in the best manner. Otherwise he deviates from Islamic manners and is unfit for what he is in charge of in governing the community, and he should fear that he may expose the interests of the community to ruin. For the reform of the community requires conveying the truth to it by these three means. The Islamic society is not free from one who is obstinate or one who obfuscates, and both cast the thorns of doubts in the path of the reformers, intentionally or unintentionally. So the way to correct him is disputation, for it is closer to persuading him and uncovering his veil.

In the Muwatta' it is related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said in a sermon he delivered at the end of his life: "O people, the sunan have been established for you, the obligations have been prescribed for you, and you have been left upon the clear path, unless you go astray through people to the right and to the left," and he struck one of his hands upon the other. Perhaps he struck his left hand upon his right hand that was holding the sword or the staff during the sermon. This striking is a sign that there is nothing beyond what he mentioned for people to seek regarding a ruling that has not previously been explained in the Shari'ah.

He placed the mention of His knowledge of who has strayed from His way before the mention of His knowledge of the guided, because the context implies a warning (ta'ridh bi-al-wa'id) to the misguided, and because clearing away (takhliyah) takes precedence over adorning (tahliyah). So the threat precedes the promise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 126:

Page 335
﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the like of what you were made to suffer. But if you are patient, it is indeed best for the patient.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]. That is: if the situation is one of invitation (da'wa), then let your invitation to them be as We have described; and if you, O believers, are retaliating against the polytheists for the harm that befell you from them, then retaliate with justice, not by exceeding the limit of what you suffered from them.

This verse is connected to what precedes it in the most complete connection, and it suffices you that the conjunctive particle (al-ʿatf) is present in it. This is a graduated arrangement of the levels of treatment: from the treatment of those who are called and admonished, to the treatment of those who are disputed with, then to the treatment of those who are repaid for their deeds. By this, the good ordering in the style of the speech is achieved.

This is the preferred view of al-Nahhas, Ibn ʿAtiyya, and Fakhr al-Din, and by this it is preferred that this verse is Meccan together with what precedes it starting from verse forty-one. This is the view of Jabir ibn Zayd, as has passed at the beginning of the surah. Ibn ʿAtiyya chose that this verse is Meccan.

It is possible that it was revealed concerning the incident of the mutilation of Hamza on the day of Uhud, which is related in a weak hadith narrated by al-Tabarani; perhaps the narrators confused it with the Prophet's ﷺ recollection of the verse when he "threatened the polytheists that he would mutilate seventy of them if God granted him victory over them."

The address is to the believers, and the Prophet ﷺ is included in it.

Al-muʿaqaba (retaliation) means requital for an evil act with that which displeases the doer of the evil.

His saying (bi-mithli ma ʿuqibtum) is a mushakala (correspondence of terms) with (ʿaqabtum): he used ʿuqibtum in the sense of "you were treated," since it came after the verb ʿaqabtum; so it is a metaphor whose basis of comparison is the mushakala.

Page 336
It is also possible that ʿuqibtum is literal, because the harm they suffered from the polytheists was intended by them as punishment for leaving the religion of their people, for reviling their idols, and for disparaging their forefathers.

The imperative in His saying (fa-ʿaqibu) is for obligation with respect to its object, which is His saying (bi-mithli ma ʿuqibtum bihi), since avoiding excess in punishment is obligatory.

In this verse there is an indication that God will give the Muslims victory over the polytheists and place them in their grip, so perhaps some of those who were tried by the polytheists will be driven by rage to excess in punishment. Thus it looks back to His saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord — for those who emigrated after they were tried﴾ [al-Nahl: 110].

He encouraged them to be patient with harm, that is, by turning away from the harm of the polytheists and by pardoning it, because it is more attractive to the hearts of enemies; so it is described as good, that is, better than taking up punishment, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Repel with that which is better, and thereupon the one between whom and you there is enmity will be as if he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34], and His saying: ﴿The recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

The pronoun of the absent (hu) refers to the patience derived from the verb (sabartum), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to righteousness﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 8]. He emphasized that patience is good with the particle of oath (lam al-qasam) for additional urging to it.

He referred to them as (al-sabirin) explicitly in the place where a pronoun would be expected, to increase the honoring of the quality of the patient; that is, patience is a predicate of the category of the patient.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 16, verse 127:

﴿So be patient. Your patience is not except by Allah. And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress because of their plotting.﴾ The Prophet (ﷺ) was singled out for the command to be patient, to indicate that his station is higher, so he is more deserving of holding to patience, taking the resolute course ('azimah) after having been permitted to retaliate against them.

[Page 337]

The clause ﴿And your patience is not except by Allah﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the coordinated clauses. Its meaning is: your patience is not achieved except through Allah's granting you success. This indicates that the patience of the Prophet (ﷺ) is great, because he suffered from the harm of the polytheists more than what the general body of Muslims suffered. So his patience is not like ordinary patience, and for this reason its attainment was by help from Allah.

He warned him against grieving over them if they did not believe, as in His saying ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 3]. Then he followed this with the instruction that his chest should not be constrained by their scheming. These are different states that arise in the soul according to the differing events that cause them. The polytheists would treat the Prophet sometimes with open harm, sometimes by turning away from listening to him and showing that they were enraged by his not following him, and at other times by plotting and scheming against him, which is devising harm in secret.

Ad-ḍayq (the constriction), with a fatḥah on the ḍād and a sukūn on the yā', is the verbal noun of (ḍāqa, to be constricted), like as-sayr and al-qawl, and the majority of reciters read it this way.

It is also said: aḍ-ḍīq, with a kasrah on the ḍād, like al-qīl, and Ibn Kathir read it this way.

This was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿and your chest is constricted by it﴾ [Hud: 12]. The intended meaning is constriction of breath, which is used metaphorically for distress and anguish, just as its opposite is used, namely expansiveness and breadth for bearing and patience. It is said: "So-and-so is narrow-chested" (ḍayyiq aṣ-ṣadr). God Most High said at the end of al-Hijr ﴿And We certainly know that your chest is constricted by what they say﴾ [al-Hijr: 97]. It is also said: "breadth of chest" (sa'at aṣ-ṣadr).

The prepositional phrase "in distress" (fī ḍayq) is used figuratively: it means that the constriction does not afflict you in the manner in which a container's contents are constrained by the container.

The particle "mā" is a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah), meaning "because of their plotting." The verb that is converted into a verbal noun was chosen because of what the present-tense verb indicates of renewal and recurrence.

[Page 338]

﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who have taqwa and those who are doers of good.﴾ This is a reason (ta'lil) for the command to limit punishment to the measure of the offense, for encouraging patience in the face of harm and pardoning those who transgress, for singling out the Prophet ﷺ with the command to be patient, for seeking help in attaining that patience through the help of Allah the Exalted, and for removing distress from himself caused by the actions of those who did not believe in him.

He gave as the reason for all of this that Allah is with those who are mindful of Him (yattaqunahu), so they stop at the limits He set for them, and with those who do good (al-muhsinin). The mu'iyyah (being "with") here is a metaphor (majaz) for support and victory.

For the side of taqwa, He used a past-tense verbal relative clause (silah fi'liyyah madiyah) to indicate that it is necessary for it to have been attained and firmly established beforehand, because it is among the necessary consequences of faith, since taqwa leads to the performance of what is obligatory, which is a right upon the responsible person. That is why he was commanded in it to limit himself to the measure of the sin.

For the side of doing good, He used the nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah) to indicate that doing good is established for them and always with them, because doing good is a virtue, so it requires being firmly rooted in the soul and well established within it.

[Page 5]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat al-Isra'. It is named in many copies of the Qur'an "Surat al-Isra'," and al-Alusi (al-Alusi) stated explicitly that it was named this because the Night Journey (al-isra') of the Prophet ﷺ is mentioned at its beginning, and it is singled out for mentioning it.

It is also called, in the time of the Companions, "Surat Bani Isra'il." In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, in the chapters on supplication, it is narrated from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ would not sleep until he recited az-Zumar and Bani Isra'il."

In Sahih al-Bukhari, it is narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said concerning Bani Isra'il, al-Kahf and Maryam: "They are among the first and oldest (al-'ataq al-ula), and they are of my old possessions (tilad)." On this basis al-Bukhari titled it in the Book of Tafsir, and al-Tirmidhi in the chapters of Tafsir. The reasoning behind this is that it mentions aspects of the history of Bani Isra'il that are not mentioned in other surahs, namely the domination over them by a people of great might (the Assyrians, al-Ashuriyyin), and then the domination over them by another people, the Romans.

It is also called Surat Subhan, because it begins with this word. This was stated in Basa'ir dhawi al-tamyiz.

[Page 6]

It is Meccan according to the majority. It was said: except for two verses from it, which are ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you﴾ [Al-Isra: 73] up to His saying "a little" (qalilan). And it was said: except for four, these two verses, and His saying ﴿And [mention] when We told you that your Lord has encompassed the people﴾ [Al-Isra: 60], and His saying ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance"﴾ [Al-Isra: 80], the verse. And it was said: except for five, these four, and His saying ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾ [Al-Isra: 107] up to the end of the surah. And it was said: except for five verses other than what preceded, namely the one beginning with His saying ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾ [Al-Isra: 33], the verse; and His saying ﴿And do not approach adultery﴾ [Al-Isra: 32], the verse; and His saying ﴿Those whom they invoke﴾ [Al-Isra: 57], the verse; and His saying ﴿Establish prayer﴾ [Al-Isra: 78], the verse; and His saying ﴿And give the relative his right﴾ [Al-Isra: 26], the verse. And it was said: except for eight, from His saying ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you﴾ [Al-Isra: 73] up to His saying ﴿a helper of authority﴾ [Al-Isra: 80].

I think the source of these statements is that the apparent rulings contained in those verses seem to indicate that those verses do not fit the situation of the Muslims before the Hijrah, so the view of the proponents of those statements prevailed that those verses are Madani. What will come is an explanation that this is not correct, when we address their interpretation.

It appears that it was revealed at a time when the community of Muslims was in Makkah, and the legislation concerning the dealings of their community was beginning to reach their souls. Rulings follow one another in it, the like of whose number is not mentioned in any other Meccan surah except Surat al-An'am, and that is from His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [Al-Isra: 23] up to His saying ﴿all that - its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord﴾ [Al-Isra: 38].

The time of the Night Journey has been disputed, and the most correct view is that it was about a year and five months before the Hijrah. If it was revealed right after the Night Journey happened to the Prophet ﷺ, then it was revealed around the year twelve after the Bi'thah (the commissioning), which is the year two before the Hijrah, in the middle of that year.

That it opens with mention of the Night Journey does not necessarily mean that it was revealed immediately after the Night Journey occurred; rather, it is possible that it was revealed some time after the Night Journey.

[Page 7]

Mentioned in it is the Night Journey to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, to honor al-Masjid al-Aqsa and to remind of its sanctity.

This surah was revealed after Surat al-Qasas and before Surat Yunus.

It is counted as the fiftieth surah in the enumeration of the order of the revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an.

Its number of verses is one hundred and ten according to the count of the people of Madinah, Makkah, al-Sham and Basrah, and one hundred and eleven according to the count of the people of Kufah.

* * *

Its purposes (aghradi-ha)

The pillar upon which the purposes of this surah are established is: affirming the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ; affirming that the Qur'an is revelation from Allah; affirming its excellence and the excellence of the one who sent it down; mentioning that it is inimitable (mu'jiz); refuting the slanders of the polytheists against it and against the one who brought it; and that they did not comprehend it, which is why they turned away from it.

And refuting their denial that the Prophet ﷺ was taken by night to al-Masjid al-Aqsa. It therefore opens with the miracle of the Night Journey as a preparation (tawti'ah) for drawing a comparison (tanzir) between the Law of Islam and the Law of Musa, peace be upon him, according to the Qur'an's custom of mentioning religious examples and parallels, and as a divine symbol that Allah gave Muhammad ﷺ excellences greater than those He gave those before him.

And that He completed for him the excellences, so nothing of them escaped him. For this reason He placed him in the sacred place that the Messengers had successively inhabited before him, and He did not make them exclusive to residing there.

[Page 8]

In that place, which is the place of descent of the Mosaic Law and the symbol of the stages of the history of Bani Isra'il and their forefathers, and which is the counterpart of al-Masjid al-Haram in that its original foundation was in the time of Ibrahim, as we shall point out when explaining His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿to al-Masjid al-Aqsa﴾ [Al-Isra: 1]. So Allah settled Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, in it after it had been abandoned and ruined, as a hint that his community will renew its glory.

And that Allah empowered him over the two sanctuaries of prophethood and of the Law, for al-Masjid al-Aqsa was not inhabited at the time of the revelation of this surah, but churches had been built around it. And that Bani Isra'il did not preserve the sanctity of al-Masjid al-Aqsa, so their corruption was a cause for their enemies to dominate them and for the destruction of al-Masjid al-Aqsa. In that is a symbol that the restoration of al-Masjid al-Aqsa will be by the hand of the community of this Messenger, whose message they denied.

Then, affirming the proofs of Allah's singular divinity, and reasoning from the sign of the night and the day and the blessings in them to establish oneness (al-wahdaniyyah).

And reminding of the blessings which Allah subjected for mankind, and the proofs in them of His singular management of creation, and what this requires of thanking the Benefactor and abandoning thanking others, and exalting Him above taking daughters.

And displaying virtues of the Law of Islam and its wisdom, and what Allah taught the Muslims of the etiquettes of dealing with their Lord, may He be glorified, and of dealing with one another, and the wisdom in their conduct and their words, and vigilance of Allah in their outward and inward states.

And from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The whole Torah is in fifteen verses of Surat Bani Isra'il," and in another narration from him: "Eighteen verses of it were in the tablets of Musa," meaning from His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Do not make with Allah another god, lest you sit reproached and forsaken﴾ [Al-Isra: 22] up to His saying ﴿Do not make with Allah another god, lest you be thrown into Hell, blamed and banished﴾ [Al-Isra: 39].

By "the Torah" he means the tablets containing the Ten Commandments. His intention is not that the Qur'an recounted what is in the Torah, but these are Qur'anic rulings that agree with what is in the Torah.

[Page 9]

Furthermore, the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's statement is that what is in the tablets is mentioned in those verses, and he does not mean that the two are the same, because those verses add rulings, among them His saying ﴿Your Lord is most knowing of what is in your souls﴾ [Al-Isra: 25] up to His saying ﴿ungrateful to his Lord﴾ [Al-Isra: 27], and His saying ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [Al-Isra: 31], and His saying ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾ [Al-Isra: 34] up to His saying ﴿That is from what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾ [Al-Isra: 39]. Along with all that is interspersed of detail and clarification, which the Ten Commandments written on the tablets lack; and the affirmation of resurrection and recompense; the urging to establish the prayers at their times; the warning against the incitement of Satan and his enmity toward Adam and his descendants; the story of his refusal to prostrate; and the warning of the punishment of the Hereafter. And the mention of what befell the nations of the causes of extermination and destruction; the threat to the polytheists that Allah is about to grant victory to Islam over their falsehood; what the Prophet ﷺ suffered from the harm of the polytheists, their seeking help from the Jews, their demands for signs, and their foolishness in their ignorance of the verses of the Qur'an, and that it is the truth.

Interspersed within all of that are digressions, warnings and admonitions containing healing and mercy, and parables that are knowledge and wisdom.
